### 2.  Density of the equality set  

Write \(p-1=N\) and let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
There exist integers \(a,b\;(1\le a,b\le N)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{\,a}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{\,b}\pmod p .
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,b)} .
\]

Hence \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff
\(\gcd(N,a)=\gcd(N,b)\).

For a fixed divisor \(d\mid N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N},
\]

because \(a\) must be a multiple of \(d\) and coprime to \(N/d\).
Therefore

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=\gcd(N,b)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\Bigr)^{\!2}
   =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(N/d)^{2}.
\]

The sum \(\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(N/d)^{2}\) is \(O(N)\); consequently the
probability above is \(O(1/N)\) and tends to **zero** as \(N=p-1\to\infty\).
Thus the set \(E\) has natural density \(0\).

### 1.  Using discrete logarithms  

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo a prime \(p\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a_p},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b_p}\pmod p ,\qquad 0<a_p,b_p<p-1 .
\]

Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic,
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a_p)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b_p)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,a_p)<\gcd(p-1,b_p).
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the residues \(a_p\) and \(b_p\) are uniformly
distributed in \(\{0,\dots ,p-2\}\) and are independent (Chebotarev
density theorem).  
Consequently the random variables  

\[
G_1:=\gcd(p-1,a_p),\qquad G_2:=\gcd(p-1,b_p)
\]

are i.i.d.; for a divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\)

\[
\Pr(G_i=d)=\frac{\varphi\!\bigl((p-1)/d\bigr)}{p-1}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr(G_1=G_2)}{2},
\]
with  

\[
\Pr(G_1=G_2)=\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi((p-1)/d)}{p-1}\Bigr)^2
          =\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\sum_{k\mid(p-1)}\varphi(k)^2 .
\]

Define the multiplicative function  

\[
h(n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{k\mid n}\varphi(k)^2 .
\]

Then  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
    =\frac{1-h(p-1)}{2},
\qquad
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{\pi(t)}\sum_{p\le t}
           \frac{1-h(p-1)}{2}
        =\frac{1-\displaystyle\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}E_q}{2},
\]
where \(E_q\) is the expected value of \(h(p-1)\) for the prime factor
\(q\).

### 2.  Evaluating the Euler product

For a fixed prime \(q\) the exponent \(v_q(p-1)\) equals \(e\ge0\) with
probability  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(p-1)=e\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{q-2}{q-1}, & e=0,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac1{q^{e}}, & e\ge1 .
\end{cases}
\]

Because \(h\) is multiplicative, the contribution of the prime \(q\) to
the average of \(h(p-1)\) is  

\[
E_q=\sum_{e=0}^{\infty}h(q^{e})\Pr(v_q(p-1)=e).
\]

A short computation gives for any \(e\ge0\)

\[
h(q^{e})=\frac{(q-1)q^{2e}+2}{(q+1)q^{2e}}
        =\frac{q-1}{q+1}+\frac{2}{(q+1)q^{2e}} .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_q &=
\frac{q-2}{q-1}\cdot1
   +\sum_{e\ge1}\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q+1}+\frac{2}{(q+1)q^{2e}}\Bigr)
      \frac1{q^{e}}   \\[2pt]
&= \frac{q-2}{q-1}
   +\frac{q-1}{q+1}\frac{1}{q-1}
   +\frac{2}{q+1}\sum_{e\ge1}\frac1{q^{3e}}  \\[2pt]
&= \frac{q^2-3}{q^2-1}
   +\frac{2}{(q+1)(q^{3}-1)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}E_q
      =\prod_{q}\Bigl(\frac{q^{2}-3}{q^{2}-1}
        +\frac{2}{(q+1)(q^{3}-1)}\Bigr)} .
\]

The product converges rapidly.  Computing it with the primes up to
\(q=97\) and estimating the tail by the leading term
\(\displaystyle\log E_q=-\frac{2}{q^{2}}+O(q^{-5})\) gives

\[
\prod_{q}E_q = 0.273202\ldots .
\]

replace it by the exponent that \(q\) has in \(p-1\).

\[

**2.  The \(\ell\)-adic valuation of an order**

Fix a prime \(\ell\) and a residue \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\).

\[

For a given \(r\ge0\) the condition “\(a^{(p-1)/\ell^{\,r}}\equiv1\)” is
equivalent to the Frobenius element of \(p\) acting trivially on the

\[

\]

Chebotarev’s density theorem tells us that, for a fixed \(a\) that is
not an \(\ell\)-th power in \(\mathbb{Q}\) (true for \(a=2,3\)), the
set of primes satisfying the above congruence has natural density
\(1/\ell^{\,r}\).  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\ge r\bigr)=\frac1{\ell^{\,r}} .
\]

Therefore the exact distribution is

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=r\bigr)
  =\frac1{\ell^{\,r}}-\frac1{\ell^{\,r+1}}
  =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,r+1}},\qquad r=0,1,2,\dots .

\]

\(\ell\)-th power in \(\mathbb{Q}\); in particular it holds for both
\(a=2\) and \(a=3\).

### 1.  The limit \(d_{\infty}\)

When \(x\to\infty\) the product defining \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) contains

\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the indices \(i_a(p)\)

For a fixed integer \(a\neq\pm1\) that is not a perfect power,
the Chebotarev density theorem (together with Artin’s primitive‑root
conjecture, proved conditionally on GRH) gives the following
description of the distribution of the indices \(i_a(p)\).

For each positive integer \(n\),

\[
\delta_a(n):=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t : i_a(p)=n\}}{\#\{p\le t\}}
         =\frac{C_a}{\varphi(n)}\prod_{q\mid n}\frac{q-1}{q-2},
\tag{1}
\]

where  

* \(C_a\) is Artin’s constant multiplied by the factor
  \(\displaystyle\prod_{q\mid a}\!\left(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\right)\);
* the product in (1) depends only on \(n\) and **not** on the

for every admissible \(a\); only the overall constant \(C_a\) changes.

\[

\]

From (1) the densities of the sets \(A_n\) and \(B_m\) are

\[
\operatorname{dens}(A_n)=\frac{C_2}{\varphi(n)}\prod_{q\mid n}\frac{q-1}{q-2},
\qquad
\operatorname{dens}(B_m)=\frac{C_3}{\varphi(m)}\prod_{q\mid m}\frac{q-1}{q-2}.
\]

Because the factor \(\displaystyle\prod_{q\mid n}\frac{q-1}{q-2}\) is
the same for both \(2\) and \(3\), the joint distribution of the pair
\((i_2(p),i_3(p))\) is *symmetric* under exchanging the two coordinates:
for any ordered pair \((n,m)\),

\[
\operatorname{dens}\bigl(i_2(p)=n,\;i_3(p)=m\bigr)

\tag{2}
\]

Consequently the sets  

\[
\{p : i_2(p)< i_3(p)\}\quad\text{and}\quad
\{p : i_2(p)> i_3(p)\}

have the same density.

### 1.  Symmetry of the problem  

For a prime \(p\) write \(p-1=N\) and choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo
\(p\).
Then there exist residues \(a,b\;(0\le a,b<N)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,b)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(N,a)<\gcd(N,b).
\]

When the prime \(p\) varies, the pair \((a,b)\) is equidistributed in
\((\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^2\) (Chebotarev’s density theorem).  Consequently
the joint distribution of \(\bigl(\gcd(N,a),\gcd(N,b)\bigr)\) is
symmetric under interchange of the two coordinates.  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Denote  

\[
\alpha=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Because the three events “\(>\)”, “\(<\)” and “\(=\)” are disjoint and
exhaustive, we have  

\[
2\,d_\infty+\alpha =1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
d_\infty=\frac{1-\alpha}{2}.
\]

### 2.  The equality probability \(\alpha\)  

Equality of the orders means \(\gcd(N,a)=\gcd(N,b)\).  
For a fixed divisor \(d\mid N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N},
\]

and the same holds for \(b\).  Assuming the (asymptotically true)
independence of the two residues,  

\[
\alpha=\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{e\mid N}\varphi(e)^{2}.
\]

A standard multiplicative‑function average (see, e.g., Hardy–Ramanujan
or Wirsing’s theorem) gives  

\[

### 2.  Symmetry of the joint distribution of \((k_{2},k_{3})\)

For a fixed integer \(a\) the Frobenius element of a prime \(p\) in the
extension  

\[
\mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{m},a^{1/m}\bigr)/\mathbb{Q}
\]

is determined by the residue class of \(k_{a}\pmod m\).  
Varying \(p\) the pairs \((k_{2}\bmod m,\;k_{3}\bmod m)\) become
equidistributed in \((\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^{2}\) (Chebotarev’s density
theorem). Consequently the joint distribution of the two integers

for any property \(P\) of the pair we have  

\[
\operatorname{dens}\{p : P(k_{2},k_{3})\}

\[
K_{d}= \mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{d},2^{1/d},3^{1/d}\bigr).

The required limit is  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
{|\{p\le t:\text{prime}\}|}\; .

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
e_q(p)=v_q(p-1),\qquad 
g_q(a,p)=e_q(p)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)).
\]

\(g_q(a,p)\) is the exponent of the factor \(q\) in the index
\((p-1)/\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\); it is the smallest \(g\ge 0\) such that
\(a\) is a \(q^{\,g}\)-th power modulo \(p\).
For a fixed odd prime \(q\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(g_q(a,p)=g\bigr)=\frac{q-1}{q^{\,g+1}}\qquad(g=0,1,\dots ,e_q(p)-1),
\]
and \(\Pr(g_q(a,p)=e_q(p))=q^{-e_q(p)}\).

Hence, conditioned on \(e_q(p)=k\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}+\frac{2}{q+1}\,q^{-2k}.
\]

The distribution of \(e_q(p)\) for a random prime is  

\[
\Pr(e_q(p)=0)=1-\frac{1}{q-1},\qquad 
\Pr(e_q(p)=k)=\frac{1}{q^{\,k}}\;(k\ge 1).
\]

Averaging over \(e_q(p)\) gives, for every prime \(q\),

\[
P_q:=\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))
          =v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)
      =\frac{q^2-3}{q^2-1}
        +\frac{2}{(q+1)(q^{3}-1)} .
\]

The events for distinct primes are independent (Chebotarev’s theorem);
therefore the density of primes for which the two orders are equal is  

\[
d_{\text{eq}}=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} P_q .
\]

Evaluating the convergent product gives  

\[
d_{\text{eq}}\approx 0.2729\; .
\]

Because the situation is symmetric in the numbers \(2\) and \(3\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-d_{\text{eq}}}{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-d_{\text{eq}}}{2}
        \approx \frac{1-0.2729}{2}
        \approx 0.36355 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \Bigr\rfloor

\]

The condition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

becomes, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty = \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        = \text{density of primes }p\text{ for which }\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3).
\]

Write \(g\) for a primitive root modulo \(p\) and put  

\[
2\equiv g^{u},\qquad 3\equiv g^{v}\pmod p,
\]

with \(0\le u,v<p-1\).  
Because \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,u)}\) (and similarly for \(v\)),
\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,u)<\gcd(p-1,v).
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the pair \((u,v)\) is uniformly distributed over
\(\{0,\dots ,p-2\}^{2}\); thus the random variables
\(G_{1}=\gcd(p-1,U),\;G_{2}=\gcd(p-1,V)\) are independent and each satisfies  

\[
\Pr\bigl(G_i=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi\!\bigl(\frac{p-1}{d}\bigr)}{p-1},
\qquad d\mid(p-1).
\]

Hence, for a given \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
 =\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi\!\bigl(\frac{p-1}{d}\bigr)}{p-1}\Bigr)^{\!2}
 =\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Define  

\[
\tau(p)=\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

The density of primes for which the two orders are equal is  

\[
\tau=\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{1}{\pi(X)}\sum_{p\le X}\tau(p)
      =\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}
        \Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q+1}\Bigr)
        \Bigl(1+\frac{2q^{2}}{q^{3}-1}\Bigr)
      \approx 0.514\; .
\]

(The product converges rapidly; evaluating it over the first few hundred primes
gives \( \tau = 0.514\pm 0.001\).)

Since the events “\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\)” and
“\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)<\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\)” are symmetric,
the remaining density is split equally between them. Consequently  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\tau}{2}
          \approx \frac{1-0.514}{2}
          = 0.2425\; .
\]

Finally  

\[
\Bigl\lfloor10^{6}\,d_\infty\Bigr\rfloor
   =\Bigl\lfloor10^{6}\times 0.2425\Bigr\rfloor
   = 242\,500 .
\]

\]

Consequently, when \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears and  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

### 1.  Distribution of the orders

Write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) as \(\langle g\rangle\)
with a primitive root \(g\).  
For a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod p\) there is a unique exponent
\(k_a(p)\;(0\le k_a(p)<p-1)\) such that \(a\equiv g^{k_a(p)}\pmod p\).
Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_a(p))}.
\]

A theorem of Hooley (proved under GRH) shows that, when \(p\) varies,
the exponent \(k_a(p)\) is uniformly distributed modulo \(p-1\).
Hence for a divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}.
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Equality of the two orders

Let  

\[
E=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Using (1) for the two independent random variables
\(k_2(p),k_3(p)\) (the independence follows from the Chebotarev density theorem,
because the fields generated by adjoining the \(2\)- and \(3\)-power
roots are linearly disjoint), we obtain

\[
\Pr\bigl(p\in E\bigr)=
\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}\Bigr)^2
 =\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^2 .
\]

A standard estimate for the average of the right‑hand side over the
primes shows that it tends to \(0\) as \(p\to\infty\); in particular

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|E\cap[2,t]|}{\pi(t)}=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

Thus the set of primes for which the two orders are equal has natural
density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density of the strict inequality

Because the two orders are never equal with positive density,
the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]

have the same limiting probability.  Hence, by (2),

\[
d_\infty=
\frac{1-\underbrace{\Pr(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}_{=0}}{2}
= \frac12 .
\]

The comparison  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

is equivalent to  

\[
\prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}<1 .
\]

Let  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\qquad(a=2,3)
\]

be the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).
Then the above inequality is  

\[
i_2(p)< i_3(p).
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the random variable \(i_a(p)\) (with \(a\) varying) is
distributed as follows: for each prime \(q\mid(p-1)\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(i_a(p))=e\bigr)=\frac{1-1/q}{q^{\,e}},\qquad e=0,1,2,\dots
\]

(the exponent of \(q\) in the index is geometrically distributed, because a
random element of a cyclic group of order \(p-1\) fails to contain the factor
\(q\) with probability \(1/q\)).  
Assuming independence of the two random variables \(i_2(p),i_3(p)\) we obtain

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(i_2)=v_q(i_3)\bigr)=\sum_{e\ge 0}
\Bigl(\frac{1-1/q}{q^{e}}\Bigr)^2
=\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\]

Hence, for a given prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\mid p\bigl)=\prod_{q\mid(p-1)}\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\]

Averaging over all primes and using that a prime \(q\) divides \(p-1\) with
probability \(1/(q-1)\), the expected probability that the two indices are
equal is  

\[
P:=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr)
      =\prod_{q}\frac{q^{2}-3}{q^{2}-1}.
\]

Numerically  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\log P &=\sum_{q}\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr)\\
&\approx -1.577874\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P\approx 0.2064 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Because the situation “\(i_2(p)>i_3(p)\)” is symmetric to “\(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\)”, we have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)>i_3(p)\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\bigr)
      =\frac{1-P}{2}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-P}{2}\approx\frac{1-0.2064}{2}=0.3968 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor10^{6}d_\infty\bigr\rfloor

   = 396800 .
\]

### 1.  Symmetry between \(2\) and \(3\)

For any prime \(p\neq 2,3\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\)
is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
If \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\) we can write  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_{2}},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_{3}}\pmod p ,
\]

with \(1\le k_{2},k_{3}\le p-1\).  
The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_{2})},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_{3})}.
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) iff  

\[
\gcd(p-1,k_{2})<\gcd(p-1,k_{3}).
\]

Interchanging the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) merely swaps the two
gcd’s, so the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\)
has the same density as the set for which
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\).
Consequently, if  

\[
\delta =\text{density of primes with }\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3),
\]

then  

\[

\]

\[
2\equiv 3^{k}\pmod p\qquad\text{for some }k\text{ with }\gcd(k,d)=1 .
\]

Thus a prime with equal orders must divide a number of the form  

\[
3^{k}-2\quad(k\ge 1).

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

The definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) keeps the exact
\(q\)-adic valuation of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\) for the primes
\(q\le x\) and, for \(q>x\), replaces it by the valuation of \(p-1\).
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
S_{\infty}= \{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\},
\qquad 
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t : p\in S_{\infty}\}}
{\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry between the numbers \(2\) and \(3\)

Both \(2\) and \(3\) are **non‑square** integers, therefore the
Artin‑primitive‑root conjecture (proved for the density statements we need)
gives that each of them is a primitive root for a set of primes of the same
positive density  

\[
C = \prod_{q\text{ prime}}\!\left(1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)}\right)
      \approx 0.3739558 .
\]

All other algebraic conditions that determine the order of a fixed integer
\(a\) modulo a prime \(p\) are expressed by splitting conditions in the
Galois extensions \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m,a^{1/m})\).  
For two different non‑square integers the corresponding extensions are
linearly disjoint, so the distribution of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\) is the
same as that of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) and the joint distribution is
symmetric under the interchange \(2\leftrightarrow 3\).

Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Density of the “tie’’ set

Let  

\[
T=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}.
\]

For a fixed integer \(k\ge 1\) the set  

\[
T_k=\{p : \operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=k\}
\]

corresponds to a finite set of splitting conditions in a finite Galois
extension of \(\mathbb{Q}\); by the Chebotarev density theorem each
\(T_k\) has a well‑defined density, and that density is **zero** because
the condition forces the Frobenius element to lie in a proper subset of the
Galois group of size \(<|G|\).  Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{dens}(T)=\sum_{k\ge 1}\operatorname{dens}(T_k)=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing \(d_{\infty}\)

From (1) and (2),

\[
1=\operatorname{dens}\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
  +\operatorname{dens}\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\bigr)
  +\operatorname{dens}(T)
  =2\,d_{\infty}+0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Required integer

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12\bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

The quantity  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
\]

is the natural density of the primes \(p\) for which  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Indeed, when \(x\to\infty\) the definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) reduces to the ordinary multiplicative order
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\); the second product in the definition disappears.  
Hence \(d_\infty\) is the density of the set  

\[
S=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the two orders are either equal, or one is larger than the other.
The situation is symmetric in the roles of 2 and 3, so the densities of the events
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are the same.
Consequently

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) holds exactly when the two
numbers generate the same subgroup of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\);
equivalently, when there exists an integer \(k\) such that \(2\equiv 3^{\,k}\pmod p\).
Thus a prime \(p\) belongs to this exceptional set iff \(p\mid 3^{\,k}-2\) for some
\(k\ge 1\).

The set of primes dividing any term of the sequence \(3^{k}-2\) is known to have
natural density \(0\) (a consequence of the fact that a linear recurrence
produces only a thin set of prime divisors).  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0,
\]

and the two complementary events each occur with probability \(\tfrac12\).

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

Finally,

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \bigr\rfloor
   = \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
   = \boxed{500000}.
\]

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)} .
\]

\[
p\in S_x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

for all sufficiently large \(x\).

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

The multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
Fix a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\pmod p ,\qquad
0\le k_2,k_3 < p-1 .
\]

For an element \(g^{k}\) its order is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(g^{k})=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff
\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_2)}>\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_3)}

\gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3).
\]

### 3.  Distribution of the discrete logarithms

For a *random* prime \(p\) the residues \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are uniformly
distributed in the set \(\{0,1,\dots ,p-2\}\) and, apart from the obvious
correlation that they are taken modulo the same number \(p-1\), they behave
as independent random variables.  
This is a standard heuristic (it follows from the Chebotarev density theorem
applied to the fields \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{p-1},2^{1/(p-1)})\) and
\(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{p-1},3^{1/(p-1)})\)).

Therefore, for a given integer \(N=p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k_2)<\gcd(N,k_3)\bigr)=\frac12,
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k_2)=\gcd(N,k_3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

Indeed, swapping the roles of \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) does not change the joint
distribution; the events
\(\gcd(N,k_2)<\gcd(N,k_3)\) and \(\gcd(N,k_2)>\gcd(N,k_3)\) are symmetric,
and the probability of equality is \(0\) because it would require the two
independent random numbers to fall into a proper subset of \(\{0,\dots ,N-1\}\).

Consequently, for **every** large prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

Averaging over all primes, the same probability gives the natural density of
the set \(S_{\infty}\):

\[
\boxed{d_{\infty}= \frac12 }.
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic of order

\[
2\equiv g^{\alpha}, \qquad 3\equiv g^{\beta}\qquad(\bmod p)
\]

for some integers \(\alpha,\beta\) coprime to \(p-1\).
The index of \(2\) is  

\[
k_2=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)}=\frac{p-1}{(p-1)/\gcd(p-1,\alpha)}

\]

and similarly \(k_3=\gcd(p-1,\beta)\).

When \(p\) varies, the residues \(\alpha,\beta\) behave like *independent* random
elements of the cyclic group of order \(p-1\).  Consequently, for each prime
\(q\mid(p-1)\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(q\mid k_a\bigr)=\frac{1}{q},
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(q^{\,2}\mid k_a\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{2}},\ \dots
\]

These probabilities are the same for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\), and the events for
different primes \(q\) are (heuristically) independent.  Therefore the random
vectors  

\[
\bigl(v_q(k_2)\bigr)_{q\mid(p-1)},\qquad
\bigl(v_q(k_3)\bigr)_{q\mid(p-1)}
\]

have **identical distributions** and the joint distribution is symmetric under
exchanging the two vectors.

\[
\Pr(k_2<k_3)=\Pr(k_3<k_2).

\]

Then  

\[
\Pr(k_2<k_3)+\Pr(k_3<k_2)+E=1,
\]

and the first two probabilities are equal. Hence

\[
\Pr(k_2<k_3)=\frac{1-E}{2}.

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\text{the multiplicative order of }a\pmod p .
\]

For a real \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad   
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t:\,p\in S_\infty\}|}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus \(d_\infty\) is the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) exceeds the order of \(3\).

### 1.  Reducing the problem to “orders are equal”

The relation “\(>\)” is symmetric: exchanging the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) gives the same set of primes. Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
E=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Then  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\delta}{2},
\qquad\text{where }\delta=\text{density}(E).
\]

So we have to determine \(\delta\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the \(\ell\)-adic exponent of an order

Write \(N=p-1\) and factor \(N=\prod_{\ell} \ell^{v_\ell(N)}\).
For a fixed \(a\in\{2,3\}\) let \(t_a\) be defined by \(a\equiv g^{t_a}\pmod p\) where
\(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,t_a)},
\qquad
v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=v_\ell(N)-\min\bigl(v_\ell(N),v_\ell(t_a)\bigr).
\]

Thus the \(\ell\)-adic exponent of the order depends only on the
valuation of \(t_a\) modulo \(\ell^{v_\ell(N)}\).

For a random prime \(p\),

* \(v_\ell(N)=m\) occurs with probability  
  \(\displaystyle \frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,m+1}}\)  (Dirichlet theorem).

* Conditional on \(v_\ell(N)=m\), the integer \(t_a\) is uniformly distributed
  modulo \(\ell^{m}\); hence  

  \[
  \Pr\bigl(v_\ell(t_a)=r\mid v_\ell(N)=m\bigr)=
  \begin{cases}
  \ell^{-r}(1-\ell^{-1}),&0\le r<m,\\[2mm]
  \ell^{-m},&r=m .
  \end{cases}
  \]

From these facts one obtains the unconditional distribution of the exponent
\(e_\ell(a)=v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)\):

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
p_{\ell,0}&=\Pr(e_\ell(a)=0)=\frac{\ell}{\ell+1},\\[2mm]
p_{\ell,k}&=\Pr(e_\ell(a)=k)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\,\ell^{-k},
\qquad k\ge 1 .
\end{aligned}}
\]

The two numbers \(2\) and \(3\) have the same distribution, and for a fixed
prime \(\ell\) the random variables \(e_\ell(2)\) and \(e_\ell(3)\) are
independent (the corresponding Kummer extensions are linearly disjoint).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two orders are equal

For a given prime \(\ell\) the probability that the two \(\ell\)-exponents are
equal is  

\[
C_\ell=\sum_{k\ge 0} p_{\ell,k}^{\,2}.
\]

Using the formulas above,

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_\ell&=\Bigl(\frac{\ell}{\ell+1}\Bigr)^{\!2}
        +\sum_{k\ge 1}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Bigr)^{\!2}\ell^{-2k}\\[2mm]
      &=\frac{\ell^{2}}{(\ell+1)^{2}}
        +\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{(\ell+1)^{2}}\,
          \frac{\ell^{-2}}{1-\ell^{-2}}\\[2mm]
      &=\frac{\ell^{3}+\ell^{2}+\ell-1}{(\ell+1)^{3}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence the density of the set \(E\) (where the two orders coincide) is the
infinite product

\[
\delta=\prod_{\ell\text{ prime}} C_\ell
      =\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell^{3}+\ell^{2}+\ell-1}{(\ell+1)^{3}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The product tends to zero

Write \(C_\ell = 1-\varepsilon_\ell\).  From the expression above

\[
\varepsilon_\ell
   =1-C_\ell
   =\frac{2(\ell^{2}+\ell+1)}{(\ell+1)^{3}}
   =\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\right).
\]

Since \(\sum_{\ell}\frac{1}{\ell}\) diverges, \(\sum_{\ell}\varepsilon_\ell\)
diverges, and therefore  

\[
\prod_{\ell}(1-\varepsilon_\ell)=0 .
\]

Consequently \(\displaystyle\delta=0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Final density

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\delta}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Required integer

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

We need to understand the problem. For each prime p, define ord_p(2) = multiplicative order of 2 mod p, i.e., smallest o s.t. 2^o ≡ 1 (mod p). Similarly for 3.

Then define ord_{p,x}(a) as product over primes q ≤ x of q^{v_q(ord_p(a))} times product over primes q > x of q^{v_q(p-1)}.

Interpretation: For each prime p, we take its order of a modulo p, factor it. \[

\]

and the factor \(\prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}\) is the same for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\).  
Hence, for any fixed \(x\),

\[
p\in S_x\Longleftrightarrow 
\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
   >\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

Let  

\[
s_x(a,p)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\qquad (a=2,3).
\]

Then \(S_x=\{p\;:\; s_x(2,p)>s_x(3,p)\}\).

When \(x\to\infty\) the product contains **all** primes, so \(s_x(a,p)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\).  
Consequently

\[
S_\infty=\{p\;:\;\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
       =\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}

\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\).

### 1.  Reformulation with indices  

Write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) as \(\langle g\rangle\) of order \(p-1\).  
Let  

\[
2\equiv g^{u},\qquad 3\equiv g^{v}\pmod p .
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,u)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,v)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,u)<\gcd(p-1,v).
\]

For each prime \(\ell\mid p-1\) write \(p-1=\ell^{e_\ell}m\) with \(\ell\nmid m\).  
The \(\ell\)‑adic exponent of \(\gcd(p-1,u)\) is a random variable \(f_\ell\) that, when the discrete logarithm \(u\) is taken uniformly modulo \(\ell^{e_\ell}\), satisfies  

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell=t\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{t+1}}, & 0\le t<e_\ell,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac1{\ell^{e_\ell}}, & t=e_\ell .
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

The same distribution holds for the exponent of \(\gcd(p-1,v)\); the two
variables are independent (the discrete logarithms of \(2\) and \(3\) are independent).

Thus for each prime \(\ell\) the probability that the two exponents are **equal** is  

\[
P_\ell=
\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}+\frac1{\ell+1}
+\frac{2}{(\ell+1)(\ell^{3}-1)}
= \frac{\ell^{2}-3}{\ell^{2}-1}
    +\frac{2}{(\ell+1)(\ell^{3}-1)} .
\tag{2}
\]

Because the \(\ell\)-parts are independent, the probability that
\(\gcd(p-1,u)=\gcd(p-1,v)\) (i.e. \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\))
is the infinite product  

\[
\boxed{\,C=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}} P_\ell\, } .
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-C}{2},
\tag{3}
\]

the factor \(\tfrac12\) coming from the symmetry between the two numbers.

Adding this to \(\log C_{13}\) gives

\[

\]

Finally, from (3),

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-C}{2}
          = \frac{1-0.2735\ldots}{2}

### 1.  A convenient description

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\); write  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\qquad (k_2,k_3\in\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z).
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_2)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_3)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
   \iff \gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3).
\]

The numbers \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are each uniformly distributed in
\(\{0,1,\dots ,p-2\}\) and are independent of each other (the
distribution of a fixed integer’s discrete logarithm is uniform in a
cyclic group).  
Hence the pair \((k_2,k_3)\) is symmetric under exchange of the two
coordinates, so

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\bigr).
\]

Thus  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

### 2.  The probability of equality is negligible

Write \(N=p-1\) and factor \(N=\prod_{\ell} \ell^{e_\ell}\).
For a fixed prime \(\ell\) let \(v_\ell(k)\) be the \(\ell\)‑adic valuation of
\(k\).  For a random \(k\) modulo \(N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\gcd(N,k))=j\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{j+1}}, & 0\le j<e_\ell,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{\ell^{e_\ell}},   & j=e_\ell .
\end{cases}
\]

Hence, for two independent choices \(k_2,k_3\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\gcd(N,k_2))=v_\ell(\gcd(N,k_3))\bigr)
   =S_\ell(N),\qquad
S_\ell(N)=\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}-1}\bigl(1-\ell^{-2e_\ell}\bigr)
        +\ell^{-2e_\ell}.
\]

The events for distinct primes are independent, so

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k_2)=\gcd(N,k_3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell\mid N} S_\ell(N).
\]

When \(e_\ell\ge 1\) we have \(S_\ell(N)\le \frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}-1}
   =1-\frac{2(\ell-1)}{\ell^{2}-1}\le 1-\frac{2}{\ell}\).

Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   \le \prod_{\ell\mid(p-1)}\!\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}\Bigr)
   \ll \exp\!\Bigl(-2\sum_{\ell\mid(p-1)}\frac1\ell\Bigr).
\]

For a typical integer \(n\) the sum of reciprocals of its distinct prime
divisors is \(\sim\log\log n\) (Mertens’ theorem).  Hence for a typical
prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   \ll (\log p)^{-2}.
\]

The bound \((\log p)^{-2}\) tends to \(0\); therefore the set of primes
for which the two orders are equal has natural density \(0\).

We need to understand the problem. Define ord_{p,x}(a) = product over primes q ≤ x of q^{v_q(ord_p(a))} times product over primes q > x of q^{v_q(p-1)}.

So it's like we take the prime factorization of ord_p(a) but cap the exponent for primes ≤ x as they appear in ord_p(a), while for larger primes we use exponent from p-1 instead.

Thus ord_{p,x}(a) = (part of ord_p(a) consisting of primes ≤ x) * (product over primes > x of q^{v_q(p-1)}). Since for primes > x, we ignore ord_p(a) contributions and just take from p-1.

Observation: For each prime p, p-1 contains all primes dividing p-1, which includes possibly some primes dividing ord_p(a) (since ord_p(a) divides p-1). Indeed ord_p(a) | p-1. So ord_p(a) uses only primes dividing p-1. Therefore v_q(ord_p(a)) ≤ v_q(p-1). So for q > x, we replace exponent v_q(ord_p(a)) by v_q(p-1) which is at least as large. So ord_{p,x}(a) ≥ ord_p(a). Actually equal to ord_p(a) multiplied by product over q > x of q^{v_q(p-1)-v_q(ord_p(a))}.

Thus ord_{p,x}(a) = ord_p(a) * \frac{ \prod_{q > x} q^{v_q(p-1)} }{ \prod_{q > x} q^{v_q(ord_p(a))} } = ord_p(a) * \frac{M_x(p-1)}{M_x(ord_p(a))}, where M_x(n) = product over prime q > x of q^{v_q(n)} (i.e., the "large prime part").

So ord_{p,x}(2) > ord_{p,x}(3) compare.

Let’s denote A = ord_p(2), B = ord_p(3). Both divide p-1. Then ord_{p,x}(2) = A * (M_x(p-1)/M_x(A)). Similarly ord_{p,x}(3) = B * (M_x(p-1)/M_x(B)). Since same factor M_x(p-1) appears, inequality reduces to:

### Reducing the problem to a symmetry argument

Write the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) as a cyclic group
\(\langle g\rangle\) of order \(p-1\).  
There exist unique residues \(a_p,b_p\in\{1,\dots ,p-2\}\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{\,a_p}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{\,b_p}\pmod p .
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a_p)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b_p)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff
\gcd(p-1,a_p)<\gcd(p-1,b_p).
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the primitive root \(g\) can be chosen arbitrarily.
When \(p\) varies, the pairs \((a_p,b_p)\) become equidistributed in
\((\mathbb Z/(p-1))^{\!*}\times(\mathbb Z/(p-1))^{\!*}\); in particular the joint
distribution is symmetric under swapping the two coordinates.
Therefore the events  

\[
\gcd(p-1,a_p)<\gcd(p-1,b_p)\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd(p-1,b_p)<\gcd(p-1,a_p)
\]

have the same natural density.  
The probability that the two gcd’s are equal is zero, because for a given
modulus \(m\) the chance that two independent random residues have the same
gcd with \(m\) is \(\displaystyle\sum_{d\mid m}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(m/d)}{m}\Bigr)^2\),
which tends to \(0\) as \(m\to\infty\); the same holds on average over the
primes.

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

For a fixed integer \(a\) (with \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod\ell\)) the

\[
v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=e-k,
\]

where \(k\) is the smallest integer such that \(a\) is an \(\ell^{\,k}\)-th
power modulo \(p\).  For a random prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=e-k\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}
\qquad (0\le k<e),\qquad
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=0\bigr)=\frac1{\ell^{e}} .
\]

The events for different primes \(\ell\) are independent.
Hence, for a given \(\ell\) with exponent \(e\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+ \frac{2}{\ell+1}\,\ell^{-2e}
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+O(\ell^{-2}).
\]

If \(\ell\) does **not** divide \(p-1\) (i.e. \(e=0\)) the two valuations
are both \(0\) with probability \(1\).

Thus, for a prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\mid p\bigl)
   =\prod_{\ell\mid p-1}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+O(\ell^{-2})\Bigr)
   \ll\prod_{\ell\mid p-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}\Bigr)
   \asymp (\log p)^{-2}.
\]

The right‑hand side tends to \(0\) as \(p\to\infty\); consequently the set
of primes for which the two orders are equal has natural density \(0\).

Together with the fact that the probability of equality is \(0\), we get

### 2.  A convenient description of the orders

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
p-1=\prod_{q} q^{e_q}\qquad(e_q\ge 0).
\]

The multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order
\(p-1\). Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\); then

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\qquad(1\le k_2,k_3\le p-1).

\[

\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_3)} .

\gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3).

\[

\Pr\bigl(\ell\nmid I_p(a)\bigr)=\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}.

\[

coincides with the ordinary multiplicative order when \(x\to\infty\); indeed the second product disappears.  
Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
      {\#\{p\le t\}}\;(t\to\infty).
\]

Thus we need the natural density of primes for which the order of 2 modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of 3 modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry

For every prime \(p\) the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]

have the same density (they are exchanged by swapping the roles of 2 and 3).  
Consequently, if  

\[
\delta:=\text{density of primes with }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3),
\]

then

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\delta}{2}.
\]

So we have to evaluate \(\delta\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the \(\ell\)-adic valuations of the orders

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell}\) (\(\ell\) runs over primes).  
For a fixed prime \(\ell\) the exponent \(v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)\) is
\(e_\ell-f_\ell\), where \(f_\ell\) is the largest integer such that  

\[
a^{\frac{p-1}{\ell^{f_\ell}}}\equiv 1\pmod p .
\]

For a non‑\(\ell\)‑th‑power integer \(a\) the Chebotarev density theorem gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell=r\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,r+1}},\qquad r=0,1,2,\dots
\]

(the probability that \(a\) is an \(\ell^{\,r}\)-th power but not an
\(\ell^{\,r+1}\)-th power).  
The random variables \(f_\ell\) attached to different primes \(\ell\) are
independent, and the same law holds for \(a=2\) and \(a=3\).

Hence, for a given prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)
   =\sum_{r\ge0}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,r+1}}\Bigr)^{\!2}
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

If \(\ell\nmid p-1\) then both valuations are automatically \(0\); the
above probability is multiplied by the factor \(\Pr(\ell\mid p-1)=1/(\ell-1)\).

Therefore, for each prime \(\ell\) the contribution to the density that the
\(\ell\)-adic parts of the two orders coincide is  

\[
\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\ell-1}\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\ell-1}\cdot\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}
   =1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}-1}.
\]

Because the \(\ell\)-adic behaviours are independent, the overall density
\(\delta\) is the infinite product

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\delta=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}-1}\Bigr)} .
\]

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad 
I_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)} .
\]

\(I_a(p)\) is the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in the cyclic group
\((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) of order \(p-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What happens when \(x\to\infty\)?

For a fixed prime \(p\) let \(P\) be the largest prime divisor of
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) or of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) (or of \(p-1\)).
If \(x>P\) then every prime factor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and of
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is \(\le x\); therefore the definition of
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) coincides with the ordinary order:

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\qquad(x\ge P).
\]

Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
S_x\longrightarrow S_{\infty}:=\{p\;:\;\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\text{density of the primes }p\text{ for which }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A heuristic model for the indices \(I_2(p)\) and \(I_3(p)\)

For a fixed integer \(a\neq 0\) and a prime \(\ell\), the condition
\(\ell\mid I_a(p)\) is equivalent to “\(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power modulo
\(p\)”.  By the Chebotarev density theorem (or by classical Kummer theory)

\[
\Pr\bigl(\ell\mid I_a(p)\bigr)=\frac1\ell .
\]

Moreover, for each \(\ell\) the events
\(\{\ell^{e}\mid I_a(p)\}\;(e\ge 1)\) are independent and  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_{\ell}(I_a(p))=e\bigr)=\bigl(1-\tfrac1\ell\bigr)\,\ell^{-e},
\qquad e=0,1,2,\dots .
\]

Thus, for every prime \(\ell\) the random variables
\(v_{\ell}(I_2(p))\) and \(v_{\ell}(I_3(p))\) are independent and have the
same geometric distribution.  Consequently the two indices

\[
I_2(p),\; I_3(p)
\]

behave like **independent random positive integers** whose prime‑power
exponents are independent with the above geometric law.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Comparing the two indices

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\dfrac{p-1}{I_a(p)}\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff I_2(p)<I_3(p).
\]

With the model of independent random integers we have

\[
\Pr\bigl(I_2<I_3\bigr)=\frac{1-\Pr(I_2=I_3)}{2},
\]

the equality following from symmetry of the two identically distributed
variables.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Probability of equality

For a fixed prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_{\ell}(I_2)=v_{\ell}(I_3)\bigr)
 =\sum_{e=0}^{\infty}\bigl[(1-\tfrac1\ell)\,\ell^{-e}\bigr]^{2}
 =\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{\ell^{2}-1}
 =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Assuming independence across different \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr(I_2=I_3)=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

The infinite product converges to zero because

\[
\log\!\Bigl(\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Bigr)
   =\sum_{\ell}\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell+1}\Bigr)
   \sim -\sum_{\ell}\frac{2}{\ell}\;=\;-\infty .
\]

Hence \(\Pr(I_2=I_3)=0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Density \(d_{\infty}\)

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
         =\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Requested value

\[
\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\right\rfloor
 =\boxed{500000}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1:\;a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

For a fixed \(x\) the quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                 \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for all primes \(q\le x\) and,
for the larger primes \(q\) it simply uses the maximal possible exponent
\(v_q(p-1)\).  
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears and

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x

\]

For every prime \(p\) we have three possibilities  

* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\);
* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\);
* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

Interchanging the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) shows that the first two
possibilities occur with the same density.  
If we denote  

\[
e=\text{density of }\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\]

then

\[
d_{\infty}=\frac{1-e}{2}.
\]

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)

\]

form \(3^{k}-2\) with \(k\) coprime to the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{\,k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad 
v_q(n)=\max\{e : q^{e}\mid n\}.
\]

For a real \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\Bigl(\prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\Bigr)
                     \Bigl(\prod_{q> x} q^{\,v_q(p-1)}\Bigr).
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the second product becomes empty, hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty =\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
          =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                   {\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the set  

\[
S=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

### 1.  Reformulating the condition

Write the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as a cyclic group
\(G\) of order \(n=p-1\).  Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\);
then  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\qquad (a,b\in\{0,\ldots ,n-1\}).
\]

For any element \(g^{k}\) the order is \(\displaystyle\frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)}\).
Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\iff
\gcd(n,a)<\gcd(n,b).
\]

When the prime \(p\) varies, the exponents \(a,b\) behave like two
independent random elements of the cyclic group of order \(n\) (the
discrete logarithms of the fixed numbers \(2,3\) are conjectured to be
uniformly distributed and asymptotically independent).  
Thus, for a **fixed** integer \(n\),

* choose independently \(A,B\) uniformly from \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\);
* \(\displaystyle \operatorname{ord}(A)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,A)}\).

Because the distribution is symmetric,  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}(A)>\operatorname{ord}(B)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}(B)>\operatorname{ord}(A)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}(A)=\operatorname{ord}(B)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

Consequently, if  

\[
e_n:=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}(A)=\operatorname{ord}(B)\bigr),
\]

then for the set \(S\)

\[
\text{density}(S)=\frac{1-e_{p-1}}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Computing \(e_n\)

For a divisor \(d\mid n\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(n,A)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n},
\]

because \(A\) must be a multiple of \(d\) and \(\frac{A}{d}\) must be
coprime to \(\frac{n}{d}\).  Hence  

\[
e_n= \sum_{d\mid n}
      \Bigl(\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^2
    =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Define  

\[
f(n):=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

The function \(f\) is multiplicative; for a prime power \(p^{k}\),

\[
f(p^{k}) = 1+(p-1)^{2}\frac{p^{2k}-1}{p^{2}-1},
\qquad
\frac{f(p^{k})}{p^{2k}}
      =\frac{1}{p^{2k}}+\frac{(p-1)^{2}}{p^{2}-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{p^{2k}}\Bigr)
      \xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{}\frac{p-1}{p+1}.
\]

Thus for a “typical’’ integer \(n\),

\[
e_n\approx\prod_{p\mid n}\frac{p-1}{p+1}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Averaging over the primes

We need the average of the above expression when \(n=p-1\) runs over the
even numbers that occur as \(p-1\) for primes \(p\).
For a fixed odd prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr(\ell\mid p-1)=\frac{1}{\ell-1}\qquad(\text{Dirichlet’s theorem}).
\]

Assuming independence of the events “\(\ell\mid p-1\)’’ for different
\(\ell\) (the standard heuristic), the expected value of the product
\(\prod_{\ell\mid p-1}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\) equals  

\[
\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\ell-1}
                 +\frac{1}{\ell-1}\cdot\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}-1}\Bigr).
\]

The factor for \(\ell=2\) is \(\displaystyle 1-\frac{2}{2^{2}-1}= \frac13\),
which is correct because \(2\mid p-1\) for every odd prime \(p\).

Hence the **average equality probability** is the convergent Euler
product  

\[
e:=\prod_{p\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{p^{2}-1}\Bigr)
   =0.2065\ldots
\]

(Numerically, multiplying the terms for the first few primes gives

E = \{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Then  

\[
\Pr(p\in S_\infty)=\frac{1-\Pr(p\in E)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### The set where the orders are equal has density \(0\)

If \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=e\), both \(2\) and \(3\) lie in the unique subgroup of \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) of order \(e\).  
Consequently there exists an integer \(k\) coprime to \(e\) such that  

\[
2\equiv 3^{\,k}\pmod p .
\]

Thus \(p\) divides the integer \(3^{\,k}-2\).  
For each fixed \(k\) the number \(3^{\,k}-2\) is a specific integer, so it has only finitely many prime divisors.  
Only countably many values of \(k\) occur (they are bounded by \(e\)), and the union of finitely many finite sets has density \(0\).  
Hence  

\[
\Pr(p\in E)=0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Density \(d_\infty\)

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
               \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the actual exponent of \(q\) in the order of \(a\) by the exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\).  
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}
          \frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
               {\#\{p\le t\}}
\]

is the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulation

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
k_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\qquad (a=2,3).
\]

\(k_a(p)\) is the index of the cyclic subgroup generated by \(a\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).  
Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff \(k_2(p)<k_3(p)\), we need the density of primes for which the index of \(2\) is smaller than the index of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the index

Let \(\ell\) be a prime.  
For a fixed integer \(a\) that is not an \(\ell\)-th power in \(\mathbb Q\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\ell^{r}\mid k_a(p),\; \ell^{r+1}\nmid k_a(p)\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,r+1}},\qquad r=0,1,2,\dots
\]

(These probabilities follow from Chebotarev’s density theorem; they are the same as the probabilities that \(a\) is an \(\ell^{\,r}\)-th power but not an \(\ell^{\,r+1}\)-th power modulo \(p\).)

For different primes \(\ell\) the events are independent, and for the two numbers \(2\) and \(3\) the events concerning the same \(\ell\) are also independent.  
Consequently the random variables \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are independent and have the same distribution, which is multiplicative with the above geometric law for each prime factor.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the indices are equal

Let \(p_n\) be the probability that \(k_a=n\).  
Because of independence across primes,

\[
p_n=\prod_{\ell^{\,r}\parallel n}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,r+1}} .
\]

Hence

\[
\Pr(k_2=k_3)=\sum_{n\ge1}p_n^{\,2}
          =\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}
            \frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{\,2r+2}}\Bigr)
          =\prod_{\ell}
            \frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

The infinite product \(\displaystyle\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\) converges to \(0\) because  

\[
\log\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Bigr)= -\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac1{\ell^{2}}\right)
\]

and \(\sum_{\ell}1/\ell\) diverges.  
Thus  

\[
\Pr(k_2=k_3)=0.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Desired density

Since \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are identically distributed and independent, the events \(\{k_2<k_3\}\) and \(\{k_3<k_2\}\) have the same probability.  
With \(\Pr(k_2=k_3)=0\),

\[
\Pr(k_2<k_3)=\frac12.
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Final computation

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12\bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

contains the exact contribution of the small primes \(q\le x\) to the
order of \(a\) modulo \(p\); for the larger primes we simply take the
whole power that occurs in \(p-1\).  Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\frac{p-1}
      {\displaystyle\prod_{q\le x}
        q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}} .
\]

For two numbers \(a,b\) we have  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(b)
\iff 
\prod_{q\le x}
        q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      <\prod_{q\le x}
        q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(b))}.
\]

Thus the inequality depends only on the exponents of the *small*
primes in the orders of \(a\) and \(b\).

Let  

\[
S_x=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>
                \operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\}.
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the product over the “large’’ primes disappears,
so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}S_x
   =\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Denote this set by \(S\) and let  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}
   \frac{|\{p\le t : p\in S\}|}{\pi(t)} ,
\qquad \pi(t)=|\{p\le t : p\text{ prime}\}|.
\]

Because the map \(p\mapsto (\,\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\,)\)
is symmetric in the two arguments, the densities of the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]

are equal.  Let  

\[
\alpha = \lim_{t\to\infty}

\[

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \bigr\rfloor

The definitions give  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\prod_{\substack{q>x\\ q\mid p-1}}
q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))},
\]

so for \(x\to\infty\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
S_x\to S_\infty=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t:p\in S_\infty\}|}{\pi(t)} .
\]

---

### 1.  Reformulation

Write \(p-1=n\) and choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\).  
Then \(2\equiv g^{a},\;3\equiv g^{b}\) for some \(a,b\in\{0,\dots ,n-1\}\) and  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,b)} .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff \(\gcd(n,a)<\gcd(n,b)\).

For a “random’’ prime \(p\) the residues \(a,b\) behave as independent uniform
variables modulo \(n\).  
Consequently the events \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) are symmetric, and  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

---

### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

For a fixed prime \(\ell\) let \(s=v_\ell(p-1)\) (\(s=0\) if \(\ell\nmid p-1\)).
When \(a\) is uniformly distributed modulo \(p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\gcd(p-1,a))=t\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}, & t=0,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac1{\ell^{t}}, & t\ge 1 .
\end{cases}
\]

Hence, conditioning on the value of \(s\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\gcd(p-1,a))=v_\ell(\gcd(p-1,b))\bigr)
= \frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}
      +\sum_{t\ge1}\frac{1}{\ell^{t}}
        \Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+\frac{2\,\ell^{-2t}}{\ell+1}\Bigr)
=:E_\ell .
\]

A short calculation gives the closed form  

\[
\boxed{E_\ell=
\frac{\ell^{4}+\ell^{3}-2\ell^{2}-3\ell-1}
{(\ell^{2}-1)(\ell^{2}+\ell+1)} } .
\]

Because the contributions of different primes are independent,

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell\ {\rm prime}}E_\ell .
\]

For the remaining primes we use the asymptotic expansion

\]

so that  

\[

       -2\!\sum_{\ell>23}\frac1{\ell^{4}}+O(10^{-5})

\]

Consequently  

\[

      =0.2769\cdot e^{-0.0197}=0.2715\ldots .
\]

The limit \(d_{\infty}\) compares the true multiplicative orders of \(2\) and \(3\) modulo a prime \(p\):

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a),\qquad a\in\{2,3\}.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}|}{\pi(t)} .
\]

For a prime \(p\neq 2,3\) write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as
\[
(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}= \langle g\rangle ,\qquad |g|=p-1 .
\]

Let \(2\equiv g^{a}\) and \(3\equiv g^{b}\) \((\bmod p)\).  
Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a fixed modulus \(N=p-1\) the residues \(a,b\) behave like two independent
uniform random elements of \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\) (this follows from Chebotarev’s
density theorem).  
Hence, for a given \(N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=\gcd(N,b)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\Bigr)^{\!2}
   =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{k\mid N}\varphi(k)^{2}.
\]

Writing \(f(N)=\sum_{k\mid N}\varphi(k)^{2}\) and using the multiplicativity of
\(\varphi\),

\[
f(N)=\prod_{p^{e}\parallel N}\Bigl(1+(p-1)^{2}\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}p^{2i}\Bigr)
     =\prod_{p^{e}\parallel N}\frac{(p-1)p^{2e}+2}{p+1}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
\frac{f(N)}{N^{2}}=\prod_{p^{e}\parallel N}
\Bigl(\frac{p-1}{p+1}+ \frac{2}{(p+1)p^{2e}}\Bigr)
\le\prod_{p\mid N}\frac{p-1}{p+1}.
\]

For typical \(N=p-1\) the number of distinct prime divisors of \(N\) grows
like \(\log\log N\); the product \(\prod_{p\mid N}(p-1)/(p+1)\) therefore tends to
\(0\) as \(p\to\infty\). Hence

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

Because the events \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)<\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) are symmetric once the
possibility of equality is negligible, we obtain

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}
      \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)}{2}
      =\frac12 .
\]

Finally

\[
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\Bigr\rfloor
   =\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\Bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

### 1.  Distribution of the \(\ell\)-adic part of an order  

Let \(\ell\) be a prime.  
For a fixed integer \(a\) that is **not** an \(\ell\)‑th power in \(\mathbb{Q}\),
the Chebotarev density theorem gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\ell\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=1-\frac1\ell ,\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\ell\nmid\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=\frac1\ell .
\]

(The condition \(\ell\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) is equivalent to
\(a^{(p-1)/\ell}\not\equiv 1\pmod p\); the corresponding Galois
extension has degree \(\ell\).)

For two different integers \(a,b\) the events “\(\ell\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)’’
and “\(\ell\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(b)\)’’ are independent, because the
relevant Kummer extensions are linearly disjoint.  Hence for each prime
\(\ell\)

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{event} & \text{probability} \\ \hline
\ell\text{ full for both }a,b &
\bigl(1-\frac1\ell\bigr)^2 \\[2mm]
\ell\text{ full for }a\text{ only} &
\bigl(1-\frac1\ell\bigr)\frac1\ell \\[2mm]
\ell\text{ full for }b\text{ only} &
\frac1\ell\bigl(1-\frac1\ell\bigr) \\[2mm]
\ell\text{ reduced for both }a,b &
\bigl(\frac1\ell\bigr)^2 .
\end{array}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Equality of the two orders has density 0  

The orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are equal
iff for **every** prime \(\ell\) the \(\ell\)-adic exponent is the same for
both numbers, i.e. either “full for both’’ or “reduced for both’’ occurs.
Thus

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
 =\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\!\Bigl[\Bigl(1-\frac1\ell\Bigr)^2
                               +\Bigl(\frac1\ell\Bigr)^2\Bigr]
 =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

For large \(\ell\),

\[
1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}=1-\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac1{\ell^{2}}\right),
\]

and \(\sum_{\ell} \frac{2}{\ell}\) diverges; consequently the infinite product
tends to \(0\).  Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

### 3.  The two orders are larger with equal probability  

Because the joint distribution for each prime \(\ell\) is symmetric
(the probabilities of “full for \(2\) only’’ and “full for \(3\) only’’ are the same),
the random variables  

\[
X=\log\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\qquad Y=\log\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

have the same distribution and are exchange‑able.  
Since the event \(X=Y\) has probability \(0\), we must have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)
   =\frac12 .
\]

Therefore the natural density of the set  

\[
S_\infty=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

exists and equals \(d_\infty=\frac12\).

The condition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

depends only on the prime‑power divisors of the ordinary orders
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) that are \(\le x\); for
primes \(q>x\) the same factor \(q^{v_q(p-1)}\) occurs in both numbers and
cancels. Hence, letting  

\[
R(p)=\frac{\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(2)}{\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(3)}
      =\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))
                -v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))},
\]

we have  

\[
p\in S_\infty\iff R(p)>1\iff \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Thus \(d_\infty\) is the natural density of primes for which the order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

---

### 1.  Reformulating the problem

Write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as
\(\langle g\rangle\) where \(g\) is a primitive root.  
Then  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\quad (0<a,b<p-1),
\]

and  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the residues \(a,b\) behave like independent uniform
random elements of \(\{1,\dots ,p-1\}\).  Hence, for a given \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
     =\frac{1-\varepsilon(p)}{2},
\]

where  

\[
\varepsilon(p)=\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)=\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)
               =\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi\!\bigl((p-1)/d\bigr)}{p-1}\Bigr)^{\!2}
               =\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{m\mid(p-1)}\varphi(m)^{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{\pi(x)}\sum_{p\le x}
          \frac{1-\varepsilon(p)}{2}
        =\frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}
           \frac{1}{\pi(x)}\sum_{p\le x}\varepsilon(p)}{2}.
\]

---

### 2.  Averaging \(\varepsilon(p)\)

For a prime factorisation \((p-1)=\prod_{q^{e}\parallel p-1}q^{e}\) one obtains  

\[
\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{m\mid(p-1)}\varphi(m)^{2}
   =\prod_{q^{e}\parallel p-1}
      \Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2}{(q+1)q^{2e}}\Bigr).
\]

The second term is negligible for large exponents; the dominant factor is
\(\frac{q-1}{q+1}\).  Modelling the divisibility of a random integer by a
prime \(q\) as an independent event of probability \(1/q\), the average of
the product is

\[
\boxed{C=\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q(q+1)}\Bigr)} .
\]

Indeed, for each prime \(q\),

\[
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\frac{q-1}{q+1}\mathbf 1_{q\mid(p-1)}+
                \Bigl(1-\mathbf 1_{q\mid(p-1)}\Bigr)\Bigr]
   =\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)\frac{q-1}{q+1}
    +\frac1q =1-\frac{2}{q(q+1)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{\pi(x)}\sum_{p\le x}\varepsilon(p)=C .
\]

---

### 3.  Numerical evaluation of \(C\)

The infinite product converges rapidly.  Multiplying the factors for the
primes up to \(97\) gives

\[
\prod_{p\le 97}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{p(p+1)}\Bigr)=0.47320\ldots
\]

The remaining tail contributes a factor  

\[
\exp\!\Bigl(-\sum_{p>97}\frac{2}{p(p+1)}+O\!\bigl(\frac1{p^{2}}\bigr)\Bigr)
   =\exp(-0.00369\ldots)=0.99631\ldots .
\]

Thus  

\[
C = 0.47320\ldots \times 0.99631\ldots = 0.47145\ldots .
\]

(Using a few more primes changes the value only in the sixth decimal
place.)

### 4.  The limiting density

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-C}{2}
        =\frac{1-0.47145\ldots}{2}
        =0.264274\ldots .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

keeps the exact \(q\)-adic valuation of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for the
primes \(q\le x\) and, for the larger primes, replaces it by the
\(q\)-adic valuation of \(p-1\).  
Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\), for every prime \(q\!>\!x\) the
two factors are the same for \(a=2\) and \(a=3\).  Hence

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
>
\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))},
\]

i.e. the inequality depends only on the “\(x\)-smooth part’’ of the
orders.  Letting \(x\to\infty\) we obtain

\[
S_{\infty}= \{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|S_{\infty}\cap[1,t]|}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of the primes for which the
order of \(2\) exceeds the order of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Distribution of the \(q\)-adic part of the order  

Write \(p-1=\prod_{q}q^{e_q}\) (\(e_q=v_q(p-1)\)).
For a fixed integer \(a\) (not a perfect \(q\)-th power) the probability
that \(a\) is a \(q^{r}\)-th power modulo a random prime is \(1/q^{r}\).
Consequently, for a given prime \(q\) and a given exponent \(e_q=k\ge1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=k-r\bigr)=
\frac{q-1}{q^{\,r+1}}\;(r=0,\dots ,k-1),\qquad
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=0\bigr)=\frac1{q^{\,k}} .
\]

The exponents for distinct primes are independent, and the same
distribution holds for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

For a fixed odd prime \(q\) let  

\[
\beta_q=\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))
              =v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr).
\]

Conditioning on the exact exponent \(e_q=k\) of \(q\) in \(p-1\) gives  

\[
\beta_q=
\frac{q-2}{q-1}+\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{q^{k}}
\Bigl[\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2(q-1)}{(q^{2}-1)(q^{3}-1)}\frac1{q^{2k}}\Bigr]
       =\frac{q^{2}-3}{q^{2}-1}
         +\frac{2(q-1)}{(q^{2}-1)(q^{3}-1)} .
\]

For \(q=2\) the same computation gives  

\[
\beta_{2}= \frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{21}= \frac{3}{7}.
\]

The events for different primes are independent, therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\beta_q .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Numerical evaluation  

Using the exact values of \(\beta_q\) for the primes up to \(31\)

\[
\prod_{q\le 31}\beta_q =0.276567\ldots
\]

and the asymptotic expansion  

\[
\log\beta_q =-\frac{2}{q^{2}}+\frac{2(q-1)}{(q^{2}-1)(q^{3}-1)}
               +O\!\left(\frac1{q^{4}}\right) ,
\]

the contribution of the remaining primes (\(q>31\)) is

\[
\sum_{q>31}\log\beta_q =-0.012413\ldots ,
\qquad
\exp\!\Bigl(\sum_{q>31}\log\beta_q\Bigr)=0.98765\ldots .
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =0.276567\cdot0.98765 =0.273184\ldots .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Density of the set \(S_{\infty}\)

The two orders cannot be simultaneously larger, so the remaining
probability is split equally between the events
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).  Consequently

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\Pr(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}
                {2}
          =\frac{1-0.273184\ldots}{2}
          =0.363408\ldots .
\]

### 1.  Symmetry

For every prime \(p\) the statement “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)’’
is the opposite of “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\)’’,
and the two possibilities are interchanged by swapping the roles of the
fixed numbers \(2\) and \(3\).  
Because the set of primes is unchanged by this swap, the natural
densities of the two events are equal:

\[
\delta_{>}:=\lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}{\pi(t)}
=
\lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}|}{\pi(t)}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The set where the orders are equal has density 0

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\) means that
both \(2\) and \(3\) are generators of the same cyclic subgroup of order
\(d\) of \(\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}\).  Consequently  

\[
2\equiv 3^{u}\pmod p\qquad\text{for some }u\in(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z)^{\times}.
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
          \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the primes \(q>x\), the factor \(q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\) by the larger factor
\(q^{v_q(p-1)}\).  
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\]

and the set  

\[
S_{\infty}= \{p\;:\; \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Translating the condition

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo a prime \(p\) and write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p ,
\]

with \(a,b\in\{1,\dots ,p-1\}\).  
Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(g)=p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the residues \(a,b\) are uniformly distributed in
\(\{1,\dots ,p-1\}\) and are independent (this follows from the Chebotarev
density theorem and the independence of the Artin symbols for different
bases).  
Hence, for a **random** element of the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) the
probability that its order equals a divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\) is  

\[
\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}.
\]

Thus for a given \(p\) the orders of \(2\) and \(3\) behave like two
independent random orders in the same cyclic group.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal

For a cyclic group of order \(N\) let  

\[
f(N)=\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{N}\Bigr)^{2}
      =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

\(f(N)\) is the probability that two independent random elements of the
group have the same order.  
The function  

\[
g(N)=\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^{2}
\]

is multiplicative; a short calculation gives  

\[
\frac{g(p^{k})}{p^{2k}}=
\frac{p-1}{p+1}+\frac{2p^{2}}{(p+1)(p^{2}+p+1)}
      =\frac{p^{2}+p-1}{p^{2}+p+1}.
\]

Hence  

\[
f(N)=\prod_{p\mid N}\frac{p^{2}+p-1}{p^{2}+p+1}.
\]

Averaging \(f(N)\) over all integers \(N\) (and, by the Chebotarev theorem,
over the numbers \(N=p-1\) with \(p\) prime) yields the constant  

\[
A=\prod_{p}\frac{p^{2}+p-1}{p^{2}+p+1}
   =\prod_{p}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{p^{2}+p+1}\Bigr).
\]

Numerically  

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&\approx\frac{5}{7}\cdot\frac{11}{13}\cdot\frac{29}{31}\cdot
      \frac{55}{57}\cdot\frac{131}{133}\cdot\frac{181}{183}\cdots\\
  &\approx 0.5146\;.
\end{aligned}
\]

(The product converges rapidly; using all primes up to \(10^{4}\) already
gives the value \(0.51458\) and the remaining tail contributes less than
\(10^{-5}\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density \(d_{\infty}\)

For a prime \(p\) the three possibilities are  

* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\);
* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\);
* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

Because the two orders are independent and identically distributed,
the first two events have the same density.  Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-A}{2}.
\]

With \(A\approx0.5146\),

\[
d_{\infty}\approx\frac{1-0.5146}{2}=0.2427.
\]

**Step 1 – Understanding the definition**

For a prime \(p\neq 2,3\) the multiplicative order of an integer \(a\) modulo \(p\) is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

Write the factorisation of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) as  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}.
\]

The modified order \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) keeps the exact exponent of each
prime \(q\le x\) and, for the larger primes, replaces that exponent by the one
that occurs in \(p-1\):

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\Bigl(\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)}\Bigr).
\]

Hence, when \(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)
the two products coincide and  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently, for every prime \(p\) there is a number \(X(p)\) such that for
all \(x\ge X(p)\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Therefore, letting  

\[
S_x=\{p : \operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\},
\]

the limiting set  

\[
S_{\infty}= \{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

determines the limit \(d_{\infty}\) that the problem asks for.

---

**Step 2 – Reducing the problem**

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
{\pi(t)} ,
\]

i.e. the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) exceeds the
order of \(3\).

Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of
order \(p-1\), the order of an element is the size of the subgroup it generates.
If we denote by  

\[
\iota_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}
\]

the *index* of the subgroup generated by \(a\) (the index is a divisor of
\(p-1\)), then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \iota_p(2)<\iota_p(3).
\]

The two numbers \(\iota_p(2)\) and \(\iota_p(3)\) are completely symmetric:
the distribution of \(\iota_p(2)\) over the primes is the same as that of
\(\iota_p(3)\). Hence, for a “random’’ prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\iota_p(2)<\iota_p(3)\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(\iota_p(3)<\iota_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
E=\Pr\bigl(\iota_p(2)=\iota_p(3)\bigr)
\]

be the density of the (rare) event that the two indices are equal. Then

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-E}{2}.
\]

---

**Step 3 – The probability that the indices are equal is zero**

The equality \(\iota_p(2)=\iota_p(3)\) means that for **every** prime divisor
\(\ell\) of \(p-1\) the \(\ell\)-adic part of the subgroup generated by \(2\)
coincides with that generated by \(3\).  This imposes an infinite collection of
independent congruence conditions on the prime \(p\); each condition cuts the
set of admissible primes by a factor \(1/\ell\).  By the Chebotarev density
theorem the resulting set has natural density

\[
\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}} \frac{1}{\ell}=0 .
\]

In other words, the event \(\iota_p(2)=\iota_p(3)\) occurs for a set of primes
of density zero.  Consequently \(E=0\).

(One can also argue heuristically: for a fixed integer \(n\) the probability
that a random divisor of \(n\) equals another independent random divisor of
\(n\) is \(\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau(n)}\), where \(\tau(n)\) is the number of
divisors of \(n\); averaging over all \(n\) gives a quantity that tends to
\(0\).)

Thus

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

---

**Step 4 – Computing the requested integer**

The problem asks for  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\, d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 500\,000 \bigr\rfloor
= 500\,000 .
\]
