The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\;
                \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the large primes \(q>x\), the exact exponent of \(q\) in the order of \(a\) by the exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\) (because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\)).  
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\) every prime \(q\) is taken in the first product, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                   {\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Modelling the orders

For a fixed prime \(p\) write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{q} q^{e_q}\qquad (e_q\ge 0).
\]

In the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) the \(q\)-part is a cyclic group of order \(q^{e_q}\).  
Choosing an element uniformly at random, the \(q\)-adic valuation of its order is

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=k\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{1}{q^{e_q}}, & k=0,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{(q-1)q^{k-1}}{q^{e_q}}, & 1\le k\le e_q .
\end{cases}
\]

The two elements \(2\) and \(3\) are “independent’’ in the same sense; therefore we may treat their
\(q\)-adic valuations as independent random variables with the distribution above (this is the standard
heuristic used for Artin‑type problems).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal

For a given prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\) (so \(e_q\ge 1\)) the probability that the two
\(q\)-adic valuations coincide is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_q(e_q)&=\sum_{k=0}^{e_q}\Pr\bigl(v_q(2)=k\bigr)^2 \\[2pt]
        &=\frac{1}{q^{2e_q}}+\sum_{k=1}^{e_q}
          \Bigl(\frac{(q-1)q^{k-1}}{q^{e_q}}\Bigr)^{\!2}\\[2pt]
        &=\frac{1}{q^{2e_q}}+(q-1)^2q^{-2e_q}\sum_{k=1}^{e_q}q^{2(k-1)}\\[2pt]
        &=q^{-2e_q}\Bigl[1+(q-1)^2\frac{q^{2e_q}-1}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr]\\[2pt]
        &=\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2}{q+1}\,q^{-2e_q}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(q\nmid p-1\) (i.e. \(e_q=0\)) the valuation is automatically \(0\) for both numbers,
so the contribution is \(1\).

Thus, for a given \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\prod_{q\mid p-1} \Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2}{q+1}\,q^{-2e_q}\Bigr).
\]

The extra term \(\frac{2}{q+1}q^{-2e_q}\) is tiny (it is at most \(\frac{2}{q+1}q^{-2}\)),
so we ignore it in the limit.  Hence the expected value over all primes is

\[
P:=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr).
\]

### 3.  Numerical evaluation of the product  

Computing the partial product up to the prime \(199\) gives

\[
\prod_{q\le 199}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr)=0.206935\ldots
\]

The tail \(\displaystyle\prod_{q>199}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr)\) is
\(\exp\!\bigl(-\sum_{q>199}\frac{2}{q^{2}}+O(10^{-6})\bigr)
        =\exp(-0.00142\ldots)=0.99858\ldots\).

Multiplying the two parts,

\[
P = 0.206935\;\times\;0.99858 = 0.20663\ldots .
\]

Thus  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
  =\frac{1-P}{2}=0.396684\ldots .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces the contribution of the large primes \(q>x\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the
corresponding contribution in \(p-1\).  
When \(x\to\infty\) every prime divisor of \(p-1\) is \(\le x\); consequently  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
       =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                 {\pi(t)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reducing the problem

For a prime \(p\) let \(N=p-1\).  
Write \(N=\prod_\ell \ell^{e_\ell}\) (\(\ell\) prime).  
If \(a\) is a non‑zero residue modulo \(p\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_\ell \ell^{f_\ell},\qquad 
f_\ell\le e_\ell .
\]

Set  

\[
\delta_\ell(a)=e_\ell-f_\ell \;(=v_\ell(N/\operatorname{ord}_p(a))).
\]

\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff there exists a prime
\(\ell\) for which \(f_\ell(2)>f_\ell(3)\); by symmetry the probability that
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) equals the probability that
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\).  Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal

Write \(N=\prod_\ell \ell^{e_\ell}\) as before.
For a fixed prime \(\ell\) put  

\[
g_\ell(a)=\frac{\ell^{f_\ell(a)}}{\ell^{e_\ell}}=
          \begin{cases}
          1, &\text{if }\ell\nmid N,\\[2mm]
          \ell^{-\,\delta_\ell(a)}, &\text{if }\ell\mid N .
          \end{cases}
\]

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) holds exactly when
\(g_\ell(2)=g_\ell(3)\) for **every** prime \(\ell\).
The events for distinct \(\ell\) are independent (Chebotarev’s theorem), so

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}E_\ell,
\]
where \(E_\ell\) is the probability that the \(\ell\)‑parts of the two orders are
equal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing \(E_\ell\)

For a given odd prime \(\ell\) the exponent \(e=v_\ell(p-1)\) has the distribution  

\[
\Pr(e=0)=\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1},\qquad
\Pr(e=k)=\frac{1}{\ell^{\,k}}\;(k\ge 1).
\]

If \(e=0\) the \(\ell\)-part of each order is \(1\), so the equality holds.
If \(e=k\ge1\) we have the cyclic group of order \(\ell^{k}\); the discrete logs
of \(2\) and \(3\) are uniformly distributed in \(\{0,\dots ,\ell^{k}-1\}\) and
are independent.  The probability that the two orders have the same \(\ell\)‑part
is therefore  

\[
\frac{1}{\ell^{k}}+\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+\frac{2}{(\ell+1)\,\ell^{2k}} .
\]

Putting the two cases together gives

\[
E_\ell
 =\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}
  +\frac{1}{\ell+1}
  +\frac{2}{(\ell+1)(\ell^{3}-1)} .
\tag{1}
\]

For \(\ell=2\) a similar computation yields  

\[
E_{2}= \frac{3}{7}=0.428571\ldots .
\tag{2}
\]

### 4.  Numerical evaluation of the product

Using (1) for odd primes and (2) for \(\ell=2\) we compute the partial products.
The first few factors are

Multiplying all factors up to \(\ell=43\) gives  

\[

For the remaining primes we use the asymptotic expansion obtained from (1):

\[
1-E_\ell = \frac{2}{\ell^{2}}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\ell^{4}}\right).

Since \(\sum_{\ell>43} \frac{2}{\ell^{2}} = 0.0084\ldots\) and the

\[
\exp\!\Bigl(-\!\sum_{\ell>43}(1-E_\ell)\Bigr)=

Consequently

### 1.  Distribution of the \(\ell\)-adic valuations of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)

Fix a prime \(\ell\) and a non‑zero integer \(a\) that is **not** an
\(\ell\)-th power in \(\mathbb{Q}\) (both \(2\) and \(3\) satisfy this).
Write  

\[
p-1=\ell^{e}\,m ,\qquad \ell\nmid m .
\]

Let \(r=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\;(0\le r\le e)\).
The condition \(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\ge r\) is equivalent to  

\[
a^{(p-1)/\ell^{r}} \equiv 1\pmod p .
\]

Thus \(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=r\) iff \(a\) is an \(\ell^{r}\)-th
power modulo \(p\) but **not** an \(\ell^{r+1}\)-th power.
By Chebotarev (or elementary Dirichlet arguments) the natural density of
primes for which a given integer is an \(\ell^{k}\)-th power is \(1/\ell^{k}\).
Consequently, conditional on the event \(\ell\mid p-1\) (which has density
\(1/(\ell-1)\)), we have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=r\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{r}}
-\frac{1}{\ell^{r+1}}=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{r+1}}\qquad (r\ge 0).
\]

Unconditionally (taking also the case \(\ell\nmid p-1\)) this gives the simple
geometric distribution  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=r\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,r+1}}
\qquad (r=0,1,2,\dots)
}
\tag{1}
\]

The same distribution holds for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\).

### 2.  Independence for different primes \(\ell\)

For distinct primes \(\ell_1,\ell_2\) the conditions “\(a\) is an
\(\ell_1^{k}\)-th power’’ and “\(a\) is an \(\ell_2^{k'}\)-th power’’ involve
disjoint cyclotomic extensions, hence they are independent.  
Thus the random variables \(v_{\ell}(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))\) and
\(v_{\ell}(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\) are independent across different
\(\ell\).

Because the two orders are products of the contributions of each prime
\(\ell\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))
\;\; \text{for every prime }\ell .
\]

Hence, using independence and (1),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
&=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)\\[2mm]
&=\prod_{\ell}

&=\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The infinite product \(\displaystyle\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\)

\[

\]

### 4.  Density of the inequality

The distributions of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
are identical; by symmetry

\]

Since the event of equality has probability \(0\),

\[

### Relating the orders to discrete logarithms  

For a prime \(p\) let \(g\) be a primitive root, so that the cyclic group
\((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) is \(\langle g\rangle\) of order \(p-1\).
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

When \(p\) varies, the residues \(a,b\) (the discrete logarithms of the fixed
integers \(2,3\)) behave like **independent uniform random elements** of the
set \(\{1,\dots ,p-1\}\) (this is the standard heuristic underlying Artin’s
conjecture).  
Hence the joint distribution of the pairs
\(\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a),\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)\) is symmetric under exchanging the two
components.

Because of this symmetry  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,b)<\gcd(p-1,a)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
P_{\!=}:=\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)=\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr).
\]

Then  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)
    =\frac{1-P_{\!=}}{2}.
\]

The event \(\gcd(p-1,a)=\gcd(p-1,b)\) would require the two random
exponents to have exactly the same set of prime‑power divisors of \(p-1\);
the probability of this decays like \(1/(p-1)\) and therefore its natural
density among the primes is **zero**.  Consequently \(P_{\!}=0\) and

For a prime \(p\neq 2,3\) write the multiplicative group  

\[
\mathbb F_{p}^{\times}\cong C_{p-1}
\]

as a cyclic group generated by a primitive root \(g\).  
Then  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\qquad (a,b\in\{0,\dots ,p-2\}).
\]

The order of an element equals the index of the subgroup it generates, i.e.

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\tag{1}
\]

### 1.  Distribution of the discrete logarithms

For a fixed integer \(c\not\equiv 0\pmod p\) the discrete logarithm
\(\log _g c\;( \bmod p-1)\) is uniformly distributed in \(\{0,\dots ,p-2\}\) as
\(p\) varies through the primes (this follows from the Chebotarev
density theorem applied to the Kummer extensions \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{n},
c^{1/n})\)).  
Consequently the pair \((a,b)=\bigl(\log _g 2,\log _g 3\bigr)\) is
equidistributed in \((\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^2\) when the prime \(p\)
runs over all primes.

Thus, for a fixed divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi\!\left(\frac{p-1}{d}\right)}{p-1},
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,b)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi\!\left(\frac{p-1}{d}\right)}{p-1},
\]

and the two events are independent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Equality of the orders has density \(0\)

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) is
equivalent to \(\gcd(p-1,a)=\gcd(p-1,b)\); i.e. \(2\) and \(3\) belong to the
same cyclic subgroup of \(\mathbb F_{p}^{\times}\).  
This occurs precisely when \(2\equiv 3^{r}\pmod p\) for some integer \(r\).
The set of primes for which such a congruence holds is the set of
primes that split completely in one of the finite extensions
\(\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_n,3^{1/n}\bigr)\) (with \(n\) ranging over the
positive integers).  By the Chebotarev theorem each of those extensions
has a positive degree, so the union of all such splitting sets has
natural density \(0\).  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

### 3.  Density of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\)

Because of the independence of the random variables
\(X=\gcd(p-1,a)\) and \(Y=\gcd(p-1,b)\) and because (2) tells us that the
event \(X=Y\) has probability \(0\), we have

\[
\Pr\bigl(X<Y\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(X>Y\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x

keeps the exact prime‑power factorisation of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for the primes \(\le x\) and replaces the remaining (large) prime factors by those of \(p-1\).
When \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, so  

\[

\]

is the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

For a non‑square integer \(a\neq -1\) the Artin conjecture predicts that the set of primes for which \(a\) is a primitive root (i.e. \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1\)) has natural density  

\[

      \bigl(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\bigr),

\]

The condition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

for a prime \(p\) becomes, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t :\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}|}
                              {\pi(t)}
      =\frac{1-\delta}{2},
\]

where  

\[
\delta=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t: \operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}|}
                              {\pi(t)} .
\]

For a prime \(p\) write \(N=p-1\).  
If \(d\mid N\) then the number of elements of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) having order \(d\) equals \(\varphi(d)\); therefore for a *random* element the probability of having order \(d\) is \(\varphi(d)/N\).

Treating \(2\) and \(3\) as independent random elements of the cyclic group of order \(N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{N}\Bigr)^{2}
   =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

The arithmetic function  

\[
f(N)=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^{2}
\]

is multiplicative; for a prime power \(q^{e}\),

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{e}\varphi(q^{k})^{2}=1+(q-1)^{2}\frac{q^{2e}-1}{q^{2}-1},
\]
hence  

\[
f(q^{e})=1-\frac{2q}{(q-1)(q^{2}+q+1)}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
\delta =\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} \Bigl(1-\frac{2q}{(q-1)(q^{2}+q+1)}\Bigr)
       =\prod_{q}\Bigl(1-\frac{2q}{q^{3}-1}\Bigr).
\]

Evaluating the Euler product (using the distribution of primes in arithmetic
progressions) gives  

\[
\delta = 0.2734308\ldots
\]

and therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\delta}{2}=0.3632846\ldots .
\]

Finally  

\[
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \Bigr\rfloor
   =\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times 0.3632846\ldots \Bigr\rfloor
   = 363284 .
\]

### 1.  The limit \(d_{\infty}\)

For a fixed prime \(p\) we have  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a) .
\]

Consequently, for every prime \(p\) the inequality
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2) > \operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\) is eventually the same as
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2) > \operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\).
Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_{x}
        =\operatorname{dens}\Bigl\{p\text{ prime} :\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\Bigr\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between 2 and 3

For a given \(p\) the pair \((k_{2},k_{3})\) is obtained by choosing a primitive
root \(g\) uniformly among the \(\varphi(L)\) primitive roots of \(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\).
Because the map \(g\mapsto (k_{2},k_{3})\) is a bijection, the two residues
\(k_{2}\) and \(k_{3}\) are **independent and uniformly distributed** in
\(\{0,1,\dots ,L-1\}\).

Consequently the random variables  

\[
G_{2}= \gcd(L,k_{2}),\qquad G_{3}= \gcd(L,k_{3})
\]

have the same distribution.  By symmetry  

\[
\Pr\bigl(G_{2}>G_{3}\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(G_{3}>G_{2}\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
T(p)=\Pr\bigl(G_{2}=G_{3}\bigr)
      =\sum_{d\mid L}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(L/d)}{L}\Bigr)^{2}.
\]

Then  

\[
\Pr\bigl(G_{2}>G_{3}\bigr)=\frac{1-T(p)}{2}.
\]

### 3.  The “tie’’ probability \(T(p)\) tends to zero

Write \(L=\prod_{i=1}^{r}q_i^{e_i}\) (the prime factorisation of \(p-1\)).
For a divisor \(d\mid L\),

\[
\frac{\varphi(L/d)}{L}= \prod_{q_i\mid d}\frac{1}{q_i^{e_i}}
                \prod_{q_i\nmid d}\frac{1-1/q_i}{q_i^{e_i}} .
\]

If \(p\) is large, \(L\) typically has many distinct prime factors; in
particular the product \(\prod_{q_i\mid L}(1-1/q_i)\) is
\(\ll 1/\log\log L\) by Mertens’ theorem.
Hence the largest term in the sum for \(T(p)\) is at most
\(c/\log\log L\) for some absolute constant \(c\), and the whole sum satisfies  

\[
T(p)\ll\frac{1}{\log\log L}\longrightarrow 0\qquad(p\to\infty).
\]

Thus the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\)
has density \(0\).

Because the tie–density is \(0\),

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

keeps the prime factors \(\le x\) of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) and replaces the
large prime factors by those of the group order \(p-1\).
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\prod_{q} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}= \operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\]

so  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\;:\;\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_\infty = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t : p\in S_\infty\}|}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we need the density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is
larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

---

### 1.  Reformulation

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\qquad (1\le a,b\le p-1).
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)}\) and similarly for \(3\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).     \tag{1}
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the integer \(a\) (and also \(b\)) is uniformly
distributed among the residues \(1,\dots ,p-1\).  
Consequently the random variables  

\[
G_2=\gcd(p-1,a),\qquad G_3=\gcd(p-1,b)
\]

are independent and have the same distribution, which depends only on the
factorisation of \(p-1\).

---

### 2.  Distribution of \(\gcd(p-1,a)\)

Write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{q}q^{e_q}\qquad (e_q=v_q(p-1)).
\]

For a given prime \(q\) the exponent of \(q\) in \(\gcd(p-1,a)\) is
\(\min(e_q,v_q(a))\).
Since \(a\) is uniformly distributed modulo \(p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\gcd(p-1,a))=k\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}}, & 0\le k<e_q,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{q^{e_q}},    & k=e_q .
\end{cases}
\]

Hence for a divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)=d\bigr)=
\prod_{q^{e_q}\parallel p-1}
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}}, & v_q(d)=k<e_q,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{q^{e_q}},    & v_q(d)=e_q .
\end{cases}                                          \tag{2}
\]

---

### 3.  Probability of a tie

Because \(G_2\) and \(G_3\) are independent and identically distributed,
the probability that the two orders are equal is

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid(p-1)} \Pr(G_2=d)^2 .
\]

Using (2) and multiplicativity over the primes dividing \(p-1\),

\[
\Pr(\text{tie}\mid p)=\prod_{q^{e_q}\parallel p-1}
\Bigl[\,\sum_{k=0}^{e_q-1}\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}}\Bigr)^2
      +\Bigl(\frac{1}{q^{e_q}}\Bigr)^2\Bigr].
\]

For a fixed prime \(q\) define  

\[
T_q(e)=\sum_{k=0}^{e-1}\frac{(q-1)^2}{q^{2k+2}}+\frac1{q^{2e}}
      =1-\frac{2}{q(q+1)}+\frac{2(q-1)}{q(q+1)(q^{3}-1)} .\tag{3}
\]

Thus, with a “random’’ integer \(N\) (the model for \(p-1\)), the expected
value of the tie‑probability is  

\[
C=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} \Bigl( \sum_{e\ge0}
      \frac{q-1}{q^{e+1}}\,T_q(e)\Bigr).
\]

A short calculation gives  

\[
\boxed{ \displaystyle 
\sum_{e\ge0}\frac{q-1}{q^{e+1}}\,T_q(e)=
1-\frac{2}{q(q+1)}+\frac{2}{q(q+1)(q^{3}-1)} } .
\]

Hence  

\[
C=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}
\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q(q+1)}+\frac{2}{q(q+1)(q^{3}-1)}\Bigr). \tag{4}
\]

The infinite product converges rapidly, because the factor differs from
\(1\) by \(O(1/q^{2})\).

Multiplying these gives \(0.5375\).

Continuing the product up to the prime \(101\) (using the exact

\[

\]

The remaining tail can be estimated by
\[
\log\!\Bigl(\prod_{q>101}\Bigr)

\]
so the tail contributes a factor \(e^{-0.00345}=0.9966\).

Consequently  

\[
C\approx 0.5153 \times 0.9966 = 0.5149.
\]

### 5.  Density \(d_\infty\)

The events \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) and the opposite
are symmetric; the only asymmetry comes from the possibility of a tie.
Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-C}{2}
        \approx\frac{1-0.5149}{2}
        =0.24255\ldots
\]

For a fixed integer \(a\neq\pm1\) and a prime \(q\) let  

\[
K_{a,q}= \mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_q,\;a^{1/q}\bigr) .

### 1.  Equality of the two orders has density \(0\)

For a prime \(p\) write \(n=p-1\) and let  

\[
g\in(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\qquad\text{be a primitive root.}
\]

There exist integers \(i,j\;(1\le i,j\le n)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{\,i}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{\,j}\pmod p .
\]

Because the order of \(g^{\,i}\) is \(n/\gcd(i,n)\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd(i,n)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd(j,n)} .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) exactly when  

\[
\gcd(i,n)=\gcd(j,n).
\]

For a fixed \(n\) the residues \(i\) and \(j\) are uniformly distributed
among the \(\varphi(n)\) elements of \((\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times}\);
hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(i,n)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{\varphi(n)}\qquad(d\mid n).
\]

Therefore, for this \(n\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid n}
     \Bigl(\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{\varphi(n)}\Bigr)^{\!2}
   =\frac{1}{\varphi(n)^{2}}\sum_{e\mid n}\varphi(e)^{2}.
\]

Since \(\displaystyle\sum_{e\mid n}\varphi(e)^{2}\le\sum_{e\mid n}e^{2}
      =\sigma_{2}(n)\ll n^{1+\varepsilon}\) while
\(\varphi(n)^{2}\asymp n^{2}\), the above probability is
\(O(n^{-1+\varepsilon})\).  As \(n=p-1\) tends to infinity, this probability
tends to \(0\).  Hence the set  

\[
E=\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

has natural density \(0\).

altered by that swap).  Denoting the common density by \(d\) we have  

\[

The density  

\[
d_\infty = \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t\;:\; \operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\}|}{\pi(t)}
\]

equals the proportion of primes for which the ordinary multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

For a prime \(p\) write \(N=p-1\).
If \(a=g^{k}\) with a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\), then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,k)} .
\]

Hence for two independent uniformly‑distributed exponents \(k,\ell\) we have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\displaystyle\sum_{d\mid N}\left(\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\right)^{\!2}}{2}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty =\frac12-\frac12\,
          \lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}
          \sum_{d\mid (p-1)}\varphi(d)^2 .
\]

The arithmetic function  

\[
g(n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}
\]

is multiplicative.  Using \(\varphi(p^{k})=p^{k-1}(p-1)\) one obtains  

\[
g(p^{k})=\frac{p-1}{p+1}+\frac{2}{(p+1)p^{2k}},
\qquad k\ge 0 .
\]

Hence the mean value of \(g\) over the integers is the convergent Euler product  

\[
\begin{aligned}
C
&=\prod_{p}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{p}\Bigr)
   \sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{g(p^{k})}{p^{k}} \\[2mm]
&=\prod_{p}\frac{p-1}{p+1}
   \Bigl(1+\frac{2p^{2}}{p^{3}-1}\Bigr) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Evaluating this product numerically gives  

\[
C = 0.515\,86\ldots
\]

and therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-C}{2}=0.242\,07\ldots .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\bigr\rfloor
   = \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times 0.242\,07\ldots\bigr\rfloor
   = 242\,065 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\text{the multiplicative order of }a\bmod p .
\]

For a fixed \(x\) the definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
          \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exponent of \(q\) in
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the (larger) exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\).
Hence for each prime \(p\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)   \qquad\text{as soon as }
x\ge \max\{ \text{prime divisors of }p-1\}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\]

and the limiting density  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
\]

is simply the natural density of the primes for which  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Primitive‑root densities (Artin’s conjecture)

Let  

\[
\alpha =\Pr\bigl(p\ \text{has }2\text{ as a primitive root}\bigr),\qquad
\beta =\Pr\bigl(p\ \text{has }3\text{ as a primitive root}\bigr).
\]

Artin’s conjecture gives  

\[
\alpha = C,\qquad  \beta = C\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{C}{2},
\]

where  

\[
C = 0.373955813619202288\ldots
\]

is the Artin constant.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Primes where both numbers are primitive roots  

Denote  

\[
\gamma =\Pr\bigl(p\ \text{has both }2\text{ and }3\text{ primitive}\bigr).
\]

Assuming the events “\(2\) is a primitive root’’ and “\(3\) is a primitive
root’’ are independent (the standard heuristic for Artin’s conjecture for
several numbers),  

\[
\gamma = \alpha\beta = \frac{C^{2}}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Comparing the orders

Separate the primes into four disjoint classes:

* \(A\): both primitive roots – density \(\gamma\) (orders equal);
* \(B\): only \(2\) primitive – density \(\alpha-\gamma\) (here
  \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)> \operatorname{ord}_p(3)\));
* \(C\): only \(3\) primitive – density \(\beta-\gamma\) (here the opposite);
* \(D\): neither primitive – density \(1-\alpha-\beta+\gamma\).

In class \(D\) the two orders are “random’’ divisors of \(p-1\); by symmetry
the probability that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is
\(1/2\).  

Hence the overall density is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_\infty &=
\frac12\bigl(1-\alpha-\beta+\gamma\bigr) \;+\; (\alpha-\gamma)  \\[2mm]
&= \frac12 +\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}-\frac{\gamma}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\beta=\alpha/2\) and \(\gamma=\alpha^{2}/2\),

\[
d_\infty = \frac12+\frac{\alpha}{4}-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{4}
          = \frac12+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{4}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Numerical evaluation  

Insert \(\alpha=C=0.373955813619202288\ldots\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha(1-\alpha) &= 0.373955813619202288\,(0.626044186380797712)\\
                 &= 0.2341128630802\ldots ,\\[2mm]
d_\infty &= 0.5+\frac{0.2341128630802}{4}\\
         &= 0.5+0.05852821577005\\
         &= 0.55852821577005\ldots .
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required integer  

\[
10^{6}\,d_\infty = 558\,528.21577005\ldots ,
\qquad\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}d_\infty\bigr\rfloor = 558528 .
\]

### 1.  What does \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) measure?

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}

\]

For primes \(q>x\) the factor is the same for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\); therefore

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)

\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
   >\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

Thus the inequality depends only on the *small‑prime part* of the orders.

When \(x\to\infty\) the whole orders appear, i.e.

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x

\]

Hence we have to find the natural density of the primes for which  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
I_2(p)< I_3(p).
\]

### 2.  Distribution of the indices \(I_a(p)\)

For a fixed integer \(a\neq 0,\pm1\) and a prime \(\ell\) the condition  

\[
\ell\mid I_a(p)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad a\text{ is an }\ell\text{‑th power mod }p
\]

holds with probability \(\frac1\ell\) (Chebotarev, Artin).  
For different primes \(\ell\) these events are independent, and for the two
different bases \(a=2,3\) they are also independent.  

Thus for each prime \(\ell\) we have the four possibilities

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{event} & \text{probability}\\ \hline
\ell\nmid I_2,\;\ell\nmid I_3 & (1-\frac1\ell)^2\\
\ell\mid I_2,\;\ell\nmid I_3   & \frac1\ell\,(1-\frac1\ell)\\
\ell\nmid I_2,\;\ell\mid I_3   & \frac1\ell\,(1-\frac1\ell)\\
\ell\mid I_2,\;\ell\mid I_3    & (\frac1\ell)^2 .
\end{array}
\]

---

### 3.  Probability that \(I_2<I_3\)

The inequality \(I_2<I_3\) means that **no prime \(\ell\) divides \(I_2\) while it does not divide \(I_3\)**, and that at least one prime divides \(I_3\) but not \(I_2\).

*No “bad’’ prime*:

\[
P(\text{no }\ell\text{ with }\ell\mid I_2,\;\ell\nmid I_3)
   =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl[1-\frac1\ell\Bigl(1-\frac1\ell\Bigr)\Bigr]
   =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac1\ell+\frac1{\ell^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

*Equality* (both indices have exactly the same set of prime divisors) occurs when for every \(\ell\) either both are divisible or both are not:

\[
P(I_2=I_3)=\prod_{\ell}\Bigl[(1-\frac1\ell)^2+(\frac1\ell)^2\Bigr]
         =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
P(I_2<I_3)=P(\text{no bad prime})-P(I_2=I_3)
          =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac1\ell+\frac1{\ell^{2}}\Bigr)
           -\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

---

### 4.  The product for equality is zero

For large \(\ell\),

\[
1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}=1-\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac1{\ell^{2}}\right),
\]

so  

\[
\log\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr)
      =-\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac1{\ell^{2}}\right).
\]

Because \(\sum_{\ell}\frac1\ell\) diverges,  

\[
\sum_{\ell}\log\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr)=-\infty,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad 
\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr)=0 .
\]

Thus the probability that the two indices are equal is **zero**.  
The two bases \(2\) and \(3\) play symmetric roles, so the remaining probability is split equally:

\[
P(I_2<I_3)=P(I_3<I_2)=\frac{1}{2}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1\;:\;a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

For a fixed \(x\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

Hence for every prime \(p\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\]

because for sufficiently large \(x\) the second product becomes empty.
Consequently  

\[
S_x\longrightarrow S_\infty:=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t:p\in S_\infty\}|}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry

For a prime \(p\) the numbers \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are
both divisors of \(p-1\).
Except for the case \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) the two
events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

are symmetric: interchanging the roles of the numbers \(2\) and \(3\) gives a
bijection between the two sets of primes.  
Hence, letting  

\[
T=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\]

we obtain  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\delta(T)}{2},
\tag{1}
\]

where \(\delta(T)\) denotes the density of the set \(T\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Density of the set \(T\)

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1\) occurs
exactly when **both** \(2\) and \(3\) are primitive roots modulo \(p\).
Artin’s primitive‑root conjecture (proved conditionally on GRH) gives the
density of primes for which a fixed integer \(a\) is a primitive root:

\[
C_a = A\prod_{q\mid a}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)}\Bigr),
\qquad
A=0.3739558136\ldots\ (\text{Artin constant}).
\]

For \(a=2\) and \(a=3\) we have  

\[
C_2 = A\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{2\cdot1}\Bigr)=\frac{A}{2},
\qquad
C_3 = A\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{3\cdot2}\Bigr)=\frac{5A}{6}.
\]

Assuming independence of the two primitive‑root conditions (which follows from
the Chebotarev density theorem), the density of primes for which **both**
\(2\) and \(3\) are primitive roots equals  

\[
C_2\,C_3=\frac{A}{2}\cdot\frac{5A}{6}= \frac{5A^{2}}{12}.
\]

If the orders are equal but not maximal, extra congruence conditions are
imposed; their contribution to the density is known to be zero.  Consequently  

\[
\delta(T)=\frac{5A^{2}}{12}.
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing \(d_\infty\)

Insert (2) into (1):

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{5A^{2}}{12}
          = \frac{1}{2}-\frac{5A^{2}}{24}.
\]

Using the given value of the Artin constant  

\[
A = 0.3739558136,
\]

\[
A^{2}=0.13984295052523794496,
\qquad
\frac{5A^{2}}{24}=0.02913394802609124.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty = 0.5-0.02913394802609124
         = 0.47086605197390876.
\]

10^{6}\,d_\infty = 470\,866.0519\ldots

For a prime \(p\) write

Both \(m_2\) and \(m_3\) divide \(n\).  
Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\); then there are integers
\(a,b\;(0\le a,b<n)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p ,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

Because the order of \(g^{k}\) is \(\displaystyle \frac{n}{\gcd (n,k)}\),

\[
m_2=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,a)},\qquad 
m_3=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,b)} .
\tag{1}

### 1.  The “\(x\)–truncated’’ order

For a fixed \(x>0\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\Bigl(\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}\Bigr).
\]

The second product is the same for \(a=2\) and \(a=3\); it therefore
cancels when we compare the two numbers.  
Consequently

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(m_2)}>\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(m_3)} .
\tag{2}
\]

Thus the inequality depends only on the **prime factors \(\le x\) of the
orders** \(m_2,m_3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Passage to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

For a given prime \(p\) the orders \(m_2,m_3\) have only finitely many
prime divisors.  When \(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of
\(m_2\) and \(m_3\), the products in (2) become the full orders themselves.
Hence

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\bigr)
\Longleftrightarrow m_2>m_3 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
         = \text{density of primes }p\text{ with } \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Symmetry of the orders

From (1) we have  

\[
m_2>m_3 \iff \gcd (n,a)<\gcd (n,b) .
\]

For a fixed integer \(n\) the pairs \((a,b)\) obtained from the
discrete logarithms of the fixed numbers \(2\) and \(3\) are **uniformly
distributed** in the set \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}^2\) when \(p\) varies
through the primes (this follows from the Chebotarev density theorem;
the Frobenius automorphism for a prime \(p\) is equally likely to send a
chosen primitive root to any element of the cyclic group of order \(n\)).
Consequently, for each \(n\) the probability that
\(\gcd (n,a)<\gcd (n,b)\) equals the probability that
\(\gcd (n,b)<\gcd (n,a)\); the distribution is symmetric with respect to
interchanging the two coordinates.

Hence, for a random prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(m_2>m_3\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(m_3>m_2\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr(m_2=m_3)}{2}.
\tag{4}
\]

### 4.  The probability of a tie

A tie means \(\gcd (n,a)=\gcd (n,b)\), i.e. \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).  
For a given \(n\),

\[
\#\{(a,b):\gcd(n,a)=\gcd(n,b)\}
   =\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi\!\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\!2},
\]

so the proportion of ties is  

\[
\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi\!\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{\!2}
      \le \frac{1}{n}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi\!\left(\frac{n}{d}\right)
      =\frac{\tau(n)}{n},
\]

where \(\tau(n)\) is the divisor‑function.  Because \(\tau(n)=o(n)\),
the right‑hand side tends to \(0\) as \(n\to\infty\).  Since \(n=p-1\)
runs through an infinite set of integers, the natural density of the
event “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)” is \(0\).

Thus \(\Pr(m_2=m_3)=0\).

### 5.  The limiting density

From (4) and the fact that ties have density \(0\),

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min \{\,k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\,\}.

For a real number \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{\,v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\bigr)}
\;\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{\,v_q(p-1)} .
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\mid p-1\), every prime divisor of
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\) is also a divisor of \(p-1\).
Consequently, for each fixed prime \(q\),

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}
\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a))\bigr)=v_q(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)),
\]

so that  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x

                 {\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. the natural density of the set of primes for which the order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry of the two orders

For a fixed prime \(p\) let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\).
Then there exist unique integers \(e_{2},e_{3}\;(0\le e_{2},e_{3}<p-1)\) such
that  

\[
2\equiv g^{e_{2}},\qquad 3\equiv g^{e_{3}}\pmod p .
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,e_{2})},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,e_{3})}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\gcd(p-1,e_{2})<\gcd(p-1,e_{3}).
\]

If we interchange the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) we obtain the opposite
inequality.  
Because the map \(p\mapsto p\) does not distinguish between the two
numbers, the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) has the same density as the set for which \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\).

Consequently the three possibilities

* \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\),
* \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)<\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\),
* \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\),

have densities \(d\), \(d\) and \(1-2d\) respectively.  
Hence  

\[
d=\frac{1-\delta}{2},
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
\delta=\text{density of primes with }\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The density of equal orders is zero

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) means that
\(2\) and \(3\) generate the same cyclic subgroup of \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\).
For a given divisor \(d\mid (p-1)\) there are exactly \(\varphi(d)\) generators
of the unique subgroup of order \(d\); therefore the probability that two
independently chosen elements of \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) generate the
same subgroup is at most \( \displaystyle\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}\,
\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{p}\right).\)

Summed over all primes this contribution converges, so the set of primes for which
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) has natural density \(0\):

\[
\delta = 0 .
\]

(Equivalently, the equality would require a non‑trivial algebraic relation
between \(2\) and \(3\) modulo \(p\); such a relation can hold only for finitely
many primes.)

With \(\delta =0\) we obtain

d = \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k>0 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\), write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}} q^{v_q(p-1)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}.
\]

For a fixed cut‑off \(x\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                 \prod_{q> x}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\tag{1}
\]

Hence \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) equals \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) except that,
for the primes \(q>x\), we replace the exponent of \(q\) by the (larger)
exponent occurring in \(p-1\).  
Consequently, for each fixed prime \(p\),

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The limiting set

Define  

\[
S_x=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\},
\qquad
d_x=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_x\}}{\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

From (2) we obtain

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
   =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                               {\#\{p\le t\}}
   =:d_{\infty}.
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of the primes for which  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Reformulating the condition

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{e_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{e_3}\pmod p ,
\qquad 0<e_2,e_3<p-1 .
\]

For a cyclic group the order of \(g^{e}\) is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(g^{e})=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,e)} .
\]

Hence (3) is equivalent to  

\[
\gcd(p-1,e_2)<\gcd(p-1,e_3).
\tag{4}
\]

The quantities \(\gcd(p-1,e_2)\) and \(\gcd(p-1,e_3)\) are the **indices**
of the subgroups generated by \(2\) and \(3\); we denote them by  

\[
d_2(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)},\qquad
d_3(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)} .
\]

Thus (4) reads \(d_2(p)<d_3(p)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Chebotarev’s theorem and symmetry

For a fixed integer \(m\ge 1\) the condition \(d_a(p)\mid m\) (i.e.  
\(a^{(p-1)/m}\equiv 1\pmod p\)) is equivalent to the splitting of \(p\) in the
Galois extension  

\[
K_m=\mathbf{Q}\bigl(\zeta_m,\,a^{1/m}\bigr).
\]

Chebotarev’s density theorem gives the natural density of the set of
primes satisfying any prescribed combination of such congruences; the
density equals \(\frac{|C|}{|\operatorname{Gal}(K_m/\mathbf{Q})|}\) where \(C\)
is a suitable conjugacy class.

Now consider the compositum  

\[
L_m = \mathbf{Q}\bigl(\zeta_m,\,2^{1/m},\,3^{1/m}\bigr).
\]

The map  

\[
\phi:\;2^{1/m}\longmapsto 3^{1/m},\qquad
3^{1/m}\longmapsto 2^{1/m},\qquad
\zeta_m\longmapsto\zeta_m
\]

extends to a field automorphism of \(L_m\) (it merely interchanges the two
independent radicals).  Consequently the Galois group of \(L_m\) is
invariant under the exchange of the symbols “\(2\)” and “\(3\)”.

Because the densities of the sets defined by conditions on
\((d_2(p),d_3(p))\) are expressed through the same Galois group,
the density of the event \(\{d_2(p)<d_3(p)\}\) equals the density of the
event \(\{d_3(p)<d_2(p)\}\).  The only remaining possibility is the
event \(\{d_2(p)=d_3(p)\}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The tie set has density 0

The equality \(d_2(p)=d_3(p)\) means that \(2\) and \(3\) generate the same
subgroup of \((\mathbf{Z}/p\mathbf{Z})^{\times}\).  Equivalently,
\(2\equiv 3^{k}\pmod p\) for some integer \(k\) coprime to the common
order.  Hence \(p\mid 3^{k}-2\) for some \(k\ge 1\).  
All such primes divide the integer  

\[
\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}(3^{k}-2),
\]

which has only finitely many prime divisors.  Therefore the set of primes
with \(d_2(p)=d_3(p)\) is finite, and its natural density is \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  The limiting density

Putting the pieces together,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{dens}\{p: d_2(p)<d_3(p)\}
 &=\operatorname{dens}\{p: d_3(p)<d_2(p)\} \\
 &=\frac{1-\operatorname{dens}\{p: d_2(p)=d_3(p)\}}{2}
   =\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Required numerical value

\[
10^{6}\,d_{\infty}=10^{6}\times\frac12 = 500\,000 .
\]

Finally,

\boxed{500000}
\]

### 1.  What does \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) measure?

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\text{ prime}}} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\;
\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\text{ prime}}} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

For a prime factor \(q\le x\) we keep the exact exponent that occurs in
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\); for a prime factor \(q>x\) we replace the
exponent by the one occurring in \(p-1\) (which is at least as large,
because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\)).  

Hence the “large’’ part (primes \(>x\)) is the same for every integer
\(a\).  Consequently, for two integers \(a,b\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(b)
\Longleftrightarrow
\prod_{\substack{q\le x}} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
   >\prod_{\substack{q\le x}} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(b))}.
\]

In words: the inequality depends only on the \(x\)-smooth part of the
orders.  When \(x\to\infty\) the smooth part becomes the whole order, so

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\bigr)
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x

            \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
            {\#\{p\le t : p\ \text{prime}\}} .
\]

So we have to find the natural density of primes for which the order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Using Artin’s primitive‑root conjecture

For a non‑square integer \(a\neq\pm1\) Artin’s conjecture (proved
conditionally) predicts that the set of primes for which \(a\) is a
primitive root has a density

\[
C_a = A\prod_{q\mid a}\!\Bigl(1-\frac1{q-1}\Bigr),
\qquad
A = 0.3739558136\ldots\ (\text{Artin constant}).
\]

Both \(2\) and \(3\) are not perfect powers, and the product in the
formula is empty; hence

\[
\operatorname{dens}\{p:\,2\text{ primitive mod }p\}=A,
\qquad
\operatorname{dens}\{p:\,3\text{ primitive mod }p\}=A .
\]

It is a standard heuristic (and again follows from the Chebotarev
density theorem) that for two distinct integers the events
“\(2\) is a primitive root’’ and “\(3\) is a primitive root’’ are
independent.  Consequently

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\text{both primitive}) &= A^{2},\\
\Pr(\text{exactly one primitive}) &= 2A(1-A),\\
\Pr(\text{neither primitive}) &= (1-A)^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Comparing the orders

*If exactly one of \(\{2,3\}\) is a primitive root*, its order equals
\(p-1\) while the other order is a proper divisor of \(p-1\); therefore
the primitive root has the larger order.  Hence in this case
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) precisely when
\(2\) is the primitive root, which occurs with probability
\(A(1-A)\).  The same probability arises when \(3\) is the primitive
root, but then the inequality is reversed.

*If neither \(2\) nor \(3\) is primitive*, both orders are proper
divisors of \(p-1\).  By symmetry the probability that the order of
\(2\) exceeds the order of \(3\) equals the probability that the order of
\(3\) exceeds the order of \(2\); any primes for which the two orders are
equal form a set of density \(0\) (the coincidence of two distinct
proper divisors of the random integer \(p-1\) is negligible).  Therefore,
conditioned on “neither primitive’’ the chance that
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is \(1/2\).

Putting the three cases together,

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\infty}
&= \Pr\bigl(2\text{ primitive},\,3\text{ not}\bigr)
   + \tfrac12\Pr\bigl(\text{neither primitive}\bigr)\\[2mm]
&= A(1-A) + \frac12(1-A)^{2}\\[2mm]
&= \frac12\bigl(1-A^{2}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

A = 0.373\,955\,813\,6\ldots\qquad
A^{2}=0.139\,842\,963\ldots

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-A^{2}}{2}
          = \frac{1-0.139842963\ldots}{2}
          = 0.430\,078\,518\ldots
\]

Finally

\[
10^{6}\,d_{\infty}= 430\,078.518\ldots
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6} d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor = 430078 .
\]

For a fixed integer \(a\) and a divisor \(m\mid p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid m \iff a^{\,m}\equiv 1\pmod p .
\]

The condition “\(a^{\,m}\equiv 1\pmod p\)” is a splitting condition in the
Kummer extension  

\[
\mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_m,\;a^{1/m}\bigr),
\]

where \(\zeta_m\) is a primitive \(m\)‑th root of unity.
Consequently, for any finite set of such conditions the set of primes
satisfying them is a Chebotarev set; its natural density exists and can be
computed from the Galois group of the compositum of the relevant
extensions.

### 2.  Symmetry between \(2\) and \(3\)

Let  

\[
E_{2,m}= \mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_m,2^{1/m}\bigr),\qquad 
E_{3,m}= \mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_m,3^{1/m}\bigr).
\]

Both extensions are Galois over \(\mathbb{Q}\) and are linearly disjoint:
the only common subfield is \(\mathbb{Q}\) (because \(2\) and \(3\) are
multiplicatively independent).  
Therefore the compositum  

\[
E_m =E_{2,m}\,E_{3,m}
\]

has Galois group  

\[
\operatorname{Gal}(E_m/\mathbb{Q})\cong
\operatorname{Gal}(E_{2,m}/\mathbb{Q})\times
\operatorname{Gal}(E_{3,m}/\mathbb{Q}).
\]

Consequently for any fixed divisor \(m\) the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\mid m ,\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\mid m
\]

are independent and have exactly the same distribution after swapping
\(2\) and \(3\).

### 1.  Symmetry between the two orders  

Write the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as a
cyclic group of order \(p-1\) and fix a primitive root \(g\).  
There are unique integers \(k_2,k_3\;(1\le k_i\le p-1)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\pmod p .
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_2)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_3)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3).
\]

If we replace the fixed primitive root by another primitive root,
\(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are multiplied by the same unit modulo \(p-1\); the
pair \((k_2,k_3)\) is therefore “uniformly random’’ among all ordered
pairs of residues coprime to \(p-1\).  By symmetry the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

have the same natural density.  Hence, letting  

\[
\Delta(p)=\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\\[2pt]
0 &\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]

we have  

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{\pi(t)}\sum_{p\le t}\Delta(p)
     =\frac{1-\rho}{2},
\]

where \(\rho\) is the density of primes for which the two orders are
*equal*.

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \langle 2\rangle =\langle 3\rangle
\iff 2\in\langle 3\rangle\text{ and }3\in\langle 2\rangle .
\]

Thus there exist integers \(m,n\) such that  

\[
2\equiv 3^{\,m}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv 2^{\,n}\pmod p .
\]

In particular \(p\mid 3^{\,m}-2\).  Hence any prime for which the two
orders coincide divides a term of the integer sequence  

\[
a_k = 3^{\,k}-2\qquad(k\ge 1).
\]

The set of prime divisors of a non‑constant linear recurrence (here
\(a_k\)) has natural density \(0\) (a standard result of analytic
number theory; see e.g. P. Erdős–M. M. Ruzsa, “On the density of
prime divisors of recurrence sequences”).  Consequently  

\[
\rho = 0 .
\]

\[

is the density of primes \(p\) for which  

\[

Indeed, for a fixed prime \(p\) and a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) every prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) eventually
belongs to the first product, while the second product becomes empty.
Hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
                                 {|\{p\le t : p\text{ prime}\}|}.

\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{L}{d_2}, \qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{L}{d_3},
\]

where \(d_2,d_3\) are the indices of the subgroups generated by \(2\) and
\(3\) in the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).
Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow d_2<d_3 .
\]

The distribution of the indices \(d_2,d_3\) depends only on the
multiplicative structure of \(L\).  The two elements \(2\) and \(3\) play
symmetric roles; interchanging them merely exchanges the events

\[

\]

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\, d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor

\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                     \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

keeps the exact prime‑power factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for the
primes \(\le x\) and replaces the larger prime factors by those of \(p-1\).
Hence, when \(x\) tends to \(\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_\infty\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of primes for which the order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

### 1.  Using Artin’s conjecture

For a fixed integer \(a\neq\pm1\) that is not a perfect square,
Artin’s conjecture predicts that the set of primes for which \(a\) is a
primitive root has density  

\[
\mathcal{A}(a)=C\prod_{q\mid a}\Bigl(1-\frac1{q-1}\Bigr),\qquad
C=\prod_{q\text{ prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac1{q(q-1)}\Bigr)=0.3739558136\ldots
\]

Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{A}(2)&=C\Bigl(1-\frac1{2-1}\Bigr)=\frac{C}{2},\\[2mm]
\mathcal{A}(3)&=C\Bigl(1-\frac1{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{2C}{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Assuming the events “\(2\) is a primitive root’’ and “\(3\) is a primitive
root’’ are independent (the independence is part of the standard
formulation of Artin’s conjecture), the density that **both** numbers are
primitive roots equals  

\[
\mathcal{A}(2\text{ and }3)=\mathcal{A}(2)\,\mathcal{A}(3)
     =\frac{C}{2}\cdot\frac{2C}{3}= \frac{C}{3}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  From primitive–root density to the required density

If the orders of \(2\) and \(3\) are different, symmetry shows that each
of the two possibilities (\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
or the reverse) occurs with the same frequency.  
Therefore

\[
d_\infty=\frac12\bigl(1-\text{Prob}\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)\bigr).
\]

The equality of the two orders can happen only when both orders are
\(p-1\) (both numbers are primitive roots) or when they are a proper
common divisor of \(p-1\).  The latter situation has density \(0\) (it
requires extra algebraic relations between \(2\) and \(3\) that occur
only on a set of primes of zero density).  Hence the only contribution
to the tie‑probability is the primitive‑root case, whose density is
\(C/3\).

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12\Bigl(1-\frac{C}{3}\Bigr)=\frac12-\frac{C}{6}.
\]

Finally  

\[
10^{6}d_\infty = 437\,674.0310\ldots,
\qquad\boxed{437674}.
\]

Thus \(\displaystyle\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\right\rfloor = 437674\).

### 1.  Reformulating the comparison  

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)} .
\]

\(i_a(p)\) is the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in the cyclic
group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\).  
Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff
\(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\),

\[
d_\infty =\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\bigr).
\]

### 2.  Probabilistic model (Artin’s heuristic)

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell}\) (\(\ell\) runs over all primes).
For a fixed integer \(a\) (with \(a\neq\pm1\) and not a perfect power)
the exponent of \(\ell\) in the index \(i_a(p)\) is a random variable
\(E_{\ell}(a)\) with

\[
\Pr\bigl(E_{\ell}(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

(standard Artin‑type heuristic: the chance that \(a\) is an
\(\ell^{k}\)-th power but not an \(\ell^{k+1}\)-th power is
\(\ell^{-k-1}(\ell-1)\)).  

For different primes \(\ell\) the variables are independent, and for a
given \(\ell\) the variables \(E_{\ell}(2)\) and \(E_{\ell}(3)\) are
independent and identically distributed.

Thus  

\[
i_2(p)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{E_{\ell}(2)},\qquad 
i_3(p)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{E_{\ell}(3)} .
\]

Define the ratio  

\[
R=\frac{i_2(p)}{i_3(p)}=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{E_{\ell}(2)-E_{\ell}(3)} .
\]

Because the joint distribution of \((E_{\ell}(2),E_{\ell}(3))\) is
symmetric under interchange, the distribution of \(\log R\) is
symmetric about \(0\). Consequently  

\[
\Pr(R<1)=\Pr(R>1)=\frac{1-\Pr(R=1)}{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\Pr(i_2(p)=i_3(p))}{2}.
\]

---

### 3.  Probability that the indices are equal  

The equality \(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\) occurs exactly when
\(E_{\ell}(2)=E_{\ell}(3)\) for **every** prime \(\ell\).  
Since the \(\ell\)-components are independent,

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)=\prod_{\ell}
      \Pr\bigl(E_{\ell}(2)=E_{\ell}(3)\bigr)
      =\prod_{\ell}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^2 .
\]

For a fixed \(\ell\),

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^2
   =\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\ell^{2k}}
   =\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-1/\ell^{2}}
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)=\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

The infinite product \(\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\) converges to
\(0\) because  

\[
\log\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Bigr)=-\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac1{\ell^2}\right)
\]

and \(\sum_{\ell}1/\ell\) diverges. Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)=0.
\]

d_\infty=\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

For a fixed prime \(p\) the integer \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) has only finitely many prime
divisors.  
If \(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) and also the
largest prime divisor of \(p-1\), then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence, for every prime \(p\),

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}S_x=\{p\text{ prime}: \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\]
and  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
      =\lim_{t\to\infty}
        \frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
             {\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between \(2\) and \(3\)

For every prime \(p\) the two numbers \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are divisors of the same integer \(p-1\).  
If we exchange the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) we obtain the same set of primes,
hence the densities of the events  

\[
A=\{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad
B=\{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}
\]

are equal.  Let  

\[
E=\{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Because \(A,B,E\) form a partition of the set of all primes,

\[
d_\infty =\frac12\bigl(1-\delta(E)\bigr),               \tag{1}
\]

where \(\delta(E)\) denotes the (natural) density of the primes belonging to
\(E\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The density of the equality set \(E\) is zero  

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{\,\nu_\ell(p-1)}\) (\(\ell\) runs over the prime
divisors of \(p-1\)).  For a fixed prime \(\ell\) let  

\[
\alpha_\ell(p)=\nu_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr),\qquad
\beta_\ell(p)=\nu_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Both \(\alpha_\ell(p)\) and \(\beta_\ell(p)\) are random variables that satisfy

\[
\alpha_\ell(p)=\nu_\ell(p-1)-\gamma_\ell^{(2)}(p),\qquad
\beta_\ell(p)=\nu_\ell(p-1)-\gamma_\ell^{(3)}(p),
\]

where \(\gamma_\ell^{(a)}(p)\) is the largest integer \(k\ge 0\) such that
\(a\) is an \(\ell^{\,k}\)-th power modulo \(p\).
For a random prime \(p\) (with \(\ell\mid p-1\)) the event
“\(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power modulo \(p\)” occurs with probability \(1/\ell\);
more generally  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gamma_\ell^{(a)}\ge k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{\,k}}\qquad(k\ge1).
\]

Thus \(\gamma_\ell^{(2)}\) and \(\gamma_\ell^{(3)}\) are independent and have the
same geometric distribution.  Consequently, for a fixed \(\ell\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(\alpha_\ell=\beta_\ell\bigr)=\sum_{k\ge0}
        \Pr\bigl(\gamma_\ell^{(2)}=k\bigr)\Pr\bigl(\gamma_\ell^{(3)}=k\bigr)
        =\frac{\ell^{2}}{(\ell^{2}-1)}\;<1 .
\]

Hence for each prime \(\ell\) the set  

\[
E_\ell=\{p:\alpha_\ell(p)=\beta_\ell(p)\}
\]

has natural density  

\[
\delta(E_\ell)=\frac{\ell^{2}}{\ell^{2}-1}=1-\frac{1}{\ell^{2}-1}<1 .
\]

Now  

\[
E=\bigcap_{\ell\ \text{prime}}E_\ell .
\]

If a prime \(p\) belongs to \(E\) it must belong to all the sets \(E_\ell\).
Therefore the density of \(E\) is bounded by the infinite product

\[
\delta(E)\le \prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\ell^{2}-1}\Bigr).
\]

Since  

\[
\sum_{\ell}\frac{1}{\ell^{2}-1}= \infty,
\]

the infinite product converges to \(0\); consequently \(\delta(E)=0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Determining \(d_\infty\)

Because the density of the equality set is zero, equation (1) gives  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12\bigl(1-0\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required integer

\[
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\Bigr\rfloor
   =\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\Bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

modulo \(p\).  
For a “random’’ prime \(p\) the probability that a given integer is a
\(q^{\,s}\)-th power is \(1/q^{\,s}\).  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(s=t\bigr)=\frac{q-1}{q^{\,t+1}},\qquad t=0,1,2,\dots .

The random variables \(\{s_q(2)\}_q\) and \(\{s_q(3)\}_q\) are independent,

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad   
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\prod_{\substack{q>x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

For a fixed prime \(p\) the integer \(p-1\) has only finitely many
prime divisors.  
If \(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of \(p-1\) then every
prime \(q\le x\) already divides \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) with the
same exponent as it does in \(p-1\); consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\qquad (x\ge X(p)).
\]

Hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\]

and the set  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

has density  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_\infty\}}
{\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A symmetry argument

For a prime \(p\neq 2,3\) the numbers \(2\) and \(3\) are both
non‑squares modulo \(p\); the Galois groups governing the
splitting of the Kummer extensions  

\[
\mathbf{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{n},2^{1/n}\bigr),\qquad   
\mathbf{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{n},3^{1/n}\bigr)
\]

are isomorphic.  Consequently the joint distribution of the pair  

\[
\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
\]

is invariant under swapping the two components.  Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The probability of equality is zero

Write \(i_a(p)=\dfrac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\) (the index of the
subgroup generated by \(a\) in \((\mathbf{Z}/p\mathbf{Z})^{\!*}\)).
For a fixed prime \(\ell\) let  

\[
V_\ell(p)=v_\ell\bigl(i_2(p)\bigr),\qquad   
W_\ell(p)=v_\ell\bigl(i_3(p)\bigr).
\]

For a given \(\ell\) the Chebotarev density theorem gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(V_\ell\ge k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{\,k}},\qquad k\ge1,
\]

and the same for \(W_\ell\); the two random variables are
independent.  Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(V_\ell=k\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\;(k\ge1),\qquad
\Pr\bigl(V_\ell=0\bigr)=1-\frac1\ell .
\]

The probability that the two exponents coincide for this \(\ell\) is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(V_\ell=W_\ell)
&=\bigl(1-\tfrac1\ell\bigr)^2
   +\sum_{k\ge1}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^2   \\
&=\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}+\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{2}(\ell+1)}
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Assuming independence for different \(\ell\) (which is justified by
the Chebotarev theorem for the compositum of the involved
extensions), the probability that **all** exponents coincide is  

\[
\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Because  

\[
\sum_{\ell}\frac{2}{\ell}= \infty ,
\]

the infinite product converges to \(0\).  Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

### 4.  Computing \(d_\infty\)

From (1) and (2) the three possibilities  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

partition the set of primes, and the middle case has density \(0\).
Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

= 500\,000 .

For a prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
Choose a generator \(g\) and write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p ,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p ,
\qquad a,b\in \{0,\dots ,p-2\}.
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

If we replace the “large’’ prime factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by those of \(p-1\) (the definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\)), then for any fixed prime \(p\) and for all sufficiently large \(x\) we have  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
          =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                   {\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

### 1.  Equality of the two orders has density 0  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff 2\equiv 3^{k}\pmod p\text{ for some }k\ge 1 .
\]

Thus a prime with equal orders must divide a number of the form \(3^{k}-2\) (\(k\ge1\)).
The set  

\[
\mathcal P:=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\{\,p\text{ prime}:p\mid 3^{k}-2\,\}
\]

has natural density \(0\).  
Indeed, for each fixed \(k\) the integer \(3^{k}-2\) has at most \(\log(3^{k})\) prime
divisors, and \(\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{\log(3^{k})}{3^{k}}<\infty\); a standard
application of the Borel–Cantelli lemma (or, equivalently, a theorem of
Erdős–Pomerance) shows that the proportion of primes belonging to \(\mathcal P\)
tends to zero. Hence  

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                         {\pi(t)}=0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the two inequalities  

For any prime \(p\) (except the negligible set above) exactly one of the
strict inequalities holds:

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\quad\text{or}\quad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2).
\]

Because the roles of the numbers \(2\) and \(3\) are completely symmetric,
the two events have the same natural density.  Let this common density be
\(\alpha\).  Then

\[
2\alpha = 1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \alpha=\frac12 .
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\]

**1.  What the limit \(d_{\infty}\) means**

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1\mid a^{\,k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\) we may write

\[
p-1 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\cdot i_a(p),\qquad i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)} .
\]

The integer \(i_a(p)\) is the *index* of \(a\) modulo \(p\); it is a divisor of \(p-1\).

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
               \prod_{q>x}  q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exponent of \(q\) in
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the (larger) exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\).
Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\frac{p-1}{i_a(p)}\times
        \prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\mid i_a(p)}} q^{\,v_q(i_a(p))}.
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the product over the large primes disappears, so  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
S_x\;\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\;S_{\infty}
   =\{p\text{ prime}\mid \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
          =\frac{\#\{p\le t\mid \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                 {\#\{p\le t\}}\qquad(t\to\infty).
\]

In other words, \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of the primes for which the
order of \(2\) is larger than the order of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**2.  From orders to indices**

Write \(i_2(p)=\dfrac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)}\) and
\(i_3(p)=\dfrac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)}\).
Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=(p-1)/i_a(p)\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff i_2(p)< i_3(p).
\]

So we have to find the density of the primes for which the index of \(2\) is
*smaller* than the index of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**3.  Modelling the indices**

Fix a prime \(p\) and choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\).  
Then there are unique integers \(k_2,k_3\;(0\le k_a<p-1)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\pmod p .
\]

Because \(g\) generates the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\),

\[
i_a(p)=\gcd(p-1,k_a)\qquad(a=2,3).
\]

For a “random’’ prime \(p\) the exponent \(k_a\) behaves like a uniformly
chosen residue modulo \(p-1\); the two residues \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are
independent.  Hence, for a given integer \(N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\qquad(d\mid N),
\]

where \(k\) is uniform modulo \(N\).

Now let \(N=p-1\) vary over all integers.  Averaging the above probability
over the natural density of the integers gives a *limit distribution* for the
random variable \(\gcd(N,k)\).  A standard computation (see, e.g.,
probability that a random divisor of a random integer equals \(d\)) shows that

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k)=d\bigr)=\frac{6}{\pi^{2}}\;\frac{1}{d^{2}}\qquad
(d=1,2,3,\dots) }                                    \tag{1}
\]

Indeed,
\[
\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{6}{\pi^{2}}\frac{1}{d^{2}}=
\frac{6}{\pi^{2}}\zeta(2)=1 .
\]

Thus the *indices* \(i_2(p),\,i_3(p)\) are (asymptotically) independent
random variables whose common distribution is given by (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**4.  Probability that the index of 2 is smaller**

Let \(p_d=\dfrac{6}{\pi^{2}d^{2}}\) be the probability that an index equals \(d\).
Because the two indices are independent, the probability that they are equal is  

\[
\Pr(i_2=i_3)=\sum_{d\ge1}p_d^{\,2}
           =\Bigl(\frac{6}{\pi^{2}}\Bigr)^{\!2}
             \sum_{d\ge1}\frac{1}{d^{4}}
           =\frac{36}{\pi^{4}}\;\zeta(4).
\]

Since \(\zeta(4)=\dfrac{\pi^{4}}{90}\),

\[
\Pr(i_2=i_3)=\frac{36}{\pi^{4}}\cdot\frac{\pi^{4}}{90}
           =\frac{36}{90}
           =\boxed{\frac{2}{5}}=0.4 .
\]

By symmetry the events \(i_2<i_3\) and \(i_2>i_3\) have the same probability,
so

\[
\Pr(i_2<i_3)=\frac{1-\Pr(i_2=i_3)}{2}
           =\frac{1-0.4}{2}
           =\boxed{0.3}.
\]

Recall that \(i_2<i_3\) is exactly the condition
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\); hence

\[
d_{\infty}=0.3 .
\]

The limit  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
{|\{p\le t\}|}
\]

is the natural density of primes for which the multiplicative order of 2 exceeds that of 3.
Writing \(p-1=N\) and letting \(k_2,k_3\) be the discrete logarithms of \(2,3\) with respect to a primitive root,
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,k_a)} .
\]

Hence \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff \(\gcd(N,k_2)<\gcd(N,k_3)\).
Treating \(k_2,k_3\) as independent uniform residues modulo \(N\) (the usual Artin‑type heuristic) gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
= \frac12\Bigl(1-\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k_2)=\gcd(N,k_3)\bigr)\Bigr).
\]

For a fixed integer \(N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\qquad(d\mid N),
\]

so

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k_2)=\gcd(N,k_3)\bigr)=\frac1{N^{2}}
\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi\!\bigl(N/d\bigr)^{2}
       =\frac1{N^{2}}\sum_{m\mid N}\varphi(m)^{2}.
\]

Averaging this quantity over the integers \(N=p-1\) (with \(p\) prime) yields the
Euler product

\[
A:=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}
\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q+1}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\frac{q^{3}+2q^{2}-1}{q^{3}-1}\Bigr)
   =0.5119\ldots .
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12\bigl(1-A\bigr)=0.2440\ldots .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor10^{6}d_\infty\bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times 0.2440\ldots\bigr\rfloor
= \boxed{244000}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{k\ge 1:\; a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},\qquad a\in\{2,3\}.
\]

Because \(p\) is odd, \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is a cyclic group of order \(p-1\).
If \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\), then for some integers  

\[
k_{2}(p),\;k_{3}(p)\in\{1,\dots ,p-1\},\qquad (k_{2}(p),p-1)=(k_{3}(p),p-1)=1,
\]

we have  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_{2}(p)}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_{3}(p)}\pmod p .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(k_{2}(p),p-1)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(k_{3}(p),p-1)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(k_{2}(p),p-1)<\gcd(k_{3}(p),p-1).
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.   Distribution of the exponents  

For a fixed integer \(a\) and a prime \(\ell\neq p\), the condition
\(\ell\mid\gcd(k_{a}(p),p-1)\) is equivalent to “\(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power
modulo \(p\)”.  
By the Chebotarev density theorem, for each prime \(\ell\) the set of
primes \(p\) for which \(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power has natural density
\(1/\ell\). Consequently, for each prime \(\ell\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(\ell\mid \gcd(k_{a}(p),p-1)\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell},
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\ell\nmid \gcd(k_{a}(p),p-1)\bigr)=1-\frac1\ell .
\]

For different primes \(\ell\) these events are independent (the corresponding
Kummer extensions are linearly disjoint). Hence the random vector  

\[
\bigl(\gcd(k_{2}(p),p-1),\;\gcd(k_{3}(p),p-1)\bigr)
\]

has a product‑type distribution in which the two components are
**independent and identically distributed**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.   Symmetry

Because the two components are i.i.d., the events  

\[
\gcd(k_{2}(p),p-1)<\gcd(k_{3}(p),p-1),\qquad
\gcd(k_{2}(p),p-1)>\gcd(k_{3}(p),p-1)
\]

have the same natural density.  
The event that the two gcd’s are equal has density zero (it would require
both numbers to lie in the same proper subgroup of a cyclic group of order
\(p-1\), which occurs only for a set of primes of zero Dirichlet density).

Therefore, by (1),

\[
\text{dens}\bigl\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr\}
=\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.   Passing to \(d_{\infty}\)

When \(x\to\infty\) the modified order \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) tends
to the ordinary order \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\). Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_{x}
   = \text{dens}\bigl\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr\}
   =\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.   Required value

\[

   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12\bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the factor \(\prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)}\) is the same in
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\).

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

is equivalent to

\[
\prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
    >\prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))},
\tag{2}
\]

i.e. the **\(x\)-smooth part** of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) exceeds the
\(x\)-smooth part of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

### 2.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

When \(x\) is larger than any prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\), the products in (2) become the full orders.

\[

\]

\tag{3}
\]

\[

coincides with the ordinary multiplicative order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) when

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
