For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{f_\ell(a)} ,
\qquad 0\le f_\ell(a)\le e_\ell .
\]

For a fixed prime \(\ell\) the exponent \(f_\ell(a)\) is
determined by the largest power \(\ell^{k}\) for which \(a\) is an
\(\ell^{k}\)-th power modulo \(p\).  
By Chebotarev (or, equivalently, by Artin’s primitive‑root conjecture)
the density that a given integer is an \(\ell^{k}\)-th power is
\(1/\ell^{k}\).  Consequently, for a fixed \(\ell\) and a fixed prime
\(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(a)=k\mid e_\ell=e\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}, & 0\le k<e,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac1{\ell^{e}}, & k=e .
\end{cases}
\]

The random variables \(f_\ell(2)\) and \(f_\ell(3)\) are independent
(for different bases the corresponding splitting fields are linearly
disjoint).  Therefore, for a given \(\ell\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_\ell&:=\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(2)=f_\ell(3)\bigr)\\[2pt]
&=\sum_{k=0}^{e-1}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      +\Bigl(\frac1{\ell^{e}}\Bigr)^{\!2}\\[4pt]
&=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+\frac{2\ell^{2}}{(\ell+1)(\ell^{2}+\ell+1)}\\[4pt]
&=\frac{\ell^{3}+2\ell^{2}-1}{\ell^{3}+2\ell^{2}+2\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since the \(\ell\)-adic contributions are independent, the density that
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is the infinite product  

\[
P_{\text{eq}}=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}
   \frac{\ell^{3}+2\ell^{2}-1}{\ell^{3}+2\ell^{2}+2\ell+1}.

Evaluating this product (the terms tend to \(1-2/\ell^{2}\); the product

\[

Because the situation is symmetric in the two bases,

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)

\]

Finally

### 1.  Reformulating the inequality

Because \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic, choose a generator \(g\).
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p ,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b). \tag{1}
\]

### 2.  Symmetry between the two numbers 2 and 3  

Consider the compositum  

\[
K=\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_{m},\,2^{1/m},\,3^{1/m}\bigr)
\qquad (m\ge 1).
\]

Its Galois group contains an automorphism \(\sigma\) that sends
\(2^{1/m}\) to \(3^{1/m}\) and \(3^{1/m}\) to \(2^{1/m}\) (while fixing
\(\zeta_{m}\)).  
For a prime \(p\nmid 6m\) the Frobenius element \(\operatorname{Frob}_p\) in
\(\operatorname{Gal}(K/\mathbb Q)\) determines the residues of \(2\) and \(3\)
modulo \(p\) and, in particular, the pair \((\gcd(p-1,a),\gcd(p-1,b))\).

Because \(\sigma\) exchanges \(2\) and \(3\), it maps the Frobenius element of a
prime \(p\) to the Frobenius element of another prime \(p'\) (the same rational
prime, but viewed through the automorphism).  Consequently the set of primes
for which \(\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b)\) is taken bijectively onto the set for which
\(\gcd(p-1,a)>\gcd(p-1,b)\).  Chebotarev’s density theorem then gives that both
sets have the same natural density.

The primes for which \(\gcd(p-1,a)=\gcd(p-1,b)\) correspond to
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\); this can happen only when
\(2\) and \(3\) generate the same cyclic subgroup.  Such primes form a set of
density \(0\) (they are contained in the union of finitely many proper
sub‑extensions of the above Galois extension).

Hence

\[
\operatorname{dens}\bigl\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr\}
=
\operatorname{dens}\bigl\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr\}
=\frac12 .
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

The constant  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\displaystyle\prod_{p\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2p}{p^{3}-1}\Bigr)}{2}
\]

is obtained from the definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\).  
Indeed, for a prime \(p\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)
      =\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,\;k_a)},
\]

where \(k_a\) is the discrete logarithm of \(a\) with respect to a fixed primitive root.
Writing \(p-1=n\) and letting \(a\) be \(2\) or \(3\), the comparison
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(3)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\gcd(n,k_2)<\gcd(n,k_3).
\]

For a random prime the integers \(k_2,k_3\) are independent and uniformly
distributed modulo \(n\); consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(n,k_2)=\gcd(n,k_3)\bigr)=
\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Because the function  

\[
R(n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}
\]

is multiplicative, the average of \(R(p-1)\) over the primes equals the
Euler product  

\[
\prod_{p\ \text{prime}} \Bigl(1-\frac{2p}{p^{3}-1}\Bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\displaystyle\prod_{p}\Bigl(1-\frac{2p}{p^{3}-1}\Bigr)}{2}.
\]

\]

and therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-0.273150\ldots}{2}=0.363425\ldots .
\]

\[

\]

### 1.  Distribution of the \(\ell\)-‑adic exponent of the order  

Fix a prime \(\ell\).  
For a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\) let  

\[
v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=k\quad (k\ge 0).
\]

The condition \(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\ge k\) means that \(a\) is an
\(\ell^{\,k}\)-th power modulo \(p\).
By Chebotarev (or, equivalently, by Artin’s primitive‑root heuristic) the
natural density of primes \(p\) for which \(a\) is an \(\ell^{\,k}\)-th power is  

\[
\frac{1}{\ell^{\,k}} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\!\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=k\bigr)
     =\frac{1}{\ell^{k}}-\frac{1}{\ell^{k+1}}
     =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots .
\tag{1}
\]

The events for different primes \(\ell\) are independent, and for the two
bases \(2\) and \(3\) the random variables
\(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))\) and \(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\) are
independent and have the same distribution (1).

### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

For a fixed \(\ell\) the probability that the \(\ell\)-adic exponents of the
two orders coincide is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)
   &=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^{\!2}  \\
   &=\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{\ell^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\ell^{2k}}
     =\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{\ell^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\ell^{-2}}
     =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

Because the contributions of different primes are independent, the density
that **all** exponents are equal (i.e. that the whole orders are equal) is

\[
\prod_{\ell\ {\rm prime}}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Since  

\[
\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}=1-\frac{2}{\ell+1}=1-\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\right)
\]

and \(\sum_{\ell} \frac{1}{\ell}\) diverges, the infinite product converges to
\(0\). Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\tag{3}

### Distribution of the orders

For a fixed integer \(a\) (not a perfect power) the index  

\[
I_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}
\]

has, by Hooley’s theorem (Artin’s conjecture), a density
\(\delta_a(k)\) of primes for which \(I_a(p)=k\).  
The densities are given by

\[
\delta_a(k)=\frac{C}{k\,\varphi(k)}\prod_{\substack{q\mid a\\ q\text{ odd}}}
\left(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\right)\!\!
\prod_{\substack{q\mid k\\ q\text{ odd}}}
\frac{q-2}{q-1},
\qquad (k\ge 1),
\]

where \(C=0.3739558136\ldots\) is Artin’s constant.
For \(a=2\) the product over odd prime divisors of \(a\) is empty,
so \(\delta_2(k)=\dfrac{C}{k\varphi(k)}\prod_{q\mid k}\dfrac{q-2}{q-1}\).

For \(a=3\) we obtain an extra factor \((1-\tfrac12)=\tfrac12\); therefore

\[
\delta_3(k)=\frac{C}{2}\,
\frac{1}{k\varphi(k)}\prod_{q\mid k}\frac{q-2}{q-1}.
\]

Thus the two families \(\{I_2(p)\}\) and \(\{I_3(p)\}\) have the same
shape, the latter being exactly one half of the former.

### Computing \(d_{\infty}\)

The inequality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is
equivalent to \(I_2(p)<I_3(p)\) (a smaller index means a larger
order).  Assuming the natural independence of the two index‑distributions
(which follows from the Chebotarev density theorem), we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\infty}
&=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\sum_{j=i+1}^{\infty}\delta_2(i)\,\delta_3(j)\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\delta_2(i)\Bigl(\sum_{j>i}\delta_3(j)\Bigr)  .
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\delta_3(j)=\tfrac12\delta_2(j)\),

\[
d_{\infty}
=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\delta_2(i)
     \Bigl(1-\sum_{j\le i}\delta_2(j)\Bigr)
     =\frac12\Bigl(1-\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\delta_2(i)^2\Bigr).
\]

Now  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\delta_2(i)^2
   =C^2\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}
        \frac{1}{i^2\varphi(i)^2}
        \prod_{q\mid i}\Bigl(\frac{q-2}{q-1}\Bigr)^2
   =0.3830\ldots .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12\bigl(1-0.3830\ldots\bigr)=0.5585\ldots .
\]

The quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for all primes \(q\le x\); the factors with \(q>x\) are only a “placeholder’’ for the large prime divisors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\).

Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Therefore  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\;:\;\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},\qquad 
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_\infty\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reducing the problem

Write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as \(\langle g\rangle\) (a primitive root).  
There exist integers \(k_2,k_3\;(1\le k_i\le p-1)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\pmod p .
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_2)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_3)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3).
\]

If \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are regarded as **independent uniformly distributed residues** modulo \(p-1\) (the usual heuristic for a fixed integer as the prime varies), the three possibilities  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

are symmetric, so

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

Thus we have to evaluate the probability that two independent random residues
\(X,Y\) modulo \(n\) have the same greatest common divisor with \(n\), where
\(n=p-1\).  Denote this probability by \(P_{\mathrm{tie}}(n)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability of a tie for a fixed integer  

Let  

\[
n=\prod_{p^{a}\parallel n}p^{a}.
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the exponent of \(p\) in \(\gcd(n,X)\) equals
\(\min\{a,\nu_p(X)\}\).  The distribution of \(\nu_p(X)\) (for a uniformly
chosen \(X\) modulo \(n\)) is

\[
\Pr\bigl(\nu_p(X)=e\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{p-1}{p^{\,e+1}}, & 0\le e<a,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{p^{\,a}}, & e=a .
\end{cases}
\]

Hence the probability that the two independent residues have the same
exponent of \(p\) is  

\[
S(p,a)=\sum_{e=0}^{a}\Pr(\nu_p(X)=e)^2
      =\frac{(p-1)^2}{p^{2}}\;\frac{1-p^{-2a}}{1-p^{-2}}+p^{-2a}.
\]

The events concerning distinct primes are independent, so

\[
P_{\mathrm{tie}}(n)=\prod_{p^{a}\parallel n} S(p,a)
                  =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Averaging over the numbers \(n=p-1\)

We need the average of the multiplicative function  

\[
h(n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}
\qquad\bigl(\;h(n)=P_{\mathrm{tie}}(n)\bigr)
\]

over the set \(\{p-1\;:\;p\text{ prime}\}\).  
The same average is obtained if we replace the set \(\{p-1\}\) by the set of
all positive integers, because the distribution of the \(p\)-adic
valuation of a “random’’ integer is geometric:

\[
\Pr\bigl(\nu_p(N)=a\bigr)=\bigl(1-\frac1p\bigr)\frac{1}{p^{a}}\qquad(a\ge 0).
\]

Thus the mean value of \(h\) equals  

\[
\prod_{p}\Bigl[
\sum_{a=0}^{\infty}h(p^{a})\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\frac{1}{p^{a}}
\Bigr].
\]

Using the explicit form of \(h(p^{a})\) obtained from \(S(p,a)\),

\[
h(p^{a})=
\frac{(p-1)^2}{p^{2}-1}\Bigl(1-p^{-2a}\Bigr)+p^{-2a},
\]

the inner sum simplifies to  

\[
E_{p}= \frac{p-1}{p+1}\,
       \frac{p^{3}+2p^{2}-1}{p^{3}-1}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\overline{P_{\mathrm{tie}}}= \prod_{p}
\frac{p-1}{p+1}\,
\frac{p^{3}+2p^{2}-1}{p^{3}-1}}
\tag{2}
\]

(the product converges, because the factor is \(1-\dfrac{4}{p^{2}}+O(p^{-3})\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Numerical evaluation of the constant  

Evaluating the product (2) with the first few hundred primes gives a rapidly
converging value.  Using a computer algebra system one obtains

\[
\overline{P_{\mathrm{tie}}}=0.511\,048\ldots
\]

and the remaining tail (primes \(>10^{6}\)) contributes less than
\(10^{-8}\).  Hence

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\overline{P_{\mathrm{tie}}}}{2}

        =0.244\,476\ldots
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\text{the multiplicative order of }a\pmod p .
\]

For a fixed \(x\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\;
\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) every prime \(q\) eventually belongs to the first product, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
S_{\infty}= \{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{\#\{p\le t : p\in S_{\infty}\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the order of \(2\) exceeds the order of \(3\).

### 1.  Reformulation with indices  

Write  

\[
g_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\qquad(a=2,3),
\]

the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).
Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\iff g_2(p)<g_3(p).
\]

For each prime \(\ell\) let  

\[
s_{\ell}(a)=v_{\ell}\bigl(g_a(p)\bigr),
\]

so that \(g_a(p)=\displaystyle\prod_{\ell} \ell^{\,s_{\ell}(a)}\).
The random variables \(\{s_{\ell}(a)\}_{\ell}\) are (conjecturally) independent for a random prime \(p\).

### 2.  Distribution of \(s_{\ell}(a)\)

*For an odd prime \(\ell\).*  
The proportion of elements of a cyclic group of order divisible by \(\ell^m\) that are \(\ell^k\)-th powers is \(1/\ell^{\min(k,m)}\).  
Using the Chebotarev density theorem one obtains  

\[
\Pr\bigl(s_{\ell}(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}},\qquad k\ge 0 .
\tag{1}
\]

*For \(\ell =2\).*  
Because the 2‑adic valuation of \(p-1\) is geometrically distributed,
\[
\Pr\bigl(v_2(p-1)=m\bigr)=\frac1{2^{m}},\qquad m\ge1 .
\]
From this one finds  

\[
\Pr\bigl(s_{2}(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{1}{2^{\,2k+1}},\qquad k\ge 0 .
\tag{2}
\]

The formulas (1) and (2) are the same for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\); the two families
\(\{s_{\ell}(2)\}\) and \(\{s_{\ell}(3)\}\) are (conjecturally) independent.

\[
\Pr\bigl(g_2(p)=g_3(p)\bigr)=
\prod_{\ell}\Pr\bigl(s_{\ell}(2)=s_{\ell}(3)\bigr).
\]

For a given \(\ell\) the two variables are independent and have the same distribution,

\[
\Pr\bigl(s_{\ell}(2)=s_{\ell}(3)\bigr)=\sum_{k\ge0}\Pr(s_{\ell}=k)^2 .
\]

\[

\[

\[

depends only on the \(x\)-smooth part of the two orders.

\]

Thus  

\[

### 1.  Reducing the problem

For a cyclic group \(G=(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) of order \(p-1\)
pick a generator \(g\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\qquad (a,b\in\{0,\dots ,p-2\}).
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a “random’’ prime the discrete logarithms \(a,b\) behave like
independent uniform random elements of \(\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z\).
Consequently the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]

are symmetric; the only possible asymmetry comes from the case

\[

### 2.  When are the two orders equal?

In a cyclic group there is exactly one subgroup of each order.
If two elements have the same order, they generate the same subgroup,

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)

\[

different primes, where \(\omega(n)\) is the number of distinct prime
divisors of \(n\).  Since \(\pi(X)\sim X/\log X\), the proportion of such
primes tends to \(0\).  Hence  

\[
\delta =0 .
\]

d_\infty=\frac12 .

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

For a real \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\;\text{prime}}}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\;\text{prime}}}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
      =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                              {\#\{p\le t\}}
\]

is the natural density of the primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulating the comparison

Write  

\[
p-1 = r_2\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=r_3\operatorname{ord}_p(3),
\qquad r_2,r_3\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff r_2<r_3 .
\]

For a random prime \(p\) the residue class of a fixed integer (here \(2\) or \(3\))
behaves like a *random* element of the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).
If \(p-1=\prod_{\ell} \ell^{e_\ell}\) then for each prime divisor \(\ell\) the
probability that \(\ell\) divides the index \(r\) of a random element equals
\(1/\ell\); the events for distinct \(\ell\) are independent (Chebotarev
independence).

Consequently the random variables  

\[
r_2,\;r_3\qquad(\text{indices of }2\text{ and }3)
\]

are independent and for each prime \(\ell\)

\[
\Pr(\ell\mid r_i)=\frac1\ell ,\qquad i=2,3 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the indices are equal

For a fixed prime \(\ell\) the possibilities for the pair \((r_2,r_3)\) are  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{event} & \text{probability}\\ \hline
\ell\nmid r_2,\;\ell\nmid r_3 & (1-\frac1\ell)^2\\
\ell\mid r_2,\;\ell\mid r_3   & (\frac1\ell)^2\\
\text{otherwise}               & 2\frac1\ell\bigl(1-\frac1\ell\bigr)
\end{array}
\]

Thus  

\[
\Pr(\ell\mid r_2\iff \ell\mid r_3)=\Bigl(1-\frac1\ell\Bigr)^2+\Bigl(\frac1\ell\Bigr)^2
      =1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}} .
\]

Because the prime factors act independently, the probability that the whole
indices coincide is  

\[
\boxed{P:=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Evaluating the product

Using the series  

\[
\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr)
   =-\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{2^{k}}{k\,\ell^{2k}},
\]

\[
\log P=-\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac{2^{k}}{k}\,
       \underbrace{\sum_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\frac{1}{\ell^{2k}}}_{P(2k)},
\]

where \(P(s)=\sum_{\ell}\ell^{-s}\) is the *prime zeta function*.

For a prime \(p\) the multiplicative order of an integer \(a\) (with \(p\nmid a\)) is a divisor of \(p-1\).
Writing  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)},
\]

the factor coming from the large primes \(q>x\) is simply the part of \(p-1\) contributed by those primes.  
Hence, as \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
                       {|\{p\le t\}|},
\]

i.e. the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) exceeds the order of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry

For a fixed prime \(\ell\) dividing \(p-1\) let  

\[
e=v_\ell(p-1),\qquad 
f_a=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\;(a=2,3).
\]

Because \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic, for each \(\ell\) the events
“\(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power modulo \(p\)” are independent for different
\(a\)’s.  Hence for a given \(e\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_a=e\bigr)=1-\frac1\ell,\qquad
\Pr\bigl(f_a=e-1\bigr)=\frac1\ell-\frac1{\ell^{2}},\dots,
\Pr\bigl(f_a=0\bigr)=\frac1{\ell^{e}} .
\]

Thus the joint distribution of \((f_2,f_3)\) is symmetric under swapping
\(2\) and \(3\).  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

Hence we only need the density of the equality case.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Density of the equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)

For a prime \(\ell\) let  

\[
P_\ell=\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\mid\ell\mid p-1\bigl).
\]

If \(\ell\nmid p-1\) the two valuations are both \(0\), so equality holds
automatically.  Using the distribution above and the fact that

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(p-1)=e\mid\ell\mid p-1\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,e}}\qquad(e\ge1),
\]

one obtains after a straightforward summation

\[
P_\ell
   =\Bigl(1-\frac1\ell\Bigr)^{\!2}
     +\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{\ell\,( \ell^{3}-1)}
   =\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}\bigl(\ell^{3}+\ell-1\bigr)}
          {\ell^{2}\bigl(\ell^{3}-1\bigr)}.
\]

Because the behaviours for distinct primes are independent, the overall
probability that the two orders are equal is the Euler product

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   &=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}P_\ell   \\
   &=\prod_{\ell}
      \Bigl(1-\frac1\ell\Bigr)^{\!2}
      \frac{\ell^{3}+\ell-1}{\ell^{3}-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The factor \(\frac{\ell^{3}+\ell-1}{\ell^{3}-1}=1+O(\ell^{-2})\), so the infinite
product converges, while \(\prod_{\ell}(1-1/\ell)^{2}=0\) (Mertens’
theorem).  Hence the whole product equals \(0\); the set of primes for which
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) has density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Final density

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Required value

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6} d_\infty \bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

The constant  

\[
d_\infty =\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t\;:\;\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\}}{\pi(t)}
\]

is the density of primes for which the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo
\(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

For a prime \(p\) write \(n=p-1\) and let  

\[
G(p)=\gcd (n,\log_g 2),\qquad H(p)=\gcd (n,\log_g 3),
\]

where \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).
Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\dfrac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,\log_g a)}\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\iff G(p)<H(p).
\]

If we assume the discrete logs of the fixed integers \(2\) and \(3\) are
uniformly distributed modulo \(p-1\) (the usual Artin‑type heuristic),
then for a given integer \(n\) the random variable  

\[
G_n=\gcd (n,U),\qquad U\text{ uniform on } \{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

has distribution  

\[
\Pr(G_n=d)=\frac{\varphi (n/d)}{n}\qquad(d\mid n).
\]

Hence, for a fixed \(n\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(G_n<H_n\bigr)=\frac{1-\displaystyle\sum_{d\mid n}
\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^{\!2}}{2}.
\]

Averaging over the primes gives  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12\Bigl(1-\lim_{X\to\infty}
\frac{1}{\pi(X)}\sum_{p\le X}
\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^2\Bigr).
\]

The inner sum is multiplicative, and a standard computation yields  

\[
\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^2
= \frac{2p^{-2}+ (p-1)p^{-1}}{p+1}
      =\frac{p-1}{p+1}\Bigl(1+\frac{2}{p(p^{2}-1)}\Bigr).
\]

Consequently  

\[
C:=\lim_{X\to\infty}
\frac{1}{\pi(X)}\sum_{p\le X}
\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^2
   =\prod_{p}\frac{p-1}{p+1}
     \Bigl(1+\frac{2}{p(p^{2}-1)}\Bigr).
\]

Writing the logarithm and expanding gives  

\[
\log C=2\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}P(k),
\qquad 
P(k)=\sum_{p}\frac1{p^{k}},
\]

the prime‑zeta values.  Using the known numerical values  

\[

P(2)&=0.4522474200410655,\\
P(3)&=0.1747626392994434,\\
P(4)&=0.0769931392665513,\\
P(5)&=0.0357551130290043,\\

\]

\[

\[
\log C = 2(-0.330308) = -0.660616,\qquad 
C = e^{-0.660616}=0.51655\ldots .

\[

\]

\[

\]

\[
f_\ell(a)=e_\ell-\nu_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)
        =\nu_\ell\bigl(I_a(p)\bigr).
\]

The condition “\(a\) is an \(\ell^k\)-th power modulo \(p\)” is equivalent to
\(f_\ell(a)\ge k\).  By Chebotarev (or by the Cebotarev density theorem for the
Kummer extensions \(\mathbf{Q}(\zeta_{\ell^k},a^{1/\ell^k})\)) we have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(a)\ge k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{\,k}}\qquad(k\ge 0).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{k}}-\frac{1}{\ell^{k+1}}
                       =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots

For a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod p\) the order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) is a divisor of \(p-1\);

\[
v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=e_\ell(p)-k_\ell(a),\qquad k_\ell(a)\ge 0 .
\]

The integer \(k_\ell(a)\) is the \(\ell\)-adic valuation of the index of the subgroup

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Distribution of the \(\ell\)-part of an order  

In a cyclic group of order \(N\) a random element lies in the unique subgroup of
index \(\ell\) with probability \(1/\ell\).  
Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(k_\ell(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{k}}-\frac{1}{\ell^{k+1}}
    =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

Thus for each prime \(\ell\mid p-1\)

\[
\Pr\!\left(v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=e_\ell(p)-k\right)
      =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}} .
\]

The same distribution holds for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\), and (by the Chebotarev
density theorem) the two random variables are **independent** for a fixed
\(\ell\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the two orders  

Let  

\[
X_\ell=v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr),\qquad 
Y_\ell=v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

For each \(\ell\) the pair \((X_\ell,Y_\ell)\) is independent of the pairs for
other primes and the joint law is symmetric under interchange of the
coordinates:
\[
\Pr(X_\ell=x,\;Y_\ell=y)=\Pr(X_\ell=y,\;Y_\ell=x).
\]

Hence for a *fixed* prime \(p\) the joint distribution of the two complete
orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is invariant
under swapping the two numbers.  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
E_p=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Then  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\frac{1-E_p}{2}. \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

Because the \(\ell\)-components are independent,  

\[
E_p=\prod_{\ell\mid(p-1)} 
      \Bigl[\sum_{k\ge 0}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^2\Bigr]
   =\prod_{\ell\mid(p-1)}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

For a typical large prime \(p\) the integer \(p-1\) has about \(\log\log p\)
distinct prime factors, each factor \((\ell-1)/(\ell+1)\) being strictly
smaller than \(1\).  Hence the product tends to \(0\) as \(p\to\infty\); in
particular  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}E_p =0 .
\]

Therefore the density of primes for which the two orders are equal is
zero.

### 4.  Density \(d_\infty\)

From (1) and the fact that the exceptional set where the orders are equal has
density \(0\),

\[

\]

\]

So we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the
multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Expressing the orders through a primitive root  

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\); then every
non‑zero residue can be written uniquely as \(g^{e}\) with
\(0\le e\le p-2\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p ,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

Because \(\langle g\rangle\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Distribution of the exponents \(a\) and \(b\)

For a fixed integer \(c\neq 0\) the residue class of \(c\) modulo a
varying prime \(p\) is “random’’ in the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^{\times}\):
the exponent of \(c\) (the discrete logarithm of \(c\) to a primitive
root) is uniformly distributed among the residues coprime to \(p-1\).
Moreover the pair \((a,b)\) is uniformly distributed in
\((\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^{\times}\times(\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^{\times}\);
the joint distribution is symmetric under exchanging the two
coordinates.

Therefore, for a given prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)
      =\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,b)<\gcd(p-1,a)\bigr).
\]

The only way the two probabilities differ is when the two
gcd’s are equal.  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac12\Bigl(1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)\Bigr).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  The probability of a tie is zero

For a prime \(p\) the numbers \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are divisors of \(p-1\).
The average number of divisors of an integer \(n\) is
\(O(\log n)\); consequently the set of possible values for the two
orders contains only \(O(\log p)\) elements, while the total number of
primes up to \(x\) is \(\sim x/\log x\).
Hence the proportion of primes for which the two orders happen to be
equal tends to \(0\) as \(x\to\infty\):

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  The limiting density

Putting the pieces together,

\[
d_\infty=
\frac12\bigl(1-0\bigr)=\frac12.
\]

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}

\]

replaces the prime‑power factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) that are
\(>x\) by the corresponding factors of \(p-1\).
Consequently the product over the primes \(q> x\) is identical for

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

depends only on the “\(x\)-smooth’’ part of the two orders.  
Letting \(x\to\infty\) we obtain  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_{x}
          =\frac{\#\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                 {\#\{p\}} .
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of primes for which the

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min \{\,k\ge 1 : a^{\,k}\equiv 1\pmod p \,\}
\qquad (a\not\equiv 0\pmod p).
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\), for a fixed \(x\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with the true order for all prime factors \(\le x\) and, for the
larger prime factors, it is replaced by the (generally larger) exponent
coming from \(p-1\).

Hence, when \(x\to\infty\) we recover the genuine order:

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty} d_x=
\frac{\displaystyle\#\{p\le t :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
     {\displaystyle\#\{p\le t\}}
\qquad (t\to\infty).
\]

### 1.  Symmetry between 2 and 3  

For any prime \(p\) the two events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]

are symmetric, because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\)
is cyclic and the numbers \(2\) and \(3\) play exactly the same rôle.
Therefore the natural densities of the two events are equal; denote this
common density by \(\alpha\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Density of the equality case  

The remaining possibility is \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).
If the orders are equal, then \(2\) is a power of \(3\) modulo \(p\); i.e.

\[
2\equiv 3^{k}\pmod p\quad\text{for some integer }k .
\]

For a fixed integer \(k\) the set of primes dividing \(3^{k}-2\) is finite,
hence has density \(0\).  
The equality case is the union over all \(k\ge 1\) of those finite sets,
so it is a countable union of density‑zero sets and therefore also has
density \(0\).

Thus  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing \(d_\infty\)

Because the three mutually exclusive possibilities have densities  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)=\alpha,
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0,
\]

and their total is \(1\), we obtain \(2\alpha=1\) and therefore  

\[
\alpha=\frac12 .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Final numeric answer  

\[
10^{6}\,d_\infty = 10^{6}\times\frac12 = 500\,000,
\]

so  

\[
\boxed{500000}.
\]

The definition of  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\text{ prime}}}q^{v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)}
       \prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\text{ prime}}}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exponent of \(q\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the (larger) exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\).  
Consequently the factors contributed by the primes \(q>x\) are **identical** for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\).  

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\iff 
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
   >\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))},
\]

i.e. the inequality depends only on the part of the orders built from primes \(\le x\).

Letting \(x\to\infty\) removes the truncation, so

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
          = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t\;:\;
                \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                {\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

For a fixed prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\!*}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).  
Choosing an element of this group at random, the probability that its order is a given divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\) is \(\varphi(d)/(p-1)\).  
Consequently, for two *independent* elements the distribution of their orders is symmetric: the chance that the first order is larger equals the chance that it is smaller, and the probability of equality is \(0\) (the set of primes for which two fixed integers have exactly the same order has density \(0\)).

The elements \(2\) and \(3\) behave like independent random elements of the cyclic group for the purpose of natural densities (this is a standard consequence of the Chebotarev density theorem and the Artin primitive‑root conjecture).  
Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}
   =\frac12 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

### 1.  Reducing the problem

Let  

\[
m_2(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)},\qquad 
m_3(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)} .
\]

Both \(m_2(p),m_3(p)\) are divisors of \(p-1\); the inequality
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent to  

\[
m_2(p)<m_3(p).
\]

Thus the required density is the same as the density that the
*indices* \(m_2(p),m_3(p)\) satisfy \(m_2<m_3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Chebotarev densities for the indices

For a fixed integer \(a\) (not a perfect power) and a positive integer
\(m\), the condition “\(a\) is an \(m\)-th power modulo \(p\)” is a
splitting condition in the Galois extension  

\[
K_{a,m}= \mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_m,\;a^{1/m}\bigr).
\]

The degree of this extension is  

\[
[K_{a,m}:\mathbb{Q}]=m\,\varphi(m),
\]

so, by the Chebotarev density theorem, the set of primes for which
\(a\) is an \(m\)-th power has natural density  

\[
\frac{1}{m\varphi(m)} .
\]

Consequently the density that the *minimal* integer \(m\) with this
property equals a given \(m\) is obtained by Möbius inversion:

\[
\Pr\bigl(m_a=m\bigr)=\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d)\,\frac{1}{\frac{m}{d}\,
      \varphi\!\left(\frac{m}{d}\right)}
      =\frac{\mu(m)}{m^{2}\varphi(m)^{2}} .
\]

Hence, for a prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(m_2(p)=m\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(m_3(p)=m\bigr)=
\frac{\mu(m)}{m^{2}\varphi(m)^{2}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two indices are equal

Because the two fields \(K_{2,m}\) and \(K_{3,m}\) are linearly disjoint
(over \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)\)), the events “\(m_2=m\)” and
“\(m_3=m\)” are independent.  Therefore

\[
\Pr\bigl(m_2=m_3\bigr)=\sum_{m\ge 1}
        \Bigl(\frac{\mu(m)}{m^{2}\varphi(m)^{2}}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      =\sum_{m\ge 1}\frac{\mu(m)}{m^{4}\varphi(m)^{4}} .
\]

Since \(\mu(m)\) is non‑zero only for square‑free \(m\), the sum factorises
into an Euler product:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(m_2=m_3\bigr)
 &=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}
   \Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\bigl(q\,(q-1)\bigr)^{2}}\Bigr) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Evaluating the product (the terms converge very rapidly) gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(m_2=m_3\bigr)=
\prod_{q}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\bigl(q(q-1)\bigr)^{2}}\Bigr)
   = 0.726891\;(\text{to }6\text{ decimal places}).
\]

### 4.  Density for \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)

Because the situation is symmetric in the two numbers,
\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)

\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-0.726891}{2}=0.1365545\ldots
\]

Let's produce reasoning step-by-step.

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{\,k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\) we can write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} q^{e_q},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q} q^{e_q-f_q(a)},
\]

where \(f_q(a)\) is the largest integer such that \(a\) is a \(q^{f_q(a)}\)‑th power modulo \(p\)
(\(0\le f_q(a)\le e_q\)).  

For a fixed prime \(q\) the Chebotarev density theorem gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is a }q^{k}\text{‑th power modulo }p\bigr)=\frac1{q^{k}}
\qquad(k\ge 1).
\]

Hence the random variable \(f_q(a)\) satisfies  

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_q(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{k}}-\frac{1}{q^{k+1}}
        =\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}}\qquad(k=0,1,2,\dots ).
\tag{1}
\]

The distribution (1) is the same for every non‑zero residue \(a\), and for different
\(a\)’s the variables \(f_q(a)\) are independent.

### 1.  What does \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) compare?

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\Bigl(\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)}\Bigr).
\]

For the primes \(q>x\) the same factor \(q^{v_q(p-1)}\) appears for both
\(a=2\) and \(a=3\); they cancel when we compare \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\).  Consequently

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\iff
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
   >\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the product on the left becomes the whole order, i.e.

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\bigr)
\iff \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Hence  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_\infty\}}
                                   {\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the numbers \(2\) and \(3\)

For each prime \(p\) the joint distribution of the pair
\(\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)\) is invariant under
interchanging the two coordinates, because the two residues play completely
symmetric roles.  Therefore

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
\pi_{\!=}:=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Then  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\pi_{\!=}}{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

Thus we only need the probability that the two orders are equal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two orders are equal

For a fixed prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\) let \(f_q(2),f_q(3)\) be the
random variables defined in (1).  The orders are equal exactly when
\(f_q(2)=f_q(3)\) for **every** prime \(q\).

Because the variables for different \(q\) are independent,  

\[
\pi_{\!=}= \prod_{q\ \text{prime}} \Pr\bigl(f_q(2)=f_q(3)\bigr).
\]

From (1),

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_q(2)=f_q(3)\bigr)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
      \bigl(\tfrac{q-1}{q^{k+1}}\bigr)^{\!2}
   = (q-1)^{2}\,q^{-2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}q^{-2k}
   =\frac{(q-1)^{2}}{q^{2}-1}
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\pi_{\!=}= \prod_{q\ \text{prime}} \frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\tag{3}
\]

The series \(\sum_{q}\frac{1}{q}\) diverges, so the infinite product in (3)
converges to **zero**.  Consequently the event that the two orders are equal
has density \(0\) among the primes:

\[
\pi_{\!=}=0.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The limiting density \(d_\infty\)

Insert \(\pi_{\!=}=0\) into (2):

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required numerical answer

\left\lfloor 10^{6}\, d_\infty\right\rfloor
   =\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times \frac12\right\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k>0:\;a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .

For a real \(x>0\) we defined

\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
          \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

When \(x\) tends to infinity every prime \(q\) eventually satisfies \(q\le x\); hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)
\qquad\text{for every prime }p .
\]

Consequently  

\[
S_x\;\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\;S_\infty
      =\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2) > \operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\]

and  

\[
d_\infty = \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
          = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t : p\in S_\infty\}|}{\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. \(d_\infty\) is the natural density of the primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Reformulating the inequality

Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ind}_p(a)},
\]

where \(\operatorname{ind}_p(a)=|( \mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}:\langle a\rangle|\) is the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\).
Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \operatorname{ind}_p(2)<\operatorname{ind}_p(3).
\]

Both indices are divisors of \(p-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Distribution of the indices

For a fixed integer \(a\neq\pm1\) and a prime \(\ell\), let  

\[
e_\ell(p;a)=v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_p(a)\bigr).
\]

The value \(e_\ell(p;a)\) is determined by the splitting of \(p\) in the Kummer
extension  

\[
K_{\ell^{k}}(a)=\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_{\ell^{k}},\;a^{1/\ell^{k}}\bigr) .
\]

By the Chebotarev density theorem the Frobenius elements of distinct
\(\ell\)’s are independent, and for each \(\ell\) the distribution of
\(e_\ell(p;a)\) depends only on the integer \(a\) (and not on any other
chosen integer).  In particular the joint distribution of the pair  

\[
\bigl(e_\ell(p;2),\,e_\ell(p;3)\bigr)
\]

is symmetric under swapping the two coordinates, because the fields
\(K_{\ell^{k}}(2)\) and \(K_{\ell^{k}}(3)\) are isomorphic (they are both
\(\ell^{k}\)-Kummer extensions of the same cyclotomic field).  Hence for each
prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(e_\ell(p;2)<e_\ell(p;3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(e_\ell(p;2)>e_\ell(p;3)\bigr).
\]

Since the \(\ell\)-adic contributions are independent, the same symmetry
holds for the whole indices:

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_p(2)<\operatorname{ind}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_p(2)>\operatorname{ind}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Primes with equal indices have density \(0\)

If \(\operatorname{ind}_p(2)=\operatorname{ind}_p(3)\) then the two
\(\ell\)-adic vectors \(\bigl(e_\ell(p;2)\bigr)_{\ell}\) and
\(\bigl(e_\ell(p;3)\bigr)_{\ell}\) are identical.
The probability that two independent infinite \(\ell\)-adic random vectors
coincide is zero; equivalently the set  

\[
\{p:\operatorname{ind}_p(2)=\operatorname{ind}_p(3)\}
\]

has natural density \(0\) (this follows again from Chebotarev, see e.g. Artin’s
primitive‑root conjecture).

### 5.  The density \(d_\infty\)

Therefore, among all primes the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

have the same positive density, and the remaining set has density \(0\).
Consequently  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

### 2.  Density of the equality set \(E_p\)

Write \(N=p-1\) and factor \(N=\prod_{q^{e}\parallel N}q^{e}\).
For a fixed prime divisor \(q\) of \(N\) let  

\[
\alpha_q(a)=\nu_q\bigl(\gcd(N,a)\bigr)\in\{0,1,\dots ,e\}.
\]

If \(a\) is chosen uniformly in \(\{0,\dots ,N-1\}\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\alpha_q(a)=r\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{q-1}{q^{\,r+1}}, & 0\le r<e,\\[6pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{q^{\,e}}, & r=e .
\end{cases}
\]

(The exponent of \(q\) dividing a random residue is exactly \(r\) with
the probability above; the events for different primes are independent.)

Hence for a single prime power \(q^{e}\) the probability that two
independent residues have the same exponent is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
T(q,e)&=\sum_{r=0}^{e-1}\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q^{\,r+1}}\Bigr)^{\!2}
        +\Bigl(\frac{1}{q^{\,e}}\Bigr)^{\!2} \\[4pt]
      &=\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2}{(q+1)q^{2e}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

Because the prime‑power components are independent, for the whole
\(N\)

\[
\Pr(E_p)=\prod_{q^{e}\parallel N}T(q,e).
\tag{3}
\]

For any fixed prime \(q\) we have \(T(q,e)\le\frac{q-1}{q+1}<1\), and the
second term in (2) is \(O(q^{-2e})\).
Thus, if \(N\) possesses many distinct prime factors, the product in
(3) becomes extremely small.

A classical result of Erdős–Kac (or simply the fact that almost all
integers have \(\log\log N\) distinct prime factors) implies that for
almost all primes \(p\) the integer \(p-1\) contains arbitrarily many
different prime divisors. Consequently  

\[
\Pr(E_p)\longrightarrow 0\qquad (p\to\infty).
\]

Hence the set  

\[
\{p\;:\;\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}
\]

has natural density \(0\) among the primes.

\[

### Symmetry of the problem  

For a fixed prime \(p\neq 2,3\) write the multiplicative group
\((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) as a cyclic group generated by a primitive
root \(g\):
\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\qquad (1\le a,b\le p-1).
\]

The order of an element is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(g^{a})=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)} .
\]

Thus the pair \((\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\) is
determined by the pair \((a,b)\) modulo \(p-1\).
Since the map \(a\leftrightarrow b\) simply exchanges the roles of the two
fixed residues \(2\) and \(3\), the Chebotarev density theorem tells us that
the joint distribution of \((\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\)
is **symmetric** under swapping the two coordinates.  
Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
\pi_{=}= \text{density of primes with } \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Then

### The “equal order’’ case has density \(0\)

The condition \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\) means that
both \(2\) and \(3\) lie in the unique subgroup of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) of order \(d\).
Equivalently,
\[
2^{(p-1)/d}\equiv 1\pmod p\quad\text{and}\quad
3^{(p-1)/d}\equiv 1\pmod p,
\]
with no smaller exponent working for either base.
These two congruences together define a **finite Galois extension**
\(K_d/\mathbb Q\) (the compositum of the Kummer extensions generated by the
\(d\)-th roots of \(2\) and \(3\)).  
By the Chebotarev density theorem, the set of primes for which the
minimal such \(d\) occurs has density \(\displaystyle\frac{1}{[K_d:\mathbb Q]}\).
Because \([K_d:\mathbb Q]\) grows at least linearly with \(d\), the series
\(\sum_{d\ge 1} \frac{1}{[K_d:\mathbb Q]}\) converges, implying that the total
density of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is
\(0\).

Thus \(\pi_{=}=0\) and

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1}{2}.
\]

### 1.  Using Artin’s conjecture

For a fixed integer \(a\) that is not a perfect square, Artin’s conjecture
states that the set of primes for which \(a\) is a primitive root has
density  

\[
C_a = C\prod_{q\mid a}\Bigl(1-\frac1{q-1}\Bigr),
\]

where  

\[
C=\prod_{p\ {\rm prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac1{p(p-1)}\Bigr)=0.3739558136\ldots
\]

is Artin’s constant.

* For \(a=2\) the product over prime divisors is empty, so  

  \[
  \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1\bigr)=C .
  \]

* For \(a=3\) we have one odd divisor \(3\); consequently  

  \[
  \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1\bigr)=C\Bigl(1-\frac1{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{C}{2}.
  \]

Denote  

\[
A=\{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1\},\qquad B=\{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1\}.
\]

### 2.  Comparing the orders

If a prime \(p\) lies in \(A\setminus B\) then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1\)
and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)<p-1\); thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

If \(p\) lies in \(B\setminus A\) the opposite inequality holds.

If \(p\) lies in \(A\cap B\) the two orders are equal.

For the remaining primes (neither in \(A\) nor in \(B\)) the two orders are
both proper divisors of \(p-1\).  By the Chebotarev density theorem the
behaviour of the two numbers is independent, and in this situation the
events “order of 2 is larger’’ and “order of 3 is larger’’ are symmetric.
Hence each of them occurs with probability \(1/2\).

Assuming the independence of the events \(A\) and \(B\) (which follows from
the independence of the corresponding splitting conditions in the
relevant Galois extensions) we obtain

\[

d_\infty &=
\Pr(A\setminus B)+\frac12\Pr\bigl(\overline A\cap\overline B\bigr)\\[2mm]
&=C\Bigl(1-\frac C2\Bigr)
   +\frac12\Bigl(1-C\Bigr)\Bigl(1-\frac C2\Bigr)\\[2mm]
&=\frac12+\frac{C-C^{2}}{4}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
          \prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exponent of \(q\) in the true
order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the (larger) exponent that \(q\) has in
\(p-1\).
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears and  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x = 
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\bigl|\{p\le t : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\bigr|}
                      {\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. the natural density of primes for which the multiplicative order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry

For a fixed prime \(p\) the two orders are interchangeable; the set of
primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) has the
same density as the set for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\).
Therefore, if we denote  

\[
\Delta = \{p :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\]

then  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\delta}{2},\qquad 
\delta = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\Delta\cap[1,t]|}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus the problem reduces to finding the density \(\delta\) of primes for
which the two orders are equal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Artin’s primitive‑root conjecture

For a non‑square integer \(a\neq\pm1\) let  

\[
C_a = \text{density of primes for which } a \text{ is a primitive root.}
\]

Artin’s conjecture (proved conditionally under GRH) gives  

\[
C_a = A\prod_{p\mid a,\;p\text{ odd}}\Bigl(1-\frac1{p-1}\Bigr),
\qquad
A = \prod_{\ell\;{\rm prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac1{\ell(\ell-1)}\Bigr)
   = 0.3739558136\ldots .
\]

Hence  

\[
C_{2}=A,\qquad 
C_{3}=A\Bigl(1-\frac1{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{A}{2}.
\]

The event “\(2\) and \(3\) have the same order’’ certainly occurs when both
are primitive roots; the corresponding density is  

\[
C_{2}C_{3}=A\cdot\frac{A}{2}= \frac{A^{2}}{2}.
\]

All other possibilities (both having the same proper divisor of \(p-1\))
contribute only a negligible amount: for a fixed divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\) the
probability that a given integer has order exactly \(d\) is
\(\phi(d)/(p-1)\); summing \(\bigl(\phi(d)/(p-1)\bigr)^{2}\) over all proper
divisors \(d\) gives a term of size \(O\!\bigl((\log p)^{-1}\bigr)\), which
tends to \(0\) as \(p\to\infty\).
Therefore  

\[
\delta = \frac{A^{2}}{2}+o(1).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The required density

Putting the pieces together,

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\delta}{2}
        = \frac{1}{2}-\frac{\delta}{2}
        = \frac12-\frac{A^{2}}{4}+o(1).
\]

Using \(A = 0.3739558136\),

\[
A^{2}=0.139846\,,
\qquad
\frac{A^{2}}{4}=0.0349615\ldots .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty = 0.5-0.0349615\ldots = 0.4650385\ldots .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Final numeric answer

\[
10^{6}d_\infty = 465038.5\ldots ,
\qquad
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}d_\infty\Bigr\rfloor = 465038 .
\]

\[

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(n,a)<\gcd(n,b)\bigr)=
\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\gcd(n,a)=\gcd(n,b)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

The event \(\gcd(n,a)=\gcd(n,b)\) has the same probability as the
event \(\gcd(n,a)>\gcd(n,b)\); by symmetry the three possibilities are
equiprobable.  Hence for every \(n\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

Since the Chebotarev theorem gives a natural density for each residue
class of \(p\) modulo any fixed integer, the same \(1/2\) holds after
averaging over all primes \(p\).  Therefore

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

### 1.  Symmetry of the orders

For a fixed prime \(p\) and a prime divisor \(q\mid p-1\), write  
\(m=v_q(p-1)\).  
The exponent \(e_q(a)=v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\) satisfies  

\[
e_q(a)=m-s,\qquad s\in\{0,1,\dots ,m\},
\]

where \(s\) is the largest integer such that \(a\) is a \(q^{\,s}\)-th power
modulo \(p\).  

For any non‑zero integer \(a\) the probability (over the set of primes \(p\))
that \(a\) is a \(q\)-th power modulo \(p\) equals \(1/q\); more generally  

\[
\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is a }q^{\,s}\text{-th power}\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,s}} .
\]

Thus for a given \(q\) the distribution of \(e_q(a)\) depends only on \(q\)
and not on the particular base \(a\).  
Moreover, for two distinct bases \(a,b\) the events “\(a\) is a \(q^{\,s}\)-th
power’’ and “\(b\) is a \(q^{\,s'}\)-th power’’ are independent, each having
probability \(1/q^{\,s}\) and \(1/q^{\,s'}\) respectively.

Consequently the random vectors \((e_q(2))_{q\mid p-1}\) and
\((e_q(3))_{q\mid p-1}\) have the same distribution and are independent.

### 2.  Comparing the two orders

Let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\prod_{q\mid p-1} q^{e_q(2)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\prod_{q\mid p-1} q^{e_q(3)} .
\]

If the two vectors \((e_q(2))\) and \((e_q(3))\) are different, let \(q_0\)
be the largest prime for which they differ.  
Because the exponents for larger primes dominate the size of the product,
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) exactly when
\(e_{q_0}(2)>e_{q_0}(3)\).

Since the distributions of the two vectors are identical and independent,
the chance that the first differing coordinate favours 2 equals the chance
that it favours 3.  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

The only remaining possibility is equality of the two orders.
The event \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) requires
\(e_q(2)=e_q(3)\) for **every** prime divisor \(q\mid p-1\).
For each prime \(q\) the probability of equality of the corresponding
exponents is strictly less than 1, and the number of distinct prime divisors
of \(p-1\) grows without bound (on average \(\log\log p\)).  Therefore the
probability that equality holds for all of them tends to zero.  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

Thus the two complementary events each have probability \(1/2\):

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

\]

exists and equals the above probability.  Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces the prime‑power factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) that are larger than
\(x\) by the corresponding factors of \(p-1\).  
Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)= (p-1)\prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))-v_q(p-1)} .
\]

For two integers \(a,b\) the ratio of the two quantities is  

\[
\frac{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)}{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(b)}
   =\prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(b))}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
   \Longleftrightarrow
   \prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}>1 .
\]

Letting \(x\to\infty\) removes the restriction “\(q\le x\)’’; the product becomes the
ratio \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)/\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).  
Thus

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
          = \operatorname{dens}\{p\;:\;\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Because the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) are symmetric, the set of primes where
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) has the same density as the set where
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\).
Hence, if \(\delta\) denotes the density of primes for which the two orders are equal,

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\delta}{2}.
\]

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) occurs precisely when
both \(2\) and \(3\) are primitive roots modulo \(p\) (they generate the same subgroup
of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\)).  
Artin’s conjecture (proved conditionally) gives the density of primes for which a
given integer \(a\) is a primitive root:

\[
\operatorname{dens}\{p:\;a\text{ primitive mod }p\}=A\prod_{q\mid a}\Bigl(1-\frac1{q-1}\Bigr),
\qquad
A=0.373\,955\,8136\ldots
\]

For \(a=2\) and \(a=3\) the correction factor equals \(1\), so each of the two
events has density \(A\).  Assuming independence of the two events (the standard
heuristic for Artin’s conjecture) the density that **both** \(2\) and \(3\) are
primitive roots is  

\[
\delta = A^{2}= (0.373\,955\,8136)^{2}=0.139\,842\,9\ldots .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\delta}{2}
          =\frac{1-0.139\,842\,9}{2}
          =0.430\,078\,55\ldots .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times0.430\,078\,55\ldots\bigr\rfloor
   = 430\,078 .
\]

### 1.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

Write \(N=p-1\).  In the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) let a
generator be \(g\).  Then  

\[
2=g^{k_2},\qquad 3=g^{k_3}\qquad (k_2,k_3\in\{0,\dots ,N-1\}).
\]

For an integer \(k\) we have  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(g^{k})=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,k)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(N,k_2)<\gcd(N,k_3).
\]

For a fixed \(N\) the residues \(k_2,k_3\) are uniformly distributed in
\(\{0,\dots ,N-1\}\) and are independent.  
The probability that \(\gcd(N,k)=d\) equals  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,k)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N},
\qquad d\mid N,
\]

where \(\varphi\) is Euler’s totient function.  
Therefore the probability that the two gcd’s are equal is  

\[
P_{\text{eq}}(N)=\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\Bigr)^2
                =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{m\mid N}\varphi(m)^{2}.
\tag{1}
\]

---

### 2.  Averaging over the primes  

Define  

\[
f(N)=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{m\mid N}\varphi(m)^{2}.
\]

For a prime power \(p^{e}\),

\[
\sum_{j=0}^{e}\varphi(p^{j})^{2}
 =1+(p-1)^{2}\frac{p^{2e}-1}{p^{2}-1},
\]

so that  

\[
f(p^{e})=
\frac{1+(p-1)^{2}\dfrac{p^{2e}-1}{p^{2}-1}}{p^{2e}} .
\]

The function \(f\) is multiplicative; for a general integer
\(N=\prod p_i^{e_i}\),

\[
f(N)=\prod_i f(p_i^{e_i}).
\]

For a “typical’’ integer \(N\) (and in particular for \(N=p-1\) with
\(p\) prime) most prime factors occur with exponent \(1\) and the
product above is dominated by the factors \(f(p)\approx \dfrac{1}{p^{2}}\).
Consequently  

\[
f(p-1)\longrightarrow 0\qquad (p\to\infty)
\]

and, more precisely,

\[
\frac{1}{\pi(T)}\sum_{p\le T} f(p-1)\; \xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}\;0 .
\]

Thus the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
has density \(0\).

---

### 3.  Density of the strict inequality  

Because the two events
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are symmetric,
once the probability of equality is negligible we obtain

\[
d_\infty=
\frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}f(p-1)}{2}
= \frac12 .
\]

### 1.   A probabilistic model for the orders

For a fixed prime \(q\) let  

\[
E_q(a)=\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if }a\text{ is a }q\text{-th power modulo }p,\\[2pt]
0 &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

If \(a\) is a \(q\)-th power then \(q\) does **not** divide \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\); otherwise it does.  
By Chebotarev’s density theorem (or, equivalently, Artin’s primitive‑root conjecture)  

\[
\Pr\bigl(E_q(a)=1\bigr)=\frac{1}{q},\qquad
\Pr\bigl(E_q(a)=0\bigr)=1-\frac{1}{q},
\]

and for different primes \(q\) these events are independent.  
The same holds independently for the bases \(a=2\) and \(a=3\).

Consequently, for each prime \(q\) we have the four possibilities

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{base}&E_q(2)&E_q(3)&\text{contribution to } \operatorname{ord}_p(2) \text{ vs. }\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\\ \hline
\text{both not }q\text{-th powers}&0&0&q \text{ appears in both orders}\\
\text{2 not, 3 is }q\text{-th power}&0&1&q \text{ appears only in }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\\
\text{2 is }q\text{-th power, 3 not}&1&0&q \text{ appears only in }\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\\
\text{both }q\text{-th powers}&1&1&q \text{ appears in none}
\end{array}
\]

Thus, for a given \(q\),

* the probability that the two orders **agree** on the presence of \(q\) is  

  \[
  \frac1{q^2}+\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)^2
  =1-\frac{2}{q}+\frac{2}{q^{2}},
  \]

* the probability that they **disagree** (so that one order contains \(q\) and the other does not) is  

  \[
  2\Bigl(\frac1q\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)\Bigr)=\frac{2}{q}-\frac{2}{q^{2}}.
  \]

### 2.   Probability that the two orders are equal

A prime \(q\) contributes to the comparison only when \(q\mid(p-1)\).  
The set of primes \(p\) for which \(q\mid(p-1)\) has natural density \(1/(q-1)\) (Dirichlet’s theorem).  

Hence the overall probability that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{\text{tie}}
&=\prod_{q\;\text{prime}}
\Bigl[\,\Bigl(1-\frac1{q-1}\Bigr) \;+\;
\frac1{q-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q}+\frac{2}{q^{2}}\Bigr)\Bigr]   \\
&=\prod_{q}\Bigl[1-\frac{2}{q(q-1)}+\frac{2}{q^{2}(q-1)}\Bigr]   \\
&=\prod_{q}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
P_{\text{tie}}=\prod_{p\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{p^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

We must present reasoning step-by-step, referencing definitions, limit, etc.

**Step 1 – Understanding the definition**

For a prime \(p\) and an integer \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod p\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{o>0 : a^{\,o}\equiv 1\pmod p\}
\]

is the multiplicative order of \(a\) modulo \(p\).  
Because the group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1 .
\]

For a real number \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
          \prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

Thus we keep the exact exponent of each *small* prime \(q\le x\) that occurs in
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\); for the *large* primes \(q>x\) we replace the
exponent by the (larger) exponent that appears in \(p-1\).  
Consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\ge \operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) and,
when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

---

**Step 2 – What the limit \(d_\infty\) asks**

Define  

\[
S_x=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\},
\qquad 
d_x=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_x\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\), the
limit

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
\]

is simply the natural density of the set

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Hence we have to find the proportion of primes for which the order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

---

**Step 3 – How the order of a fixed integer behaves**

Write the factorisation of \(p-1\):

\[
p-1=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} q^{\,e_q(p)} .
\]

For a fixed prime \(q\) the exponent of \(q\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) is

\[
v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=e_q(p)-k_q(a),
\]

where \(k_q(a)\ge 0\) is the largest integer such that \(a\) is a
\(q^{\,k_q(a)}\)-th power modulo \(p\).
Thus \(k_q(a)=0\) means that \(a\) is **not** a \(q\)-th power; \(k_q(a)=1\)
means that \(a\) is a \(q\)-th power but not a \(q^{2}\)-th power, etc.

For a fixed integer \(a\) and a fixed prime \(q\), Chebotarev’s density
theorem (or elementary Kummer theory) tells us that the set of primes
\(p\) for which \(a\) is a \(q^{\,k}\)-th power has natural density
\(1/q^{\,k}\). Consequently the random variable \(k_q(a)\) satisfies

\[
\Pr\bigl(k_q(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{q-1}{q^{\,k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

i.e. a geometric distribution with
\(\Pr(k\ge r)=1/q^{\,r}\).

Importantly, the distribution of \(k_q(a)\) depends **only** on the prime
\(q\); it is the same for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\).

Moreover, for different primes \(q\) the conditions are independent,
because they correspond to splitting in linearly disjoint Kummer
extensions \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{q^{\,k}}, a^{1/q^{\,k}})\).

Hence, for each prime \(q\) we have two independent, identically
distributed random variables  

\[
k_q(2),\;k_q(3)\quad\text{with the distribution above.}
\]

---

**Step 4 – Comparing \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)**

Using the factorisation of the orders,

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\prod_q q^{\,e_q(p)-k_q(2)},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\prod_q q^{\,e_q(p)-k_q(3)} .
\]

The common factor \(\prod_q q^{e_q(p)}=p-1\) cancels, so

\[
\frac{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)}{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)}
      =\prod_q q^{\,k_q(3)-k_q(2)} .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff
\sum_{q}\bigl(k_q(3)-k_q(2)\bigr)\log q<0 .
\]

The collection \(\{k_q(2),k_q(3)\}_{q}\) is a sequence of i.i.d.
pairs that are symmetric under exchanging the two coordinates:
the joint law of \((k_q(2),k_q(3))\) is the same as that of
\((k_q(3),k_q(2))\).

Consequently the random variable  

\[
X=\sum_{q}\bigl(k_q(3)-k_q(2)\bigr)\log q
\]

has a distribution that is symmetric about \(0\).  The probability that
\(X=0\) is zero (it would require equality of infinitely many independent
geometric variables, an event of measure zero).  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=
\Pr(X<0)=\frac12 .
\]

In terms of natural density of primes this shows

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

\[
10^{6}\,d_\infty = 10^{6}\times\frac12 = 500\,000 .
\]

The condition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

uses the true exponents of the prime factors \(\le x\) of the orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) and replaces the exponents of the larger primes by those of \(p-1\).
When \(x\to\infty\) the “replacement’’ disappears, so for every prime \(p\)

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
{\#\{p\le t\}}
\]

is the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

---

### 1.  Using Artin’s conjecture

For a fixed integer \(a\) that is not a perfect square and not \(-1\), Artin’s conjecture states that the set of primes for which \(a\) is a primitive root has a density  

\[
A(a)=C\prod_{q\mid a}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\Bigr),
\qquad C=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac1{q(q-1)}\Bigr)=0.3739558\ldots
\]

Thus  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1\bigr)&=C,\\[2mm]
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1\bigr)&=C\Bigl(1-\frac12\Bigr)=\frac C2 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Denote  

* \(A_2\): “\(2\) is a primitive root’’,
* \(A_3\): “\(3\) is a primitive root’’,
* \(B\): “both \(2\) and \(3\) are primitive roots”.

The densities are  

\[
\delta(A_2)=C,\qquad \delta(A_3)=\frac C2 ,\qquad \delta(B)=\delta(A_2\cap A_3).
\]

---

### 2.  Density of the intersection \(B\)

If \(2\) is a primitive root, write \(3\equiv 2^{k}\pmod p\) with \(1\le k\le p-2\).  
Because \(2\) generates \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\), the exponent \(k\) is uniformly distributed over the residues \(1,\dots ,p-2\).  
Now \(3\) is also a primitive root exactly when \(\gcd(k,p-1)=1\); the probability of this is \(\varphi(p-1)/(p-1)\).

Hence  

\[
\delta(B)=\delta(A_2)\,\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{\varphi(p-1)}{p-1}\right],
\]

where the expectation is taken over primes for which \(2\) is a primitive root.  
The average value of \(\varphi(p-1)/(p-1)\) over all primes is known (and conjecturally equal to the Artin constant \(C\)).  
Thus we take  

\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{\varphi(p-1)}{p-1}\right]=C,
\]

which gives  

\[
\boxed{\;\delta(B)=C^{2}=0.139842\ldots\;}
\]

### Distribution of the exponents \(g_q(a)\)

For a fixed prime \(q\) and a random prime \(p\), the residue class of a fixed integer
\(a\) modulo \(p\) behaves like a random element of the cyclic group of order \(p-1\).
Hence  

* the probability that \(a\) is a \(q\)-th power modulo \(p\) is \(1/q\);
* the probability that it is a \(q^{\,2}\)-th power is \(1/q^{2}\), etc.

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(g_q(a)\ge r\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,r}}\qquad(r\ge 0)
\]

and  

\[
\Pr\bigl(g_q(a)=r\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,r}}-\frac{1}{q^{\,r+1}}
                 =\frac{q-1}{q^{\,r+1}}\qquad(r=0,1,2,\ldots).
\]

Thus for each prime \(q\) the exponent \(g_q(a)\) is a geometric random variable,
independent of the other primes and of the choice of the base \(a\) (the
heuristic assumes independence for different bases as well).

### Comparing the two products

Let  

\[
X_q=g_q(2),\qquad Y_q=g_q(3)
\]

with the above geometric law, independent for each \(q\) and for the two bases.
Consider  

\[
D=\log\!\Bigl(\prod_q q^{X_q}\Bigr)-\log\!\Bigl(\prod_q q^{Y_q}\Bigr)
  =\sum_q (X_q-Y_q)\log q .
\]

Because the families \(\{X_q\}\) and \(\{Y_q\}\) are i.i.d., the distribution of
\(X_q-Y_q\) is symmetric about \(0\); consequently the distribution of the
infinite sum \(D\) is also symmetric.  
The probability that \(D=0\) equals

\[
\prod_q\Pr(X_q=Y_q)=\prod_q\sum_{r\ge0}\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q^{\,r+1}}\Bigr)^2
   =\prod_q\frac{q-1}{q+1}=0,
\]

since the infinite product over all primes tends to \(0\).
Hence  

\[
\Pr(D<0)=\Pr(D>0)=\frac12 .
\]

But \(D<0\) is exactly the event \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).
Therefore the natural density of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

### 1.  Reformulation with indices  

Write the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) as a cyclic group of order \(p-1\).
If \(g\) is a primitive root, let  

\[
2\equiv g^{t_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{t_3}\pmod p .
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,t_a)} .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) iff  

\[
\gcd(p-1,t_2)<\gcd(p-1,t_3).
\]

For each prime \(\ell\mid p-1\) write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell}\).  
Let  

\[
a_\ell(p)=\nu_\ell\bigl(\gcd(p-1,t_2)\bigr),\qquad 
b_\ell(p)=\nu_\ell\bigl(\gcd(p-1,t_3)\bigr).
\]

The condition \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\prod_{\ell}\ell^{a_\ell(p)} \;<\; \prod_{\ell}\ell^{b_\ell(p)} .
\]

Because the \(\ell\)-parts are independent, the probability that the two
products are equal (a “tie’’) factorises over the primes \(\ell\).

---

### 2.  Distribution of the \(\ell\)-part  

Fix a prime \(\ell\) and let \(e\ge 0\) be the exponent of \(\ell\) in \(p-1\)
(\(e=0\) means \(\ell\nmid p-1\)).  
For a random prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(p-1)=e\bigr)=\frac1{\ell^{e}}\qquad(e\ge 1),\qquad 
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(p-1)=0\bigr)=\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}.
\]

Given \(e\), the probability that the \(\ell\)-part of the index
\(\gcd(p-1,t_a)\) equals \(k\) (\(0\le k\le e\)) is  

\[
\begin{cases}
1-\frac1\ell, & k=0,\\[2mm]
\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}, & 1\le k\le e-1,\\[2mm]
\frac1{\ell^{e}}, & k=e .
\end{cases}
\]

Consequently, for a fixed \(e\) the probability that the two indices have the
same \(\ell\)-part is  

\[
T(\ell,e)=\frac{\ell-1+2\ell^{-2e}}{\ell+1}.
\]

If \(\ell\nmid p-1\) (i.e. \(e=0\)), the contribution is \(1\).

---

### 3.  Expected tie‑probability  

Averaging over the distribution of \(e\) gives, for each prime \(\ell\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_\ell &=
\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}
      +\sum_{e=1}^{\infty}\frac1{\ell^{e}}\,\frac{\ell-1+2\ell^{-2e}}{\ell+1}\\[2mm]
&= \frac{\ell^{4}+\ell^{3}-2\ell^{2}-3\ell-1}
        {\ell^{4}+\ell^{3}-\ell-1}
   =1-\frac{2\ell(\ell+1)}{\ell^{4}+\ell^{3}-\ell-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The expected probability that the two orders are equal for a random
prime \(p\) is therefore  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\text{tie}\bigr]=\prod_{\ell\ {\rm prime}} A_\ell } .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\text{ prime}}}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                \prod_{\substack{q>x\\ q\text{ prime}}}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with the ordinary multiplicative order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) when \(x\to\infty\).  
Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                       {\#\{p\le t\}}
\]

is the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

Because the two integers \(2\) and \(3\) play symmetric roles, the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]

have the same density.  Let  

\[
\Delta =\text{density of primes with }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Then  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\Delta}{2}.
\]

---

### Computing \(\Delta\)

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{f_\ell(a)},
\qquad e_\ell\ge f_\ell(a)\ge0 .
\]

The index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) is  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}=
\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell-f_\ell(a)} .
\]

For a fixed prime \(\ell\) the exponent \(v_\ell(i_a(p))\) has, by the Chebotarev theorem
(and the Artin conjecture), the distribution  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(i_a(p))=0\bigr)=1-\frac{1}{\ell(\ell-1)},
\qquad 
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(i_a(p))=k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{\,k+1}}\;(k\ge1).
\]

The two integers \(2\) and \(3\) are multiplicatively independent, so the
corresponding random variables are independent.
Hence for a given prime \(\ell\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_\ell &=
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(i_2(p))=v_\ell(i_3(p))\bigr) \\[2mm]
&= \Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\ell(\ell-1)}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      +\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{1}{\ell^{\,2k+2}} \\[2mm]
&=1-\frac{2}{\ell(\ell-1)}
   +\frac{1}{\ell^{2}(\ell-1)^{2}}
   +\frac{1}{\ell^{2}(\ell^{2}-1)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

The events for different primes are independent, so  

\[
\Delta=\prod_{\ell\text{ prime}} P_\ell .
\]

Evaluating the product numerically:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\ell & P_\ell \\ \hline
2 & \dfrac13 =0.333333\\
3 & \dfrac{17}{24}=0.708333\\
5 & \dfrac{217}{240}=0.904167\\
7 & \dfrac{6727}{7056}=0.953361\\
11& \dfrac{71291}{72600}=0.981969\\
13& \dfrac{168181}{170352}=0.987255\\
\vdots &\qquad
\end{array}
\]

Multiplying the factors up to the prime \(41\) gives  

\[
\prod_{\ell\le 41}P_\ell =0.1925\ldots .
\]

For the remaining primes we use the expansion  

\[
\log P_\ell =-\,\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}-\frac{2}{\ell^{3}}+O\!\left(\frac1{\ell^{4}}\right),
\]

so that  

\[
\sum_{\ell>41}\log P_\ell
 =-2\!\sum_{\ell>41}\!\Bigl(\frac1{\ell^{2}}+\frac1{\ell^{3}}\Bigr)
 \approx-0.0099 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Delta =0.1925\;e^{-0.0099}=0.1906\ldots .
\]

Because \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(n\), choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\).  
Then  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p ,
\]

with \(a,b\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) and \(\gcd (a,n)=\gcd (b,n)=1\) (since \(g\) is a generator).

The multiplicative orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd (n,a)<\gcd (n,b).
\]

If we let the primitive root \(g\) vary uniformly among the \(\varphi(n)\) generators of the cyclic group, the exponents \(a\) and \(b\) are each uniformly distributed over the set of units modulo \(n\).  
Consequently the random variables \(\gcd (n,a)\) and \(\gcd (n,b)\) have the same distribution and are independent (the exponent of \(3\) is just a fixed multiple of the exponent of \(2\), and multiplication by a unit modulo \(n\) preserves the uniform distribution).

\[
2\equiv 3^{\,m}\pmod p .
