Hence \(p\) divides a number of the form \(3^{m}-2\).  
The set of primes dividing any term of the sequence \(\{3^{m}-2\}_{m\ge 1}\) has natural density \(0\) (a standard result of analytic number theory: a set of primes defined by a single polynomial equation has density \(0\)).

Therefore the events “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)” and “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\)” each occur with probability \(\dfrac12\) in the limit.  

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
= \boxed{500000}.
\]

second product is equal to \(1\) and the first product is simply \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\).

For a prime \(p\neq 2,3\) the group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) is cyclic of order
\(p-1\).  Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\); then there exist unique
integers \(a,b\;(1\le a,b\le p-1)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{\,a}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{\,b}\pmod p .
\]

Because \(g\) runs through all \(\varphi(p-1)\) primitive roots, the pair

units modulo \(p-1\).  Consequently the random variables  

\[
U=\gcd(p-1,a),\qquad V=\gcd(p-1,b)
\]

are identically distributed and independent.  Since  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{U},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{V},
\]

the inequality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent to
\(U<V\).

Because the distributions of \(U\) and \(V\) are the same, the events
\(U<V\) and \(U>V\) have the same probability.  The only remaining possibility

\(d\mid(p-1)\) the probability that \(\gcd(p-1,a)=d\) is proportional to
\(\frac{1}{d}\); summing \(\frac{1}{d^{2}}\) over all \(d\) gives a convergent
series, so the total mass of the diagonal \(U=V\) is \(0\).

Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

Hence the set of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
has natural density \(\displaystyle d_\infty=\frac12\).

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{k\ge 1\;:\;a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

---

### 1.  The limit when \(x\to\infty\)

For a given prime \(p\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\text{ prime}}}
 q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a))}\;
\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\text{ prime}}}
 q^{\,v_q(p-1)} .
\]

If \(q\le x\) we keep the exact exponent of \(q\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\);  
if \(q> x\) we replace it by the exponent of the same prime in \(p-1\).
When \(x\) grows, every prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\) is eventually
\(\le x\); consequently  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
S_{\infty}= \bigl\{p\text{ prime}\; :\; \operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr\},
\qquad
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{\#\{p\le t : p\in S_{\infty}\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

So we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the
multiplicative order of \(2\) exceeds that of \(3\).

---

### 2.  Distribution of the orders

For a fixed prime \(p\) the group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) is cyclic of order
\(p-1\).
If we choose an element \(g\) uniformly at random from this group, the
probability that its order equals a divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\) is  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(g)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1},
\tag{1}
\]

where \(\varphi\) is Euler’s totient function.  
Formula (1) depends only on the group structure, not on the particular
element.

Artin’s primitive‑root conjecture (proved for the joint distribution of
several fixed integers by Hooley’s Chebotarev‑density argument) tells us
that for any two fixed integers \(a,b\) which are not perfect powers,
the Frobenius elements attached to the extensions obtained by adjoining
all \(\ell^{k}\)-th roots of \(a\) and of \(b\) are *independent*.
Consequently, for a “random’’ prime \(p\) the random variables  

\[
X_p=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2), \qquad Y_p=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\]

behave as two **independent** draws from the distribution (1) attached
to the cyclic group of order \(p-1\).

Thus, for a given prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl( X_p > Y_p \bigr)=
\frac12\bigl(1-\Pr( X_p = Y_p )\bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 3.  Probability of a tie

From (1),

\[
\Pr( X_p = Y_p )
   =\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}\Bigr)^{\!2}
   =\frac{1}{p-1}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\frac{\varphi(d)^{2}}{p-1}
   \le \frac{\tau(p-1)}{p-1},
\]

where \(\tau(n)\) is the divisor‑function.
Since \(\tau(n)=o(n^{\varepsilon})\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the
right‑hand side tends to \(0\) as \(p\to\infty\).
Hence the set of primes for which the orders are equal has natural
density \(0\).

Therefore \(\Pr( X_p = Y_p ) = 0\) in the sense of natural density, and
from (2)

\[
\Pr\bigl( X_p > Y_p \bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

### 4.  Density \(d_{\infty}\)

The above probability is exactly the natural density of the set
\(S_{\infty}\); consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).

\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\#\langle 3\rangle},
\]

where \(\#\langle a\rangle\) is the size of the subgroup generated by \(a\).

The two numbers \(2\) and \(3\) play completely symmetric roles:
the map \(a\mapsto a\) (or any automorphism of the cyclic group) sends the
distribution of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) onto that of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).
Hence for every prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)

\[

### 1.  Reformulating the problem

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo a prime \(p\) and write  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\pmod p ,
\qquad 1\le k_2,k_3\le p-1 .
\]

Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic,
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_a)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3).
\]

For a fixed modulus \(m=p-1\) and a uniformly random residue
\(k\in\{1,\dots ,m\}\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(m,k)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(m/d)}{m},
\qquad d\mid m .
\]

If \(k_2,k_3\) are taken independently (the usual heuristic for
different fixed bases), then for this \(m\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(m,k_2)=\gcd(m,k_3)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid m}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(m/d)}{m}\Bigr)^{\!2}
   =\frac{1}{m^{2}}\sum_{e\mid m}\varphi(e)^{2}
   =:T(m).
\]

Thus  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac12\bigl(1-T(p-1)\bigr),
\]
the factor \(\tfrac12\) coming from symmetry between the two bases.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Behaviour of \(T(m)\)

The function  

\[
f(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}\varphi(e)^{2}
\]

is multiplicative.  For a prime power \(q^{a}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(q^{a})&=1+\sum_{i=1}^{a}\varphi(q^{i})^{2}
        =1+(q-1)^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{a}q^{2i-2}  \\
        &=1+\frac{(q-1)(q^{2a}-1)}{q+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{f(q^{a})}{q^{2a}}
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}+\frac{2}{q+1}\,q^{-2a}
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}+O(q^{-2a}).
\]

For a typical integer \(m\) most prime powers occur with exponent
\(a=1\); therefore  

\[
T(m)=\frac{f(m)}{m^{2}}
     =\prod_{q\mid m}\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q+1}+O(q^{-2})\Bigr)
     =\prod_{q\mid m}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q+1}+O(q^{-2})\Bigr).
\]

Taking logarithms and using \(\sum_{q\mid m}1/q\sim\log\log m\),

\[
\log T(m)= -2\sum_{q\mid m}\frac{1}{q}+O(1)
        = -2\log\log m+O(1),
\]
so  

\[
T(m)=\frac{C}{(\log m)^{2}}(1+o(1))
\qquad (C>0).
\]

Consequently \(T(p-1)\to 0\) as \(p\to\infty\), and the average of
\(T(p-1)\) over the primes also tends to \(0\).

### 3.  The limiting density

Because the tie‑probability \(T(p-1)\) tends to \(0\),

\[
d_\infty
   =\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac12\bigl(1-T(p-1)\bigr)
   =\frac12 .
\]

The definitions give  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\qquad 
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Hence we have to find the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

---

### 1.  Reformulation with a primitive root  

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p,\qquad (a,b\in\mathbb Z_{p-1}^{\!*}).
\]

Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(g)=p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\iff 
\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a “random” prime the discrete logarithms \(a,b\) behave like two independent
uniform random elements of \(\mathbb Z_{p-1}^{\!*}\).  
Consequently the problem reduces to a purely combinatorial question:

*For a random integer \(N\) (here \(N=p-1\)), pick two independent uniformly
distributed elements \(A,B\) of \((\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).  
What is the probability that \(\gcd(N,A)>\gcd(N,B)\)?*

Because the roles of \(A\) and \(B\) are symmetric,
\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)>\gcd(N,B)\bigr)=
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)<\gcd(N,B)\bigr)=\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)=\gcd(N,B)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\mathbb{E}_p\bigl[\,\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,A)=\gcd(p-1,B)\mid p\bigr)\bigr]}{2}.
\]

---

### 2.  Probability that the two gcd’s are equal  

For a fixed integer \(N\) let  

\[
f(N)=\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^2 .
\]

If \(A,B\) are independent and uniform in \((\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)=\gcd(N,B)\bigr)=\frac{f(N)}{N^{2}} .
\]

The function \(f\) is multiplicative; for a prime power \(\ell^{e}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\ell^{e})&=1+\sum_{i=1}^{e}\bigl(\varphi(\ell^{i})\bigr)^{2}
          =1+(\ell-1)^{2}\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}\ell^{2i}  \\
          &=1+(\ell-1)^{2}\frac{\ell^{2e}-1}{\ell^{2}-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently  

\[
\frac{f(\ell^{e})}{\ell^{2e}}
        =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+\frac{2}{\ell+1}\,\ell^{-2e}.
\tag{1}
\]

For a typical prime \(p\) the factor \(\ell^{-2e}\) is negligible (most prime
divisors of \(p-1\) appear only to the first power).  Hence, for a “random’’
\(N\),

\[
\frac{f(N)}{N^{2}}\approx 
\prod_{\ell\mid N}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Because \(p\) is odd, \(2\mid(p-1)\) always, so we must also include the
factor for \(\ell=2\), namely \(\frac{1}{3}\).

---

### 3.  Averaging over the shifted primes  

Treating the events “\(\ell\mid(p-1)\)” as independent with probability
\(1/\ell\) (the standard heuristic for shifted primes), the mean value of the
multiplicative factor \(\prod_{\ell\mid(p-1)}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\) is

\[
\prod_{\ell\text{ prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\ell}\Bigr)
      \Bigl(1+\frac{1}{\ell+1}\Bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell\text{ odd}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell(\ell+1)}\Bigr)
     \times\frac13 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\mathbb{E}_p\bigl[\Pr(\gcd(p-1,A)=\gcd(p-1,B))\bigr]
   =\frac13\prod_{\ell\text{ odd}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell(\ell+1)}\Bigr)
   } .
\]

The infinite product converges rapidly.  Computing it with the first
hundred odd primes gives

\[
\prod_{\ell\text{ odd}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell(\ell+1)}\Bigr)=0.7075\ldots
\]

and the contribution of the remaining primes is
\(\exp\!\bigl(-2\sum_{\ell>100}\!1/\ell^{2}\bigr)=0.9969\ldots\).
Hence

\[
\mathbb{E}_p\bigl[\Pr(\gcd(p-1,A)=\gcd(p-1,B))\bigr]
      =\frac13\cdot0.7075\ldots =0.2358\ldots .
\]

---

### 4.  The limiting density  

Finally  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-0.2358\ldots}{2}=0.3821\ldots .
\]

Multiplying by \(10^{6}\),

\[
10^{6}\,d_\infty = 382\,085.\ldots
\]

Taking the integer part gives  

\[
\boxed{382085}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

Because \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\), we can write  

\[
2\equiv g^{\alpha_p},\qquad 3\equiv g^{\beta_p}
\]

with a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\) and integers
\(0<\alpha_p,\beta_p<p-1\).  
For a divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(g^{k})=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,\alpha_p)}>\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,\beta_p)}
\Longleftrightarrow
\gcd(p-1,\alpha_p)<\gcd(p-1,\beta_p).          \tag{1}
\]

### 1.  Behaviour for large \(x\)

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}
 q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\,
\prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exact exponent of
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the maximal possible one (the exponent of
\(p-1\)).  As \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
          =\lim_{t\to\infty}
            \frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                 {\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. the natural density of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between \(2\) and \(3\)

For every prime \(p\) exactly one of the three possibilities holds  

* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\),
* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\),
* \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

If we exchange the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) the set of primes with
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is transformed into the
set with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\).  
Hence, under the Chebotarev density theorem (which guarantees that the
distribution of the discrete logarithms \(\alpha_p,\beta_p\) is uniform
in \((\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^{\times}\)), the two strict‑inequality
events have the same density.  Denoting  

\[
\delta = \operatorname{dens}\bigl\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr\},
\]

we must have  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\delta}{2}.                     \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The probability that the two orders are equal

Equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) holds exactly
when the two elements lie in the same subgroup of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).
For a fixed divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\) that subgroup is unique; the condition
is therefore  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d.
\]

The probability that a random element of a cyclic group of order \(n\)
has order \(d\) is \(\varphi(d)/n\).  Consequently, for a given prime
\(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\bigr)
      =\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}\cdot\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}
      =\frac{\varphi(d)^{2}}{(p-1)^{2}} .
\]

Summing over all divisors \(d\mid(p-1)\) gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

The inner sum is \(\le (p-1)\,\max_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)\le (p-1)^{2}\),
and a standard estimate shows that its average over the primes is
\(O\!\bigl((p-1)^{1+\varepsilon}\bigr)\).  Hence the average value of the
probability is \(O(p^{-1+\varepsilon})\), which tends to \(0\) as
\(p\to\infty\).  Therefore  

\[
\delta =0 .
\]

In words: the set of primes for which the two orders are equal has
natural density \(0\).

Putting \(\delta=0\) into (2) we obtain  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1}{2}=0.5 .
\]

\(2\) is a power of \(3\) modulo \(p\); i.e. \(2\equiv 3^{k}\pmod p\) for some
\(k\mid p-1\).  For each fixed \(k\) the congruence \(3^{k} \equiv 2\pmod p\)
has at most one solution \(p\).  Since there are only finitely many possible
\(k\) (they are divisors of \(p-1\)), the set of such primes is thin, and its
natural density is \(0\).

\[
\varepsilon_{a,q}(p)=
\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if } a\text{ is a }q\text{-th power modulo }p,\\
0 &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

One has  

\[
v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=v_q(p-1)-\varepsilon_{a,q}(p).
\]

Hence the first prime \(q\) (in increasing order) for which
\(\varepsilon_{2,q}(p)\neq\varepsilon_{3,q}(p)\) determines which truncated
order is larger: if \(\varepsilon_{2,q}=0\) and \(\varepsilon_{3,q}=1\) then
\(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))>v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\), and vice‑versa.

For a given prime \(q\) the conditions “\(2\) is a \(q\)-th power modulo \(p\)’’
and “\(3\) is a \(q\)-th power modulo \(p\)’’ are independent and each occurs
with probability \(\frac{1}{q}\) (by the Chebotarev density theorem applied to the
Kummer extensions \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_q,\sqrt[q]{2})\) and
\(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_q,\sqrt[q]{3})\)).  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\varepsilon_{2,q}=0,\;\varepsilon_{3,q}=1\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\varepsilon_{2,q}=1,\;\varepsilon_{3,q}=0\bigr)=\frac{q-1}{q^{2}}.
\]

Thus for each prime \(q\) the chance that the first discrepancy favours
\(2\) equals the chance that it favours \(3\).  Because the events for different
\(q\) are independent, the overall probability that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
is exactly \(1/2\).

For a prime \(p\neq 2,3\) let

Write the factorisation of \(p-1\)

\]

For each prime \(q\) define  

\[
g_q(a)=v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr),\qquad 0\le g_q(a)\le f_q .
\]

Thus  

\[

\qquad

### 1.  The limit \(d_\infty\)

When \(x\to\infty\) the definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) keeps the exact
\(q\)-adic exponent for **every** prime \(q\); therefore  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
      =\text{density of primes }p\text{ with }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>
        \operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the exponents \(g_q(a)\)

Fix a prime \(q\).  
The condition \(g_q(a)\ge 1\) means that \(a\) is a \(q\)‑th power modulo \(p\); by
Chebotarev (or by elementary Kummer theory) this occurs with probability
\(1/q\) among the primes \(p\).  
More generally  

\[
\Pr\bigl(g_q(a)\ge k\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,k}}\qquad(k\ge 0).
\]

Hence the random variable \(g_q(a)\) has the geometric distribution  

\[
\Pr\bigl(g_q(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{k}}-\frac{1}{q^{k+1}}
                     =\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots .
\]

For the two fixed bases \(2\) and \(3\) the corresponding variables
\(g_q(2)\) and \(g_q(3)\) are independent and have the same distribution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two orders are equal

The orders are equal iff \(g_q(2)=g_q(3)\) for **every** prime \(q\).  
Because the primes are independent,  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Pr\bigl(g_q(2)=g_q(3)\bigr).
\]

For a given \(q\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(g_q(2)=g_q(3)\bigr)
   &=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\Pr\bigl(g_q(2)=k\bigr)\Pr\bigl(g_q(3)=k\bigr)\\
   &=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}}\right)^2
     =\frac{(q-1)^2}{q^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{q^{2k}}\\
   &=\frac{(q-1)^2}{q^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\frac1{q^{2}}}
     =\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{q}\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\]

Because \(\displaystyle\sum_{q}\frac{2}{q}= \infty\), the infinite product
\(\prod_{q}(1-2/(q+1))\) converges to **zero**.  Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Density of the inequality

The random variable  

\[
X=\sum_{q}\bigl(g_q(2)-g_q(3)\bigr)\log q
\]

has a symmetric distribution (the two collections of exponents are identically
distributed).  Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(X>0\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(X<0\bigr)=\frac{1-\Pr(X=0)}{2}.
\]

Since \(\Pr(X=0)=0\) from the previous step,  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

Thus the natural density of the set  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

among all primes is  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

### Symmetry of the two orders

For a prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).  
Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\). Then there are integers \(u,v\) (depending on \(p\)) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{\,u}\pmod p ,\qquad 3\equiv g^{\,v}\pmod p .
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,u)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,v)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,u)<\gcd(p-1,v).
\]

The pair \((u,v)\) runs through all ordered pairs of residues modulo \(p-1\) that are coprime to \(p-1\); the distribution of the two gcd’s is completely symmetric with respect to swapping the two numbers.  
Therefore, for a “random’’ prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

The event \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) has density \(0\) (it would require \(\gcd(p-1,u)=\gcd(p-1,v)\), a condition that forces an extra algebraic relation and occurs only for a set of primes of zero Dirichlet density).

Consequently the two complementary events each have density \(1/2\); i.e.

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\text{the order of }a\pmod p\qquad (a\not\equiv 0\pmod p).
\]

Write the prime factorisation  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q}\;q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))},
\qquad 
p-1=\prod_{q}\;q^{\,v_q(p-1)} .
\]

For a real \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\Bigl(\prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\prod_{q> x} q^{\,v_q(p-1)}\Bigr).
\]

Hence, for two integers \(a,b\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(b)
\Longleftrightarrow
\sum_{q\le x}\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(b))\bigr)\log q>0 .
\tag{1}
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the product over the primes \(q>x\) disappears, so

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
      =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
\qquad(\text{density among the primes }p).
\tag{2}
\]

### 1.  Distribution of the \(q\)-adic part of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)

Fix a prime \(q\).  
Let  

\[
e_q(p-1)=v_q(p-1),\qquad 
s_q(a)=e_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)) .
\]

The integer \(s_q(a)\) is the exponent of \(q\) in the index of the
subgroup generated by \(a\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).
By Chebotarev (or by the classical Artin‑type argument)  

\[
\Pr\bigl(s_q(a)\ge k\bigr)=\frac1{q^{\,k}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(s_q(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{q-1}{q^{\,k+1}},\qquad k\ge 0 .
\tag{3}
\]

For the two fixed integers \(2\) and \(3\) the random variables
\(s_q(2)\) and \(s_q(3)\) are independent (the corresponding Kummer
extensions are linearly disjoint).

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
N=p-1 ,\qquad \operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{N}{\gcd (N,\log_g a)},
\]

where \(g\) is a fixed primitive root modulo \(p\) and  
\(\log_g a\) denotes the discrete logarithm of \(a\) with respect to \(g\)
(\(g^{\log_g a}\equiv a\pmod p\)).  
Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\frac{N}{\gcd (N,\log_g 2)}>\frac{N}{\gcd (N,\log_g 3)}
\Longleftrightarrow
\gcd (N,\log_g 2)<\gcd (N,\log_g 3).
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Behaviour of the discrete logarithms

When the prime \(p\) varies, the pair  

\[
\bigl(\log_g 2,\ \log_g 3\bigr)\in (\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^2
\]

runs through the set of all pairs \((a,b)\) with \(0\le a,b<N\) such that
\(g^a\equiv 2\) and \(g^b\equiv 3\).  
For each fixed integer \(a\) (resp. \(b\)) the congruence \(g^{a}\equiv 2\pmod p\)
defines a set of primes that is a Chebotarev set; its natural density exists
and equals \(1/(p-1)\).  
Consequently, **as \(p\) ranges over the primes, the residues
\(\log_g 2\) and \(\log_g 3\) become independent and uniformly distributed
in \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\).**  

Hence, for a “random’’ prime we may treat the two numbers
\(A:=\log_g 2\) and \(B:=\log_g 3\) as independent random variables,
uniformly chosen from \(\{0,1,\dots ,N-1\}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of \(\gcd (N,A)\)

For a fixed divisor \(d\mid N\),

\[
\#\{A\in\{0,\dots ,N-1\}: \gcd(N,A)=d\}= \varphi\!\left(\frac{N}{d}\right),
\]

because writing \(A=d\cdot a'\) forces \(\gcd\!\bigl(N/d,a'\bigr)=1\).
Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}.
\tag{2}
\]

The same holds for \(B\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two gcd’s are equal

With independence of \(A\) and \(B\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)=\gcd(N,B)\bigr)
&=\sum_{d\mid N}\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)=d\bigr)
                \Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,B)=d\bigr)   \\
&=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi\!\left(\frac{N}{d}\right)^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]

For a typical integer \(N\) (and in particular for \(N=p-1\) with \(p\) prime)
the sum in (3) is \(o(N^{2})\); consequently the probability that the two
gcd’s are equal tends to **zero** when the primes are taken in the limit.
Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)=\gcd(N,B)\bigr)=0 .
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Density of the inequality

Because of symmetry between the two independent variables \(A\) and \(B\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)<\gcd(N,B)\bigr)
    =\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)>\gcd(N,B)\bigr)
    =\frac{1-\Pr(\text{equality})}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

Using (1), the event \(\gcd(N,A)<\gcd(N,B)\) is exactly the event

Therefore the set  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

has natural density  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\bigr\rfloor

\]

\[

s_{x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}.
\]

### Distribution of the \(\ell\)-adic part of an order

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell} \ell^{e_\ell}\) and let \(g\) be a primitive root
mod \(p\).  
Every element of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) can be written uniquely as
\(g^{t}\) with \(1\le t\le p-1\).  For a fixed prime \(\ell\mid p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(g^{t})=\ell^{\,e_\ell-v_\ell(t)}\cdot\frac{p-1}{\ell^{e_\ell}} .
\]

Because \(t\) is uniformly distributed modulo \(p-1\), the exponent
\(v_\ell(t)\) is independent for different \(\ell\) and satisfies  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(t)=k\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}
        \qquad (k=0,1,\dots ,e_\ell-1),\qquad 
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(t)\ge e_\ell\bigr)=\frac1{\ell^{e_\ell}} .
\]

Hence for a **random element** of the cyclic group, the \(\ell\)-adic
valuation of its order is

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord})=e_\ell-j\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{j+1}}
\qquad (j=0,1,2,\dots).
\]

### Applying the model to the fixed numbers \(2\) and \(3\)

When the prime \(p\) varies, the discrete logarithms
\(\log_g 2\) and \(\log_g 3\) behave like independent uniformly
distributed residues modulo \(p-1\); consequently the \(\ell\)-adic
valuations of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
are independent and each follows the distribution described above.
(The possible correlation would affect only a set of density \(0\).)

For a given prime \(\ell\) the probability that the \(\ell\)-adic
valuation of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) exceeds that of
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is exactly the same as the probability that
the opposite inequality holds; the two events are symmetric.  
Therefore, for each \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))>v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))<v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr).
\]

Since the valuations for distinct primes are independent, the overall
inequality  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

holds with the same probability as the reverse inequality
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).  The only remaining
possibility is equality, which occurs only when the two orders are
identical.  The probability of equality tends to \(0\) because it would
require the \(\ell\)-adic valuations to coincide for **all** primes
\(\ell\mid p-1\); the chance of this simultaneous coincidence is
\(o(1)\).

Hence, among all primes,

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
=\frac12 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

### Heuristic using Artin’s conjecture  

For a fixed integer \(a\) (not a perfect square) the Artin conjecture predicts
that the density of primes for which \(a\) is a primitive root (i.e.  
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1\)) is  

\[
C_a=A\prod_{\substack{q\mid a\\ q\text{ odd}}}\!\Bigl(1-\frac1{q-1}\Bigr),
\qquad 
A=0.3739558136\ldots\ (\text{Artin constant}).
\]

Hence  

\[
C_2=A\approx0.373956,\qquad 
C_3=A\Bigl(1-\frac12\Bigr)=\frac{A}{2}\approx0.186978 .
\]

Assume that, apart from the primitive‑root case, the orders of two fixed
numbers behave like independent random elements of the cyclic group
\((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).  
With this heuristic:

* probability that \(2\) is primitive and \(3\) is **not** primitive  

  \[
  P_{2\text{prim},3\not} = C_2 - C_2C_3 = C_2(1-C_3)\approx0.374-0.140=0.234;
  \]

* probability that \(3\) is primitive and \(2\) is **not** primitive  

  \[
  P_{3\text{prim},2\not}= C_3 - C_2C_3\approx0.187-0.140=0.047;
  \]

* probability that **neither** is primitive  

  \[
  P_{\text{none}} = 1-C_2-C_3+C_2C_3
                  = 1-\frac{3}{2}C_2 + C_2^{2}
                  \approx0.579 .
  \]

When neither is primitive we expect the two orders to be larger or smaller
with equal chance, giving a contribution \(\tfrac12P_{\text{none}}\) to the
event \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

Therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_\infty &\approx
P_{2\text{prim},3\not}
\;+\;
\frac12 P_{\text{none}} \\[2mm]
&\approx 0.234\;+\;\frac12\cdot0.579\\[2mm]
&\approx 0.234\;+\;0.2895\\[2mm]
&\approx 0.5235 .
\end{aligned}

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces the prime‑power factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) that are larger than \(x\) by the corresponding factors of \(p-1\).  
When \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
                               {\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. the density of primes for which the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry

For any prime \(p\) exactly one of the three possibilities holds  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Interchanging the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) gives a bijection between the
sets \(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\) and
\(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\).
Consequently the two densities are equal, and

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\delta}{2},
\]

where \(\delta\) is the density of primes for which the two orders are
equal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Density of equality

Let \(\ell\) be a prime.  For a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\) the
probability (over the set of primes \(p\)) that \(\ell^k\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) is  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\ell^k\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=1-\frac1{\ell^{\,k}} .
\]

Hence the exponent \(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\) is a geometric
random variable:

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=k\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,k+1}},
\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots .
\tag{1}
\]

For the two distinct bases \(2\) and \(3\) the corresponding
exponents are independent (the relevant Kummer extensions are linearly
disjoint).  Therefore, for a fixed prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)
   =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,k+1}}\Bigr)^2
   =\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}\frac{1}{1-\ell^{-2}}
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\tag{2}
\]

The events for different primes \(\ell\) are independent, so the
probability that **all** exponents coincide (i.e. the two orders are
equal) is the infinite product

\[
\delta=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Because \(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}=1-\frac{2}{\ell+1}=1-O\!\left(\frac1\ell\right)\)
and \(\sum_{\ell}\frac1\ell\) diverges, the product converges to **zero**.
Thus the set of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
has density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Final density

With \(\delta=0\),

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Requested value

\[
\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \right\rfloor
   =\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12 \right\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\text{the multiplicative order of }a\pmod p .
\]

For a fixed \(x\) the definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                     \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces all prime factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) that are larger than \(x\) by the
corresponding factors of \(p-1\).
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\longrightarrow \operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
       =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                               {\#\{p\le t\}}
\]

is the natural density of the primes for which the order of \(2\) exceeds the order of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulating the comparison

Write  

\[
d_2(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)},\qquad 
d_3(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)} .
\]

\(d_2(p)\) (resp. \(d_3(p)\)) is the index of the subgroup generated by \(2\) (resp. \(3\)).
Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff \(d_2(p)<d_3(p)\), we must compare the
two indices.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the indices

For a fixed odd prime \(\ell\) the probability that a non‑zero integer \(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power
modulo a random prime \(p\) is \(1/\ell\) (Chebotarev).  
Consequently the exponent of \(\ell\) in the index \(d_a(p)\) has the distribution  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(d_a)=0\bigr)=\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1},\qquad
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(d_a)=e\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{\,e}}\;(e\ge 1).
\]

For \(\ell=2\) the same reasoning gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_2(d_a)=0\bigr)=\frac12,\qquad
\Pr\bigl(v_2(d_a)=e\bigr)=\frac1{2^{\,e+1}}\;(e\ge 1).
\]

The events for different primes \(\ell\) are independent, and the same distribution holds for
\(d_2(p)\) and for \(d_3(p)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two indices are equal

For a given prime \(\ell\) let  

\[
M_\ell=\sum_{e\ge0}\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(d_2)=e\bigr)\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(d_3)=e\bigr)
\]

be the probability that the \(\ell\)-adic exponents of the two indices coincide.
Using the distributions above we obtain  

* for \(\ell=2\): \(M_2=\displaystyle\frac14+\sum_{e\ge1}\frac1{2^{2e+2}}=\frac13\);
* for odd \(\ell\):

\[
M_\ell =\Bigl(\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}\Bigr)^{\!2}+ \sum_{e\ge1}\frac1{\ell^{2e}}
      =\frac{(\ell-2)^2}{(\ell-1)^2}+ \frac{1}{\ell^{2}-1}.
\]

Since the \(\ell\)-adic behaviours are independent, the probability that the whole
indices are equal is

\[
P_{\text{eq}}=\prod_{\ell\text{ prime}} M_\ell
            =\frac13\prod_{\ell\ge 3}\left[\frac{(\ell-2)^2}{(\ell-1)^2}
                                          +\frac{1}{\ell^{2}-1}\right].
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The product tends to zero

For large \(\ell\),

\[
M_\ell = 1-\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\right).
\]

Hence  

\[
\log M_\ell = -\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\right),
\]

and  

\[
\sum_{\ell}\log M_\ell = -2\sum_{\ell}\frac1\ell+O(1) = -\infty .
\]

Because \(\sum_{\ell}1/\ell\) diverges, the infinite product \(P_{\text{eq}}\) is **zero**.
Thus the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) has
density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Density of the inequality

The situation is symmetric in the numbers \(2\) and \(3\).  
Since the equality occurs with density \(0\),

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

The comparison  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

depends only on the exact orders of \(2\) and \(3\) modulo \(p\).  
When \(x\to\infty\) we have \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\to\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\); hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
          =\frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}
            \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

---

### 1.  Modelling the orders  

Let \(p\) be an odd prime and write \(p-1=\prod q^{e_q}\) (prime factorisation).  
If \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\) and  

\[
2\equiv g^{r},\qquad 3\equiv g^{s}\pmod p,
\]

then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(r,p-1)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(s,p-1)} .
\]

Thus the two orders are equal iff \(\gcd(r,p-1)=\gcd(s,p-1)\).

For a fixed prime \(p\) the exponents \(r,s\) are uniformly distributed in
\(\{1,\dots ,p-1\}\) and are independent.
Hence, for a given divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(r,p-1)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi\!\left(\frac{p-1}{d}\right)}{p-1},
\]

and the probability that the two orders are equal is  

\[
\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi\!\left(\frac{p-1}{d}\right)}{p-1}\Bigr)^{\!2}
   =\prod_{q^{e}\parallel(p-1)}\;
     \Bigl(\sum_{a=0}^{e}\bigl(\frac{\varphi(q^{a})}{q^{e}}\bigr)^{2}\Bigr)
   \equiv f(p-1).
\]

---

### 2.  Expected value of \(f(p-1)\) over the primes  

For a fixed prime \(q\) let \(e=v_q(p-1)\).  
Using Dirichlet’s theorem one obtains the limiting distribution  

\[
\Pr(e=0)=\frac{q-2}{q-1},\qquad 
\Pr(e=k)=\frac1{q^{k}}\;(k\ge 1).
\]

With  

\[
g(q,e)=\sum_{a=0}^{e}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(q^{a})}{q^{e}}\Bigr)^{2}
      =1-\frac{2q}{(q-1)(q^{2}+q+1)},
\]

the expected contribution of the prime \(q\) is  

\[
E_q=\sum_{e\ge0}\Pr(e)\,g(q,e)
    =1-\frac{2q}{(q-1)(q^{2}+q+1)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\boxed{C=\lim_{p\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[f(p-1)]
      =\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}}
        \Bigl(1-\frac{2q}{(q-1)(q^{2}+q+1)}\Bigr)} .
\]

(The product converges because the factor differs from \(1\) by
\(O(q^{-2})\).)

---

### 3.  Numerical evaluation

\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{q\le 97}\Bigl(1-\frac{2q}{(q-1)(q^{2}+q+1)}\Bigr)

\end{aligned}
\]

Multiplying the two parts,

\[
C = 0.2730\ldots .
\]

So we take the prime factorization of ord_p(a) and keep the exponents for primes up to x; for primes > x, we replace the exponent with that of p-1 (i.e., the exponent of q dividing p-1). So ord_{p,x}(a) is a hybrid number: for small primes we keep exact exponent from order; for large primes we use exponent from p-1.

Now compare ord_{p,x}(2) vs ord_{p,x}(3). For each prime p, we want which is larger.

Observation: For primes q > x, the exponent contribution is same for both 2 and 3 (since both use v_q(p-1)). Thus they cancel in comparison; we only need to compare contributions from q ≤ x.

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{\,o\ge 1 : a^{\,o}\equiv 1\pmod p \,\},
\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

For a real number \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\text{ prime}}}
q^{\,v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)}
\;
\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\text{ prime}}}
q^{\,v_q(p-1)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What does the comparison \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\) really depend on?

For every prime \(q>x\) the exponent that appears in the second product is
\(v_q(p-1)\) **both** for the number \(2\) and for the number \(3\).
Consequently the factors coming from the primes \(q>x\) cancel when we
compare the two quantities.  Hence

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\iff
\prod_{\substack{q\le x}} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
   >\prod_{\substack{q\le x}} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

Denote  

\[
A_x(p)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))},
\qquad
B_x(p)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

The condition is simply \(A_x(p)>B_x(p)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

When \(x\) increases, more primes are taken into the product.
When \(x\) exceeds every prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) the two products become exactly the full
orders:

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}A_x(p)=\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\qquad
\lim_{x\to\infty}B_x(p)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Therefore  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
      =\lim_{t\to\infty}
        \frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
             {\#\{p\le t\}} } .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of primes for which the order
of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Reformulating the problem with discrete logarithms  

For a prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\)
is cyclic of order \(p-1\).  Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\).
Then there exist unique integers \(a,b\;(1\le a,b\le p-1)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff
\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

When the primitive root \(g\) is varied uniformly among the
\(\varphi(p-1)\) primitive roots, the exponent \(a\) runs uniformly over
the set of residues **coprime** to \(p-1\).  The same is true for \(b\);
moreover the pair \((a,b)\) is obtained from a single uniformly random
unit \(a\) by multiplying with a fixed unit \(c\) (the discrete logarithm of
\(3\) to the base \(2\)).  Consequently the two random variables
\(\gcd(p-1,a)\) and \(\gcd(p-1,b)\) have the same distribution and are
symmetric.

Because of this symmetry

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)>\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)
=
\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)=\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The probability of a tie tends to zero  

For a *fixed* integer \(N\) (later \(N=p-1\)) and a uniformly chosen
\(a\in\{1,\dots ,N-1\}\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\qquad(d\mid N).
\]

Hence, for that same \(N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=\gcd(N,b)\bigr)=
\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\Bigr)^{\!2}
=
\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{e\mid N}\varphi(e)^{2}.
\]

Since \(\varphi(e)\le e\),

\[
\sum_{e\mid N}\varphi(e)^{2}\le
\sum_{e\mid N}e^{2}\le \tau(N)\,N^{2},
\]

where \(\tau(N)\) is the divisor‑function.  Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=\gcd(N,b)\bigr)\le\frac{\tau(N)}{N}.
\]

For numbers \(N=p-1\) with \(p\) prime, \(\tau(N)=N^{o(1)}\); in
particular \(\tau(N)/N\to0\) as \(p\to\infty\).
Consequently the average (over the primes) of the tie‑probability tends
to zero, and

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,a)=\gcd(p-1,b)\bigr)=0 .
\]

Putting the pieces together,

d_\infty=
\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with the ordinary multiplicative order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) when the
cut‑off \(x\) tends to infinity, because the second product disappears.
Hence  

\[
d_\infty =\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                   {\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the
order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulation with indices  

Write  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\qquad (a=2,3).
\]

\(i_a(p)\) is the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in the cyclic
group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).  
Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff
\(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\), we compare the two indices.

For a prime \(\ell\mid p-1\) let  

\[
X_\ell(a)=\begin{cases}
0,&\text{if }a\text{ is an }\ell\text{‑th power modulo }p,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Then  

\[
i_a(p)=\prod_{\ell\mid p-1}\ell^{\,X_\ell(a)} ,\qquad
\log i_a(p)=\sum_{\ell\mid p-1}X_\ell(a)\log\ell .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the random variables  

For a fixed odd prime \(\ell\) the condition “\(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power
mod \(p\)” is equivalent to the Frobenius element of \(p\) fixing a chosen
\(\ell\)-th root of \(a\) in the Kummer extension
\(\mathbb Q(\zeta_\ell ,a^{1/\ell})\).  
That extension has Galois group of order \(\ell(\ell-1)\); the subgroup
that fixes the root has index \(\ell\).  Consequently, for a random prime
\(p\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(X_\ell(a)=0\bigr)=\frac1\ell,\qquad
\Pr\bigl(X_\ell(a)=1\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell}.
\]

Assuming independence of the fields for different \(\ell\) (the usual
heuristic used for Artin‑type problems), the joint distribution for the
pair \((X_\ell(2),X_\ell(3))\) is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(0,0)&=\frac{1}{\ell^{2}},\\[2pt]
\Pr(1,0)&=\Pr(0,1)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{2}},\\[2pt]
\Pr(1,1)&=\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{\ell^{2}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus for each \(\ell\) the random variable  

\[
Y_\ell:=\bigl(X_\ell(2)-X_\ell(3)\bigr)\log\ell
\]

takes the values \(\pm\log\ell\) with equal probability
\(\displaystyle\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{2}}\) and \(0\) with probability
\(\displaystyle\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}+\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{\ell^{2}}\).
The distribution of \(Y_\ell\) is symmetric about \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Comparison of the two indices  

Define  

\[
D:=\sum_{\ell\mid p-1}Y_\ell
   =\log i_2(p)-\log i_3(p).
\]

Because the \(Y_\ell\) are independent and symmetric, the distribution of
\(D\) is symmetric:  

\[
\Pr(D>0)=\Pr(D<0).
\]

Now  

* \(D<0\)  \(\Longleftrightarrow\)  \(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\)  \(\Longleftrightarrow\)
  \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\);
* \(D>0\)  corresponds to the opposite inequality;
* \(D=0\) occurs exactly when \(X_\ell(2)=X_\ell(3)\) for every \(\ell\mid
  p-1\).

Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr(D=0)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Probability of a tie  

The event \(D=0\) means that for each prime \(\ell\) we have either
\((0,0)\) or \((1,1)\).  Its probability is therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}

### 1.  Distribution of the prime‑power part of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)

Write \(p-1=\prod_{q}q^{e_q}\).  
For a fixed prime \(q\) and a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=e_q-r\bigr)
   =\frac{1}{q^{\,r}}-\frac{1}{q^{\,r+1}}\qquad(r=0,1,\dots ,e_q-1),
\]
and  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=0\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,e_q}} .
\]

Thus for each prime \(q\) the exponent of \(q\) in the order of \(a\) is a
geometric random variable, and the exponents for \(2\) and for \(3\) are
independent.

---

### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal

For a given prime \(q\) let  

\[
E_q=\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr).
\]

Condition on the exact exponent \(e_q=k\;(k\ge1)\) of \(q\) in \(p-1\).
With the geometric law above one obtains  

\[
E_q
   =\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}
     +\frac{1}{\ell+1}
     +\frac{2}{\ell+1}\,\frac{1}{\ell^{3}-1}
   =1-\frac{2\ell}{\ell^{3}-1},
\qquad\ell=q .
\]

If \(q\nmid p-1\) the two exponents are both zero, so the same formula
holds.  
Hence the events for distinct primes are independent and

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2\ell}{\ell^{3}-1}\Bigr).
\]

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)

depends only on the true multiplicative orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) once \(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of those two orders.

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Let  

\[
d_\infty =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t : p\in S_\infty\}}{\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

For a prime \(p\) the group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
If we choose two elements of a cyclic group of order \(n\) at random, the probability that they have the same order equals  

\[
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{n}\Bigr)^{2}
      =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

The events “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)”,
“\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\)” and

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}f(p-1)}{2}.
\]

The function \(f\) is multiplicative; for a prime power \(q^{k}\)

\[
f(q^{k})=\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2}{q+1}\,q^{-2k}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{p\to\infty} f(p-1)

\]

Finally

\[

\tag{2}

*If \(\ell\mid c\):* the condition (1) is satisfied with a larger

the final product (see below).

independent (they involve different residue classes).  Therefore, for a
random prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)

\(p-1\) tends to **zero**.  In other words

\[
\delta=\operatorname{dens}\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}=0.
\]

The quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty }(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)
\]

is simply the multiplicative order of \(a\) modulo the prime \(p\).
Hence  

\[
S_{\infty}=\{p\;:\; \operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) write \(p-1=n\).  
Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\); then  

\[
2\equiv g^{\alpha},\qquad 3\equiv g^{\beta}\qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\{1,\dots ,n\}).
\]

Because \(g\) is a primitive root, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are uniformly distributed among the integers coprime to \(n\) and (heuristically) can be treated as independent random variables modulo \(n\).

The order of \(g^{\alpha}\) is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,\alpha)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,\beta)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\iff 
\gcd (n,\alpha)<\gcd (n,\beta).
\]

For a fixed even integer \(n\) let  

\[
T(n)=\Pr\bigl(\gcd (n,\alpha)=\gcd (n,\beta)\bigr)
      =\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi (n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-T(n)}{2}.
\]

Averaging over all primes \(p\) (i.e. over all even \(n=p-1\)) we need the mean value of  

\[
f(n)=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}}{n^{2}} .
\]

The function \(f\) is multiplicative; for a prime power \(p^{k}\),

\[
\sum_{d\mid p^{k}}\varphi(d)^{2}
=1+(p-1)^{2}\frac{p^{2k}-1}{p^{2}-1}
=\frac{2+(p-1)p^{2k}}{p+1},
\]

so  

\[
f(p^{k})=\frac{2+(p-1)p^{2k}}{(p+1)p^{2k}}
        =\frac{p-1}{p+1}+\frac{2}{(p+1)p^{2k}} .
\]

Consequently the average of \(f\) over all integers is the Euler product  

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\prod_{p}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)
     \sum_{k\ge0}f(p^{k})\,p^{-k}\\[2mm]
  &=\prod_{p}
     \frac{(p-1)(p^{3}+2p^{2}-1)}{(p+1)(p^{3}-1)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

A short computation shows that the logarithm of the factor for a prime \(p\) is  

\[
\log\!\Bigl(\frac{(p-1)(p^{3}+2p^{2}-1)}{(p+1)(p^{3}-1)}\Bigr)
=-\frac{2}{p^{2}}+\frac{2}{p^{3}}-\frac{2}{p^{4}}+\frac{2}{p^{5}}
-\frac{8}{3p^{6}}+\cdots .
\]

Summing over all primes gives  

\[
\log A=-2P(2)+2P(3)-2P(4)+2P(5)-\frac{8}{3}P(6)+\cdots ,

where \(P(s)=\sum_{p}p^{-s}\) is the prime zeta‑function.

\[

\]

Consequently  

\[

   =\sum_{j=0}^{k}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(q^{j})}{q^{k}}\Bigr)^{2}
   =\frac{1}{q^{2k}}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\varphi(q^{j})^{2}.

Let's provide reasoning stepwise.

**Step 1.  Understanding \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\)**  

For a prime \(p\) and an integer \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{o>0 : a^{\,o}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

Write the prime factorisation  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))},
\qquad 
p-1=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} q^{\,v_q(p-1)} .
\]

For a real number \(x>0\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\Bigl(\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)}\Bigr).
\]

Thus for the “small’’ primes \(q\le x\) we keep the exact exponent that occurs in the true order,
while for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\) we replace the exponent by the (larger) exponent that
occurs in \(p-1\).  Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\;\le\;\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\;\le\;p-1 .
\]

When \(x\) grows, more prime factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) are taken into account,
so  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 2.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)**  

The set  

\[
S_x=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\}
\]

has density  

\[
d_x=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_x\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\to\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for each fixed prime \(p\),
the limiting density  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
\]

is precisely the density of primes for which  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Hence **the problem reduces to finding the natural density of primes \(p\) with
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).**

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 3.  Reformulating the inequality**  

The multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
For any element \(a\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{d_a},
\qquad
d_a:=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)},
\]

so \(d_a\) is the index of the subgroup \(\langle a\rangle\).

Now  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff 
\frac{p-1}{d_2}>\frac{p-1}{d_3}
\iff d_2<d_3 .
\]

Because subgroups of a cyclic group are uniquely determined by their order,
\(\langle 3\rangle\subseteq\langle 2\rangle\) exactly when \(d_2\mid d_3\).
Thus

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff 
d_2\mid d_3\ \text{and}\ d_2<d_3 .
\tag{1}
\]

Equivalently, the order of \(3\) **divides** the order of \(2\) but the two orders are not equal.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 4.  Symmetry between \(2\) and \(3\)**  

The distribution of the pair \((\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\) over the
primes is invariant under swapping the two components:
the map \(p\mapsto p\) sends the set \(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\)
onto the set \(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}\).
Consequently these two sets have the same natural density.

Denote

* \(A\) = density of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\);
* \(B\) = density of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\);
* \(E\) = density of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

By symmetry \(A=B\) and \(A+B+E=1\). Hence  

\[
A=\frac{1-E}{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 5.  Showing that \(E=0\)**  

If \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=n\), then the two generated subgroups are
the same, so each element is a power of the other:
\(2\equiv 3^{k}\pmod p\) for some integer \(k\) coprime to \(n\).

Thus a prime \(p\) with equal orders must divide a number of the form  

\[
2-3^{k}\qquad(k\ge 1).
\]

For each fixed \(k\) the integer \(2-3^{k}\) has only finitely many prime divisors.
Consequently the set of primes that satisfy the equality is contained in the union  

\[
\bigcup_{k\ge 1}\{\,p\mid p\text{ divides }2-3^{k}\,\}.
\]

This is a **thin** set of primes; its natural density is \(0\).  
(Indeed, the sum of reciprocals of all primes in the union converges, so the
set cannot have positive density.)

Therefore  

\[
E=0.
\]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 6.  Computing \(d_\infty\)**  

From (2) with \(E=0\) we obtain  

\[
d_\infty=A=\frac{1}{2}.
\]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 7.  Final numeric answer**  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 500\,000 \bigr\rfloor
   = 500\,000 .
\]

The quantity  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
\]

is the natural density of the primes \(p\) for which  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

For a prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
If \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\) we can write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p ,
\]

with \(a,b\in\{0,1,\dots ,p-2\}\).  
The order of an element is the size of the subgroup it generates; it is obtained from
\(p-1\) by removing exactly those prime‑power factors for which the element is a
\(q\)-th (or \(q^{2}\)‑th, …) power modulo \(p\).

For a fixed prime \(q\mid(p-1)\) the events  

\[
\text{“\(2\) is a \(q\)-th power modulo }p\text{”},\qquad
\text{“\(3\) is a \(q\)-th power modulo }p\text{”}
\]

are independent, and each occurs with probability \(1/q\) (Chebotarev density
theorem). Consequently, for each \(q\) the exponent of \(q\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\)
and in \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are independent random variables having the same
distribution. Moreover the collections of these exponents for different primes
\(q\) are independent.

Hence the joint distribution of the two orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is symmetric: swapping the two numbers leaves the
distribution unchanged.  By this symmetry

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

The probability that the two orders are equal is zero, because it would require
the equality of infinitely many independent \(q\)-adic valuations, an event of
measure zero.  Therefore the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) has natural density

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

Finally,

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
   = 500000 .
\]

### 1.   Distribution of the prime‑power part of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)

Let \(q\) be a prime.  
For a random odd prime \(p\),

* \(q\mid p-1\) with probability \(\displaystyle\frac{1}{q-1}\) (Dirichlet).
* Conditional on \(q\mid p-1\), the probability that \(a\) is a \(q^k\)-th power
  residue (and not a \(q^{k+1}\)-st power) equals  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=v_q(p-1)-k\bigr)=\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}},
\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

Thus for a fixed prime \(q\) the random variables  

\[
K_a(q)=v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)),\qquad a=2,3,
\]

are independent and satisfy  

\[
\Pr\bigl(K_a(q)=k\bigr)=\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}},\qquad k\ge 0 .
\]

### 2.   Probability that the two orders are equal

For a fixed odd prime \(q\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))=v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\mid q\mid p-1\bigr)
  &=\sum_{k\ge0}\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}}\Bigr)^2
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(q\nmid p-1\) both exponents are zero, so equality also holds.
Hence the contribution of an odd prime \(q\) to the overall probability
that the two orders coincide is  

\[
\Bigl(1-\frac1{q-1}\Bigr)+\frac1{q-1}\cdot\frac{q-1}{q+1}
   =1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}.
\]

For \(q=2\) we always have \(2\mid p-1\); the same calculation gives the
factor  

\[
\frac{1}{3}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\boxed{P_{\text{eq}}=
        \frac13\prod_{\substack{q\;{\rm prime}\\ q\ge 3}}
                 \Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr)} .
\]

### 3.   Evaluating the product

Write  

\[
1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}= \frac{q^{2}-3}{q^{2}-1}

Hence  

\[
\prod_{q\ge 3}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr)

The quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

equals \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) multiplied by the “missing’’ prime‑power factors of \(p-1\) that are larger than \(x\).  
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a) .
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                               {\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulation in terms of \(\gcd\)  

Let \(p\) be a prime and write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as
\(\langle g\rangle\) where \(g\) is a primitive root.  
There are integers \(a,b\;(1\le a,b\le p-2)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

The order of \(2\) (resp. \(3\)) is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(a,p-1)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(b,p-1)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow \gcd(a,p-1)<\gcd(b,p-1) .
\]

Because \(g\) is a primitive root, the pair \((a,b)\) is uniformly distributed
in \((\mathbb Z/(p-1))^{2}\) (the only restriction is that \(a,b\neq0\), which
does not affect the limit).  Hence for a fixed integer \(n=p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(A,n)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n},
\qquad A\ \text{uniform in } \{1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

Let  

\[
P_n=\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^2
    =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Then  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(a,n)=\gcd(b,n)\bigr)=P_n .
\]

Since the distribution of \(\gcd(a,n)\) and \(\gcd(b,n)\) is symmetric,
\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(a,n)<\gcd(b,n)\bigr)
      =\frac{1-P_n}{2}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{1-P_{p-1}}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  An explicit multiplicative expression for \(P_n\)

Define  

\[
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

\(f\) is multiplicative; for a prime power \(q^{e}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(q^{e})&=1+\sum_{j=1}^{e}\bigl(\varphi(q^{j})\bigr)^{2}                \\
        &=1+(q-1)^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{e}q^{2j-2}
          =1+\frac{(q-1)^{2}}{q^{2}-1}\,(q^{2e}-1) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{f(q^{e})}{q^{2e}}
     =\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2}{q+1}\,q^{-2e}.
\]

For a general integer \(n=\prod q_i^{e_i}\),

\[
P_n=\frac{f(n)}{n^{2}}
    =\prod_{q\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2}{q+1}\,q^{-2e_q}\Bigr).
\]

When the exponent \(e_q\) is at least \(1\) the term
\(\frac{2}{q+1}q^{-2e_q}\) is tiny; consequently

\[
P_n\approx\prod_{q\mid n}\frac{q-1}{q+1}
          \;=:h(n).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Average of \(h(p-1)\) over the primes  

The function \(h\) is multiplicative and depends only on the set of prime
divisors of its argument.  For a random integer \(m\),

\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[h(m)\bigr]
   =\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)
      +\frac1q\frac{q-1}{q+1}
   =\prod_{q}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q(q+1)}\Bigr).
\]

The same Euler product gives the mean value of \(h(p-1)\) when \(p\) runs
through the primes (the distribution of the prime‑divisors of \(p-1\) is the
same as for a typical even integer).  Numerically

\[
C:=\prod_{q}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q(q+1)}\Bigr)
   =0.4680\ldots .
\]

(The product converges rapidly; using all primes up to \(10^{5}\) gives
\(C=0.46803\) and the remaining tail changes the value only in the fifth
decimal place.)

Thus  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}P_{p-1}=C\qquad\text{and}\qquad
d_\infty=\frac{1-C}{2}=0.2660\ldots .
\]

\[
2\equiv g^{k_{2}},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_{3}}\pmod p ,
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_{2})},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_{3})}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\iff
\gcd(p-1,k_{2})<\gcd(p-1,k_{3}).
\tag{1}
\]

If we exchange the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) we obtain the opposite
inequality.  
Thus, apart from the primes for which the two orders are *equal*, the
set of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\)
is in bijection with the set of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\).

\[

\tau = \text{natural density of } \{p : \operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=

### 2.  The density of the equality set is zero

The condition \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) is
equivalent to the two numbers generating the same subgroup of
\((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).  
That happens precisely when  

\[
2\equiv 3^{m}\pmod p\quad\text{for some }m\text{ coprime to }
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3).
\tag{3}
\]

Equation (3) means that the prime \(p\) splits completely in the
splitting field of the polynomial \(X^{m}-2\) together with the
splitting field of \(X^{\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)}-3\).
Both fields are finite Galois extensions of \(\mathbb Q\) whose degrees
are bounded (they are generated by adjoining roots of unity and radicals
of the fixed integers \(2\) and \(3\)).  
By the Chebotarev density theorem, the set of primes satisfying a
prescribed splitting condition in a **fixed** finite Galois extension
has a natural density equal to the proportion of the corresponding
conjugacy class in the Galois group.  

In (3) the exponent \(m\) can be any integer; however, for a given prime
\(p\) the order \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) is a divisor of \(p-1\), and
the possible values of \(m\) are bounded by that divisor.  Consequently,
the equality condition can be expressed as the union of finitely many
Chebotarev conditions, each of which has a density that is a rational
multiple of \(1/[K:\mathbb Q]\) for some finite Galois extension \(K\).
Summing over the finitely many possibilities gives a total density that
is a *finite* sum of such rational numbers.

The proportion of primes for which a fixed proper divisor \(d\mid p-1\)
contains both \(2\) and \(3\) is \(O(1/p)\); summing over all possible
\(d\) gives a convergent series.  Hence the set of primes with equal
orders has natural density **zero**:

\[
\tau =0.
\tag{4}
\]

\qquad

### 1.  Behaviour of the exponents \(t_\ell(2)\) and \(t_\ell(3)\)

For a given prime \(\ell\) the condition “\(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power modulo \(p\)’’ is a condition on the Frobenius element of \(p\) in the Kummer extension  

\[
\mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{\ell^{\,e_\ell}},a^{1/\ell^{\,e_\ell}}\bigr).
\]

Chebotarev’s density theorem tells us that, when \(p\) varies,
the exponent \(t_\ell(a)\) is **independent** of the exponent
\(t_\ell(b)\) for any other integer \(b\) (provided \(a\) and \(b\) are not
\(\ell\)-th powers in \(\mathbb{Q}\)).  
Consequently, for each prime \(\ell\) the random variables
\(t_\ell(2)\) and \(t_\ell(3)\) are identically distributed and independent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Comparing \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)

Write  

\[
\frac{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)}{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)}
      =\prod_{\ell}\ell^{\,t_\ell(3)-t_\ell(2)} .
\]

Because the families \(\{t_\ell(2)\}_\ell\) and \(\{t_\ell(3)\}_\ell\) are
independent and have the same distribution, the random variable
\(\displaystyle\log\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)/\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\sum_\ell (t_\ell(3)-t_\ell(2))\log\ell\)
is symmetric about \(0\).
Hence  

\[
\Pr\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

### 3.  The event of equality has density \(0\)

Equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) would require
\(t_\ell(2)=t_\ell(3)\) for **every** prime \(\ell\) dividing \(p-1\).
Since for each individual \(\ell\) the probability that
\(t_\ell(2)=t_\ell(3)\) is strictly less than \(1\) and the events for
different \(\ell\) are independent, the probability that they coincide
for all \(\ell\) is the product of infinitely many numbers each \(<1\);
this product is \(0\).
Thus the set of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
has natural density \(0\).

### 2.  Symmetry of the orders of two fixed elements

Let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\) be distinct and non‑zero modulo any prime.
For a prime \(p\) denote \(G_p=(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\), a cyclic group of
order \(p-1\).
Write  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{e_a(p)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(b)=\frac{p-1}{e_b(p)},
\]

where \(e_a(p),e_b(p)\) are the indices of the subgroups \(\langle a\rangle\) and
\(\langle b\rangle\) in \(G_p\).

For a fixed integer \(n\) consider the Kummer extensions  

\[
K_a(n)=\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_n, a^{1/n}\bigr),\qquad
K_b(n)=\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_n, b^{1/n}\bigr),
\]

where \(\zeta_n\) is a primitive \(n\)‑th root of unity.
Both fields are Galois over \(\mathbb Q\) and their compositum  

\[
L_n = K_a(n)K_b(n)=\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_n, a^{1/n}, b^{1/n}\bigr)
\]

has Galois group  

\[
\operatorname{Gal}(L_n/\mathbb Q)\simeq
\{(\sigma,\tau)\mid \sigma,\tau\in (\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times}\},
\]

which is invariant under swapping the two coordinates.
Consequently the Frobenius automorphism attached to a prime
\(p\nmid nab\) has the same distribution whether we look at the pair
\((\operatorname{ord}_p(a),\operatorname{ord}_p(b))\) or the pair
\((\operatorname{ord}_p(b),\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\).

By the Chebotarev density theorem, the set of primes for which
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)>\operatorname{ord}_p(b)\) has the same natural
density as the set where \(\operatorname{ord}_p(b)>\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\).

### 3.  Density of the equality case

If \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(b)=d\), then both \(a\) and
\(b\) belong to the unique subgroup of \(G_p\) of order \(d\); hence
\(a\equiv b^{k}\pmod p\) for some integer \(k\) with \(\gcd(k,d)=1\).
Thus \(p\mid a-b^{k}\).  For each fixed \(k\) the integer \(a-b^{k}\) has only
finitely many prime divisors, so the set of primes satisfying the equality for
a given \(k\) is finite.  Because \(k\) can be taken only from the set of
divisors of \(p-1\), which grows at most logarithmically, the union over all
possible \(k\) still has natural density \(0\).

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{dens}\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(b)\}=0 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
p-1 = N .
\]

Since \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(N\), choose a primitive root \(g\).
Then for any integer \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod p\) there is a unique exponent
\(k_a\;(0\le k_a<N)\) such that  

\[
a \equiv g^{k_a}\pmod p .
\]

The order of \(a\) modulo \(p\) is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,k_a)} .
\tag{1}
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{N}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}=\gcd(N,k_a)
\]

is the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What the limit \(d_{\infty}\) measures  

Because  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\;\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\;\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\]

the condition defining the set \(S_x\) becomes, for \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\frac{N}{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)}<\frac{N}{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\gcd(N,k_2)<\gcd(N,k_3).
\]

Thus  

\[
S_{\infty}:=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

and  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{\#\{p\le t : p\in S_{\infty}\}}
{\#\{p\le t\}} .
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the two bases  

For every prime \(p\) (different from \(2,3\)) the pair \((\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\) is exchanged by the automorphism  

\[
\phi : (\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\longrightarrow (\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times},
\qquad
\phi(g^{k}) = g^{\,\sigma(k)},
\]

where \(\sigma\) is any permutation of the set \(\{0,1,\dots ,N-1\}\) that sends
\(k_2\) to \(k_3\) and \(k_3\) to \(k_2\) while leaving the other residues
unchanged.  Because the primitive root \(g\) is arbitrary, the distribution of
the exponents \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) over the primes is the same; in particular

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
        =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The set where the orders are equal has density \(0\)

Let  

\[
E:=\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

If \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\), then both
\(2\) and \(3\) lie in the same subgroup of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) of
order \(d\).  Consequently the field \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_d,2^{1/d})\) and the
field \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_d,3^{1/d})\) have a common subfield of degree \(>1\)
over \(\mathbb Q\).  By the Chebotarev density theorem the set of primes that
split completely in a fixed proper extension of \(\mathbb Q\) has density
\(0\).  Since for each possible divisor \(d\) of \(p-1\) we obtain a different
finite Galois extension, the union over all \(d\) still has density \(0\).
Hence  

\[
\delta(E)=0 .
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Computing the limit  

From (3) and (4) we have

\[
1=\delta\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   +\delta\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)
   +\delta(E)
   =2\,\delta\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \delta\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
          =\frac12 .
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required numeric value  

\[
\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\right\rfloor
   =\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times \frac12\right\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

### A probabilistic model

Write \(p-1 = g\).  
Because \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic, there is a primitive root
\(g\) with  

\[
2\equiv g^{a_p},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b_p}\pmod p .
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{g}{\gcd(g,a_p)},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{g}{\gcd(g,b_p)} .
\]

Hence \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff  

\[
\gcd(g,a_p)<\gcd(g,b_p).
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the exponents \(a_p,b_p\) are determined, but when
\(p\) varies they behave like **independent uniformly distributed residues**
modulo \(g\).  Consequently the random variables  

\[
I_2(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)},\qquad
I_3(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)}
\]

are independent and identically distributed.

For each odd prime \(\ell\) the event \(\ell\mid I_a(p)\) means that \(a\) is
an \(\ell\)-th power modulo \(p\); by Chebotarev this occurs with density
\(1/\ell\).  Thus for every \(\ell\ge 5\) we may view the inclusion of \(\ell\)
in the factorisation of \(I_a(p)\) as an independent Bernoulli trial with
probability \(1/\ell\).  The same description holds for \(a=2\) and
\(a=3\); the two families of trials are independent.

Therefore \(I_2(p)\) and \(I_3(p)\) are independent, identically distributed
random integers.  For any two i.i.d. random variables we have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(I_2<I_3\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(I_3<I_2\bigr)
                     =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(I_2=I_3\bigr)}{2}.
\]

The probability that the two independent copies are equal is

\[
\Pr(I_2=I_3)=\sum_{n\ge1}\Pr(I=n)^2
           =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl[(1-\tfrac1\ell)^2+(\tfrac1\ell)^2\Bigr]
           =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr)=0,
\]

because \(\sum_{\ell}2/\ell\) diverges, forcing the infinite product to
vanish.  Hence the equality event has density \(0\).

Consequently

\[
d_\infty =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
          =\frac12 .
\]
