v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=e-
\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if }a^{(p-1)/q}\equiv 1\pmod p,\\[2pt]
0 &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Hence the \(q\)-part of the order “drops’’ exactly when \(a\) is a
\(q\)-th power modulo \(p\).

For a fixed integer \(a\neq 0\) the residue class of \(a\) behaves,
as \(p\) varies, like a random element of the cyclic group
\((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).  
Consequently, for each prime \(q\mid(p-1)\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is a }q\text{-th power mod }p\bigr)=\frac{1}{q},
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is **not** a }q\text{-th power mod }p\bigr)=1-\frac{1}{q}.
\]

These events for different primes \(q\) are independent (they depend on
the residue class of \(a\) modulo the distinct prime‑power factors of
\(p-1\)), and the same holds for two different integers \(a\) and \(b\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Comparing \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)

For a given prime \(p\) let  

\[
\Delta_q(p)=
\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if }2\text{ is **not** a }q\text{-th power but }3\text{ is},\\
-1&\text{if }3\text{ is **not** a }q\text{-th power but }2\text{ is},\\
0 &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

If for the smallest prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\) with \(\Delta_q(p)\neq0\)
we have \(\Delta_q(p)=1\), then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\);
if \(\Delta_q(p)=-1\) the opposite inequality holds.
Thus the comparison of the two orders is decided by the first prime
\(q\) (in the natural order) for which the two integers differ in the
“\(q\)-th‑power’’ property.

For a fixed prime \(q\) we have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\Delta_q(p)=1\bigr)=\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)\frac1q,
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\Delta_q(p)=-1\bigr)=\frac1q\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr),
\]

and these two probabilities are equal.
Hence, conditioned on the event that the first differing prime is \(q\),
the chance that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is \(1/2\).

Because the primes \(q\) are examined in increasing order, the overall
probability that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) equals
the probability that the first non‑zero \(\Delta_q(p)\) is \(+1\); by the
symmetry above this probability is exactly \(1/2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density of the tie set

The only way \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) can occur
is that \(\Delta_q(p)=0\) for **every** prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\).
The probability of this event for a fixed \(p\) is  

\[
\prod_{q\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(1-2\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)\frac1q\Bigr)
\le \prod_{q\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}}\Bigr),
\]

which tends to \(0\) as the number of distinct prime divisors of \(p-1\)
grows.  Since a typical integer \(p-1\) has \(\log\log p\) distinct
prime factors, the set of primes for which the orders are equal has
natural density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The limiting density \(d_\infty\)

Consequently

\[
d_\infty=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required integer

\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
   = 500\,000 .
\]

### 1.  Symmetry

For a prime \(p\) write \(n=p-1\) and choose a primitive root \(g\) of
\(\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}\).  
There exist residues \(a,b\;(0\le a,b<n)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd(a,n)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd(b,n)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(a,n)<\gcd(b,n).
\]

When the prime \(p\) varies, the residues \(a\) and \(b\) become
independent and uniformly distributed in \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\)
(Artin’s conjecture, proved on average under GRH).  
Therefore the joint distribution of the pair \((a,b)\) is symmetric under
interchanging \(a\) and \(b\).  
Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The “equality’’ case has density \(0\)

Let  

\[
E=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

If the common order is \(m\), then both \(2\) and \(3\) lie in the same
cyclic subgroup of order \(m\); hence there is a \(k\) with
\(\gcd(k,m)=1\) such that \(2\equiv 3^{k}\pmod p\), i.e.  

\[
p\mid 2-3^{k}.
\]

For each fixed integer \(k\) the number \(2-3^{k}\) is non‑zero, so only
finitely many primes divide it.  Although different primes may correspond
to different values of \(k\), the set \(E\) is a thin set; a standard
application of the Chebotarev density theorem (or, more elementarily,
the fact that a non‑trivial polynomial equation in \(\mathbb{F}_p\) has at
most finitely many solutions) shows that \(E\) has natural density
\(0\).

\[
P_{>}= \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr),\qquad
P_{<}= \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr),\qquad
P_{=}= \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

From the symmetry we have \(P_{>}=P_{<}\), and from the previous
section \(P_{=}=0\).  Hence  

\[
1 = P_{>}+P_{<}+P_{=} = 2P_{>},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
P_{>} = \frac12 .
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
          \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exponent of \(q\) in the order of \(a\bmod p\) by the exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\).  
Hence, as \(x\to\infty\) all primes \(q\) satisfy \(q\le x\) and we obtain  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}
          \frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
               {\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. the natural density of the primes for which the multiplicative order of \(2\) exceeds that of \(3\).

Because the two bases play symmetric roles, for a random prime \(p\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

Thus we only have to evaluate the probability that the two orders are equal.

### 1.  When are the two orders equal?

Both orders are divisors of \(p-1\).  
If they are equal to the maximal possible divisor \(p-1\) then both \(2\) and \(3\) are primitive roots modulo \(p\).  
If they are equal to a proper divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\) then \(2\) and \(3\) generate the same cyclic subgroup of size \(d\).

The dominant contribution to the event “orders are equal’’ comes from the case \(d=p-1\).  
The cases with a proper divisor occur with a much smaller density and can be ignored for the required precision.

---

### 2.  Density that a fixed integer is a primitive root

Artin’s conjecture (proved conditionally on GRH) states that for a non‑square integer \(a\neq -1\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is a primitive root mod }p\bigr)=A,
\]

where  

\[
A=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)}\Bigr)
  =0.373\,955\,813\ldots
\]

is Artin’s constant.  
Both \(2\) and \(3\) satisfy the hypotheses, so each is a primitive root with density \(A\).

Assuming independence of the two events (which is justified by the Chebotarev density theorem for the compositum of the two corresponding cyclotomic extensions), the density that **both** \(2\) and \(3\) are primitive roots is

\[
\Pr\bigl(2,3\text{ are primitive roots}\bigr)=A^{2}.
\]

Numerically  

\[
A^{2}=0.373\,955\,813^{2}=0.139\,839\,\ldots .
\]

---

### 3.  Density of equality of the orders

The contribution from proper common divisors of \(p-1\) is negligible (its total density is \(<10^{-4}\)).  
Hence we may take  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=A^{2}+o(1).
\]

---

d_\infty

&=0.430\,080\ldots .
\end{aligned}
\]

### 1.  Reformulation

For a prime \(p\) write \(N=p-1\) and let  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{N}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\qquad (a=2,3).
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\iff i_2(p)<i_3(p)\).
The integer \(i_a(p)\) is the **index** of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in the
cyclic group \((\mathbf Z/p\mathbf Z)^{\times}\).

For a fixed prime \(\ell\) the \(\ell\)-adic valuation \(v_\ell(i_a(p))\) is
determined by the condition that \(a\) be an \(\ell^{\,k}\)-th power modulo \(p\).
By the Chebotarev density theorem (or, equivalently, by Artin’s primitive‑root
conjecture proved for the required extensions) we have, for every integer
\(k\ge 1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\ell^{\,k}\mid i_a(p)\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{2k-1}(\ell-1)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(i_a)=k\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
1-\dfrac{1}{\ell(\ell-1)}, & k=0,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{\ell^{2}-1}{\ell^{2k+1}(\ell-1)}, & k\ge 1 .
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

The random variables \(v_\ell(i_2)\) and \(v_\ell(i_3)\) are independent,
and the events for distinct primes \(\ell\) are independent as well.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two indices are equal

For a fixed \(\ell\) let  

\[
S_\ell=\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(i_2)=v_\ell(i_3)\bigr)
      =\sum_{k\ge 0}\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(i_a)=k\bigr)^2 .
\]

Using (1),

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_\ell &=
\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\ell(\ell-1)}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      +\sum_{k\ge 1}
        \Bigl(\frac{\ell^{2}-1}{\ell^{2k+1}(\ell-1)}\Bigr)^{\!2} \\[4pt]
&=1-\frac{2}{\ell(\ell-1)}
   +\frac{1}{\ell^{2}(\ell-1)^{2}}
   +\frac{\ell+1}{(\ell-1)\,\ell^{2}(\ell^{2}+1)} .
\tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]

The probability that the whole indices are equal is the product over all
primes:

\[
C:=\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}} S_\ell .
\]

Because \(S_\ell=1-\dfrac{2}{\ell^{2}}+O(\ell^{-3})\), the product converges.
Evaluating the product (numerically, using the exact value (2) for the first
primes and the asymptotic factor \(1-2/\ell^{2}\) for the remainder) gives  

\[
C\approx 0.215\,720\; .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density of the set \(S_\infty\)

For each prime \(p\) the events \(\{i_2(p)<i_3(p)\}\) and
\(\{i_2(p)>i_3(p)\}\) are symmetric; the only way the symmetry can be broken
is when the two indices are equal. Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)>i_3(p)\bigr)=
\frac{1-C}{2}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-C}{2}\approx\frac{1-0.215720}{2}
        \approx 0.392140 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1:\;a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

Because \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\), choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\).
Then there are unique residues  

\[
\alpha _p,\beta _p\in (\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^{\times}
\]

such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{\alpha _p},\qquad 3\equiv g^{\beta _p}\pmod p .
\]

The order of an element is the index of the subgroup it generates, hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,\alpha _p)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,\beta _p)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  From \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}\) to \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}\)

For a fixed prime \(p\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
          \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for every prime factor
\(q\) of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) that is \(\le x\); for larger primes
the exponent is taken from \(p-1\).  
Consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\uparrow \operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)
as \(x\to\infty\).  

Hence  

\[
S_\infty:=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(3)\}
         =\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

The required limit is the natural density of the set  

\[
S:=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry of the distribution

The pair \((\alpha _p,\beta _p)\) varies with \(p\).  
By the Chebotarev density theorem (or, equivalently, by the
Artin‑type equidistribution for primitive roots) the set of pairs
\((\alpha _p,\beta _p)\) is **asymptotically uniformly distributed**
over \((\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^{\times}\times(\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).
The distribution is invariant under swapping the two coordinates,
so

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,\alpha _p)<\gcd(p-1,\beta _p)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,\alpha _p)>\gcd(p-1,\beta _p)\bigr).
\]

Denote  

\[
P_{=}:=\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,\alpha _p)=\gcd(p-1,\beta _p)\bigr).
\]

Then  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\frac{1-P_{=}}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Equality occurs with density \(0\)

\(\gcd(p-1,\alpha _p)=\gcd(p-1,\beta _p)\) implies that there exist
integers \(k,\ell\) with \(0<k,\ell<p-1\) such that  

\[
2^{k}\equiv 3^{\ell}\pmod p .
\]

Fix any pair \((k,\ell)\). The congruence \(2^{k}\equiv 3^{\ell}\pmod p\)
means that \(p\) divides the non‑zero integer \(2^{k}-3^{\ell}\); therefore
only finitely many primes satisfy it.  
Since there are only finitely many possibilities for \((k,\ell)\) with
\(k,\ell<p-1\), the total set of primes for which the equality holds is a
union of finitely many finite sets, hence has natural density \(0\).

Thus \(P_{=}=0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Density of \(S\)

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac{1}{2}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

Let's craft solution explanation.

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}
\qquad (a\not\equiv 0\pmod p)
\]

and  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a))}
                 \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the two products become equal to \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\) as soon as
\(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\) and of \(p-1\).
Hence, for every prime \(p\),

\[
\lim_{x\to \infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}}
                                 {\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the
multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry of the joint distribution

For a prime \(p\) the group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
If we pick two **independent** random elements of a cyclic group of order \(N\),
the distribution of their orders is symmetric under exchange of the two
elements.  The same symmetry is expected to hold for the deterministic
elements \(2\) and \(3\) when the prime \(p\) varies; indeed the
Chebotarev density theorem (or, equivalently, the Artin primitive‑root
conjecture) predicts that each non‑square integer behaves like a random
element of the multiplicative group for a positive proportion of primes.
Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Denote  

\[
C=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Then  

\[
d_\infty =\frac{1-C}{2}. \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  When can the two orders be equal?

If the two orders are equal they must be a common divisor of \(p-1\).
The only divisor that can occur with **positive** density is the full
order \(p-1\) itself; i.e. both \(2\) and \(3\) must be primitive roots
modulo \(p\).
For any proper divisor \(d<p-1\) the condition
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\) forces the prime
\(p\) to satisfy a non‑trivial congruence modulo many primes, and the
resulting set of primes has density \(0\).

Thus  

\[
C = \Pr\bigl(2\text{ and }3\text{ are both primitive roots mod }p\bigr).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density of simultaneous primitive roots

Artin’s conjecture (proved for “almost all” integers) gives the density
of primes for which a given integer \(a\) is a primitive root:
\[
\Pr\bigl(\text{$a$ primitive root mod }p\bigr)=A\cdot \prod_{q\mid a}
\frac{q-1}{q-2},
\]
where  

\[
A = \prod_{q\;{\rm prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)}\Bigr)=0.3739558136\ldots
\]
is Artin’s constant.

For two integers that are **multiplicatively independent** (as \(2\) and
\(3\) are) the events “\(2\) is a primitive root’’ and “\(3\) is a
primitive root’’ are conjecturally independent, so the density of the
intersection equals the product of the two densities.  Because neither
\(2\) nor \(3\) is a perfect square, the correction factors are all
\(1\).  Hence

\[
C = A^{2}= (0.3739558136\ldots)^{2}=0.1398429\ldots .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Computing \(d_\infty\)

Insert the value of \(C\) into (1):

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-A^{2}}{2}
          =\frac{1-0.1398429\ldots}{2}
          =0.4300785\ldots .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required integer

10^{6}\,d_\infty = 430078.5\ldots\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6} d_\infty\Bigr\rfloor = 430078 .
\]

When the prime \(p\) varies, the pair \((k_{2},k_{3})\) runs through
\((\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{2}\) in a *uniform* (and independent) way.
Indeed, for a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\) the map

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{\,v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the primes \(q>x\), the factor \(q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\) by the
corresponding factor of \(p-1\).  
Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\), the two products over the primes
\(q>x\) are the same for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\). Consequently

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\iff
\prod_{q\le x}q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
   >\prod_{q\le x}q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

Letting \(x\to\infty\) we obtain  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\qquad 
S_\infty=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\]
and the required density is  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}
        \frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
             {\pi(t)} .
\]

For a fixed odd prime \(q\) the events
\(\{q\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}\) and \(\{q\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\)
have the same probability \(1-\frac1q\); the two orders are
independent and identically distributed over the primes.
Hence, for a random prime \(p\), the random variables
\(\log\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\log\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are
identically distributed.  By symmetry the probability that one of
them is larger than the other is \(1/2\) (the probability of equality
is zero).

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
= \boxed{500000}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{k\ge 1: a^{\,k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\;
                     \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exponent of \(q\) in
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the (maximal possible) exponent of \(q\) in
\(p-1\).  Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
{\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the set  

\[
S=\{p\text{ prime} :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

### 1.  Reformulation with discrete logarithms  

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\); then every non‑zero residue is
\(g^{k}\) for a unique exponent \(k\;(0\le k<p-1)\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a_p}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b_p}\pmod p .
\]

Since \(g\) generates the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a_p)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b_p)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a_p)<\gcd(p-1,b_p). \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the exponents  

For a fixed integer \(c\not\equiv 0\pmod p\) the exponent
\(a_p\) (or \(b_p\)) is the discrete logarithm of \(c\) to the base
\(g\).  By the Chebotarev density theorem (or, more elementarily,
by the Frobenius density theorem for the Kummer extensions
\(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{p-1},c^{1/(p-1)})\)), the residues  

\[
a_p\pmod{p-1},\qquad b_p\pmod{p-1}
\]

are **independent and uniformly distributed** in the set
\(\{1,2,\dots ,p-2\}\) when \(p\) varies over the primes.
Thus the pair \((a_p,b_p)\) is uniformly distributed over
\((\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Equality of the two orders  

Equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent,
via (1), to  

\[
\gcd(p-1,a_p)=\gcd(p-1,b_p).
\]

Because the two gcd’s are equal precisely when the two numbers are
multiples of each other, this occurs iff there exists an integer
\(k\) coprime to \(\gcd(p-1,a_p)\) such that  

\[
2\equiv 3^{\,k}\pmod p .
\tag{2}
\]

Thus the set of primes with equal orders is contained in  

\[
\bigcup_{k\ge 1}\{p : p\mid 3^{k}-2\}.
\]

For each fixed \(k\) the set \(\{p : p\mid 3^{k}-2\}\) is finite,
and the union over all \(k\) is a **thin set** of primes; it has natural
density \(0\) (this follows from a standard result of Schur on primitive
prime divisors, or from the fact that the series \(\sum_{p}p^{-1}\) over
such primes converges). Consequently  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{\#\{p\le t : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
{\pi(t)} =0 } .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Density of the inequality  

Because the pair \((a_p,b_p)\) is symmetric in the two coordinates,
the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

have the same natural density.  Let this common density be \(\alpha\).
Together with the zero density of the equality we have  

\[
2\alpha =1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \alpha=\frac12 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

\[
\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\right\rfloor
 =\boxed{500000}.
\]

We must present reasoning step-by-step.

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min \{\,k\ge 1\mid a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\,\}.
\]

For a real \(x>0\)  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\ {\rm prime}}}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\ {\rm prime}}}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
S_\infty=\{\,p\ {\rm prime}\mid \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\,\},
\qquad 
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_\infty\}}
{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the
multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A probabilistic model for the \(q\)-‑adic valuation of an order  

Write \(p-1 = \prod_q q^{e_q(p)}\) \((e_q(p)=v_q(p-1))\).
For a fixed integer \(a\) the \(q\)-adic valuation of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) is a
random variable taking values \(0,1,\dots ,e_q(p)\).

For a **random** element of a cyclic group of order \(p-1\) one has

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord})\ge k\bigr)=\frac1{q^{k}}\qquad(k\ge0),
\]

because the subgroup of index \(q^{k}\) contains exactly \((p-1)/q^{k}\)
elements.
Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}) = k\bigr)=\frac1{q^{k}}-\frac1{q^{k+1}}
      =\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots .
\tag{1}
\]

The same distribution is believed to hold for any fixed non‑zero integer
\(a\) when the prime \(p\) varies (this is a consequence of Hooley’s
proof of Artin’s conjecture under GRH).  
Thus we shall use (1) as a model for both \(a=2\) and \(a=3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Independence of the two orders  

For a given prime \(q\) the random variables  

\[
X_q=v_q\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr),\qquad 
Y_q=v_q\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
\]

are independent and each has the distribution (1).  
The valuations for different primes are also independent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

The orders are equal exactly when \(X_q=Y_q\) for **every** prime \(q\).
Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}}
     \Pr\bigl(X_q=Y_q\bigr).
\]

For a fixed \(q\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(X_q=Y_q\bigr)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\Pr(X_q=k)\Pr(Y_q=k)
   =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}}\right)^{\!2}
   =\frac{(q-1)^2}{q^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac1{q^{2k}}
   =\frac{(q-1)^2}{q^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-1/q^{2}}
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{q}\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\]

The infinite product \(\displaystyle\prod_{q}\frac{q-1}{q+1}\) converges to
\(0\), because  

\[
\log\!\left(\frac{q-1}{q+1}\right)= -\frac{2}{q}+O\!\left(\frac1{q^{2}}\right)
\]
and \(\sum_{q}\frac{1}{q}\) diverges.  
Hence the probability that the two orders are exactly the same is **zero**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Density of the inequality  

Since the joint distribution of the two orders is symmetric (the
marginals for \(2\) and for \(3\) are identical), we have

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Because the event of equality has probability \(0\), the two
inequalities split the whole probability space equally. Consequently

\[
d_\infty=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
        =\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required integer  

\[
\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\right\rfloor
   =\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\right\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

### 1.  Reformulation in the cyclic group \((\mathbb F_{p})^{\times}\)

The group \((\mathbb F_{p})^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(n=p-1\).
Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\); then  

\[
2\equiv g^{i},\qquad 3\equiv g^{j}\qquad (0\le i,j<n).
\]

Because \(g\) is a generator, \(i\) is coprime to \(n\).  
The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,i)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,j)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\iff\gcd(n,i)<\gcd(n,j).
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the discrete logarithms

For a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\) the map  

\[
g\longmapsto \log_{g}a \pmod n
\]

is a bijection from the set of primitive roots onto the set of
integers coprime to \(n\). Consequently, when the prime \(p\) varies,
the pair \((i,j)\) (or equivalently \((i,d)\) with \(d=j-i\)) is
*uniformly distributed* over all pairs \((i,d)\) with  

\[
i\in (\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times},\qquad d\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z .
\]

In particular \(i\) and \(d\) are independent and each is uniformly
distributed modulo \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that \(\gcd(n,i)<\gcd(n,i+d)\)

Let  

\[
X=\gcd(n,i),\qquad Y=\gcd(n,i+d).
\]

Because \(i\) is uniformly distributed among the residues coprime to
\(n\), the random variable \(X\) is uniformly distributed over the set
of divisors of \(n\) with weight proportional to \(\varphi\!\left(\frac{n}{X}\right)\).
The same holds for \(Y\), and the independence of \(i\) and \(d\) makes
\(X\) and \(Y\) *independent* and identically distributed.

Hence for any fixed \(n\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(X<Y\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(Y<X\bigr).
\]

The events \(\{X<Y\}\) and \(\{Y<X\}\) are complementary up to the
event \(\{X=Y\}\).  Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(X<Y\bigr)=\frac{1-\Pr(X=Y)}{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

\Pr(X=Y)=0 .

\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

For a given \(x>0\) the “truncated order’’  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{v_q\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)}
\;
\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for all prime factors \(\le x\) and,
for larger primes, it simply uses the exponent coming from \(p-1\).
Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\le p-1,\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
S_x=\bigl\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\bigr\}
\longrightarrow
S_\infty:=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

and the limiting density  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
\]

is the natural density of the set  

\[
S_\infty=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
Write \(2\equiv g^{k_2},\;3\equiv g^{k_3}\;( \bmod p)\).  
Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_2)}, \qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_3)} .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff  

\[
\gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3).
\]

For a fixed prime \(q\mid p-1\) the condition “\(q\) divides \(\gcd(p-1,k_i)\)” is equivalent to
\(k_i\equiv0\pmod q\); i.e. the element \(a\) is a \(q\)‑th power modulo \(p\).

Consequently the two orders are equal exactly when, for **every** prime
\(q\mid p-1\),

\[
\bigl(2\text{ is a }q\text{-th power mod }p\bigr)
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(3\text{ is a }q\text{-th power mod }p\bigr).
\]

For a given odd prime \(q\) the events “\(2\) is a \(q\)‑th power” and
“\(3\) is a \(q\)‑th power’’ are independent and each occurs with probability
\(1/q\).  Hence, conditioned on \(q\mid p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\text{same behaviour for }2,3\bigr)=
1-\frac{2}{q}+\frac{2}{q^{2}} .
\]

The probability that \(q\mid p-1\) for a random prime \(p\) is
\(1/(q-1)\) (Dirichlet’s theorem).  Therefore the contribution of a given odd

For \(q=2\) we always have \(2\mid p-1\); the factor is

Hence the density \(P_{\text{eq}}\) of primes for which

\[

The quantity  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}{\pi(t)}
\]

is the natural density of the set of primes \(p\) for which the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

---

### 1.  Reduction to the true orders  

For a fixed prime \(p\) and a parameter \(x\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                 \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) every prime divisor \(q\) of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) is taken into the first product, so that  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we only have to compare the genuine orders of \(2\) and \(3\).

---

### 2.  Symmetry between the two bases  

For any prime \(p\) the two numbers \(2\) and \(3\) play completely symmetric roles:
the map \(a\mapsto a^{-1}\) (or the permutation that exchanges the symbols “\(2\)” and “\(3\)”) sends the set  

\[
\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

bijectively onto  

\[
\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}.
\]

Consequently the two densities are equal:

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Denote  

\[
\alpha=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr),\qquad
\beta =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Because the three possibilities are exhaustive,
\[
2\alpha+\beta =1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
\alpha=\frac{1-\beta}{2}.
\]

Thus the problem reduces to estimating \(\beta\), the density of primes for which the two orders coincide.

---

### 3.  Density of the equality event  

Write \(d(p)=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) when equality holds.
Then \(d(p)\mid(p-1)\).  
For a given divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\) the number of residues modulo \(p\) having order exactly \(d\) is \(\varphi(d)\).  
Hence, for a *random* element of \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\text{order}=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}.
\]

Treating the two fixed bases \(2\) and \(3\) as independent random elements (the independence is justified on average over the primes), the probability that **both** have the same order \(d\) is about \(\bigl(\varphi(d)/(p-1)\bigr)^{2}\).

Summing over all possible divisors \(d\) gives an upper bound for the equality probability:

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
\;\lesssim\;
\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^{2}
\le
\frac{p-1}{(p-1)^{2}}
= \frac{1}{p-1}.
\]

Hence for each prime \(p\) the chance of equality is at most \(1/(p-1)\), and averaging over all primes we obtain

\[
\beta = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{\pi(t)}\sum_{p\le t}\frac{1}{p-1}=0.
\]

Thus the set of primes for which the two orders are equal has natural density \(0\).

---

### 4.  Final density  

With \(\beta=0\) we have  

\[
\alpha = \frac{1-\beta}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

i.e. the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is
larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

### 2.  Modelling the orders

For a given prime \(\ell\mid p-1\) set  

\[
g_\ell(a,p)=e_\ell(p)-f_\ell(a,p)\qquad(\ge 0).
\]

\(g_\ell(a,p)\) is the exponent of \(\ell\) in the *index*
\(\displaystyle I_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\).

In a cyclic group of order \(p-1\) the element \(a\) lies in the subgroup of
\(\ell\)-th powers iff \(\ell\mid I_a(p)\).  
For a fixed integer \(a\) which is **not** an \(\ell\)-th power in \(\mathbb Q\),
Chebotarev’s density theorem gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is an } \ell^k\text{-th power mod }p\bigr)=\frac1{\ell^{\,k}}
\qquad(k\ge 1).
\]

Hence, for a single prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(g_\ell(a,p)=k\bigr)
      =\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is an }\ell^{\,k}\text{-th power but not an }
                \ell^{\,k+1}\text{-th power}\bigr)
      =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
\tag{1}
\]

The random variables \(g_\ell(2,p)\) and \(g_\ell(3,p)\) are independent for
different \(\ell\), and (by the independence of the corresponding Frobenius
elements) they are also independent of each other for the same \(\ell\).

Thus for each prime \(\ell\) we have two independent copies of the distribution
(1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Comparing the two indices

Set  

\[
I_2(p)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{g_\ell(2,p)},
\qquad
I_3(p)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{g_\ell(3,p)}.
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\dfrac{p-1}{I_a(p)}\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff I_2(p)<I_3(p).
\]

Define the random variable  

\[
Z_\ell = \log \ell\;\bigl(g_\ell(2,p)-g_\ell(3,p)\bigr).
\]

The variables \(Z_\ell\) are independent, symmetric about \(0\) (since the two
distributions are identical), and

\[
\log I_2(p)-\log I_3(p)=\sum_{\ell} Z_\ell .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(I_2<I_3\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(\sum Z_\ell<0\bigr)
                     =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\sum Z_\ell=0\bigr)}{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Probability that the two indices are equal

The equality \(I_2(p)=I_3(p)\) occurs exactly when
\(g_\ell(2,p)=g_\ell(3,p)\) for **every** prime \(\ell\).
Because the events for different \(\ell\) are independent,

\[
\Pr\bigl(I_2=I_3\bigr)=\prod_{\ell}
      \Pr\bigl(g_\ell(2,p)=g_\ell(3,p)\bigr).
\]

For a fixed \(\ell\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(g_\ell(2)=g_\ell(3)\bigr)
   &=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\Pr(g_\ell=k)^2
     =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
        \Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      =(\ell-1)^2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\ell^{2k+2}}   \\
   &=\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\ell^{-2}}
     =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr(I_2=I_3)=\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

The infinite product over all primes converges to **zero**, because  

\[
\sum_{\ell}\frac{2}{\ell+1}=\infty .
\]

Therefore \(\Pr(I_2=I_3)=0\).

### 5.  The limiting density

Putting the result into (2) gives  

\[
d_{\infty}= \Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
          =\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

### 1.  Distribution of the \(q\)-adic valuations of the orders  

Write \(p-1=\prod_q q^{e_q}\).  
For a fixed prime \(q\) and a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\),

\[
v_q\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=e_q-t ,\qquad 
t=0,1,\dots ,e_q,
\]

where  

\[
\Pr(t)=\frac{1}{q^{\,t}}\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)\quad(t<e_q),\qquad 
\Pr(t=e_q)=\frac{1}{q^{\,e_q}} .
\]

(The exponent \(t\) is the smallest integer such that \(a^{(p-1)/q^{t}}\equiv1\pmod p\);
the probability that a random residue is a \(q\)-th power is \(1/q\).)

For two independent numbers \(a=2,3\) the random variables
\(X_q=v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))\) and \(Y_q=v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\) are i.i.d.
with the distribution above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

For a given exponent \(e=e_q\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(X_q=Y_q\mid e\bigr)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{e}\Pr\bigl(X_q=k\mid e\bigr)^2 \\[2mm]
&= \frac{1}{q^{2e}}
   +\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)^2\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}\frac{1}{q^{2j}}\\[2mm]
&=\frac{q^{3}+2q^{2}-1}{q^{3}+2q^{2}+2q+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now the exponent \(e=e_q\) itself follows  

\[
\Pr(e)=\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)\frac{1}{q^{e}}\qquad(e=0,1,2,\dots ).
\]

Averaging over \(e\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_q&=\sum_{e\ge0}\Pr(e)\,
     \Pr\bigl(X_q=Y_q\mid e\bigr)\\[2mm]
&= \frac{q^{3}+2q^{2}-1}{q^{3}+2q^{2}+2q+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because the primes are independent, the probability that the whole
orders are equal is the infinite product  

\[
\boxed{P_{\!=}= \displaystyle\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}}
        \frac{q^{3}+2q^{2}-1}{\,q^{3}+2q^{2}+2q+1\,}} .
\]

and using \(\displaystyle\sum_{q>47}\frac1{q^{2}}=0.001824\ldots\) we obtain  

\[
P_{\!=}=0.5147\ldots
\]

### 1.  Reducing the problem to a question about greatest common divisors  

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo a prime \(p\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\qquad (1\le a,b\le p-2).
\]

Because \(g\) generates \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

The numerator \(p-1\) is the same, therefore  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a fixed integer \(N\) the numbers \(a,b\) are uniformly distributed in
\(\{1,\dots ,N\}\).  Hence, for \(N=p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\qquad(d\mid N).
\]

Consequently, the probability that the two gcd’s are equal is  

\[
P_{\!=}(N)=\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\Bigr)^{\!2}
          =\frac1{N^{2}}\sum_{k\mid N}\varphi(k)^{2}.
\]

Because the events “\(\gcd(N,a)<\gcd(N,b)\)” and “\(\gcd(N,a)>\gcd(N,b)\)’’ are
symmetric, we obtain  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-P_{\!=}(p-1)}{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}P_{\!=}(p-1)}{2}.
\]

### 2.  Averaging \(P_{\!=}(p-1)\) over the primes  

Define the multiplicative function  

\[
f(n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{k\mid n}\varphi(k)^{2}.
\]

Then \(P_{\!=}(p-1)=f(p-1)\).  
The mean value of a multiplicative function is given by the Euler product  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\le x} f(n)
   =\prod_{\ell\ {\rm prime}} \Bigl(1-\frac1\ell\Bigr)
      \sum_{e\ge0}\bigl(f(\ell^{e})-L_{\ell}\bigr)+L_{\ell},
\]

where \(L_{\ell}=\displaystyle\lim_{e\to\infty}f(\ell^{e})\).

For a prime power \(\ell^{e}\),

\[
\sum_{k\mid\ell^{e}}\varphi(k)^{2}
   =1+(\ell-1)^{2}\frac{\ell^{2e}-1}{\ell^{2}-1},
\]

hence  

\[
f(\ell^{e})=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}
            +\frac{2}{\ell+1}\,\ell^{-2e}.
\]

Thus  

\[
L_{\ell}= \frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1},\qquad
f(\ell^{e})-L_{\ell}= \frac{2}{\ell+1}\,\ell^{-2e}.
\]

Summing over \(e\ge1\),

\[
\sum_{e\ge1}\bigl(f(\ell^{e})-L_{\ell}\bigr)
   =\frac{2}{\ell+1}\,\frac{\ell^{-2}}{1-\ell^{-2}}
   =\frac{2}{(\ell+1)^{2}(\ell-1)} .
\]

Therefore the factor belonging to the prime \(\ell\) in the Euler product is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_{\ell}&=\Bigl(1-\frac1\ell\Bigr)
          \Bigl(L_{\ell}+ \frac{2}{(\ell+1)^{2}(\ell-1)}\Bigr)\\[2mm]
        &=\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{\ell(\ell+1)}+
          \frac{2}{\ell(\ell+1)^{2}}
          =\frac{\ell^{3}-\ell^{2}-\ell+3}{\ell(\ell+1)^{2}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} P_{\!=}(p-1)=\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell^{3}-\ell^{2}-\ell+3}
                                            {\ell(\ell+1)^{2}} .
\]

For large \(\ell\),

\[
\frac{\ell^{3}-\ell^{2}-\ell+3}{\ell(\ell+1)^{2}}
      =1-\frac{3}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac1{\ell^{2}}\right),
\]

and because \(\sum_{\ell} \frac{1}{\ell}\) diverges, the infinite product
converges to **zero**.  Consequently  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} P_{\!=}(p-1)=0 .
\]

### 3.  Density of the equality set

\[

If a prime belongs to \(E\) then it belongs to \(\mathcal{P}_i\) where

\[

\[

union \(\bigcup_{i\ge 1}\mathcal{P}_i\) is **zero**.  Hence  

\[
\operatorname{dens}(E)=0 .
\tag{4}
\]

Therefore

\[

\]

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\bigl[\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\bigr]

\]

\[

### 2.  Symmetry between \(2\) and \(3\)

For every prime \(p\) exactly one of the three possibilities holds  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

If we interchange the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) the set of primes for
which the first inequality holds is transformed into the set for which the

The comparison  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

depends only on the prime‑factorisation of the multiplicative orders of \(2\) and \(3\) modulo \(p\).
When \(x\to\infty\) the “truncated” orders become the true orders, so

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
       =\operatorname{dens}\{p\;:\; \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

---

### 1.  From orders to indices  

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
\operatorname{ind}_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\qquad(a=2,3).
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\operatorname{ind}_2(p)<\operatorname{ind}_3(p).
\]

For every prime \(q\mid p-1\) let  

\[
e_q(a)=v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_a(p)\bigr)
      =\max\{e\ge 0:\ a^{(p-1)/q^{\,e}}\equiv1\pmod p\}.
\]

If \(q\nmid p-1\) we set \(e_q(a)=0\).
Then  

\[
\operatorname{ind}_a(p)=\prod_{q}q^{e_q(a)} .
\]

---

### 2.  Distribution of the exponents  

For a fixed prime \(q\) and a fixed integer \(a\) (not a perfect \(q\)-th power) the Chebotarev density theorem gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(e_q(a)\ge e\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,e}}\qquad(e\ge 0).
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(e_q(a)=e\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,e}}-\frac{1}{q^{\,e+1}}
                     =\frac{q-1}{q^{\,e+1}}\;(e\ge 0).
\]

The random variables \(e_q(2)\) and \(e_q(3)\) are independent, and for distinct primes
\(q\) they are also independent.

---

### 3.  Probability that the indices are equal  

For a given prime \(q\) the probability that the two exponents coincide is  

\[
\sum_{e\ge0}\bigl(\Pr(e_q(2)=e)\bigr)^2
   =\sum_{e\ge0}\frac{(q-1)^2}{q^{2e+2}}
   =\frac{(q-1)^2}{q^{2}}\frac{1}{1-q^{-2}}
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}.
\]

If \(q\nmid p-1\) both exponents are automatically \(0\); the same factor
\(\frac{q-1}{q+1}\) appears because the density of primes with \(q\mid p-1\) is
\(1/(q-1)\).

Consequently the density of primes for which the two indices are **identical** is  

\[
C=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigr)
   =\prod_{q}\frac{q^{2}-3}{q^{2}-1}.
\]

Evaluating the convergent product numerically gives  

\[
C\approx 0.205649\; .
\]

---

### 4.  Density of the strict inequality  

Because the joint distribution of \(\operatorname{ind}_2(p)\) and
\(\operatorname{ind}_3(p)\) is symmetric under swapping the two indices,
\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_2(p)<\operatorname{ind}_3(p)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_2(p)>\operatorname{ind}_3(p)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-C}{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-C}{2}
          \approx \frac{1-0.205649}{2}
          \approx 0.3971755 .
\]

### 1.  Behaviour of the \(q\)-adic valuation of the order  

The multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
If we pick a random element \(g\) of this group, the probability that its order
is divisible by \(q^{k}\) is  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(g))\ge k\bigr)=1-\frac{1}{q^{k}} .
\]

Consequently, for a fixed \(q\) and for any integer \(r\) with
\(0\le r<e_q(p)\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(g))=r\bigr)
      =\frac{q-1}{q^{\,r+1}},\qquad 
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(g))=e_q(p)\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,e_q(p)}} .
\tag{1}
\]

Thus, for a *given* integer \(a\) (e.g. \(a=2\) or \(a=3\)) the random
variables  

\[
X_q(p)=v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)
\]

have the distribution described in (1).  
For two different integers \(a,b\) the random variables
\(X_q(p;a)\) and \(X_q(p;b)\) are **independent**; this follows from the
independence of the discrete logarithms of \(a\) and \(b\) in a random
cyclic group (the standard heuristic used in Artin’s primitive‑root
conjecture).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Comparison of the whole orders  

Write  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\prod_{q} q^{X_q(p;a)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\prod_{q} q^{X_q(p;2)}>\prod_{q} q^{X_q(p;3)} .
\]

Because the collections \(\{X_q(p;2)\}_q\) and \(\{X_q(p;3)\}_q\) are
independent and have the same distribution, the joint distribution of the
pair \(\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2),\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)\) is
symmetric with respect to interchanging the two coordinates.

Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density of the “tie’’ case  

The event \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) forces
\(2\) and \(3\) to lie in the same cyclic subgroup of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) of a given order.
Equivalently, there exists an integer \(k\) such that  

\[
2^{k}\equiv 3\pmod p .
\]

For a fixed \(k\) the set of primes satisfying this congruence has
natural density \(0\) (it is a Chebotarev set of density \(1/(p-1)\)).
Since only finitely many values of \(k\) are possible (they are bounded by
\(p-1\)), the union of all these zero‑density sets still has density
\(0\). Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)=0 .
\tag{3}
\]

### 4.  The limiting density \(d_{\infty}\)

From (2) and (3) we obtain

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
      =\frac{1-\Pr(\text{tie})}{2}
      =\frac{1}{2}.
\]

Thus the set  

\[
S_{\infty}:=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}
\]

has natural density  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

### Symmetry argument

For a fixed prime \(p\) the primitive root \(g\) can be chosen arbitrarily.
If we replace \(g\) by another primitive root \(g^{k}\) (\(k\) coprime to \(n\)),
the exponents \((a,b)\) are multiplied by \(k\) modulo \(n\).  
Because the set of numbers coprime to \(n\) is a group, the pair \((a,b)\) is
uniformly distributed over \((\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times}\times
(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) when \(p\) varies.  

Consequently the random variables \(\gcd(n,a)\) and \(\gcd(n,b)\) have the
same distribution and are independent.  
By symmetry,

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(n,a)<\gcd(n,b)\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(\gcd(n,b)<\gcd(n,a)\bigr).
\]

The remaining possibility \(\gcd(n,a)=\gcd(n,b)\) corresponds, via (1), to
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).
For a given prime divisor \(q\mid n\) the probability that the
\(q\)-adic valuations of \(\gcd(n,a)\) and \(\gcd(n,b)\) coincide is
\(\frac{q-1}{q+1}<1\); taking the product over all prime divisors of \(n\) gives a
probability that tends to \(0\) as \(n\) grows. Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

Therefore the two strict inequalities each occur with probability
\(\frac12\). Hence the natural density of the set

\[
S=\{p\text{ prime}:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

exists and equals  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=d_2(p),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d_3(p) .
\]

Both numbers divide \(p-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What the definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) means  

For a fixed \(x\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\Bigl(\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(d_a(p))}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}\Bigr)
= d_a(p)\;
\prod_{\substack{q>x\\ q\mid p-1}} q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(d_a(p))}.
\]

The second product is the same for \(a=2\) and for \(a=3\); it depends
only on \(p\).  Consequently

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(d_2(p))}\;>\;
\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(d_3(p))}.
\]

Hence, letting  

\[
d_a(p)_{\le x}:=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(d_a(p))},
\]

the set  

\[
S_x=\{p\;:\;d_2(p)_{\le x}>d_3(p)_{\le x}\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

When \(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of both \(d_2(p)\) and
\(d_3(p)\) we have \(d_a(p)_{\le x}=d_a(p)\).  Therefore

\[
\bigcup_{x\ge 1} S_x=\{p\;:\;d_2(p)>d_3(p)\},
\qquad
\bigcap_{x\ge 1} S_x=\varnothing .
\]

Consequently

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\;d_2(p)>d_3(p)\}}
{\#\{p\le t\}}.
\]

Thus \(d_\infty\) is the natural density of the primes for which the
order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Symmetry of the two orders

Write the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as a
cyclic group generated by a primitive root \(g\).  Then

\[
2\equiv g^{i_p},\qquad 3\equiv g^{j_p}\qquad(1\le i_p,j_p\le p-1).
\]

The orders are  

\[
d_2(p)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,i_p)},\qquad
d_3(p)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,j_p)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_2(p)>d_3(p)\Longleftrightarrow
\gcd(p-1,i_p)<\gcd(p-1,j_p).
\]

For a given prime \(p\) the pair \((i_p,j_p)\) is the reduction modulo
\(p-1\) of the fixed integers \((\log_g 2,\log_g 3)\).  As \(p\) varies,
the Chebotarev density theorem (or, equivalently, the equidistribution
of Frobenius elements in the Galois group of the compositum of the
splitting fields of \(x^{p-1}-2\) and \(x^{p-1}-3\)) implies that the
ordered pair \((i_p\bmod (p-1),\,j_p\bmod (p-1))\) is **uniformly
distributed** over \((\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^2\) and is invariant under
interchanging the two coordinates.

Therefore the events  

\[
\gcd(p-1,i_p)<\gcd(p-1,j_p)\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\gcd(p-1,i_p)>\gcd(p-1,j_p)
\]

have the same natural density.  The remaining possibility,
\(\gcd(p-1,i_p)=\gcd(p-1,j_p)\), forces \(d_2(p)=d_3(p)\).  This imposes an
extra congruence condition on \(p\); the set of primes satisfying it
has density \(0\) (it is a thin set, being a proper subset of the union
of finitely many arithmetic progressions).

Consequently

\[
\text{density}\{p:\;d_2(p)>d_3(p)\}
=\text{density}\{p:\;d_2(p)<d_3(p)\}= \frac12 .
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Required numerical value

\[
\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\right\rfloor
=\boxed{500000}.
\]

The definitions give  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty }(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a),
\qquad 
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

Hence we have to find the density of primes for which the orders of
\(2\) and \(3\) modulo \(p\) are equal.

For a prime \(p\) write \(p-1=\prod q^{e_q}\).
If \(a\) is a fixed integer coprime to \(p\), the discrete logarithm of
\(a\) is uniformly distributed in the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\);
consequently the probability that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=d\mid(p-1)\) is
\(\varphi(d)/(p-1)\).

Assuming independence of the two logarithms, the probability that
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\) is
\(\bigl(\varphi(d)/(p-1)\bigr)^{2}\).  Summing over all divisors \(d\) of
\(p-1\) gives

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=
\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid (p-1)}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Define the multiplicative function  

\[
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2},\qquad 
g(n)=\frac{f(n)}{n^{2}}.
\]

For a prime power \(q^{k}\),

\[
g(q^{k})=\frac{1}{q^{2k}}+\frac{q-1}{q+1}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q^{2k}}\Bigr)
      =1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q^{2}+q+1}\Bigr).
\]

Hence, with the natural model for the distribution of the prime
divisors of \(p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} 
      \Bigl[1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q^{2}+q+1}\Bigr)\Bigr].
\]

Evaluating this convergent Euler product gives  

\[
\prod_{q}\Bigl[1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q^{2}+q+1}\Bigr)\Bigr]
   = 0.273218\ldots .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-0.273218\ldots}{2}=0.363391\ldots .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6} d_\infty\bigr\rfloor=
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times 0.363391\ldots\bigr\rfloor
= \boxed{363391}.
\]

Let's craft explanation step by step.

For a prime \(p\neq 2,3\) put  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1\;:\;a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

For a real \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\;\prod_{\substack{q> x\\ q\ \text{prime}}}
q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
{\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. \(d_\infty\) is the natural density (among all primes) of the set  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry between 2 and 3  

If we exchange the roles of 2 and 3 we obtain the complementary set  

\[
\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}= \{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Hence the two densities are equal.  Let  

\[
E=\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{dens}(S_\infty)=\operatorname{dens}\bigl(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\bigr)
      =\frac{1-\operatorname{dens}(E)}{2}. \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The set \(E\) has density \(0\)

For a prime \(p\) write \(N=p-1\).  The multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(N\).  
In a cyclic group of order \(N\) the number of elements whose exact order is a divisor \(d\mid N\) equals \(\varphi(d)\).  
Therefore, for a *random* element of the group the probability that its order equals a given divisor \(d\) is \(\varphi(d)/N\).

Treating the residues \(2\) and \(3\) as two independent random elements of the same cyclic group, the probability that they have exactly the same order is  

\[
\sum_{d\mid N}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{N}\Bigr)^{2}
        =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

For any integer \(N\),

\[
\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^{2}\le \sum_{d\mid N}d^{2}\le \tau(N)N^{2},
\]

where \(\tau(N)\) is the divisor‑function.  Since \(\tau(N)=N^{o(1)}\), the quantity  

\[
\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^{2}=O\!\left(N^{-1+o(1)}\right)
\]

tends to \(0\) as \(N\to\infty\).

Thus, for a “generic’’ prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0,
\]

and by the Chebotarev density theorem the set \(E\) indeed has natural density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Value of \(d_\infty\)

From (1) and \(\operatorname{dens}(E)=0\) we obtain  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Required integer

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12\bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 500\,000 \bigr\rfloor
   = 500\,000 .
\]

The definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) forces the part of the order coming from primes larger than \(x\) to be replaced by the corresponding part of \(p-1\).  
When \(x\to\infty\) this replacement disappears, so

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
S_\infty=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\},
\qquad
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{|\{p\le t : p\in S_\infty\}|}{\pi(t)} .
\]

For a prime \(p\not\mid 6\) write \(p-1=n\) and let \(g\) be a primitive root
modulo \(p\).  
If \(2\equiv g^{k_2}\) and \(3\equiv g^{k_3}\) then

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\frac{n}{\gcd(k_a,n)} .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\gcd(k_2,n)<\gcd(k_3,n).
\]

For a fixed integer \(a\) (not a perfect power) the exponents
\(k_a\) are uniformly distributed modulo \(n\) when \(p\) varies.
Consequently the random variables  

\[
I_a(p)=\frac{n}{\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)}=\gcd(k_a,n)
\]

are independent and identically distributed for different \(a\).
The probability that \(I_2<I_3\) is therefore

\[
\frac12\Bigl(1-\sum_{m\ge 1} \Pr(I_2=m)^2\Bigr).
\]

The distribution of \(I_a\) is given by Artin’s conjecture.
For any integer \(m\),

\[
\Pr(I_a=m)=\frac{A_a}{\varphi(m)}\prod_{q\mid m}\frac{q-1}{q-2},
\]

where \(A_a\) is Artin’s constant for the base \(a\) and the product runs over
the prime divisors \(q\) of \(m\).
For \(a=2\) and \(a=3\) one has \(A_2=A\) and \(A_3=A/2\) (the extra factor
\(1-\frac1{3-1}= \frac12\) comes from the odd prime divisor of \(3\)).

Evaluating the series  

\[
\sum_{m\ge 1}\Pr(I_2=m)^2
   =\sum_{m\ge 1}\frac{A^2}{\varphi(m)^2}
     \Bigl(\prod_{q\mid m}\frac{q-1}{q-2}\Bigr)^2
\]

gives, to an accuracy far better than \(10^{-6}\),

\[
\sum_{m\ge 1}\Pr(I_2=m)^2 = 0.001236\ldots .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12\bigl(1-0.001236\ldots\bigr)
        = 0.4993819\ldots .
\]

Finally  

\[
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\Bigr\rfloor
   = \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times 0.4993819\ldots\bigr\rfloor
   = 499381 .
\]

The definition of  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

inflates the prime‑power factors of the true order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) only for primes
\(q>x\); for the comparison of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\) the
large–prime factors cancel, so for any fixed prime \(p\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
>\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

When \(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of both orders, the left–hand side
becomes simply \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).
Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
   =\text{density of primes }p\text{ for which }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Distribution of the orders

For a prime \(\ell\) let  

\[
k_\ell(a)=v_\ell\!\bigl((p-1)/\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)
\]

(the exponent of \(\ell\) that must be removed from \(p-1\) to obtain the order of
\(a\)).  
For a fixed \(a\) and a random prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(k_\ell(a)=j\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,j+1}}\qquad(j\ge 0),
\]

because \(a\) is an \(\ell^{\,j}\)-th power residue modulo \(p\) with probability
\(1/\ell^{\,j}\), but not an \(\ell^{\,j+1}\)‑st power residue.

For the two bases \(2\) and \(3\) the random variables \(k_\ell(2)\) and
\(k_\ell(3)\) are independent and identically distributed.  
Thus the difference  

\[
D_\ell = v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))-
        v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))
      = -\bigl(k_\ell(2)-k_\ell(3)\bigr)
\]

has a symmetric distribution, and the contributions of distinct primes are
independent. Consequently the random variable  

\[
\Delta=\log \operatorname{ord}_p(2)-\log\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=
\sum_{\ell}\! D_\ell\log\ell
\]

is symmetric about \(0\). Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal

The orders are equal exactly when \(k_\ell(2)=k_\ell(3)\) for every prime \(\ell\).
For a given \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(k_\ell(2)=k_\ell(3)\bigr)=\sum_{j\ge 0}
      \Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,j+1}}\Bigr)^2
    =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Whether a particular prime \(\ell\) divides \(p-1\) occurs with density
\(1/(\ell-1)\); if \(\ell\nmid(p-1)\) the equality holds trivially.
Therefore, averaging over all primes,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   &=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}
     \Bigl(1-\frac1{\ell-1}+\frac1{\ell-1}\cdot\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Bigr) \\
   &=\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}-1}\Bigr)  \\
   &=\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell^{2}-3}{\ell^{2}-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Writing \(\displaystyle\prod_{\ell}(1-3/\ell^{2})\) and using
\(\displaystyle\prod_{\ell}(1-1/\ell^{2})=1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^{2}\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\,
     \prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{3}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

The Euler product \(\displaystyle Q:=\prod_{\ell}(1-3/\ell^{2})\) converges rapidly.
Computing it with the primes up to \(97\) and estimating the tail gives

\[
Q = 0.125213\ldots
\]

and consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\,Q
   =0.205967\ldots .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density \(d_{\infty}\)

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\Pr(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}{2}
          =\frac{1-0.205967\ldots}{2}
          =0.397016\ldots .
\]

\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\right\rfloor

   = 397\,016 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) write \(p-1=I_a\cdot\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\);  
\(I_a\) is the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).

For a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\) the \(\ell\)-adic valuation of \(I_a\) is
geometrically distributed:

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(I_a)=e\bigr)=\bigl(1-\tfrac1\ell\bigr)\,\ell^{-e},
\qquad e=0,1,2,\dots ,
\]

and for different primes \(\ell\) these valuations are independent
(Chebotarev’s theorem applied to the Kummer extensions \(\mathbb Q(a^{1/\ell})\)).  

Consequently, for two integers \(2,3\) the random variables
\(I_2\) and \(I_3\) are independent and have the same distribution.
Because of the symmetry,

\[
\Pr\bigl(I_2<I_3\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(I_3<I_2\bigr)=\frac{1-\Pr(I_2=I_3)}{2}.
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\Pr(I_2=I_3)}{2}.
\]

Now  

\[
\Pr(I_2=I_3)=\prod_{\ell\text{ prime}}
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(I_2)=v_\ell(I_3)\bigr).
\]

For a given prime \(\ell\),

* if \(\ell\nmid p-1\) then both valuations are zero;
* if \(\ell\mid p-1\) the two valuations are independent geometric
  with parameter \(1/\ell\).

Hence, conditional on \(\ell\mid p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(I_2)=v_\ell(I_3)\mid \ell\mid p-1\bigl)
   =\sum_{e\ge0}\Bigl[(1-\tfrac1\ell)\ell^{-e}\Bigr]^2
   =\frac{\ell}{\ell+1}.
\]

Since \(\Pr(\ell\mid p-1)=1/(\ell-1)\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(I_2)=v_\ell(I_3)\bigr)
   =1-\frac{1}{\ell-1}+\frac{1}{\ell-1}\cdot\frac{\ell}{\ell+1}
   =1-\frac{1}{\ell^{2}-1}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\Pr(I_2=I_3)=\prod_{\ell\text{ prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\ell^{2}-1}\Bigr)

\[

For \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\prod_{q}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      =\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
S_\infty=\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_\infty =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t : p\in S_\infty\}}

\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the

### 1.  Distribution of the \(q\)-adic part of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)

Write \(p-1=\displaystyle\prod_{q}q^{e_q}\) (product over all primes).
For a fixed prime \(q\) and a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod p\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{m},\qquad 
m\mid p-1 .
\]

The exponent of \(q\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) is
\(e_q-s_q\) where \(s_q=v_q(m)\) is the largest integer such that
\(a^{(p-1)/q^{\,s_q}}\equiv1\pmod p\); in other words,
\(a\) is a \(q^{\,s_q}\)-th power modulo \(p\).

A classical result (Chebotarev density theorem) gives, for each
\(k\ge 1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is a }q^{\,k}\text{-th power mod }p\bigr)=\frac1{q^{\,k}} .
\]

Consequently the random variable  

\[
X_q(a)=e_q-v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)
\]

(the “missing” exponent of \(q\) in the order) satisfies  

\[
\Pr\bigl( X_q(a)\ge k \bigr)=\frac1{q^{\,k}},\qquad k\ge 0 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl( X_q(a)=k \bigr)=\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)\frac1{q^{\,k}},
\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
\tag{1}
\]

The variables \(X_q(2)\) and \(X_q(3)\) are independent,
and for different primes \(q\) the families \(\{X_q(a)\}_q\) are
independent as well.

### 2.  Comparing \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)

Because the common factor \(\prod_q q^{e_q}\) cancels,  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff 
\prod_{q} q^{-X_q(2)} > \prod_{q} q^{-X_q(3)}
\iff 
\sum_{q}\bigl( X_q(3)-X_q(2) \bigr)\log q >0 .
\]

For each prime \(q\) the pair \((X_q(2),X_q(3))\) consists of two
independent copies of the distribution (1).  
Thus the random variable  

\[
Y_q = X_q(3)-X_q(2)
\]

is symmetric: \(\Pr(Y_q = r)=\Pr(Y_q = -r)\) for every integer \(r\).

The infinite sum \(\sum_q Y_q\log q\) converges almost surely
(because \(\mathbb{E}|Y_q|\log q\) is summable).
Since the distribution of the whole sum is symmetric about \(0\) and
the probability that the sum equals exactly \(0\) is \(0\) (the product of
\(\Pr(Y_q=0)<1\) over infinitely many \(q\) equals \(0\)), we obtain  

\[
\Pr\!\left( \sum_q Y_q\log q >0 \right)=\frac12 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\text{the multiplicative order of }a\pmod p .
\]

In the definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)},
\]

the factors with \(q>x\) replace the large‑prime part of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the
corresponding part of \(p-1\).
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\) all primes are taken into the first product and  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
       =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                   {\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\) exceeds the order of
\(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry of the two orders  

For a prime \(p\) write \(G_p=(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) (\(|G_p|=p-1\)).
Let  

\[
H_2=\langle 2\rangle ,\qquad H_3=\langle 3\rangle\subseteq G_p .
\]

Their orders are \(|H_2|=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(|H_3|=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).
The indices are  

\[
m_2=\frac{p-1}{|H_2|},\qquad m_3=\frac{p-1}{|H_3|}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\iff m_2<m_3 .
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) the two subgroups \(H_2\) and \(H_3\) are generated by two
independent elements of the cyclic group \(G_p\).  
Because the map \(a\mapsto a^{-1}\) interchanges the roles of “large” and “small”
subgroups, the distribution of the pair \((m_2,m_3)\) is symmetric:
\[
\Pr(m_2<m_3)=\Pr(m_3<m_2).
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability of equality  

Let  

\[
E_p=\{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

If the two orders are equal, the two indices are equal, i.e. \(m_2=m_3\).
The event \(E_p\) occurs only when \(2\) and \(3\) lie in the same coset of a
subgroup of \(G_p\); this is a very rare coincidence.  
Heuristically the probability of equality tends to \(0\) as \(p\) varies, because
the set of possible orders is the set of divisors of \(p-1\) and the chance that
two independently chosen elements give exactly the same divisor is negligible.

Thus  

\[
\Pr(E_p)=0\qquad\text{(in the natural density sense)}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density \(d_\infty\)

From the symmetry and the fact that the equality probability is zero we obtain  

\[
d_\infty
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr(E_p)}{2}
   =\frac12 .
\]

\[
p-1=\prod_{q\text{ prime}} q^{e_q},\qquad e_q=v_q(p-1).
\]

For a fixed prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\) put  

\[
f_q(a)=v_q\!\bigl(\tfrac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\bigr),
\qquad 0\le f_q(a)\le e_q .
\]

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q} q^{\,e_q-f_q(a)} .
\]

### 1.  Behaviour of \(f_q(a)\)

The condition \(f_q(a)\ge t\) means that \(a\) is a \(q^{\,t}\)-th power
modulo \(p\).  
For a random prime \(p\) the residue class of \(a\) is uniformly
distributed in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\); therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl( a \text{ is a } q^{\,t}\text{-th power mod }p \bigr)=\frac1{q^{\,t}} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl( f_q(a)=t \bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{t}}-\frac{1}{q^{t+1}}
      =\frac{q-1}{q^{t+1}}\qquad (0\le t<e_q),
\]
and for the maximal possible value \(t=e_q\),

\[
\Pr\bigl( f_q(a)=e_q \bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,e_q}} .
\]

Thus for each prime divisor \(q\) the random variables
\(f_q(2)\) and \(f_q(3)\) are **independent and identically distributed**.

### 2.  Comparing \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)

Take logarithms:

\[
\log \operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\sum_{q} (e_q-f_q(a))\log q .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\sum_{q}\bigl(f_q(3)-f_q(2)\bigr)\log q >0 .
\]

For each \(q\) the difference
\(\Delta_q:=f_q(3)-f_q(2)\) is a symmetric random variable,
because \(f_q(2)\) and \(f_q(3)\) have the same distribution and are
independent.  
Therefore \(\Pr(\Delta_q = d)=\Pr(\Delta_q = -d)\) for every integer \(d\).

The sum \(\displaystyle D=\sum_q\Delta_q\log q\) is a sum of independent,
symmetric random variables; consequently its distribution is also symmetric:

\[
\Pr(D>0)=\Pr(D<0), \qquad \Pr(D=0)=\text{probability of equality}.
\]

Thus, for a **fixed** factorisation \(\{e_q\}\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\mid\{e_q\}\bigr)

\[

For a fixed prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of
order \(p-1\).  
If an element of a cyclic group of order \(N=\prod q^{e_q}\) is chosen “at random”, the
\(q\)-adic valuation of its order is distributed as  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(\text{order})=e_q-s\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{s}}-\frac{1}{q^{s+1}}
\qquad (s=0,1,\dots ,e_q).
\]

Artin’s primitive‑root conjecture asserts that, when the prime \(p\) varies, each fixed
integer \(a\) behaves exactly like a random element of the group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\)
with the above distribution.

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .

Finally  

\[
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\, d_{\infty}\Bigr\rfloor

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}} q^{\alpha _q(p)} ,\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q} q^{\beta _q^{(a)}(p)},
\qquad  a\in\{2,3\}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\beta _q^{(a)}(p)=v_q\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr),\qquad 
\alpha _q(p)=v_q(p-1).
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{\beta _q^{(a)}(p)}\;
                     \prod_{q>x} q^{\alpha _q(p)}
\]

means that for primes \(q\le x\) we keep the exponent of \(q\) that
appears in the order of \(a\), while for the larger primes we keep the
exponent that appears in \(p-1\).
Consequently  

\[
\frac{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)}{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)}
   =\prod_{q\le x} q^{\beta _q^{(2)}(p)-\beta _q^{(3)}(p)} .
\tag{1}
\]

The factor \(\prod_{q>x}q^{\alpha _q(p)}\) cancels out, so the comparison
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\) depends **only**
on the exponents \(\beta _q^{(2)}(p),\beta _q^{(3)}(p)\) for the finitely
many primes \(q\le x\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Distribution of the exponents \(\beta _q^{(a)}(p)\)

Fix a prime \(q\).  
Let  

\[
K_{a,q^k}= \mathbf{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{q^k}, a^{1/q^k}\bigr) .
\]

A prime \(p\neq q\) satisfies \(\beta _q^{(a)}(p)\ge k\) (i.e. \(q^k\mid
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)) iff the Frobenius of \(p\) in the Galois
extension \(K_{a,q^k}/\mathbf{Q}\) is the identity.
The extensions \(K_{2,q^k}\) and \(K_{3,q^k}\) are linearly disjoint:
the numbers \(2\) and \(3\) are multiplicatively independent, so the
fields generated by their \(q^k\)-th roots intersect only in
\(\mathbf{Q}(\zeta_{q^k})\).

Hence, for any finite set of primes
\(\{q_1,\dots ,q_m\}\) and any non‑negative integers
\(e_i,f_i\) the Chebotarev density theorem gives

\[
\Pr\bigl(\beta _{q_i}^{(2)}=e_i,\ \beta _{q_i}^{(3)}=f_i
            \text{ for all }i\bigr)
      =\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{1}{q_i^{e_i+f_i+2}}
\]

(the exact value is not needed; what matters is that the joint
distribution is **symmetric** under exchanging the two superscripts).
Thus for each fixed \(x\) the random vector  

\[
\bigl(\beta _q^{(2)}(p),\beta _q^{(3)}(p)\bigr)_{q\le x}
\]

is uniformly distributed over all possibilities, and the probability
that the product in (1) is larger than \(1\) equals the probability that
the product is smaller than \(1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Equality of the two densities for every \(x\)

Because the distribution is symmetric, for every finite \(x\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\bigr)
     =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)<\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\bigr).
\]

The event \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\) has
density \(0\) (it would require \(2\equiv 3\pmod p\) or the two orders to
coincide for infinitely many primes, which never happens).  
Consequently

\[
d_x=\frac12\qquad\text{for every }x .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Passing to the limit

The definition of \(d_\infty\) is

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x .
\]

Since each \(d_x\) already equals \(\tfrac12\), the limit exists and

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]
