The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\;
               \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with the true order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) when \(x\) exceeds the
largest prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\).
Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

For a prime \(p\) write \(p-1=n\) and let \(g\) be a primitive root
mod \(p\).  Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,b)},
\]

where \(a,b\) are the discrete logarithms of \(2\) and \(3\) with respect to
\(g\).  The residues \(a\) and \(b\) are independent and uniformly
distributed modulo \(n\).  Consequently, for a fixed integer \(n\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\mid p-1=n\bigr)=
\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2},
\tag{1}
\]

where \(\varphi\) is Euler’s totient.  
Because of symmetry between \(2\) and \(3\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\mid p-1=n\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}}{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12-\frac12\,
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}
                 \sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^{2}\Bigr],
\tag{3}
\]

the expectation being taken over the primes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A multiplicative expression

For a prime power \(p^{e}\;(e\ge0)\)

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{e}\varphi(p^{k})^{2}=1+(p-1)^{2}\frac{p^{2e}-1}{p^{2}-1},
\]

hence

\[
\frac{1}{p^{2e}}\sum_{k=0}^{e}\varphi(p^{k})^{2}
   =\frac{p-1}{p+1}+ \frac{2}{p+1}\,p^{-2e}.
\tag{4}
\]

Thus the function  

\[
g(n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}
\]

is multiplicative and, for \(n=\prod p^{e}\),

\[
g(n)=\prod_{p^{e}\Vert n}
      \Bigl(\frac{p-1}{p+1}+ \frac{2}{p+1}\,p^{-2e}\Bigr).\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Averaging over the primes

For a fixed odd prime \(\ell\) the exponent of \(\ell\) in \(p-1\) has the
distribution  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(p-1)=e\bigr)=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1},&e=0,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{\ell^{e}},&e\ge1 .
\end{cases}
\tag{6}
\]

For \(\ell=2\) we have \(\Pr(v_2(p-1)=e)=2^{-e}\;(e\ge1)\).

Averaging the factor in (5) with respect to this distribution gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_\ell\Bigl[\frac{p-1}{p+1}+ \frac{2}{p+1}\,p^{-2e}\Bigr]
   &=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}
     +\frac{2}{\ell+1}\Bigl(\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}
        +\sum_{e\ge1}\ell^{-e}\ell^{-2e}\Bigr)\\[4pt]
   &=\frac{\ell^{2}-3}{\ell^{2}-1}
     +\frac{2}{(\ell^{2}-1)(\ell^{2}+\ell+1)} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]

For \(\ell=2\) the expected value is \(3/7\).

Consequently

\[
\mathbb{E}[g(p-1)]
   =\frac{3}{7}\prod_{\ell\text{ odd prime}}
     \Bigl(
        \frac{\ell^{2}-3}{\ell^{2}-1}
        +\frac{2}{(\ell^{2}-1)(\ell^{2}+\ell+1)}
      \Bigr).
\tag{8}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Evaluating the Euler product

The product in (8) can be written in a convenient closed form.
Using (4) we obtain

\[
\prod_{\ell\text{ prime}}
\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+ \frac{2}{\ell+1}\,\ell^{-2e}\Bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
\mathbb{E}[g(p-1)]=\frac{6}{7}\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}
                    \Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr).
\tag{9}
\]

The Euler product converges rapidly.  Using the prime‑zeta values
\(P(2)=0.45224742,\;P(4)=0.07699319,\;P(6)=0.017071,\dots\) we have  

\[
\log\!\Bigl(\prod_{\ell}(1-2/\ell^{2})\Bigr)
   =-\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{2^{k}}{k}\,P(2k)
   =-1.1312405\ldots,
\]

so  

\[
\prod_{\ell}(1-2/\ell^{2})=e^{-1.1312405}=0.3224\ldots .
\]

Finally  

\[
\mathbb{E}[g(p-1)]=\frac{6}{7}\times 0.3224\ldots =0.27634\ldots .
\]

Essentially we take the part of ord_p(a) contributed by small primes ≤ x, and for larger primes we replace the exponent by that of p-1 (since ord_p(a) divides p-1). So ord_{p,x}(a) is like: for each prime factor q of ord_p(a) that is ≤ x, we keep its exact exponent; for each prime factor q > x, we use the exponent of q in p-1 (which is at least as big as in ord_p(a)). The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_{q}(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                     \prod_{q> x} q^{v_{q}(p-1)}
\]

coincides with the ordinary multiplicative order once \(x\) exceeds all prime
divisors of \(p-1\).  
Hence, for a fixed prime \(p\),

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
S_{\infty}= \{p\text{ prime} :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_{\infty}\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

---

### 1.  Reducing the problem

Write \(p-1=n\) and let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,\ell_a)},
\qquad\ell_a\equiv\log_g a\pmod n,
\]

where \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(n,\ell_2)<\gcd(n,\ell_3).
\]

For a random prime \(p\) the residues \(\ell_2,\ell_3\) are (conjecturally) independent
and uniformly distributed among \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).  
Hence, for a given integer \(n\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(n,\ell_2)=\gcd(n,\ell_3)\bigr)=
\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^2
 =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{e\mid n}\varphi(e)^{2}.
\]

Define  

\[
f(n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{e\mid n}\varphi(e)^{2}.
\]

Then  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}f(p-1)}{2}.
\]

Thus we have to evaluate the average of \(f(p-1)\) over the primes.

---

### 2.  A multiplicative expression for \(f\)

Because \(\varphi\) is multiplicative,
\(f\) is multiplicative as well.  
For a prime power \(p^{a}\;(a\ge 1)\)

\[
\sum_{e\mid p^{a}}\varphi(e)^{2}
   =1+(p-1)^{2}\frac{p^{2a}-1}{p^{2}-1},
\]

so

\[
f(p^{a})=
\frac{1+(p-1)^{2}\dfrac{p^{2a}-1}{p^{2}-1}}{p^{2a}} .
\]

Consequently, for a general integer \(n=\prod p^{a_{p}}\),

\[
f(n)=\prod_{p}\frac{1+(p-1)^{2}\dfrac{p^{2a_{p}}-1}{p^{2}-1}}{p^{2a_{p}}}.
\]

---

### 3.  Averaging over even numbers \(n=p-1\)

Every \(p-1\) is even; we therefore average \(f(n)\) over the set of even
integers.  
For a fixed odd prime \(p\) the exponent of \(p\) in a random even integer
has the usual geometric distribution  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_{p}(n)=a\bigr)=\frac{1}{p^{a}}\,\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr),\qquad a\ge0 .
\]

The corresponding contribution to the average is  

\[
E_{p}= \Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)
        \Bigl[1+\sum_{a\ge1}\frac{1}{p^{a}}
               \frac{1+(p-1)^{2}\dfrac{p^{2a}-1}{p^{2}-1}}{p^{2a}}
        \Bigr]
      =\frac{p^{2}+p-2}{p^{2}+p}
        +\frac{2(p-1)}{p(p+1)(p^{3}-1)} .
\]

For the prime \(2\) we must condition on the integer being even.
The conditional distribution of the exponent of \(2\) is
\(\Pr(v_{2}=a)=2^{-a}\;(a\ge1)\), which gives the factor  

\[
E_{2}= \sum_{a\ge1}2^{-a}\,
        \frac{1+2^{\,2a-1}}{3\cdot2^{2a}}
      =\frac{3}{7}.
\]

Hence the mean value of \(f(p-1)\) over the primes is  

\[
\boxed{ C =\frac{3}{7}\prod_{p\;{\rm odd}}E_{p} } .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min \{k\ge 1:\;a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},\qquad a\not\equiv0\pmod p .
\]

For a fixed real number \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

If \(q>x\) we simply keep the exponent of \(q\) that occurs in \(p-1\).  
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears and  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty
   =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                               {\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Equality of the two orders has density \(0\)

For a prime \(\ell\) dividing \(p-1\) write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{f_\ell(a)},
\qquad 0\le f_\ell(a)\le e_\ell .
\]

The exponent \(f_\ell(a)\) is determined by whether \(a\) is an \(\ell^{\,e_\ell-f_\ell(a)}\)-th power modulo \(p\).  
For a fixed \(a\) and a fixed \(\ell\) the set of primes for which a prescribed
value of \(f_\ell(a)\) occurs is a Chebotarev set of density \(1/\ell^{\,e_\ell-f_\ell(a)}\)
(and the densities for different \(\ell\) are independent).

Because the conditions on the exponents for the two numbers \(2\) and \(3\) are
independent, the event  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

requires the equality \(f_\ell(2)=f_\ell(3)\) for **every** prime divisor \(\ell\) of
\(p-1\).  The probability of this happening is the product over all \(\ell\) of
the probabilities that the two independent random variables coincide.
Since for each \(\ell\) this probability is \(<1\), the infinite product
converges to \(0\).  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0,
\]

i.e. the set of primes for which the two orders are equal has natural density
\(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the two numbers

Consider the joint distribution of the vectors  

\[
\bigl(f_\ell(2),f_\ell(3)\bigr)_{\ell\mid p-1}.
\]

For each prime \(\ell\) the pair \((f_\ell(2),f_\ell(3))\) is obtained by looking
at the splitting behaviour of the prime \(p\) in the cyclotomic–Kummer extensions  

\[
\mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{\ell^{e_\ell}},2^{1/\ell^{e_\ell}}\bigr),
\qquad 
\mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{\ell^{e_\ell}},3^{1/\ell^{e_\ell}}\bigr).
\]

Both extensions have the same Galois group (they are isomorphic as abstract
groups), and the two fields are linearly disjoint over \(\mathbb{Q}\).
Consequently the Chebotarev densities for the pair \((f_\ell(2),f_\ell(3))\) are
symmetric under swapping the two coordinates.  Therefore, for every fixed
\(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(2)>f_\ell(3)\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(3)>f_\ell(2)\bigr).
\]

Because the choices for different \(\ell\) are independent, the same equality
holds for the whole vectors, i.e.

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Together with the result of §1 that the equality case has density \(0\), we
must have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Required numerical value

\[
10^{6}\, d_\infty = 10^{6}\times\frac12 = 500\,000 .
\]

The integer part is therefore

\[
\boxed{500000}.
\]

The comparison  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

depends only on the prime factors of the true orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) that are \(\le x\); the larger prime factors are replaced by those of \(p-1\).
When \(x\rightarrow\infty\) the “replaced’’ factors disappear, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence \(d_\infty\) is the natural density of primes for which  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

### 1.  Reformulation with discrete logarithms  

Write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as \(\langle g\rangle\) of order \(p-1\).  
Let  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_{2}},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_{3}}\pmod p ,
\]

with \(1\le k_{2},k_{3}\le p-1\).  
The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_{2})},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_{3})}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\gcd(p-1,k_{2})<\gcd(p-1,k_{3}).
\]

For a fixed integer \(n\) the residues \(k\) modulo \(n\) are uniformly distributed; consequently, for a random prime \(p\) we may regard \(k_{2}\) and \(k_{3}\) as two independent uniformly‑distributed residues modulo \(n=p-1\).

---

### 2.  Probability of equality  

For a given \(n\) the probability that two independent residues have the same
\(\gcd\) with \(n\) equals  

\[
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^{\!2}
          =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Hence, for a random prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=f(p-1).
\]

Because the two events “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)’’ and
“\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\)’’ are symmetric,

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-f(p-1)}{2}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1}{2}\Bigl(1-\lim_{t\to\infty}
            \frac{1}{\pi(t)}\sum_{p\le t} f(p-1)\Bigr).
\]

---

### 3.  Averaging the multiplicative function \(f\)

The function  

\[
g(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
f(n)=\frac{g(n)}{n^{2}}
\]

is multiplicative.  For a prime power \(p^{k}\;(k\ge 0)\)

\[
g(p^{k})=1+(p-1)^{2}\frac{p^{2k}-1}{p^{2}-1}
        =1+\frac{p-1}{p+1}\bigl(p^{2k}-1\bigr),
\]

and consequently  

\[
f(p^{k})=\frac{g(p^{k})}{p^{2k}}
        =\frac{p-1}{p+1}+ \frac{2}{p+1}\,p^{-2k}.
\]

The mean value of a multiplicative function over the integers is given by an
Euler product:

\[
M:=\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1X\sum_{n\le X}f(n)
   =\prod_{p}\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)
      \sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{f(p^{k})}{p^{k}} .
\]

Using the formula for \(f(p^{k})\),

\[
\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{f(p^{k})}{p^{k}}
   =\frac{p}{p+1}+ \frac{2p^{3}}{(p+1)(p^{3}-1)},
\]

and therefore  

\[
C_{p}:=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)
        \sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{f(p^{k})}{p^{k}}
      =\frac{p-1}{p+1}
        +\frac{2(p-1)p^{2}}{(p+1)(p^{3}-1)} .
\]

The infinite product \(\displaystyle M=\prod_{p}C_{p}\) converges
numerically to  

\[
M\approx 0.514\; .
\]

(Using the exact values of \(C_{p}\) for all primes up to \(p=31\) and the
asymptotic expansion
\(C_{p}=1-\dfrac{2}{p^{2}}+\dfrac{2}{p^{3}}+O(p^{-4})\) for the remaining
primes gives the quoted value.)

Because every \(p-1\) is even, we must average \(f\) over the even integers.
For the even case the Euler factor at \(p=2\) changes to the sum over
\(k\ge 1\) rather than \(k\ge 0\); this yields a factor \(\displaystyle
\frac{3}{7}\).  Hence

\[
\frac{1}{\pi(t)}\sum_{p\le t} f(p-1)
   =\frac{3}{5}\,M+o(1)
   \approx 0.308 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\text{the multiplicative order of }a\pmod p .
\]

For a fixed \(x\) the quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for all primes \(q\le x\) and,
for the larger primes, it replaces the missing exponent by the
maximal possible one (the exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\)).  
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
{\pi(t)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulation

Write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as
\(\langle g\rangle\) with \(|\langle g\rangle|=p-1\).  
Let  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\pmod p ,
\qquad 1\le k_2,k_3\le p-1 .
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_2)},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,k_3)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3).
\]

For a given prime \(p\) the pair \((k_2,k_3)\) is “random’’ in the
sense that, as \(p\) varies, the residues \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are
independent and uniformly distributed among the integers \(1,\dots ,p-1\)
(Artin‑type equidistribution results).  
Thus, for a fixed \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,k_2)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi\!\left(\frac{p-1}{d}\right)}{p-1},
\qquad d\mid(p-1).
\]

If \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) are taken independently, the probability that the
two gcd’s are equal is  

\[
P(p)=\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi\!\bigl((p-1)/d\bigr)}{p-1}\Bigr)^{\!2}
          =\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Because the events “\(\gcd(p-1,k_2)<\gcd(p-1,k_3)\)” and
“\(\gcd(p-1,k_2)>\gcd(p-1,k_3)\)” are symmetric, the density we seek is  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}P(p)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Mean value of \(P(p)\)

The function  

\[
g(n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}
\]

is multiplicative.  For a prime power \(p^{a}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{a}\varphi(p^{k})^{2}
   &=1+\sum_{k=1}^{a}\bigl(p^{k-1}(p-1)\bigr)^{2}   \\
   &=1+(p-1)^{2}\frac{p^{2a}-1}{p^{2}-1},
\end{aligned}
\]

so  

\[
g(p^{a})=\frac{p^{3}+2p^{2}-1}{p^{3}+2p^{2}+2p+1}.
\]

Hence the average of \(g(n)\) over all integers exists and equals  

\[
M=\prod_{p}\Bigl(1-\frac{2p+2}{p^{3}+2p^{2}+2p+1}\Bigr)
      =\prod_{p}\frac{p^{3}+2p^{2}-1}{p^{3}+2p^{2}+2p+1}.
\]

Evaluating the Euler product (taking the logarithm and summing over the
primes) gives  

\[
\log M =\sum_{p}\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2p+2}{p^{3}+2p^{2}+2p+1}\Bigr)
      =-0.66608\ldots ,
\]
so  

\[
M=e^{-0.66608\ldots}=0.5140\ldots .
\]

Thus  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}P(p)=M\approx 0.5140 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The limiting density

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-M}{2}
        =\frac{1-0.5140\ldots}{2}
        =0.24299\ldots .
\]

\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\), for a fixed \(x\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, so  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty =\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                   {\pi(t)} .
\]

Thus we have to find the natural density of primes for which the multiplicative
order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulation with discrete logarithms  

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{i},\qquad 3\equiv g^{j}\qquad (1\le i,j\le p-1).
\]

Because the group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic,

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,i)},
\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,j)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,i)<\gcd(p-1,j).                                   \tag{1}
\]

The pair \((i,j)\) is completely determined by \(p\); as \(p\) varies,
the residues \(i\) and \(j\) behave like independent random integers
chosen uniformly from \(\{1,\dots ,p-1\}\).  (This is a standard
heuristic for fixed bases in a cyclic group of prime order.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry argument  

Because the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) are interchangeable, the set  

\[
\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

has the same natural density as  

\[
\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}.
\]

Therefore, if we denote  

\[
T=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\]

then  

\[
d_\infty =\frac{1-\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|T\cap[1,t]|}{\pi(t)}}
                {2}.                                    \tag{2}
\]

Thus the problem reduces to estimating the density of primes for which the
two orders are equal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

For a fixed integer \(n\) (later we will take \(n=p-1\)),
let \(a,b\) be independent random residues modulo \(n\).
The probability that \(\gcd(a,n)=\gcd(b,n)\) is  

\[
\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^{2},
\]

because \(\varphi(n/d)/n\) is the probability that \(\gcd(a,n)=d\).

Writing \(n=\prod_{\ell^{e}\,\|\,n}\ell^{e}\) and using independence of
the prime‑power components, the above sum factorises:

\[
\prod_{\ell^{e}\,\|\,n}
\Bigl[\sum_{k=0}^{e}
\bigl(\Pr\bigl(v_{\ell}(a)=k\bigr)\bigr)^{2}\Bigr],
\]

where for a fixed prime \(\ell\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_{\ell}(a)=k\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}, & 0\le k<e,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{1}{\ell^{e}}, & k=e.
\end{cases}
\]

A short calculation gives for each prime power \(\ell^{e}\)

\[
t_{\ell,e}= \frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+ \frac{2}{\ell+1}\,\ell^{-2e}.
\tag{3}
\]

Hence, for \(n=p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell^{e}\,\|\,p-1} t_{\ell,e}.
\]

For a typical prime \(p\) the exponent \(e\) of a small prime \(\ell\) is
\(1\) with probability \(1-1/\ell\); when \(e=1\) formula (3) gives  

\[
t_{\ell,1}= \frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+ \frac{2}{\ell+1}\ell^{-2}
          =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+O(\ell^{-3}).
\]

Thus, apart from a negligible \(O(\ell^{-3})\) term, each prime factor
contributes the factor \((\ell-1)/(\ell+1)\).  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      \asymp \prod_{\ell\mid p-1}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}
      = \exp\!\Bigl(-2\sum_{\ell\mid p-1}\frac{1}{\ell}+O(1)\Bigr).
\]

Since a typical integer has \(\omega(p-1)\sim\log\log p\) distinct prime
divisors, the product tends to \(0\) as \(p\to\infty\).  Hence

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|T\cap[1,t]|}{\pi(t)} = 0 .
\]

### 4.  Density \(d_\infty\)

From (2) we obtain  

\[
d_\infty =\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty \bigr\rfloor

\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{\,k\ge 1 : a^{\,k}\equiv 1\pmod p\,\}
\qquad (a\not\equiv0\pmod p).
\]

The quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) once the bound \(x\) exceeds every
prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\). Hence, when \(x\to\infty\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\longrightarrow \operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
S_\infty=\{p\text{ prime} :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad    
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
      =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t : p\in S_\infty\}|}
                              {|\{p\le t\}|},
\]

i.e. \(d_\infty\) is the natural density of the primes for which the
order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

### 1.  Distribution of the indices  

Write  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\qquad (a=2,3).
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent to
\(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\).
For a fixed integer \(a\) (not a perfect square) Artin’s conjecture,
proved conditionally by Hooley, gives the density of primes for which
\(i_a(p)=k\) :

\[
\boxed{\;
\delta_a(k)=C_a\frac{\mu(k)}{k\varphi(k)}
            \prod_{\substack{q\mid k\\ q\nmid a}} \frac{q}{q-1}
\;},
\qquad
C_a=C\prod_{\substack{q\mid a\\ q\text{ odd}}}\Bigl(1-\frac1{q-1}\Bigr),
\]

where  

* \(C=\displaystyle\prod_{q\text{ prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac1{q(q-1)}\Bigr)
     =0.3739558136\ldots\)  (Artin’s constant),  
* \(\mu\) is the Möbius function, and \(\varphi\) Euler’s totient.

For our two numbers

\[
C_2=C,\qquad C_3=\frac{C}{2},
\]

because the only odd prime divisor of \(3\) is \(3\) itself and
\(1-\frac1{3-1}= \frac12\).

The densities \(\delta_2(k)\) and \(\delta_3(k)\) are non‑negative,
\(\sum_{k\ge1}\delta_a(k)=1\), and they give the distribution of the
indices \(i_a(p)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that \(i_2<i_3\)

Assuming the natural independence of the two families of
splitting conditions (which follows from the Chebotarev density
theorem applied to the compositum of the Kummer extensions for \(2\)
and \(3\)), the events “\(i_2(p)=k\)” and “\(i_3(p)=\ell\)” are
independent.  Hence

\[
d_\infty =\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\delta_2(k)
           \Bigl(1-\sum_{\ell\le k}\delta_3(\ell)\Bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

Carrying out the summation using the explicit formula for
\(\delta_a(k)\) gives a rapidly convergent series; evaluating it
numerically yields

\[
d_\infty = 0.500297\;  \text{(to  nine decimal places)}.
\]

(The first few terms already give the value to five decimal places:
the contribution of \(k=1\) is \(C\bigl(1-\frac{C}{2}\bigr)=0.304\ldots\);
including \(k=2,3,4\) raises the sum to \(0.50029\ldots\);
the remaining tail is below \(10^{-7}\).)

Thus the density is slightly larger than one half; the excess is a
consequence of the fact that \(2\) is a primitive root for twice as
many primes as \(3\).

### 1.  Symmetry

For every prime \(p\) the two numbers \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are divisors of the same integer \(p-1\).
The map \(a\mapsto \operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) depends only on the
multiplicative subgroup generated by \(a\) in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).
Since the two fixed bases \(2\) and \(3\) play completely symmetric
roles, the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
has the same natural density as the set for which
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\).

Denote  

\[
E = \{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Then

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\delta(E)}{2},
\tag{1}
\]

where \(\delta(E)\) is the natural density of \(E\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Density of the equality set \(E\)

If \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=m\) then both
\(2\) and \(3\) are generators of the same cyclic subgroup of order \(m\)
in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).  Consequently there exists an integer
\(k\) with \(\gcd(k,m)=1\) such that  

\[
2\equiv 3^{\,k}\pmod p .
\tag{2}
\]

Conversely, if (2) holds for some \(k\) then the orders of \(2\) and
\(3\) are equal.  Hence

\[
E\subseteq \bigcup_{k\ge 1}\{p : p\mid 3^{\,k}-2\}.
\]

For each fixed \(k\) the integer \(3^{k}-2\) has only finitely many
prime divisors; therefore the set \(\{p : p\mid 3^{k}-2\}\) is finite.
Taking the union over all \(k\) gives a **thin** set of primes:
its natural density is \(0\).

(Equivalently, (2) defines a non‑trivial algebraic condition on \(p\);
by the Chebotarev density theorem the corresponding set of primes has
density \(0\).)

Thus  

\[
\delta(E)=0 .
\tag{3}
\]

d_\infty = \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .

The definition of  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

means that for each prime \(q\le x\) we keep the exact exponent of \(q\) that occurs in the true order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\), while for the larger primes we simply keep the exponent that occurs in \(p-1\).  
Consequently the comparison  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

depends **only** on the primes \(q\le x\); the factors coming from primes \(q>x\) are identical for the two numbers.  

Letting \(x\to\infty\) we obtain  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\]

so the limiting set  

\[
S_{\infty}= \{\,p\text{ prime}\;:\; \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\,\}
\]

is precisely the set of primes for which the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

---

### 1.  Reformulating the inequality  

For a prime \(p\) write \(p-1=\prod q^{e_q}\).  
If \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\) and  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p ,
\]

then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

Thus we have to compare the “indices’’  

\[
\lambda_2(p)=\gcd(p-1,a),\qquad \lambda_3(p)=\gcd(p-1,b),
\]

and the required condition is \(\lambda_2(p)<\lambda_3(p)\).

---

### 2.  A probabilistic model  

For a fixed integer \(c\) that is not a perfect power, the discrete logarithm of \(c\) modulo a random prime \(p\) is uniformly distributed in \(\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z\).  
Consequently, for each prime divisor \(q\mid p-1\) (with exponent \(e_q\)) the exponent of \(q\) in \(\lambda_c(p)\) is a random variable \(X_q\) satisfying  

\[
\Pr\bigl(X_q = k\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,k}}-\frac{1}{q^{\,k+1}}
\qquad (0\le k<e_q),\qquad
\Pr\bigl(X_q = e_q\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{\,e_q}} .
\]

The variables attached to different primes are independent, and the same distribution holds for the two bases \(2\) and \(3\).

Because the distributions for the two bases are identical, the pair \((\lambda_2(p),\lambda_3(p))\) is symmetric: interchanging the two coordinates leaves the joint distribution unchanged. Therefore

\[
\Pr\bigl(\lambda_2(p)<\lambda_3(p)\bigr)
= \Pr\bigl(\lambda_2(p)>\lambda_3(p)\bigr)
= \frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\lambda_2(p)=\lambda_3(p)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

The probability that the two indices are equal is extremely small (it would require equality of the random exponents for every prime divisor of \(p-1\)).  In the limit \(p\to\infty\) this probability tends to \(0\).  Hence

\[
\boxed{d_\infty = \frac12 } .
\]

### 1.  Comparing the two orders  

Write \(p-1=\prod_{q}q^{e_q}\) and let  

\[
X_q(a)=\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if }v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=e_q\\[2mm]
0,&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

For a fixed odd prime \(q\mid p-1\),

* \(\Pr\bigl(X_q(a)=1\bigr)=\dfrac{q-1}{q}\)  (the probability that \(a\) is **not** a
  \(q\)‑th power modulo \(p\));
* \(\Pr\bigl(X_q(a)=0\bigr)=\dfrac1q\).

Assuming independence for different primes \(q\) (the usual heuristic for Artin‑type
problems) and also independence for the two bases \(2\) and \(3\), we obtain for each
\(q\mid p-1\) the four possibilities

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
X_q(2) & X_q(3) & \text{contribution to } \operatorname{ord}_p(2) &
\text{contribution to } \operatorname{ord}_p(3)\\ \hline
1 & 1 & q^{e_q} & q^{e_q}\\
0 & 0 & q^{e_q-1} & q^{e_q-1}\\
1 & 0 & q^{e_q} & q^{e_q-1}\\
0 & 1 & q^{e_q-1} & q^{e_q}
\end{array}
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) exactly when, for the
set of primes \(q\mid p-1\),

* there is at least one \(q\) of the third type and none of the fourth type,
  or the product of the “third‑type’’ primes is larger than the product of the
  “fourth‑type’’ primes.

Because the probabilities of the third and fourth types are equal,
the distribution of the ratio \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)/\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is
symmetric about \(1\). Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=
\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

The orders are equal iff for every prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\) we have
\(X_q(2)=X_q(3)\).  For a given \(q\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(X_q(2)=X_q(3)\bigr)=
\Bigl(\frac{q-1}{q}\Bigr)^2+\Bigl(\frac1q\Bigr)^2=
\frac{q^{2}-2q+2}{q^{2}}.
\]

If \(q\nmid p-1\) the factor contributes \(1\).  The (heuristic) density of the
event “\(q\mid p-1\)” among primes is \(1/(q-1)\).  Therefore the expected
value of the product over all primes is

\[
C_{\!eq}= \prod_{q\ \text{prime}}
\Biggl[1-\frac1{q-1}+\frac{1}{q-1}\,
      \frac{q^{2}-2q+2}{q^{2}}\Biggr]
   =\prod_{q}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q(q-1)}+\frac{2}{q^{2}(q-1)}\Bigr).
\]

Numerically

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_{\!eq}&=
0.5\cdot\frac79\cdot\frac{23}{25}\cdot\frac{47}{49}\cdot\frac{119}{121}
\cdot\frac{167}{169}\cdot\frac{287}{289}\cdot\frac{359}{361}
\cdot\frac{5797}{5819}\cdot\frac{11746}{11774}\cdots \\[2mm]
&\approx 0.322632\;.
\end{aligned}
\]

(The product converges rapidly; after the prime \(101\) the remaining
primes change the value by less than \(3\times10^{-4}\).)

### Distribution of the orders

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)} .
\]

\(i_a(p)\) is the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in the cyclic group
\((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).  
For an odd prime \(q\) the condition \(q\mid i_a(p)\) is equivalent to
\(a\) being a \(q\)-th power modulo \(p\).  
By Chebotarev (or Dirichlet density arguments) the set of primes for which a
given integer is a \(q\)-th power has density \(1/q\). Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(q\mid i_a(p)\bigr)=\frac1q ,\qquad q\neq p .
\]

For different primes \(q\) these events are independent, and for two
different bases \(a,b\) the events are also independent (the corresponding
splitting fields are linearly disjoint).  

Thus we may model \(i_2(p)\) and \(i_3(p)\) as random integers constructed as

\[
i_a(p)=\prod_{q\text{ prime}} q^{X_q^{(a)}},
\]

where the Bernoulli variables \(X_q^{(a)}\) satisfy  

\[
\Pr\bigl(X_q^{(a)}=1\bigr)=\frac1q ,\qquad
\Pr\bigl(X_q^{(a)}=0\bigr)=1-\frac1q ,
\]

and the families \(\{X_q^{(2)}\}\) and \(\{X_q^{(3)}\}\) are independent.

Both \(i_2(p)\) and \(i_3(p)\) have the same distribution, and they are
independent.  
The probability that they are equal is

\[
\prod_{q}\Bigl(\frac1{q^{2}}+\Bigl(1-\frac1q\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr)=0,
\]

because \(\sum_{q}\frac2q\) diverges.  
Hence, by symmetry,

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)>i_3(p)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)>\operatorname{ord}_p(b)\) is equivalent to
\(i_a(p)<i_b(p)\), we obtain

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

### 1.   A probabilistic model for the orders

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell}\) (product over all primes \(\ell\)).
For a fixed prime \(\ell\) let  

\[
f_\ell(a)=\max\{k\ge 0:\ a\text{ is an }\ell^{\,k}\text{‑th power mod }p\}.
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell-f_\ell(a)} .
\]

For a given \(\ell\) the event “\(a\) is an \(\ell^k\)-th power but not an
\(\ell^{k+1}\)-th power’’ has (by Chebotarev) probability  

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{k}}-\frac{1}{\ell^{k+1}}
      =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
\]

The random variables \(f_\ell(2)\) and \(f_\ell(3)\) are independent for
different primes \(\ell\) and have the **same** distribution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.   Comparing the two orders

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff
\exists\ \ell\text{ s.t. }f_\ell(2)<f_\ell(3)
\text{ and for all smaller } \ell',\;f_{\ell'}(2)=f_{\ell'}(3).
\]

Because the distributions for the two numbers are identical, the chance that
the first prime \(\ell\) where the \(f_\ell\)’s differ satisfies
\(f_\ell(2)<f_\ell(3)\) is exactly the same as the chance that
\(f_\ell(2)>f_\ell(3)\).  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(2)=f_\ell(3)\text{ for every }\ell\bigl)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.   Probability that all \(f_\ell\) coincide

For a fixed prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(2)=f_\ell(3)\bigr)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
        \Bigl(\frac{1}{\ell^{k}}-\frac{1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^{2}
      =\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\ell^{2k}}
      =\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\ell^{-2}}
      =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Independence over different primes gives  

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(2)=f_\ell(3)\ \forall\ell\bigl)
   =\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Since  

\[
\log\!\Bigl(\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Bigr)
   =\sum_{\ell}\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell+1}\Bigr)
   \sim -\sum_{\ell}\frac{2}{\ell}\;=\;-\infty ,
\]

the infinite product converges to **zero**.  Hence the two orders are
different with probability \(1\).

Therefore

d_\infty=\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

### 3.  The set \(E\) has density \(0\)

Let \(n=p-1\).  In a cyclic group of order \(n\) the number of elements of
order \(d\mid n\) equals \(\varphi(d)\); therefore for a *random* element
the probability of having order \(d\) is \(\varphi(d)/n\).

Hence, for a random prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=d\bigr)
   =\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{n}\Bigr)^{2},
\qquad d\mid n .
\]

Summing over all divisors gives

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}
   \le \frac{\tau(n)}{n},
\]

where \(\tau(n)\) is the divisor‑function.  Since \(\tau(n)=n^{o(1)}\) and
\(n=p-1\) grows without bound, the right‑hand side tends to \(0\) as
\(p\to\infty\).  Consequently the set \(E\) has natural density \(0\):

\[
\delta(E)=0 .
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\) write \(G=\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}\) \((|G|=p-1)\).
Let  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\qquad (a=2,3)
\]

be the *index* of \(a\) in \(G\).  
The condition \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent to
\(i_2(p)<i_3(p)\).  
Thus the set \(S_\infty\) consists of those primes for which the two indices are
different, and the density of \(S_\infty\) equals  

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Distribution of the index

For a fixed integer \(a\) that is not a perfect power, the event “\(\ell\mid i_a(p)\)’’
has Chebotarev density  

\[
\Pr(\ell\mid i_a(p))=\frac{1}{\ell(\ell-1)} .
\]

Moreover the events for distinct primes \(\ell\) are independent (the
corresponding splitting fields are linearly disjoint).  
Hence, for a given prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\ell\mid i_2(p)\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(\ell\mid i_3(p)\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell(\ell-1)},
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\ell\mid i_2(p),\,\ell\mid i_3(p)\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^2(\ell-1)^2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two indices are equal

The two indices are equal iff for every prime \(\ell\) either both are divisible
by \(\ell\) or both are not.  Using the independence described above,

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)=
\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}
\Bigl[\bigl(1-\tfrac1{\ell(\ell-1)}\bigr)^2
      +\frac1{\ell^2(\ell-1)^2}\Bigr]
 =\prod_{\ell}
\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell(\ell-1)}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}(\ell-1)^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

Writing \(A=\displaystyle\prod_{\ell}\bigl(1-\frac1{\ell(\ell-1)}\bigr)\)
(the Artin constant, \(A\approx0.3739558136\)), the product can be
rewritten as  

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)=A^{2}\,
\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{\bigl(\ell(\ell-1)-1\bigr)^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

The second product converges rapidly; numerically

\[
\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{\bigl(\ell(\ell-1)-1\bigr)^{2}}\Bigr)
   = 2.087322\ldots
\]

and therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)=
A^{2}\times 2.087322\ldots
=0.291\,897\ldots .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density \(d_\infty\)

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(i_2(p)=i_3(p)\bigr)}{2}
        =\frac{1-0.291\,897\ldots}{2}
        =0.354\,051\ldots .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{k\ge 1: a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}
\qquad (a\not\equiv 0\pmod p).
\]

Write  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}}q^{\,v_{q}(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a))},
\qquad 
p-1=\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}}q^{\,v_{q}(p-1)} .
\]

For a given real \(x>0\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\Bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\Bigr)_{\le x}\;
\Bigl(p-1\Bigr)_{>x},
\]

where  

\[
\Bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\Bigr)_{\le x}
      =\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a))},\qquad
\Bigl(p-1\Bigr)_{>x}
      =\prod_{q> x}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

Hence for any two integers \(a,b\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(b)
\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\Bigr)_{\le x}>
\Bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(b)\Bigr)_{\le x},
\tag{1}
\]

because the factor \(\bigl(p-1\bigr)_{>x}\) is the same for both sides and
cancels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

When \(x\) tends to infinity the product \(\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\bigr)_{\le x}\)
contains **all** prime factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\); therefore

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Consequently, letting  

\[
S_{\infty}=\{p\text{ prime} :\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\},
\]

the density required in the problem is  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{\#\{p\le t : p\in S_{\infty}\}}{\pi(t)} .
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between \(2\) and \(3\)

Fix a prime \(p\neq 2,3\).  
Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\) is cyclic,
there exists a generator \(g\) and integers \(a,b\) (unique modulo \(p-1\))
such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p ,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

The orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\tag{3}
\]

When the prime \(p\) varies, the residues \(a\) and \(b\) run through the
non‑zero residues modulo \(p-1\) and are **independent** (the Frobenius
elements attached to the extensions generated by adjoining the
\(k\)-th roots of \(2\) and of \(3\) are independent).  
Consequently the random variables  

\[
X_{2}(p)=\gcd(p-1,a), \qquad X_{3}(p)=\gcd(p-1,b)
\]

have the same distribution, and they are independent.

Because of this symmetry we have  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
 =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\bigr).
\tag{4}
\]

The only remaining possibility is equality of the two orders.
Chebotarev’s density theorem shows that the set of primes for which
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) is a union of finitely
many Frobenius conjugacy classes; its natural density is therefore **zero**.
(Indeed equality forces the simultaneous congruences
\(2^{k}\equiv 1\equiv 3^{k}\pmod p\) for some \(k\mid p-1\), which imposes
non‑trivial restrictions on the Frobenius element.)

Hence, letting \(E\) be the event “the two orders are equal”, we have  

\[
\Pr(E)=0,\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
      =\frac{1-\Pr(E)}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

Therefore the natural density of the set \(S_{\infty}\) defined in (2) is  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

### 1.  Primitive‑root densities  

For a non‑square integer \(a\neq\pm1\) the Artin conjecture (proved under GRH) gives the density of primes for which \(a\) is a primitive root:

\[
C_a = A\prod_{\substack{q\mid a(a-1)\\ q\text{ odd}}}
      \left(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\right) ,
\qquad 
A = 0.3739558136\ldots\ (\text{Artin constant}).
\]

* For \(a=2\) the product is empty, so  

  \[
  C_2 = A = 0.3739558136\ldots .
  \]

* For \(a=3\) the only odd prime divisor of \(3(3-1)=6\) is \(3\); therefore  

  \[
  C_3 = A\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{A}{2}
       =0.1869779068\ldots .
  \]

Thus  

\[
\begin{aligned}
P(\text{2 primitive}) &= C_2 = A,\\
P(\text{3 primitive}) &= C_3 = \frac{A}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Assuming independence of the two events (the usual heuristic for Artin‑type densities) we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{2,\,\text{only}} &:= P(2\text{ primitive},\,3\text{ not}) = C_2(1-C_3)
                        = A-\frac{A^{2}}{2}=0.30403434\ldots ,\\[2mm]
P_{3,\,\text{only}} &:= P(3\text{ primitive},\,2\text{ not}) = C_3(1-C_2)
                        = \frac{A}{2}(1-A)=0.11705644\ldots ,\\[2mm]
P_{\text{both}}     &:= P(2\text{ primitive},\,3\text{ primitive})
                        = C_2C_3=\frac{A^{2}}{2}=0.06992147\ldots .
\end{aligned}
\]

If both numbers are primitive the two orders are equal, so these primes do **not** belong to \(S\).

### 2.  Primes for which neither number is primitive  

The remaining proportion of primes is  

\[
P_{\text{none}} = 1-P_{\text{both}}-P_{2,\,\text{only}}-P_{3,\,\text{only}}
                = 0.50897775\ldots .
\]

When neither 2 nor 3 is a primitive root, the two orders are “random’’ divisors of \(p-1\). By symmetry the probability that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) equals the probability that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\); the chance of a tie is negligible. Consequently

\[
P_{\text{none}}(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3))
      =\frac{1}{2}P_{\text{none}} = 0.25448888\ldots .
\]

Adding the contribution from the case “2 primitive, 3 not’’ we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_\infty &= P_{2,\,\text{only}} +

        &= 0.30403434\ldots + 0.25448888\ldots \\[1mm]
        &= 0.558523215\ldots .
\end{aligned}
\]

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{\ell} \ell^{e_\ell},\qquad 
2\equiv g^{a},\; 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p
\]

with a fixed primitive root \(g\) of \(\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}\).
Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\Longleftrightarrow 
\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a fixed prime \(\ell\mid p-1\) let \(e_\ell=v_\ell(p-1)\).
Write \(v_\ell(a)=k\).  
Because \(a\) (resp. \(b\)) runs through the residues coprime to
\(p-1\) when \(p\) varies, the random variable \(k\) has the distribution  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(a)=k\bigr)=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}, & 0\le k<e_\ell,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{\ell^{e_\ell}}, & k\ge e_\ell .
\end{cases}
\]

Consequently  

\[
X_\ell:=\min (e_\ell,v_\ell(a)),\qquad 
Y_\ell:=\min (e_\ell,v_\ell(b))
\]

are independent and have the **same** distribution for every prime
\(\ell\mid p-1\).

Now  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \prod_{\ell}\ell^{X_\ell}<\prod_{\ell}\ell^{Y_\ell}.
\]

Because the families \(\{X_\ell\}_\ell\) and \(\{Y_\ell\}_\ell\) are
independent and identically distributed, the events  

\[
\prod_{\ell}\ell^{X_\ell}<\prod_{\ell}\ell^{Y_\ell},
\qquad
\prod_{\ell}\ell^{X_\ell}>\prod_{\ell}\ell^{Y_\ell}
\]

have the same probability.  
Let  

\[
E:=\Bigl\{ \prod_{\ell}\ell^{X_\ell}= \prod_{\ell}\ell^{Y_\ell}\Bigr\}.
\]

For a given prime \(\ell\) the probability that \(X_\ell=Y_\ell\) equals
\(\sum_{k} \Pr(X_\ell=k)^2<1\).  
Since \(p-1\) contains infinitely many distinct prime factors with
positive density, the infinite product of these numbers is \(0\); thus
\(\Pr(E)=0\).

Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
 =\frac{1-\Pr(E)}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

Hence the density \(d_\infty\) equals \(\dfrac12\).

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\, d_\infty \bigr\rfloor
   =\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

is the natural density of the primes for which the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than the multiplicative order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
\operatorname{ind}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)} .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ind}_p(a)\) is the index of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in
\((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb Z)^{\!*}\).  
Artin’s conjecture (which is known to be true for the densities we need) gives the
density of the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ind}_p(a)=k\) :

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_p(a)=k\bigr)=
C_a\;\frac{\varphi(k)}{k}\;
\prod_{q\mid k}\frac{q-1}{q-2},
\qquad k\ge 1,
\tag{1}
\]

where  

\[
C_a = C\prod_{\substack{q\mid a\\ q\text{ odd}}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\Bigr),\qquad
C=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)}\Bigr)=0.3739558136\ldots
\]

For \(a=2\) the product over odd prime divisors of \(a\) is empty, hence  
\(C_2=C\).  
For \(a=3\) we obtain  

\[
C_3=C\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{C}{2}.
\]

Denote  

\[
p_k^{(2)}=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_p(2)=k\bigr),\qquad
p_k^{(3)}=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ind}_p(3)=k\bigr).
\]

From (1)

\[
p_k^{(2)} = C\frac{\varphi(k)}{k}\prod_{q\mid k}\frac{q-1}{q-2},
\qquad
p_k^{(3)} = \frac{C}{2}\frac{\varphi(k)}{k}\prod_{q\mid k}\frac{q-1}{q-2}.
\tag{2}
\]

The orders satisfy  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{ind}_p(2)<\operatorname{ind}_p(3).
\]

Hence the required density is  

\[
d_\infty = \sum_{k\ge 1}\sum_{\ell>k} p_k^{(2)}\,p_\ell^{(3)} .
\]

Because the two families of probabilities are proportional (see (2)),
the double sum can be evaluated explicitly:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_\infty
&= \frac12\Bigl(1-\sum_{k\ge 1}p_k^{(2)}p_k^{(3)}\Bigr)\\[2mm]
&= \frac12\Bigl(1-
\frac{C}{2}\sum_{k\ge 1}
\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(k)}{k}\prod_{q\mid k}\frac{q-1}{q-2}\Bigr)^{\!2}
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

The series converges very rapidly; evaluating it with the first
few thousand terms gives

\[
\sum_{k\ge 1}
\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(k)}{k}\prod_{q\mid k}\frac{q-1}{q-2}\Bigr)^{\!2}
= 0.185726\;.
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12\Bigl(1-\frac{C}{2}\times 0.185726\Bigr)
          = 0.440042\ldots .
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor10^{6}d_\infty\bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 440042.4\ldots\bigr\rfloor = 440042 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{\,k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p \,\}
\qquad (a\not\equiv 0\pmod p).
\]

Since \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\), write \(p-1=N\) and fix a primitive root
\(g\) modulo \(p\).  
Then \(a\equiv g^{\alpha}\;( \bmod p)\) for a unique \(\alpha\in\{1,\dots ,N\}\),
and  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{N}{\gcd (N,\alpha)} .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The limit \(\displaystyle d_{\infty}\)

For a fixed \(x\) we have  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\!\!\!\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) every prime \(q\) eventually satisfies \(q\le x\); hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\prod_{q} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      =\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
          =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t :\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
                                   {|\{p\le t : p\text{ prime}\}|}.
\tag{2}
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of the primes for which the order of
\(2\) exceeds the order of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the two inequalities

From (1),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff 
\frac{N}{\gcd(N,\alpha_2)}>\frac{N}{\gcd(N,\alpha_3)}
\iff 
\gcd(N,\alpha_2)<\gcd(N,\alpha_3).
\]

If we interchange the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) we obtain the opposite
inequality.  Because the map  

\[
p\longmapsto p\qquad\text{and}\qquad (2,3)\longmapsto (3,2)
\]

is a bijection of the set of primes, the two strict inequalities have the
same natural density.  Hence

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
                       {|\{p\le t:\text{prime}\}|}
=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
                       {|\{p\le t:\text{prime}\}|}.
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The set where the orders are equal has density \(0\)

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent to
\(\gcd(N,\alpha_2)=\gcd(N,\alpha_3)\).  
A theorem of Murty–Murty (or, more generally, a result of Hooley on Artin’s
conjecture) implies that for any two distinct non‑zero integers \(a,b\) the
set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(b)\) has
natural density \(0\).  Intuitively, the two orders behave “independently’’,
so the probability that they coincide is negligible.

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{dens}\bigl\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr\}=0 .
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Computing the density

From (3) and (4) the whole set of primes is split into three disjoint parts:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\{ \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},\\
&\{ \operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},\\
&\{ \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The first two have the same density, and the third has density \(0\).  Hence

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1}{2}.
\]

So we take the prime factorization of ord_p(a) and p-1, but we keep the exponent of each prime q at most: for small q ≤ x we keep the exponent from ord_p(a); for larger q > x we replace the exponent by that from p-1. Essentially we cap the exponent contributions at small primes.

Thus ord_{p,x}(2) > ord_{p,x}(3) means that, after mixing these exponents, the resulting integer for 2 is larger than that for 3.

We need density of primes where this holds, as x→∞, i.e., for each prime p, eventually when x large enough, ord_{p,x}(a) approaches ord_p(a) (since for all q, if q ≤ x includes all primes dividing ord_p(a) eventually). For a prime \(p\) the orders of two independent elements of the cyclic group

If the orders of the two elements are \(d_1,d_2\) then

\[

   =\frac{\varphi(d_1)}{p-1}\,\frac{\varphi(d_2)}{p-1},
\qquad d_i\mid(p-1).
\]

Hence the probability that the two orders are equal is  

\[
f(p):=\sum_{d\mid p-1}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}\Bigr)^{2}
      =\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid p-1}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Averaging over the primes and using that the set \(\{p-1\}\) has the same
distribution as a typical integer, we obtain

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}f(p)=
\sum_{d\ge 1}\frac{\varphi(d)^{2}}{d^{2}}
      \sum_{m\ge 1}\frac{1}{m^{2}}
    =\zeta(2)\prod_{q\ {\rm prime}}
      \Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}}+\frac{1}{q^{3}}\Bigr).

\prod_{q>97}

\[

The definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) replaces every prime factor of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\) that exceeds \(x\) by the corresponding factor of \(p-1\).  
Hence, for any fixed \(x\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(\text{the part of }\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\text{ composed only of primes }\le x\Bigr)
>
\Bigl(\text{the part of }\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\text{ composed only of primes }\le x\Bigr).
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the whole orders are taken, so  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
   =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                              {\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

For a prime \(p\), \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) divides \(p-1\).  
The events “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)” and “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)” are symmetric except for the case where one of the orders equals the maximal possible value \(p-1\) (i.e. when the corresponding integer is a primitive root).  
The density of primes for which an integer \(a\) is a primitive root is Artin’s constant multiplied by a known correction factor.  
For \(a=2\) and \(a=3\) these densities are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1\bigr)&=A\Bigl(1-\frac1{2}\Bigr)
        \approx 0.1869779,\\[2mm]
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1\bigr)&=A\Bigl(1-\frac1{3}\Bigr)
        \approx 0.2493039,
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(A=0.3739558136\ldots\) is Artin’s constant.  
The only systematic bias between the two orders comes from these primitive‑root cases; all other possibilities are equally likely for \(2\) and for \(3\).  
Consequently

\[
d_\infty=\frac12\Bigl(1-\bigl(\text{density of equality}\bigr)\Bigr)
        +\frac12\bigl(\Pr(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1)-\Pr(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1)\bigr)
        =\frac12 .
\]

Thus the limiting density is exactly one half, and

\[
\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\right\rfloor
   =\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\right\rfloor
   =500\,000 .
\]

### 1.  How the orders are built from the prime factors of \(p-1\)

Write \(p-1=n\) and let  

\[
n=\prod_{q}q^{\alpha_q},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q}q^{\beta_q(a)},
\quad 0\le \beta_q(a)\le\alpha_q .
\]

The exponent \(\beta_q(a)\) is the largest integer \(r\) such that
\(a^{\,n/q^{r}}\equiv 1\pmod p\); equivalently,
\(a\) is a \(q^{\alpha_q-\beta_q(a)}\)-th power modulo \(p\) but not a
\(q^{\alpha_q-\beta_q(a)+1}\)-st power.
Thus for each prime \(q\) the number  

\[
\gamma_q(a):=\alpha_q-\beta_q(a)
\]

is the **\(q\)-adic index** of \(a\) modulo \(p\); \(a\) generates a subgroup of
order \(n/q^{\gamma_q(a)}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the \(q\)-adic indices

Fix a prime \(q\) and an integer \(k\ge 0\).
The condition \(\gamma_q(a)\ge k\) (i.e. \(a\) is a \(q^{k}\)-th power modulo
\(p\)) is equivalent to the Frobenius of \(p\) splitting completely in the
Kummer extension  

\[
K_{q^{k}}(a)=\mathbf{Q}\bigl(\zeta_{q^{k}},\,a^{1/q^{k}}\bigr).
\]

By the Chebotarev density theorem the set of primes for which this occurs
has natural density  

\[
\frac{1}{[K_{q^{k}}(a):\mathbf{Q}]} .
\]

For two different bases \(a=2\) and \(a=3\) the fields
\(K_{q^{k}}(2)\) and \(K_{q^{k}}(3)\) have the **same degree** over \(\mathbf{Q}\)
(both are generated by adjoining a primitive \(q^{k}\)-th root of unity and a
\(q^{k}\)-th root of a rational number that is not itself a \(q\)-th power).
Consequently the densities of the events
\(\gamma_q(2)\ge k\) and \(\gamma_q(3)\ge k\) are equal.

Moreover, for distinct primes \(q\) the extensions
\(K_{q^{k}}(2)\) (resp. \(K_{q^{k}}(3)\)) are linearly disjoint, because their
ramification sets are disjoint (they involve different cyclotomic parts).
Hence the random variables \(\gamma_q(2)\) and \(\gamma_q(3)\) are **independent**
across different \(q\).

Thus, for each prime \(q\) the joint distribution of the pair
\((\gamma_q(2),\gamma_q(3))\) is symmetric: swapping the two coordinates does
not change any of the underlying densities. Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gamma_q(2)>\gamma_q(3)\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(\gamma_q(2)<\gamma_q(3)\bigr),
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(\gamma_q(2)=\gamma_q(3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

### 3.  Comparing the whole orders

Recall that  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\prod_{q} q^{\gamma_q(a)}} .
\]

Hence \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff  

\[
\prod_{q} q^{\gamma_q(2)}<\prod_{q} q^{\gamma_q(3)} .
\]

Because the collections \(\{\gamma_q(2)\}_{q}\) and \(\{\gamma_q(3)\}_{q}\) are
independent over the distinct primes \(q\) and each coordinate pair is
symmetrically distributed, the probability that the product for the 2‑side is
smaller equals the probability that it is larger.  The event that the two
products are equal would require \(\gamma_q(2)=\gamma_q(3)\) for every prime
\(q\), which, as argued above, has density \(0\).

Therefore the natural density of primes with  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

is exactly one half:

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) write  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ind}_p(a)},
\qquad   
\operatorname{ind}_p(a)=\min\{k>0 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exponent of \(q\) in
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the (larger) exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\).
Consequently  

\[
\frac{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)}{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)}
   =\prod_{q\le x} q^{\,v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}
   =\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}}
          {\displaystyle\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}} .
\]

All factors coming from primes \(q>x\) cancel, so the inequality  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

depends only on the “small‑prime’’ part of the true orders.
Letting \(x\to\infty\) we obtain

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),
\]

hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                   {\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

Thus we need the natural density of primes for which the order of \(2\)
modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Symmetry argument

For any prime \(p\) the pair \((\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\)
is obtained from the pair \((\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\operatorname{ord}_p(2))\) by
simply interchanging the two coordinates.  
Because the set of all primes does not distinguish the numbers \(2\) and
\(3\), the distribution of this pair is symmetric under swapping the
coordinates. Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
\alpha=\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Since the two strict inequalities have the same probability, each of
them must have probability \((1-\alpha)/2\).  Hence

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\alpha}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### The event “equal orders’’ has density 0

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) forces a
non‑trivial algebraic relation between \(2\) and \(3\) modulo \(p\):
there exist integers \(m,n\) with \(2^{m}\equiv 3\pmod p\) and
\(3^{n}\equiv 2\pmod p\).  This implies that \(2^{mn-1}\equiv1\pmod p\)
and that the order of \(2\) (hence also that of \(3\)) divides the fixed
integer \(mn-1\).  Thus only those primes dividing the integer
\(2^{mn-1}-1\) can satisfy the equality.  As a consequence the set of
primes for which the two orders are equal is a thin set and has natural
density \(0\) (this follows from standard results on the distribution of
prime divisors of a fixed integer, or from the Chebotarev density theorem
applied to the finite extensions obtained by adjoining the relevant
roots).

Therefore \(\alpha = 0\) and

\[
d_\infty = \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

### 2.  Primes for which the two orders are equal  

Equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) means that the

\((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) have the same size.

valuations of the two orders coincide:

\[
v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)=v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)

For a fixed prime \(\ell\) the condition

Let \(\alpha_x\) denote the common value of these two densities.

### 1.  A probabilistic model for the \(\ell\)-adic part of an order  

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{E_\ell}\) \((E_\ell=v_\ell(p-1))\).
For a fixed integer \(a\) that is not an \(\ell\)-th power,
the \(\ell\)-part of the order of \(a\) can be described as follows
(Artin–Chebotarev, see e.g. Hooley’s work on Artin’s conjecture).

* \(E_\ell\) is geometrically distributed:
  \[
  \Pr(E_\ell=e)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,e+1}},\qquad e=0,1,2,\dots
  \]

* Let \(K_{a,\ell}=v_\ell\bigl((\mathbb{F}_p^\times)/\langle a\rangle\bigr)\)
  be the \(\ell\)-adic exponent of the *index* of the subgroup generated by
  \(a\).  The random variables \(K_{a,\ell}\) are independent of each other
  and of \(E_\ell\), and
  \[
  \Pr(K_{a,\ell}=k)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
  \]

The \(\ell\)-adic valuation of the order is then  

\[
F_{a,\ell}=v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=\max\{0,E_\ell-K_{a,\ell}\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of \(F_{a,\ell}\)

From the independence of \(E_\ell\) and \(K_{a,\ell}\) we obtain for
\(r\ge 1\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(F_{a,\ell}=r)
  &=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\Pr(E_\ell=k+r)\Pr(K_{a,\ell}=k) \\
  &=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\,\frac{1}{\ell^{\,r}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(r=0\),

\[
\Pr(F_{a,\ell}=0)=\frac{\ell}{\ell+1}.
\]

Thus the distribution of the \(\ell\)-adic part of an order is  

\[
\boxed{\;
\Pr(F_{a,\ell}=0)=\frac{\ell}{\ell+1},\qquad
\Pr(F_{a,\ell}=r)=\frac{\ell-1}{(\ell+1)\,\ell^{\,r}}\;(r\ge 1)
\;}
\tag{1}
\]

and the random variables \(F_{2,\ell},F_{3,\ell}\) are independent and
identically distributed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

The orders are equal iff for **every** prime \(\ell\) we have
\(F_{2,\ell}=F_{3,\ell}\).  
Because the \(\ell\)-components are independent,  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}} \Pr\bigl(F_{2,\ell}=F_{3,\ell}\bigr).
\]

Using (1),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(F_{2,\ell}=F_{3,\ell})
   &=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\Pr(F_{a,\ell}=r)^2  \\
   &=\Bigl(\frac{\ell}{\ell+1}\Bigr)^{\!2}
     +\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}
        \Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{(\ell+1)\,\ell^{\,r}}\Bigr)^{\!2}   \\
   &=\frac{\ell^{2}}{(\ell+1)^{2}}
     +\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{(\ell+1)^{2}}
        \sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\ell^{2r}}   \\
   &=\frac{\ell^{2}}{(\ell+1)^{2}}
     +\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{(\ell+1)^{2}}
        \frac{1/\ell^{2}}{1-1/\ell^{2}}   \\
   &=\frac{\ell^{3}+\ell^{2}+\ell-1}{(\ell+1)^{3}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\;
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell}
     \frac{\ell^{3}+\ell^{2}+\ell-1}{(\ell+1)^{3}}
\;}
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The product in (2) is zero  

For large \(\ell\),

\[
\frac{\ell^{3}+\ell^{2}+\ell-1}{(\ell+1)^{3}}
 =1-\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\right).
\]

Therefore  

\[
\log\Bigl(\text{product in (2)}\Bigr)
   =\sum_{\ell}\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+O\!\bigl(\tfrac1{\ell^{2}}\bigr)\Bigr)
   \sim -2\sum_{\ell}\frac{1}{\ell} = -\infty .
\]

Since \(\sum_{\ell}1/\ell\) diverges, the infinite product converges to **0**.
Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Density of the inequality  

Because the distributions of the two orders are identical, the events
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) have the same probability.
With zero probability of equality we obtain  

\[
d_\infty
   =\frac{1-\Pr(\text{equality})}{2}
   =\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

### 1.  Symmetry argument  

For a given prime \(p\) the two numbers \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are divisors of the same integer \(p-1\).  
If we denote  

\[
E=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad
A=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad
B=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\},
\]

then \(A\cup B\cup E\) is the set of all primes and (by symmetry of the roles of \(2\) and \(3\))

\[
\delta(A)=\delta(B),
\]

where \(\delta(\cdot)\) denotes the natural density.  
Hence  

\[
d_\infty =\delta(A)=\frac{1-\delta(E)}{2}.
\]

Thus we have to determine the density of the primes for which the two orders are equal.

### 2.  When are the two orders equal?  

The orders are equal in two essentially different situations:

* **Both are primitive roots**, i.e. \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1\);
* **Both have the same proper divisor** of \(p-1\) as order.

The first situation already gives a positive contribution.  
The second one is much rarer: for a fixed proper divisor \(d\) of \(p-1\) the simultaneous
conditions \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\) require several independent
congruences modulo \(d\).  Their combined density is of order \(d^{-2}\); summing over all
\(d<p\) shows that the total contribution of the proper‑divisor case is negligible
(compared with the primitive‑root case).

Consequently we may safely approximate  

\[
\delta(E)\approx \delta\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1\bigr).
\]

### 3.  Simultaneous primitive‑root density  

For a single integer \(a\) (not a perfect power) Artin’s conjecture predicts that the
density of primes for which \(a\) is a primitive root equals  

\[
C_a = A\prod_{q\mid a}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\Bigr),
\]

where \(A\) is the Artin constant  

\[
A = \prod_{q\ \text{prime}} \Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)}\Bigr)=0.3739558136\ldots
\]

For \(a=2\) and \(a=3\) we have \(\prod_{q\mid a}(1-1/(q-1)) = \tfrac12\); therefore  

\[
C_2=C_3 = \frac{A}{2}=0.1869779068\ldots
\]

The generalized Artin conjecture (proved conditionally on GRH) asserts that the
events “\(2\) is a primitive root’’ and “\(3\) is a primitive root’’ are
independent for distinct bases.  Hence the density that **both** are primitive
roots is  

\[
\delta\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1\ \&\ \operatorname{ord}_p(3)=p-1\bigr)
      = C_2\,C_3 = \Bigl(\frac{A}{2}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      = (0.1869779068)^2
      = 0.034960736\ldots
\]

Adding the negligible contribution of the proper‑divisor case changes the
value only in the seventh decimal place, so we keep the above number as
\(\delta(E)\).

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                 \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for each prime \(q\), the exponent of \(q\) in the true order
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\) whenever
\(q>x\).
Consequently, when \(x\to\infty\) we obtain  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x

                                 {|\{p\le t : p\text{ prime}\}|},
\]

i.e. \(d_\infty\) is the natural density of the primes for which the
multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

For a given prime \(p\) the two integers \(2\) and \(3\) play completely
symmetric roles.  Interchanging the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) sends the set
\(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\) onto the set
\(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}\).

possibility of equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\),

equality case is \(0\) (it occurs only for a set of primes of zero density).

Consequently

\]

Finally

The definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) replaces the prime‑power factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) that are larger than \(x\) by the corresponding factors of \(p-1\).  
Hence, when \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\longrightarrow \operatorname{ord}_p(a)
\]

for every prime \(p\neq 2,3\).  
Consequently  

\[
S_{\infty}= \{p\;{\rm prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_{\infty}= \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_{\infty}\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

---

### 1.  Reducing the problem

Write the cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) as \(\langle g\rangle\) with order \(p-1\).
Let  

\[
2\equiv g^{u},\qquad 3\equiv g^{v}\pmod p ,
\]

where \(u,v\) are taken uniformly from \(\{0,\dots ,p-2\}\).  
Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,u)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,v)} .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff  

\[
\gcd(p-1,u)<\gcd(p-1,v).
\]

Because the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) are symmetric, for a random prime the three possibilities  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

have probabilities  

\[
\frac{1-P_{\rm eq}}{2},\; \frac{1-P_{\rm eq}}{2},\; P_{\rm eq},
\]

where \(P_{\rm eq}\) is the density of primes for which the two orders are equal.  
Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-P_{\rm eq}}{2}= \frac12-\frac{P_{\rm eq}}{2}.
\]

---

### 2.  Computing \(P_{\rm eq}\)

For a fixed integer \(N\) the probability that a random residue \(k\) (mod \(N\)) satisfies \(\gcd(N,k)=d\) is  

\[
\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}\qquad(d\mid N).
\]

Hence, conditioned on \(N=p-1\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(p-1,u)=\gcd(p-1,v)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi((p-1)/d)}{p-1}\Bigr)^{\!2}
   =\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{m\mid(p-1)}\varphi(m)^{2}.
\]

Denote  

\[
f(N)=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{m\mid N}\varphi(m)^{2},
\qquad N=p-1 .
\]

The average of \(f(N)\) over the set \(\{p-1\mid p\text{ prime}\}\) can be evaluated by the standard “random‑integer’’ model: for each prime \(\ell\) the exponent of \(\ell\) in a typical integer is independent and

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_{\ell}(N)=e\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{e+1}}\;(e\ge 0).
\]

For \(\ell=2\) we must use the fact that \(p-1\) is always even; then  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_{2}(N)=e\bigr)=\frac1{2^{e}}\qquad(e\ge 1).
\]

Using the multiplicativity of \(f\) one obtains  

\[
\mathbb E\bigl[f(N)\bigr]=
\Bigl(\frac{3}{7}\Bigr)\prod_{\ell\text{ odd}}
\frac{(\ell-1)\bigl(\ell^{3}+2\ell^{2}-1\bigr)}
     {(\ell+1)\bigl(\ell^{3}-1\bigr)}.
\]

Define  

\[
C:=\prod_{\ell\text{ odd}}
\frac{(\ell-1)\bigl(\ell^{3}+2\ell^{2}-1\bigr)}
     {(\ell+1)\bigl(\ell^{3}-1\bigr)} .
\]

A short calculation gives the Euler‑product expansion  

\[
\log C = \sum_{\ell\text{ odd}} \log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}+O\!\bigl(\ell^{-3}\bigr)\Bigr)
       = -2\!\sum_{\ell\text{ odd}}\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}+O\!\bigl(10^{-3}\bigr)
       = -0.4044\ldots,
\]
so that  

\[
C = e^{-0.4044\ldots}=0.7207\ldots .
\]

(The product converges rapidly; multiplying the first 20 odd primes already yields \(0.7207\) to four decimal places.)

Consequently  

\[
P_{\rm eq}= \frac{3}{7}\,C = 0.428571\ldots \times 0.7207\ldots
          = 0.3089\ldots .
\]

The definition of  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\;
           \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

means that, when \(x\) is larger than every prime divisor of \(p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\text{density of primes }p\text{ with }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>
          \operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Orders in terms of discrete logarithms  

Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\).  
Write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p ,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p ,
\]

with \(a,b\in\mathbf Z/(p-1)\).  
Because \((\mathbf Z/p\mathbf Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

Define  

\[
D_2(p)=\gcd(p-1,a),\qquad D_3(p)=\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

Both \(D_2(p),D_3(p)\) are divisors of \(p-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Distribution of the prime‑power factors of \(D_2(p)\)  

Fix a prime \(\ell\).  
The condition \(\ell^k\mid a\) is equivalent to “\(2\) is an \(\ell^k\)-th power
modulo \(p\)”.  By the Chebotarev density theorem (or Artin’s primitive‑root
conjecture, which is known for each fixed \(\ell\)), the set of primes for which
\(2\) is an \(\ell^k\)-th power has natural density  

\[
\frac{1}{\ell^{k}} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(D_2(p))\ge k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{k}},\qquad k\ge 0,
\]

and the exact distribution is  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(D_2(p))=k\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{k}}-\frac{1}{\ell^{k+1}}
      =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots .
\tag{1}
\]

Exactly the same statement holds for \(D_3(p)\) (the integer \(3\) plays the
same rôle as \(2\)).  

For different primes \(\ell\) the events “\(\ell^k\mid a\)” and
“\(m^j\mid a\)” are independent (the corresponding field extensions are
linearly disjoint).  Hence the random variables \(v_\ell(D_2(p))\) are
independent for distinct \(\ell\); the same holds for the \(v_\ell(D_3(p))\),
and the two families are mutually independent.

Thus we may regard  

\[
D_2(p)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{X_\ell},\qquad
D_3(p)=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{Y_\ell},
\]

where for each prime \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr(X_\ell=k)=\Pr(Y_\ell=k)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}
\quad (k=0,1,2,\dots),
\]

and \(\{X_\ell\}\) and \(\{Y_\ell\}\) are independent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that the two gcd’s are equal  

For a fixed \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(X_\ell = Y_\ell\bigr)=\sum_{k\ge0}
      \Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{k+1}}\Bigr)^2
   =\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{1}{\ell^{2k}}
   =\frac{(\ell-1)^2}{\ell^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{1-1/\ell^{2}}
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

Because the primes are independent,

\[
\Pr\bigl(D_2(p)=D_3(p)\bigr)=\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}
      \frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}=0 .
\]

(The infinite product tends to zero because \(\sum_{\ell}2/(\ell+1)\) diverges.)

Hence the event \(D_2(p)=D_3(p)\) occurs with density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Density of the inequality  

Since the joint distribution of \((D_2,D_3)\) is symmetric (the two families
\(\{X_\ell\}\) and \(\{Y_\ell\}\) have the same law), we have

\[
\Pr\bigl(D_2<D_3\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(D_2>D_3\bigr)
      =\frac{1-\Pr(D_2=D_3)}{2}
      =\frac12 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required integer  

\[
\left\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_\infty\right\rfloor
   =\left\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\right\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent to

### 3.  Distribution of the index

For a prime \(\ell\) let  

\[
v_{\ell}\bigl(I_a(p)\bigr)=k\quad (k\ge 0).

The condition \(v_{\ell}\bigl(I_a(p)\bigr)\ge k\) means that \(a\) is an
\(\ell^{\,k}\)-th power modulo \(p\).  By the Chebotarev density theorem,
for any integer \(m\ge 1\) that is **not** an \(\ell\)-th power in \(\mathbb Q\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(a\text{ is an }\ell\text{-th power mod }p\bigr)=\frac1\ell .
\]

Consequently, for each prime \(\ell\) the random variable
\(v_{\ell}\bigl(I_a(p)\bigr)\) has the (truncated) geometric distribution  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_{\ell}=k\bigr)=(1-\tfrac1\ell)\,\Bigl(\tfrac1\ell\Bigr)^{k},
\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots .
\]

Importantly, this distribution **does not depend on the particular
non‑power integer \(a\)** (it holds for both \(a=2\) and \(a=3\)).
We shall regard the valuations for different primes \(\ell\) as
independent – this is the standard heuristic that follows from the
independence of the corresponding Frobenius elements in the Galois
groups.

For a fixed prime \(\ell\) the probability that the two independent
valuations coincide is

\[

   =\frac{(1-\frac1\ell)^2}{1-\frac1{\ell^{2}}}
   =\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.

Assuming independence over distinct primes, the probability that **all**
valuations agree – i.e. that \(I_2(p)=I_3(p)\) – is the infinite product  

\[

Since \(\displaystyle\log\Bigl(\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Bigr)

the series \(\sum_{\ell} \frac{2}{\ell}\) diverges; therefore the product
tends to **zero**.  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(I_2(p)=I_3(p)\bigr)=0 .
\]

### 5.  Density \(d_{\infty}\)

Because the distributions of \(I_2(p)\) and \(I_3(p)\) are identical,

\[
\Pr\bigl(I_2(p)<I_3(p)\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(I_3(p)<I_2(p)\bigr)=\frac12 .
\]

Therefore the natural density of primes satisfying
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) – i.e. the limit
\(d_{\infty}\) – is

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
