### 1.  Symmetry between 2 and 3  

For a fixed prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \(\mathbf{F}_p^{\times}\) is cyclic
of order \(p-1\).  Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\) and write  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\qquad (0\le a,b<p-1).
\]

Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

If we interchange the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) we obtain the opposite inequality.
Because the pair \((a,b)\) is uniformly distributed among the \((p-1)^2\)
possibilities when \(p\) varies (this is a standard consequence of the
Chebotarev density theorem applied to the Kummer extensions
\(\mathbf{Q}(\zeta_n,2^{1/n})\) and \(\mathbf{Q}(\zeta_n,3^{1/n})\)),
the two events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]

have the same natural density among the primes.

### 2.  Primes for which the two orders are equal  

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\gcd(p-1,a)=\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a given integer \(d\mid p-1\) this means that both \(2\) and \(3\) lie in the
unique subgroup of order \((p-1)/d\); equivalently  

\[
\frac{2}{3}\in\bigl(\mathbf{F}_p^{\times}\bigr)^{d}.
\]

Thus a prime with equal orders must satisfy a congruence of the form  

\[
\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\qquad\text{for some }k\mid(p-1).
\]

For each fixed \(k\) the set of primes for which \((2/3)^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\)
has natural density \(0\) (it is the set of primes that split completely in the
abelian extension \(\mathbf{Q}(\zeta_k,\,(2/3)^{1/k})\), which has degree
\(\ge k>1\)).  The union over all \(k\ge 1\) of these zero‑density sets is still
of density \(0\).  Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{dens}\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}=0 .
\]

Let

A=\{p : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},\qquad

From the symmetry proved in §1,
\(\displaystyle \operatorname{dens}(A)=\operatorname{dens}(B)\).
Since the set where the two orders are equal has density \(0\),

\[
\operatorname{dens}(A)+\operatorname{dens}(B)=1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\operatorname{dens}(A)=\frac12 .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .

distributed in its Galois group.  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_\ell(a)=k\mid \ell\mid p-1\bigr)=\frac{1}{\ell^{\,k+1}}\qquad(k=0,1,\dots ,e_\ell) .
\]

In particular \(\Pr(f_\ell(a)=0\mid \ell\mid p-1)=1/\ell\) and
\(\Pr(f_\ell(a)>0\mid \ell\mid p-1)=1-1/\ell\).

\]

### 1.  A convenient description

Let \(p\) be a prime and write the (cyclic) multiplicative group
\(\mathbf F_{p}^{\times}\) as \(\langle g\rangle\) with \(|\langle g\rangle|=p-1\).
If  

\[
2\equiv g^{a},\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p ,
\]

then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\iff \gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).
\]

For a fixed \(N=p-1\) the residues \(a,b\) are *independent* and
uniformly distributed in \(\{0,1,\dots ,N-1\}\).
Therefore, for a given integer \(N\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_N&:=\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)<\gcd(N,b)\bigr)  \\
   &=\frac{1-\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=\gcd(N,b)\bigr)}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two gcd’s are equal

For a divisor \(d\mid N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N},
\]

so  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,a)=\gcd(N,b)\bigr)=
\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(N/d)^{2}
    =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{k\mid N}\varphi(k)^{2}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
P_N=\frac{1}{2}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{k\mid N}\varphi(k)^{2}\Bigr).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Averaging over the primes

We need the average of \(P_{p-1}\) when \(p\) runs over the primes.
Because the function  

\[
F(N)=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{k\mid N}\varphi(k)^{2}
\]

is multiplicative, write \(N=\prod_{q^{e}\parallel N}q^{e}\) and obtain  

\[
F(N)=\prod_{q^{e}\parallel N}
      \frac{S(q^{e})}{q^{2e}},\qquad
S(q^{e})=1+(q-1)^{2}\frac{q^{2e}-1}{q^{2}-1}.
\]

For a random integer the exponent \(e\) of a prime \(q\) follows the
distribution \(\Pr(e)=\frac{1-1/q}{q^{e}}\) \((e\ge 0)\).
Hence the expected contribution of the prime \(q\) is  

\[
E_q=\sum_{e\ge 0}\frac{S(q^{e})}{q^{2e}}\frac{1-1/q}{q^{e}}
     =\frac{q-1}{q+1}\;\frac{q^{3}+2q^{2}-1}{q^{3}-1}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\mathbb{E}[F(p-1)]=\prod_{q\text{ prime}}E_q .
\]

For larger primes we use the expansion

Hence  

\[
\prod_{q>19}E_q = e^{-0.0200}=0.9802\ldots .

Putting the two parts together,

\[
\mathbb{E}[F(p-1)]\approx 0.5255\times0.9802 = 0.5149\ldots .

### 1.  Behaviour of the \(\ell\)-adic part of the order

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell} \ell^{e_\ell}\) (product over all primes \(\ell\)).  
For a fixed prime \(\ell\mid p-1\) let  

\[
X_\ell(p)=\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if } \ell^{e_\ell}\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\\[2pt]
0 &\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\qquad
Y_\ell(p)=\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if } \ell^{e_\ell}\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\\[2pt]
0 &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

In the cyclic group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) of order \(p-1\) a random element has its full \(\ell\)-adic exponent with probability \(1-\frac1\ell\) (the complement is the subgroup of index \(\ell\)).  
Hence, for each \(\ell\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(X_\ell=1\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(Y_\ell=1\bigr)=1-\frac1\ell,
\qquad
\Pr\bigl(X_\ell=0\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(Y_\ell=0\bigr)=\frac1\ell .
\]

The events concerning the two different bases \(2\) and \(3\) are independent, and the events for different primes \(\ell\) are also independent (they depend on distinct \(\ell\)-power residues).

### 2.  Comparing the two orders

The orders are compared by looking at the largest prime \(\ell\) for which the \(\ell\)-adic parts differ.  
Because the distributions of \(X_\ell\) and \(Y_\ell\) are identical, the chance that \(X_\ell=1,\;Y_\ell=0\) equals the chance that \(X_\ell=0,\;Y_\ell=1\).  
Therefore, for any prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\]

Let \(E\) be the event that the two orders are equal. Then

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr(E)}{2}.
\]

### 3.  Probability of equality

Equality occurs exactly when for **every** prime \(\ell\mid(p-1)\) we have either
both \(X_\ell=Y_\ell=1\) or both \(X_\ell=Y_\ell=0\).  
For a given \(\ell\) this has probability  

\[
(1-\tfrac1\ell)^2+\bigl(\tfrac1\ell\bigr)^2
   =1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}} .
\]

Hence, conditioning on the (random) factorisation of \(p-1\),

\[
\Pr(E)=\prod_{\ell\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

The product over the primes dividing \(p-1\) tends to \(0\) as the number of such primes grows, because  

\[
\sum_{\ell\mid(p-1)}\frac{2}{\ell}=+\infty
\]

(the sum of reciprocals of the prime divisors of the integers is divergent).  
Thus the set of primes for which the two orders are equal has natural density \(0\).

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

The definition

uses the full order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) for the primes \(q\le x\) and

Hence, for two integers \(a,b\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(b)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
   >\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(b))},
\]

because the second product (over \(q>x\)) is the same for \(a\) and \(b\).

### 1.  The limit \(d_\infty\)

When \(x\to\infty\) the first product contains **all** prime factors of the
order, so

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}
   \frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
        {|\{p\le t:\text{prime}\}|},
\]

i.e. \(d_\infty\) is the natural density of primes for which the order of
\(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

---

### 2.  Distribution of the \(\ell\)-adic part of an order

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{e_\ell}\) (\(\ell\) prime).  
For a fixed integer \(a\not\equiv0\pmod p\) the \(\ell\)-adic valuation
\(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))\) is a random variable.
In a cyclic group of order \(N\) a random element has

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord})\ge k\bigr)=\frac1{\ell^{k}}
\qquad(k\ge0),
\]

hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord})=r\bigr)=\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,r+1}}
\qquad(r=0,1,2,\dots).
\tag{1}
\]

This distribution depends only on the prime \(\ell\); it is the same for
\(a=2\) and for \(a=3\).  Moreover, for a given prime \(\ell\) the two
variables \(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))\) and
\(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\) are independent (the reductions of \(2\)
and \(3\) behave like independent random elements of the cyclic group).

---

### 3.  Comparing the whole orders

Let  

\[
X=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))},\qquad
Y=\prod_{\ell}\ell^{v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

Because the \(\ell\)-components are independent and have the same law (1),
the joint distribution of \((X,Y)\) is symmetric under swapping the two
coordinates.  Therefore  

\[
\Pr\bigl(X>Y\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(Y>X\bigr).
\]

The probability that the two orders are equal is  

\[
\prod_{\ell}\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))
                    =v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}=0,
\]

so ties occur with density \(0\).  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac12.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

---

### 4.  Required integer

\Bigl\lfloor10^{6}\,d_\infty\Bigr\rfloor

   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

The quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{\substack{q\le x}}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
        \prod_{\substack{q>x}}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with the ordinary order \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) when \(x\to\infty\).  
Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\frac{|\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
               {|\{p\text{ prime}\}|}
        =\frac{1-\rho}{2},
\]

where  

\[
\rho=\lim_{p\to\infty}\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
\]

is the density of primes for which the two orders are equal.

---

### 1.  Probability that the two orders are equal for a fixed prime \(p\)

Write \(p-1=\prod_{r}r^{e_r}\) (product over prime divisors \(r\)).  
Let \(a,b\) be the discrete logarithms of \(2,3\) with respect to a primitive
root modulo \(p\).  For a given prime \(r\),

\[
v_r\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)=e_r-\min\bigl(v_r(a),e_r\bigr),\qquad
v_r\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=e_r-\min\bigl(v_r(b),e_r\bigr).
\]

Thus the two orders are equal iff  

\[
\min\bigl(v_r(a),e_r\bigr)=\min\bigl(v_r(b),e_r\bigr)
\qquad\text{for every }r\mid(p-1).
\]

For a fixed \(r\) and exponent \(e=e_r\) the probability (over the random
choice of the residues \(a,b\) modulo \(r^{e}\)) that the above equality holds
is  

\[
P_r(e)=\frac{r-1}{r+1}+\frac{2}{r+1}\,r^{-2e}.
\tag{1}
\]

Consequently, for a given prime \(p\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\prod_{r\mid(p-1)} P_r\!\bigl(v_r(p-1)\bigr)
      \equiv g(p-1).
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 2.  Averaging over the primes

For a “random’’ prime the exponents \(v_r(p-1)\) are distributed as  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_r(p-1)=e\bigr)=\bigl(1-\frac1r\bigr)\frac1{r^{\,e}}\qquad(e\ge0).
\]

Hence the expected contribution of a single prime \(r\) to the product (2) is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_r&=\sum_{e\ge0}P_r(e)\Bigl(1-\frac1r\Bigr)\frac1{r^{\,e}}\\[2mm]
   &=\frac{r^{3}+2r^{2}-1}{\,r^{3}+2r^{2}+2r+1\,}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The average value of \(g(p-1)\) over all primes is therefore the infinite
Euler product  

\[
\rho=\prod_{r\ \text{prime}}E_r
     =\prod_{r}\frac{r^{3}+2r^{2}-1}{r^{3}+2r^{2}+2r+1}
     \;=\;0.5145\ldots
\]

(the product converges rapidly; multiplying the first 20 primes already gives
\(0.5146\) and the remaining primes change the value by less than \(10^{-4}\)).

---

### 3.  Density \(d_{\infty}\)

Finally  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\rho}{2}
          =\frac{1-0.5145\ldots}{2}
          =0.24275\ldots .
\]

### 1.  Primitive‑root densities  

For a fixed integer \(a\) which is not a perfect square and not \(-1\), Artin’s conjecture (proved conditionally on GRH) states that the set of primes for which \(a\) is a primitive root has a density  

\[
C_a = A\prod_{q\mid a}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\Bigr),
\]

where  

\[
A = 0.3739558136\ldots
\]

is Artin’s constant.

* For \(a=2\) the product is empty, so  

\[
C_2 = A = 0.3739558136\ldots .
\]

* For \(a=3\) the only odd prime divisor is \(3\); therefore  

\[
C_3 = A\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{A}{2}=0.1869779068\ldots .
\]

Thus  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha &= C_2 = 0.3739558136\ldots ,\\[2mm]
\beta  &= C_3 = 0.1869779068\ldots .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 2.  Comparing the two orders  

Write \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1\) when \(a\) is a primitive root for \(p\); otherwise \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)<p-1\).

The possibilities for a prime \(p\) are  

| case | probability | relation of orders |
|------|-------------|--------------------|
| both \(2\) and \(3\) are primitive roots | \(\alpha\beta\) | equal (not counted) |
| \(2\) primitive, \(3\) not | \(\alpha(1-\beta)\) | \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) |
| \(3\) primitive, \(2\) not | \(\beta(1-\alpha)\) | opposite |
| neither primitive | \((1-\alpha)(1-\beta)\) | orders are “random’’; by symmetry the chance that one exceeds the other is \(1/2\). |

Hence the density \(d_\infty\) of primes with \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_\infty &=
\alpha(1-\beta)
+\frac12\,(1-\alpha)(1-\beta)\\[2mm]
&= \alpha-\alpha\beta+\frac12-\frac12\alpha-\frac12\beta+\frac12\alpha\beta\\[2mm]
&= \frac12\bigl(1-\alpha\beta\bigr)+\frac12(\alpha-\beta).
\end{aligned}
\]

Substituting the numerical values \(\alpha=0.3739558136\) and \(\beta=0.1869779068\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_\infty &=
0.3739558136\,(1-0.1869779068)
+\frac12\,(1-0.3739558136)(1-0.1869779068)\\[2mm]
&= 0.304034338336\;+\;0.254493877431\\[2mm]
&= 0.558528215767\ldots .
\end{aligned}
\]

\end{cases}
\]

### 1.  From \(S_x\) to the limit set \(S_\infty\)

Define  

\[
S_x=\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\},
\qquad
d_x=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in S_x\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) increases with \(x\) and converges to
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\), the sets \(S_x\) stabilize:

\[
S_\infty:=\{p: \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},
\qquad 
d_\infty:=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x .
\]

Thus we only have to evaluate the natural density of the primes for which the
multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).

### Symmetry argument

For a prime \(p>3\) the group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of
order \(p-1\).  Choose a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\).  
Then there exist unique exponents \(u,v\in\{1,\dots ,p-1\}\) such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{u}\pmod p,\qquad 3\equiv g^{v}\pmod p .
\]

Their orders are  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,u)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,v)} .
\]

If we replace the primitive root \(g\) by another primitive root
\(g^{k}\) (\(k\) coprime to \(p-1\)), the pair \((u,v)\) is multiplied by the
same factor \(k\) modulo \(p-1\).  Consequently, as the prime \(p\) varies,
the unordered pair \(\{\gcd(p-1,u),\gcd(p-1,v)\}\) is equally likely to be in
either order.  There is no arithmetic bias favouring one of the two
possibilities, because the map \((u,v)\mapsto (v,u)\) is a bijection of the
set of admissible pairs.

The event \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) would require
\(\gcd(p-1,u)=\gcd(p-1,v)\).  This imposes an extra algebraic condition on
\(p\) (essentially that \(2\cdot3^{-1}\) be a perfect \(d\)-th power
modulo \(p\) for some divisor \(d\mid p-1\)), which is known to occur for
a set of primes of density \(0\).  Hence the equality case does not affect
the limiting proportion.

Therefore the set of primes for which \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)
has the same natural density as its complement, and that density is

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .
\]

### 1.  Orders expressed via powers modulo \(p\)

The multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order
\(p-1\).  
Fix a primitive root \(g\) modulo \(p\).  
Then  

\[
2\equiv g^{t_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{t_3}\qquad (t_2,t_3\in\mathbb Z/(p-1)).
\]

For any integer \(a\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,t_a)} .
\]

Thus the prime‑power factor \(q^{e}\) of \(p-1\) is removed from the order of
\(a\) exactly when \(a\) is a \(q\)-th power modulo \(p\); it is removed twice
when \(a\) is a \(q^{2}\)-th power, etc.

### 2.  Distribution of “being a \(q^{k}\)-th power”

For a fixed prime \(q\) the Kummer extension  

\[
\mathbb Q(\zeta_{q^{k}},\; a^{1/q^{k}})
\]

has Galois group of size \(q^{k}(q-1)\).  
By the Chebotarev density theorem the set of primes \(p\) for which
\(a\) is a \(q^{k}\)-th power modulo \(p\) has natural density \(1/q^{k}\).

Consequently, for each prime \(q\) the random variable  

\[
X_q(a)=\max\{k\ge 0 : a\text{ is a }q^{k}\text{-th power mod }p\}
\]

satisfies  

\[
\Pr\bigl(X_q(a)=k\bigr)=\frac{q-1}{q^{k+1}},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots .
\]

The variables \(X_q(2)\) and \(X_q(3)\) are independent (the corresponding
fields are linearly disjoint), and for a given \(q\) they have the same
distribution.

Write  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\prod_{q\mid p-1} q^{e_q-X_q(2)},
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\prod_{q\mid p-1} q^{e_q-X_q(3)},
\]

where \(e_q=v_q(p-1)\).  
The factor \(q^{e_q}\) cancels, so

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff
\sum_{q\mid p-1}\bigl(X_q(3)-X_q(2)\bigr)\log q <0 .
\]

For each prime \(q\) the difference  

\[
D_q:=X_q(3)-X_q(2)

has a **symmetric** distribution, because \(X_q(2)\) and \(X_q(3)\) are
i.i.d. Hence  

\[
\Pr(D_q = d)=\Pr(D_q = -d)\qquad (d\in\mathbb Z).
\]

The variables \(\{D_q\}_{q\mid p-1}\) are independent, so the sum
\(\sum_{q\mid p-1} D_q\log q\) is a symmetric random variable about \(0\).

\[
\Pr\Bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\Bigr)

For a real \(x>0\)

\[

\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
  >\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

### 1.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

When \(x\) exceeds every prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) the two products above become the full
orders. Hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}S_x=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\equiv S_\infty ,
\]

and  

\[
d_\infty =\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x

### 2.  Primes with equal orders have density 0  

The equality \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\) means that
both \(2\) and \(3\) lie in the same subgroup of \(\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}\) of
order \(d\).  Equivalently, the prime \(p\) splits completely in the
composite field  

\[
K_d=\mathbb{Q}\bigl(\zeta_d,\;2^{1/d},\;3^{1/d}\bigr),
\]

where \(\zeta_d\) is a primitive \(d\)‑th root of unity.  
For every fixed \(d\ge 2\) the field \(K_d\) has degree at least \(d>1\);
by the Chebotarev density theorem the set of primes that split completely
in \(K_d\) has natural density \(1/[K_d:\mathbb{Q}]\le 1/d\).  
Summing over all possible \(d\),

\[
\sum_{d\ge 2}\frac{1}{d}<\infty ,
\]

so the set \(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\) has
natural density \(0\).

### 3.  Symmetry between 2 and 3  

For a fixed integer \(a\neq\pm 1\) the distribution of the order

splitting behaviour of the fields \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m,a^{1/m})\).

of fields are *independent* because the numbers \(2\) and \(3\) are
multiplicatively independent.  Consequently the joint distribution of the
pair \((\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\) is invariant under
interchanging the two coordinates.

Hence, apart from the negligible set where the orders are equal,
the events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

have the same natural density.  Since their densities sum to \(1\),

\[
d_\infty =\frac{1}{2}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) write \(n=p-1\).  
If \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\) then  

\[
2\equiv g^{k_2},\qquad 3\equiv g^{k_3}\qquad (0\le k_2,k_3<n).
\]

The order of an element \(g^{k}\) is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(g^{k})=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,k)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow  
\gcd (n,k_2)<\gcd (n,k_3).
\]

For a fixed \(n\) the numbers \(k_2\) and \(k_3\) behave like independent
uniform residues modulo \(n\); therefore, for a given \(n\)

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi (n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^2
   =\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)^{2}}{2}.
\]

### 1.  Equality of the two orders has density \(0\)

If \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) then the subgroups generated
by \(2\) and \(3\) coincide, i.e. \(2\equiv 3^{m}\pmod p\) for some integer
\(m\).  Thus \(p\mid 2-3^{m}\).  For each fixed \(m\) the integer
\(2-3^{m}\) has only finitely many prime divisors, and there are only countably
many possible values of \(m\).  Consequently the set of primes for which the
two orders are equal has natural density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the numbers \(2\) and \(3\)

Apart from the negligible set of primes where the orders are equal,
the two events  

\[
A=\{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\},\qquad
B=\{\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\}
\]

are symmetric: interchanging the roles of the fixed integers \(2\) and \(3\)
does not change any of the underlying algebraic conditions that determine
the orders.  Hence the natural densities of \(A\) and \(B\) must be the same.

Because the three possibilities \(A\), \(B\) and “orders equal’’ exhaust all

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min \{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad 
\operatorname{ind}_p(a)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\operatorname{ind}_p(2)<\operatorname{ind}_p(3) .
\tag{1}
\]

### 1.  From \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}\) to the ordinary order  

For a fixed prime \(p\) let \(q_{\max}= \max\{q\;:\; q\mid p-1\}\).
If \(x\ge q_{\max}\) then every prime divisor of \(p-1\) is \(\le x\);
consequently the definition of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) uses the
exact exponent of each prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\), i.e.

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\qquad (x\ge q_{\max}).
\]

Hence for every prime \(p\),

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\mathbf 1_{ \{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\}}
   =\mathbf 1_{\{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}} .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
          = \lim_{t\to\infty}
            \frac{\#\{p\le t : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                 {\pi(t)} .
\tag{2}
\]

So we have to find the natural density of primes for which
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Artin’s primitive‑root densities  

For an integer \(a\) which is not a perfect square and \(a\neq -1\) the
Artin conjecture (proved conditionally on GRH) gives the density of
primes for which \(a\) is a primitive root:

\[
\delta(a)=C\prod_{q\mid a(a^2-1)}\!\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q-1}\Bigr),
\qquad
C=0.3739558136\ldots\;(\text{Artin constant}).
\]

Applying this to \(a=2\) and \(a=3\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha &:=\delta(2)=C,
\\[2mm]
\beta  &:=\delta(3)=C\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{C}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]

Thus  

\[
\alpha\approx0.3739558136,\qquad 
\beta\approx0.1869779068 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Splitting the set of primes  

Write \(P\) for the set of all primes.  Partition \(P\) into

* \(P_{2}\): primes for which \(2\) is a primitive root,
* \(P_{3}\): primes for which \(3\) is a primitive root,
* \(P_{0}=P\setminus(P_{2}\cup P_{3})\): primes for which neither is primitive.

The densities of these three subsets are \(\alpha ,\beta\) and
\(1-\alpha-\beta\), respectively.

*If a prime belongs to \(P_{2}\setminus P_{3}\) then
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).*
Conversely, if \(p\in P_{3}\setminus P_{2}\) then
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\).

Hence the contribution of the first two sets to the required density is  

\[
\alpha(1-\beta)-\beta(1-\alpha)=\alpha-\beta .
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The remaining primes  

For the primes in \(P_{0}\) (neither \(2\) nor \(3\) is a primitive root)
the orders of \(2\) and \(3\) are governed by the same random process:
for each prime divisor \(q\mid p-1\) the events

\[
\bigl\{2\text{ is a }q\text{th power mod }p\bigr\},
\qquad
\bigl\{3\text{ is a }q\text{th power mod }p\bigr\}
\]

have the same probability \(1/q\) and are independent for distinct
\(q\).  Consequently, conditioned on \(p\in P_{0}\), the random variables
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) have identical
distributions and are symmetric.  Therefore

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\mid p\in P_{0}\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\mid p\in P_{0}\bigr)
=\frac12 .
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Putting everything together  

Using (2)–(5),

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\infty}
&= \underbrace{\bigl(\alpha-\beta\bigr)}_{\text{bias from primitive roots}}
   \;+\;
   \frac12\bigl(1-\alpha-\beta\bigr) \\
&= \frac12 + \frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Insert the values (3):

\[
\alpha-\beta = C-\frac{C}{2}= \frac{C}{2},
\qquad
d_{\infty}= \frac12 + \frac{C}{4}.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 + \frac{0.3739558136}{4}
          = 0.5934889534\ldots
\]

### 1.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

For a fixed prime \(p\) we have  

\[
O_{p}(a)\mid p-1 .
\]

Hence for every prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\),

\[
v_{q}\bigl(O_{p}(a)\bigr)\le v_{q}(p-1).
\]

Consequently the definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\prod_{\substack{q\le x}} q^{\,v_{q}(O_{p}(a))}
\prod_{\substack{q> x}} q^{\,v_{q}(p-1)}
\]

gives a number that is \(\le p-1\) and that coincides with the true
order as soon as all prime factors of \(O_{p}(a)\) are \(\le x\).
When \(x\to\infty\) every prime divisor of \(O_{p}(a)\) is eventually
\(\le x\); therefore  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=O_{p}(a)} .
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty}d_{x}

                                 {\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of the primes for which the
order of \(2\) is larger than the order of \(3\).

For a fixed integer \(m\ge 1\) the condition \(O_{p}(a)=m\) means  

\[
a^{m}\equiv 1\pmod p\quad\text{and}\quad a^{d}\not\equiv 1\pmod p

\[
\#\{p\le t: O_{p}(a)=m\}=O\!\left(\frac{\pi(t)}{\log t}\right)
\]

and the set \(\{p:O_{p}(2)=O_{p}(3)\}\) has natural density \(0\).

\[
G_p=(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\qquad\text{and}\qquad |G_p|=p-1 .

\(G_p\) is cyclic; let \(g\) be a (fixed) generator.  
There are unique integers  

\[
a\;( \bmod p-1),\qquad b\;(\bmod p-1)
\]

such that  

\[
2\equiv g^{a}\pmod p ,\qquad 3\equiv g^{b}\pmod p .
\]

The order of an element \(g^{u}\) in a cyclic group is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(g^{u})=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,u)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,b)} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\gcd(p-1,a)<\gcd(p-1,b).                                    \tag{1}
\]

### 1.  Distribution of the logarithms \(a\) and \(b\)

If we replace the generator \(g\) by any other generator, the pair
\((a,b)\) is multiplied by a unit modulo \(p-1\).  
Because the set of generators of \(G_p\) is the set of units of
\(\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z\), the pair \((a,b)\) is uniformly distributed
over \((\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z)^2\).

Thus, for a *fixed* integer \(N\) the random variables  

\[
X=\gcd(N,A),\qquad Y=\gcd(N,B) 
\]

(with \(A,B\) independent and uniformly distributed modulo \(N\))
have the same distribution as the two quantities occurring in (1) with
\(N=p-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal

For a given divisor \(d\mid N\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)=d\bigr)=\frac{\varphi(N/d)}{N}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\gcd(N,A)=\gcd(N,B)\bigr)=
\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi\!\left(\frac{N}{d}\right)^{2}
   =\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{k\mid N}\varphi(k)^{2}.               \tag{2}
\]

Writing \(N=\prod_{i}p_i^{e_i}\) and using the multiplicativity of the
right–hand side gives  

\[
\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{k\mid N}\varphi(k)^{2}
   =\prod_{p_i\mid N}
      \Bigl[\frac{p_i-1}{p_i+1}+ \frac{2}{p_i+1}\,p_i^{-2e_i}\Bigr].
\]

All factors are \(<1\) and the factor belonging to the prime \(2\) is
\(1/3\).  Consequently the product tends to \(0\) when the number of
distinct prime factors of \(N\) grows.  

For a “typical’’ prime \(p\) the integer \(p-1\) has many distinct
prime divisors; by the Erdős–Kac theorem the number of distinct prime
factors of \(p-1\) tends to infinity with \(p\).  Therefore

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =o(1)\qquad(p\to\infty).                                   \tag{3}
\]

### 3.  Density of the set \(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}\)

Because the distribution of the pair \((\gcd(p-1,a),\gcd(p-1,b))\) is
symmetric, (1) shows that, apart from the negligible event of equality,

\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty=\frac12 .

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min \{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

For a real \(x>0\) the quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

coincides with the part of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) whose prime
factors are \(\le x\); the factor coming from the primes \(>x\) is the
same for every \(a\).  
Consequently

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
      >\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

Thus \(p\in S_x\) exactly when the **\(x\)-smooth part** of
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) exceeds the \(x\)-smooth part of
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

When \(x\to\infty\) the smooth part becomes the whole order, so

\[
d_\infty = \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
          = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                                    {\pi(t)} .
\]

Hence we have to find the natural density of the primes for which the
multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Heuristic model

For a fixed prime \(p\) the group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) is cyclic
of order \(p-1\).  
If we pick an element of this cyclic group uniformly at random, the
probability that its order equals a divisor \(d\mid (p-1)\) is

\[
\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1},
\]

because there are exactly \(\varphi(d)\) elements of order \(d\).

The two numbers \(2\) and \(3\) are *fixed* elements, but by the
Chebotarev density theorem (and, under GRH, by Hooley’s theorem on
Artin’s primitive‑root conjecture) the residues of \(2\) and of \(3\)
behave, as \(p\) varies, like two independent uniformly‑distributed
elements of the cyclic group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\).
Therefore we may model the pair \((\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3))\)
as two independent random orders with the distribution described above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the orders are equal

With the independence assumption,

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(d)}{p-1}\Bigr)^{2}
   =\frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}}\sum_{d\mid(p-1)}\varphi(d)^{2}.
\]

For a given integer \(N\),

\[
\sum_{d\mid N}\varphi(d)^{2}\le \tau(N)\,(\max_{d\mid N}\varphi(d))^{2}
        \ll (\log N)\,N^{2},
\]

so the above probability is \(\ll \dfrac{\log p}{p}\), which tends to
\(0\) as \(p\to\infty\).  Consequently the set of primes for which the
orders are equal has density \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Probability that one order exceeds the other

Since the events “\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)” and
“\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\)” are symmetric,
and the probability of equality is \(0\), we obtain

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
    =\frac{1-\Pr(\text{equality})}{2}
    =\frac{1}{2}.
\]

Hence the natural density of the set  

\[
\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

exists and equals \(\displaystyle d_\infty=\frac12\).

The constant  

\[
C=\prod_{p\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{p^{2}}\Bigr)
\]

is the limiting probability that the orders of \(2\) and \(3\) modulo a prime are equal.  
Indeed, for a prime \(p\) the events “the \(\ell\)-adic exponent of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) equals that of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\)” are independent for each prime \(\ell\); the probability for a fixed \(\ell\) is  

\[
1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}} .
\]

Hence  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=C .
\]

Because the two numbers play symmetric roles, the remaining primes are split equally between the cases
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).  
Therefore

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-C}{2}.
\]

Evaluating the Euler product numerically (e.g. by multiplying the factors for the first several hundred

\[

\qquad
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-0.322634}{2}=0.338683.
\]

Finally  

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times 0.338683\ldots \bigr\rfloor
= 338683 .
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1: a^{\,k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1 ,\qquad 
d_a(p):=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}\in\mathbb N .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)>\operatorname{ord}_p(b)
\Longleftrightarrow d_a(p)<d_b(p) .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.   The limit \(d_{\infty}\)

For a fixed \(x\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

If \(q\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) then \(q\le x\) for all sufficiently large
\(x\); consequently  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
          =\lim_{t\to\infty}
            \frac{\#\{p\le t\mid \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
                 {\pi(t)} .
\]

So we have to find the natural density of primes for which  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.   Influence of the quadratic character

Let \(\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)\) denote the Legendre symbol.
If \(\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)=1\) (i.e. \(a\) is a quadratic residue) then  

\[
a^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\equiv 1\pmod p,
\]

so \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid\frac{p-1}{2}\); consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\le\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]

If \(\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)=-1\) then \(a^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\equiv-1\pmod p\); the
order cannot divide \(\frac{p-1}{2}\) and therefore must be a multiple of
\(\frac{p-1}{2}\). In particular the order is “large’’ (it is at least
\(\frac{p-1}{2}\) and often equals \(p-1\)).

Thus the quadratic character of a base determines whether its order is
typically small (\(+1\)) or typically large (\(-1\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.   The joint distribution of \(\bigl(\frac{2}{p},\frac{3}{p}\bigr)\)

The residues of odd primes modulo \(\operatorname{lcm}(8,12)=24\) are  

\[
1,5,7,11,13,17,19,23 .
\]

From the well‑known formulas  

\[
\Bigl(\frac{2}{p}\Bigr)=
\begin{cases}
 1,&p\equiv 1,7\pmod 8,\\
-1,&p\equiv 3,5\pmod 8,
\end{cases}
\qquad
\Bigl(\frac{3}{p}\Bigr)=
\begin{cases}
 1,&p\equiv 1,11\pmod{12},\\
-1,&p\equiv 5,7\pmod{12},
\end{cases}
\]

we obtain the table

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
p\bmod 24 &\bigl(\frac{2}{p},\frac{3}{p}\bigr)\\\hline
1,23 & (1,1)\\
5,19 & (-1,-1)\\
7,17 & (1,-1)\\
11,13& (-1,1)
\end{array}
\]

Each of the four possibilities occurs for exactly one quarter of the odd
primes, i.e.

\[
\Pr\Bigl(\Bigl(\frac{2}{p},\frac{3}{p}\Bigr)=(\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3)\Bigr)=\frac14
\qquad(\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3\in\{\pm1\}).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.   Comparison of the orders

*If \(\bigl(\frac{2}{p},\frac{3}{p}\bigr)=(-1,1)\)*, then \(2\) is a non‑residue
and \(3\) a residue; consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) is typically
large (at least \((p-1)/2\)) whereas \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\le (p-1)/2\).
Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) for **all** such primes.

*If \(\bigl(\frac{2}{p},\frac{3}{p}\bigr)=(1,-1)\)*, the situation is reversed,
so \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) never occurs.

*If the two symbols are equal* (both \(+1\) or both \(-1\)), the two bases
play completely symmetric roles: the joint distribution of
\(\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)\) is invariant
under swapping the two coordinates. Hence, conditioned on the event
\(\bigl(\frac{2}{p},\frac{3}{p}\bigr)=(1,1)\) or \((-1,-1)\), the probability
that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) equals the probability
that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\); each is therefore
\(\tfrac12\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.   Density \(d_{\infty}\)

Putting the four cases together,

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\infty}
&= \Pr\bigl(\bigl(\tfrac{2}{p},\tfrac{3}{p}\bigr)=(-1,1)\bigr)
   +\frac12\Pr\bigl(\bigl(\tfrac{2}{p},\tfrac{3}{p}\bigr)=(1,1)\bigr)
   +\frac12\Pr\bigl(\bigl(\tfrac{2}{p},\tfrac{3}{p}\bigr)=(-1,-1)\bigr)\\[2mm]
&= \frac14 +\frac12\cdot\frac14 +\frac12\cdot\frac14
   =\frac12 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.   Required integer

\[
\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\Bigr\rfloor
   =\Bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times\frac12\Bigr\rfloor
   =\boxed{500000}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min\{k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\},
\qquad a\not\equiv 0\pmod p .
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\), write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{q\text{ prime}} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

For a fixed real \(x>0\) the quantity  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\Bigl(\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\Bigr)
                         \Bigl(\prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)}\Bigr)
\]

contains the **\(x\)-smooth part** of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) (the product over the
primes \(\le x\)) and, for the larger primes, simply the corresponding part of
\(p-1\).
Hence the factor \(\displaystyle\prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)}\) is the same for
\(a=2\) and for \(a=3\).  Consequently

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
   >\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\tag{1}
\]

Thus a prime \(p\) belongs to  

\[
S_x=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)\}
\]

iff the **\(x\)-smooth part** of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) exceeds the
\(x\)-smooth part of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).

### 1.  Passing to the limit \(x\to\infty\)

When \(x\to\infty\) the product over the primes \(\le x\) in (1) becomes the
full order; therefore

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}S_x
   =\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Denote this set by \(S_\infty\).  
The required density is  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t: p\in S_\infty\}}
                              {\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the two numbers

The two integers \(2\) and \(3\) are **multiplicatively independent**,
i.e. no power of one equals a power of the other.  
For a prime \(p\) the pair \(\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)\)
depends only on the Frobenius element of \(p\) in the compositum of the
Kummer extensions  

\[
\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_n,2^{1/n}\bigr),\qquad 
\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_n,3^{1/n}\bigr) \qquad (n\ge 1).
\]

The Galois group of the compositum is the direct product of the two
individual Galois groups; consequently the joint distribution of the two
orders is **invariant under swapping the two coordinates**.  
Therefore the natural densities of the three mutually exclusive events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

must satisfy  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
    =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)<\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The probability of equality is zero

For a fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) the condition \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=d\) means that

* \(p\) splits completely in \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_d,2^{1/d})\) and also in
  \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_d,3^{1/d})\),
* but does **not** split completely in any proper sub‑extension (otherwise
  the order would be a proper divisor of \(d\)).

The two splitting conditions are independent, and each of them has a
Chebotarev density of order \(1/d\).  Their intersection therefore has density
\(O(1/d^{2})\).  Summing over all possible \(d\) we obtain

\[
\sum_{d\ge 1} O\!\left(\frac{1}{d^{2}}\right)<\infty .
\]

Hence the set of primes for which the two orders are equal has natural
density **zero**.  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=0 .
\tag{3}
\]

### 4.  Computing \(d_\infty\)

From (2) and (3)

\[
d_\infty
 =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
 =\frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

The comparison  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\]

for a fixed prime \(p\) depends only on the orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) modulo \(p\).  
Indeed, letting \(n=p-1\) and writing  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,\log_g a)},
\]

where \(g\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\), we obtain  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}{\pi(t)} .
\]

---

### 1.  Reformulation

Write \(n=p-1\) and let  

\[
a=\log_g 2,\qquad b=\log_g 3\quad(\bmod n).
\]

Both \(a\) and \(b\) are uniformly distributed in \(\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\) and are independent (Chebotarev).  
Then  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,a)},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd (n,b)} .
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) iff  

\[
\gcd (n,a)<\gcd (n,b).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf 1_{\gcd (n,a)=\gcd (n,b)}\right]}{2}
      =\frac{1-\mathbb{E}[f(n)]}{2},
\]

where  

\[
f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi (n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^2
     =\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{m\mid n}\varphi(m)^2 .
\]

---

### 2.  The average of \(f(p-1)\)

The function \(f\) is multiplicative.  
For a prime power \(q^e\;(e\ge 1)\)

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{e}\varphi(q^{k})^{2}
     =1+(\,q-1\,)^{2}\frac{q^{2e}-1}{q^{2}-1},
\]

hence  

\[
f(q^{e})=\frac{1}{q^{2e}}
          +\frac{q-1}{q+1}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q^{2e}}\Bigr)
        =\frac{q-1}{q+1}+\frac{2}{q+1}\,q^{-2e}.
\]

For a prime \(q\) the exponent \(e\) of \(q\) in \(p-1\) (with \(p\) prime) satisfies  

\[
\Pr(e=0)=1-\frac{1}{q-1},\qquad 
\Pr(e=k)=\frac{1}{q^{k}}\;(k\ge 1).
\]

Therefore the expected contribution of the prime \(q\) is  

\[
g_q
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}
     +\frac{2}{q+1}\,
       \mathbb{E}[q^{-2e}]
   =\frac{q-1}{q+1}
     +\frac{2}{q+1}
       \Bigl(\frac{q-2}{q-1}+\frac{1}{q^{3}-1}\Bigr) .
\]

After simplification

\[
\boxed{g_q=1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}+\frac{2}{(q+1)(q^{3}-1)}} .
\]

The primes are independent, so

\[
\mathbb{E}[f(p-1)]=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}} g_q .
\]

The definition of  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                 \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

means that for a fixed prime \(p\) the factor coming from the “large’’ primes
\(q>x\) tends to \(1\) when \(x\to\infty\).  Hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
        =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t\;:\;
          \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
          {\pi(t)},
\]

i.e. the natural density of the set of primes for which the multiplicative
order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is larger than that of \(3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reducing the comparison to prime‑factor exponents  

Write  

\[
p-1=\prod_{q}q^{e_q},\qquad 
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q}q^{f_q(a)},\qquad   0\le f_q(a)\le e_q .
\]

For a given prime divisor \(q\) of \(p-1\) the exponent \(f_q(a)\) is
determined by whether \(a\) is a \(q^k\)-th power modulo \(p\):
\[
f_q(a)=\max\{k\le e_q : a^{(p-1)/q^k}\equiv1\pmod p\}.
\]

For a “random’’ prime \(p\) the events that \(2\) and \(3\) are \(q^k\)-th
powers are independent, and  

\[
\Pr\bigl(f_q(a)=k\mid e_q=v\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{1}{q^{k}}-\frac{1}{q^{k+1}}, & k<v,\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1}{q^{v}}, & k=v .
\end{cases}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Probability that the two orders are equal  

The orders are equal iff for every prime \(q\) we have \(f_q(2)=f_q(3)\).
Hence, with the independence just described,

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}P_q,
\]
where  

\[
P_q=\sum_{v=0}^{\infty}\Pr(v_q(p-1)=v)\,
      \sum_{k=0}^{v}
      \Bigl(\frac{1}{q^{k}}-\frac{1}{q^{k+1}}\Bigr)^{\!2}
      \qquad (\text{with the convention } \frac{1}{q^{v+1}}=0).
\]

Using \(\Pr(v_q(p-1)=v)=(1-1/q)/q^{\,v}\) (the usual geometric distribution
for the exponent of a prime divisor of a random integer) and evaluating the
inner sum gives  

\[
P_q=\frac{q^{2}+q-1}{\,q^{2}+q+1\,}
      =1-\frac{2}{q^{2}+q+1}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\frac{q^{2}+q-1}{q^{2}+q+1}}
\tag{1}
\]

The infinite product converges rapidly; multiplying the factors for all
primes up to \(97\) already yields \(0.5153\).  The remaining tail contributes
\(\exp\!\bigl(-\!\sum_{q>97}2/q^{2}+O(1/q^{3})\bigr)
 =0.9965\).  Consequently

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
      =0.5134\;(\text{to }5\text{ decimal places}).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Density of the inequality  

Because the roles of \(2\) and \(3\) are symmetric,

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)
   =\frac{1-\Pr(\text{equality})}{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-0.5134}{2}=0.2433\;( \text{to }4\text{ decimal places}).
\]

\]

\frac{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)}{\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(b)}
   =\prod_{q\le x} q^{a_q-b_q},
\]

because the factors with \(q>x\) cancel (they are both \(q^{e_q}\)).
Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\iff 
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}>1 .
\tag{1}
\]

When \(x\to\infty\) the product on the left of (1) becomes the whole
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)/\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\); thus

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}S_x=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty =\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x
          =\lim_{t\to\infty}
            \frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
                 {|\{p\le t:\;p\text{ prime}\}|}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Symmetry of the two orders

The multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic of order
\(p-1\).  
Let \(g\) be a primitive root modulo \(p\); then

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,\,k_2)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,\;k_3)},
\]

where \(2\equiv g^{k_2}\) and \(3\equiv g^{k_3}\) (\(1\le k_2,k_3\le p-1\)).
Thus the size of the subgroup generated by \(2\) (resp. \(3\)) is determined
solely by the integer \(\gcd(p-1,k_2)\) (resp. \(\gcd(p-1,k_3)\)).
For a fixed prime \(p\) the pair \((k_2,k_3)\) is uniformly distributed
among the \((p-1)^2\) possibilities, because the map
\(p\mapsto (k_2,k_3)\) is a bijection between the set of primitive roots
\(g\) and the set of exponent pairs.

Consequently, for a given \(p\) the events

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]

have exactly the same probability when \(p\) varies over the primes.
The only remaining possibility is equality of the two orders.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Equality occurs with density 0

Because the cyclic group of order \(p-1\) contains **exactly one**
subgroup of each divisor of \(p-1\), the equality  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\]

means that both \(2\) and \(3\) lie in the same subgroup.
Equivalently, the element \(2\cdot 3^{-1}\) must be a \((p-1)/d\)-th power
modulo \(p\) for some divisor \(d\mid(p-1)\).
For each fixed divisor \(d\) this condition defines a proper subfield of
the cyclotomic field \(\mathbf Q(\zeta_{p-1})\); Chebotarev’s density theorem
implies that the set of primes satisfying it has natural density \(0\).
A countable union of zero‑density sets still has density \(0\).
Hence  

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{|\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
     {|\{p\le t:\;p\text{ prime}\}|}=0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The limiting density

From the symmetry and the fact that equality occurs with density \(0\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)>\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\bigr)
   =\frac12 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty = \frac12 .
\]

10^{6}\,d_\infty = 10^{6}\times\frac12 = 500\,000 .
\]

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x}q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\;
          \prod_{q>x}q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

can be rewritten as  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\frac{p-1}
       {\displaystyle\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\mid(p-1),\,q\nmid \operatorname{ord}_p(a)}}
          q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}} .
\]

Hence, for two integers \(a,b\),

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(b)
\Longleftrightarrow 
\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\mid(p-1),\,q\nmid \operatorname{ord}_p(a)}}
          q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
      \;<\;
\prod_{\substack{q\le x\\ q\mid(p-1),\,q\nmid \operatorname{ord}_p(b)}}
          q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(b))}.
\]

Letting \(x\to\infty\) the products on the right disappear, and we obtain  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p,\infty}(b)=\operatorname{ord}_p(b).
\]

Thus  

\[

\]

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,a)},\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,b)} .
\]

Because \(a\) and \(b\) are independent and uniformly distributed in
\(\mathbb Z_n\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
   =\frac12\Bigl(1-\sum_{d\mid n}\Bigl(\frac{\varphi(n/d)}{n}\Bigr)^2\Bigr)
   =\frac12-\frac12\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k\mid n}\varphi(k)^2}{n^{2}} .

The definition of  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
               \prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

means that for a fixed prime \(p\) all the prime‑power factors of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) that are \(\le x\) are kept, while the larger prime‑power factors are replaced by the corresponding factors of \(p-1\).

For each prime \(p\) there is an integer  

\[
X(p)=\max\{q\;:\;q\text{ prime},\;q\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\text{ or }\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}.
\]

When \(x\ge X(p)\) we have \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\).
Hence, for every prime \(p\),

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{p\in S_x\}} \xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{} 
\mathbf 1_{\{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}} .
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty}d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}}
{\pi(t)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A probabilistic model for the orders

Write \(p-1=\prod_{\ell} \ell^{e_\ell}\) (\(\ell\) prime).
For a fixed prime \(\ell\) the exponent of \(\ell\) in \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\)
is  

\[
v_\ell\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\bigr)=e_\ell -
\max\{k\ge 0 : a^{(p-1)/\ell^{\,k}}\equiv 1\pmod p\}.
\]

For a random non‑zero residue \(a\) the events “\(a\) is an \(\ell\)-th power
mod \(p\)” are independent and have probability \(1/\ell\).  
Hence, for a *random* element of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=e_\ell-j\bigr)=
\frac{\ell-1}{\ell^{\,j+1}}\qquad (j=0,\dots ,e_\ell-1),
\]
and \(\Pr\bigl(v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=0\bigr)=\ell^{-e_\ell}\).

Assuming that the two elements \(2\) and \(3\) behave like independent
random elements (the dependence between them is negligible for the
density we seek), the probability that the \(\ell\)-adic exponents of
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are equal is  

\[
\sum_{j=0}^{e_\ell}\Bigl(\Pr\bigl(v_\ell=e_\ell-j\bigr)\Bigr)^2
   \;=\; \frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}+O\!\left(\ell^{-2e_\ell}\right).
\]

Thus, for a prime \(p\),

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\mid p\bigl)
   =\prod_{\ell\mid p-1}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Expected value over the primes

The set of primes for which a given prime \(\ell\) divides \(p-1\) has
Dirichlet density \(1/(\ell-1)\).  Treating the events “\(\ell\mid p-1\)’’ as
independent gives the average value of the product above:

\[
C:=\mathbb{E}_p\!\left[\prod_{\ell\mid p-1}\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\right]
   =\prod_{\ell\ \text{prime}}
      \Biggl(1-\frac{1}{\ell-1}+\frac{1}{\ell-1}\cdot\frac{\ell-1}{\ell+1}\Biggr)
   =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{(\ell-1)(\ell+1)}\Bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-C}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Numerical evaluation of \(C\)

We compute the convergent product  

\[
C=\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}-1}\Bigr)
   =\prod_{\ell}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{(\ell-1)(\ell+1)}\Bigr).
\]

Multiplying the factors for the first several primes:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell=2 &: \frac13,\\
\ell=3 &: \frac34,\\
\ell=5 &: \frac{11}{12},\\
\ell=7 &: \frac{23}{24},\\
\ell=11&: \frac{59}{60},\\
\ell=13&: \frac{83}{84},\\
\ell=17&: \frac{143}{144},\\
\ell=19&: \frac{179}{180},\\
\ell=23&: \frac{263}{264},\dots
\end{aligned}
\]

Carrying the product up to the prime \(97\) gives  

\[
P_{97}=0.207351\ldots
\]

The remaining tail contributes  

\[
\sum_{\ell>97}\log\!\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{\ell^{2}-1}\Bigr)
   =-\,\sum_{\ell>97}\frac{2}{\ell^{2}-1}+O\!\Bigl(\sum_{\ell>97}\frac{1}{\ell^{4}}\Bigr)
   =-0.00365\ldots .
\]

Thus  

\[
\log C = \log P_{97} -0.00365\ldots = -1.5785\ldots,
\qquad
C = e^{-1.5785\ldots}=0.20630\ldots .
\]

\[

\]

Finally

\qquad
\left\lfloor 10^{6}d_\infty\right\rfloor = \boxed{396840}.
\]

\[

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\min \{k\ge 1\;:\;a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\}
\qquad (a\not\equiv 0 \pmod p).
\]

Write  

\[
p-1 = \prod_{q\ \text{prime}} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\) we have  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\prod_{q} q^{v_q(p-1)-v_q(i_a)},
\qquad 
i_a:=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}
\]

where \(i_a\) is the *index* of the subgroup generated by \(a\) in the cyclic group
\((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).

---

### 1.  Behaviour of \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) when \(x\to\infty\)

By definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
\prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

If \(q>x\) then \(v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))=0\) (all prime factors of
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) are \(\le p-1\)). Hence for any fixed prime \(p\)

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\prod_{q} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}= \operatorname{ord}_p(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty} S_x =\{\,p\ \text{prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2) >
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\,\}.
\]

Thus  

\[
d_\infty = \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
        = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\{p\le t : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>
          \operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}|}
          {|\{p\le t : p\text{ prime}\}|}.
\]

The problem reduces to finding the natural density of the primes for which
the order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds the order of \(3\) modulo \(p\).

---

### 2.  Distribution of the orders

For a fixed integer \(a\neq\pm1\) the subgroup generated by \(a\) in the
cyclic group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is “random’’ as \(p\) varies.
The index  

\[
i_a(p)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(a)}
\]

is therefore distributed like a random divisor of \(p-1\):
\[
\Pr\bigl(i_a(p)=d\bigr)=\frac{1}{d}+o(1)\qquad (d\mid p-1).
\]

(Indeed, the probability that a random element of a cyclic group of order
\(N\) lies in the unique subgroup of index \(d\) is \(1/d\); the fixed
integer \(a\) behaves uniformly in the same way when \(p\) runs through the
primes – this is the standard heuristic underlying Artin’s conjecture.)

Hence the random variables \(i_2(p)\) and \(i_3(p)\) are *independent* and
each satisfies  

\[
\Pr\bigl(i_a(p)=d\bigr)=\frac{1}{d}+o(1).
\]

Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=\dfrac{p-1}{i_a(p)}\), we have  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2) > \operatorname{ord}_p(3)
\iff i_2(p) < i_3(p).
\]

For two independent positive integer‑valued random variables with the same
distribution, the events \(\{i_2<i_3\}\) and \(\{i_2>i_3\}\) have the same
probability, while the event \(\{i_2=i_3\}\) has probability zero
(the equality of two independent random integers occurs with density zero).
Consequently  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2) > \operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)=\frac12.
\]

Thus the set  

\[
\{p\text{ prime} : \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\}
\]

has natural density \( \displaystyle d_\infty = \frac12\).

The density \(d_{\infty}\) is the proportion of primes for which the ordinary multiplicative orders satisfy  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

For a prime \(p\) write \(p-1=\prod_{q}q^{e_q}\).
For a fixed prime \(q\) the exponent \(v_q(p-1)=e_q\) satisfies  

\[
\Pr\bigl(v_q(p-1)=e\bigr)=\frac{1}{q^{e}}\qquad(e\ge 1),\qquad
\Pr\bigl(v_q(p-1)=0\bigr)=1-\frac1{q-1}.
\]

Hence, for a fixed odd prime \(q\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_q&=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\frac{q-1}{q+1}+ \frac{2}{(q+1)q^{2v_q(p-1)}}\Bigr] \\
&=1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}+\frac{2}{(q+1)(q^{3}-1)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

For the prime \(2\),

\[
E_2=\sum_{e\ge 1}\frac{1}{2^{e}}\frac{1+2^{1-2e}}{3}= \frac{3}{7}.
\]

Because the contributions of distinct primes are independent, the expected value of the “tie’’ probability  

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\bigr)
\]

is  

\[
P_{\text{tie}}=
\frac{3}{7}\prod_{\substack{q\ \text{odd prime}}}
\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}+\frac{2}{(q+1)(q^{3}-1)}\Bigr).
\]

The infinite product converges rapidly.  Computing it up to \(q=67\) gives  

\[
\prod_{q\le 67}\Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}+\frac{2}{(q+1)(q^{3}-1)}\Bigr)
 = 0.6388\; .
\]

The remaining tail (primes \(q>67\)) contributes a factor  

\[
\exp\!\Bigl(-2\sum_{q>67}\frac{1}{q^{2}}\Bigr)=
\exp(-0.0055)=0.9945 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\prod_{q\ \text{odd}} \Bigl(1-\frac{2}{q^{2}-1}+\frac{2}{(q+1)(q^{3}-1)}\Bigr)
 \approx 0.6388\times0.9945 = 0.6353 .
\]

Consequently  

\[
P_{\text{tie}}\approx\frac{3}{7}\times0.6353=0.27227 .
\]

Finally  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-P_{\text{tie}}}{2}
          \approx \frac{1-0.27227}{2}=0.363865 .
\]

Hence  

\[

\qquad\Bigl\lfloor10^{6}d_{\infty}\Bigr\rfloor = \boxed{363865}.
\]

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{\,k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\,\}.
\]

Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic,
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\mid p-1\) for every \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) tends to

For a fixed prime \(p\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\bigr)}\;
\prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

If \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}}
{\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of the set  

\[
S:=\{p\text{ prime }:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the two numbers

For a fixed prime \(p\) the two events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)
\]

have the same probability, because the map  

\[
a\longmapsto a^{-1}\pmod p
\]

is a bijection of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) that interchanges the
orders of \(2\) and \(3\).  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
E=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}.
\]

Then for every prime \(p\),

\[
\mathbf 1_{S}(p)+\mathbf 1_{S^{c}}(p)+\mathbf 1_{E}(p)=1,
\]

where \(S^{c}\) denotes the set \(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\}\).
Taking densities and using the symmetry gives  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\delta(E)}{2},
\tag{1}
\]

where \(\displaystyle\delta(E)=\lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in E\}}{\#\{p\le t\}}\) (if it exists).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The set where the two orders are equal has density 0

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
2\in\langle 3\rangle\subset (\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists k\ge 1:\; 2\equiv 3^{\,k}\pmod p .
\]

Thus every prime in \(E\) divides a number of the form  

\[
2-3^{k}\qquad(k=1,2,\dots ).
\]

For a fixed \(k\) the integer \(2-3^{k}\) has only finitely many prime
divisors; consequently the set  

\[
\bigcup_{k\ge 1}\{\,p\mid p\mid 2-3^{k}\,\}
\]

is a countable union of finite sets, hence it has natural density \(0\).
Therefore  

\[
\delta(E)=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

(One can also view this as a special case of a general result: the set of
primes for which two fixed non‑zero integers generate the same cyclic
subgroup of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) has Dirichlet density \(0\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Computing \(d_{\infty}\)

Putting (2) into (1) we obtain  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required integer

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 500\,000 \bigr\rfloor
= 500\,000 .
\]
